events.title: Crude oil dives to session low on Iran peace talk hopes ahead of midterms
events.summary: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Trump prefers not to use military force and would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically." Iranian authorities also signaled that a deal is still possible, following two days of talks mediated by Qatar, as long as demands are implemented tangibly, according to Al Jazeera. However, concerns over the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts will likely linger in the near term. Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday after U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically. Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for January delivery fell 6.07% to $106.54 a barrel as of 8:55 a.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December declined 6.2% to $97.65 per barrel. Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections. The president "hasn't made a decision," Rubio told reporters over the weekend. "What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful," the secretary of state said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully." The news come following reports that both the U.S. and Iran are preparing for more military strikes after the midterm elections. Reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate that the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response." Concerns over the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts will likely linger in the near term. "Attacks on ships and refineries in the Middle East and on civilians in Ukraine continue, doing little to inspire confidence in the prospects for lasting ceasefires in the foreseeable future," said Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates. "Nonetheless, hope springs eternal," Varga added. —CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

events.title: A fresh wave of cyberattacks has hit Europe’s supermarket refrigerators, destroying food across countries
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. A second wave of cyberattacks is suspected to have hit supermarket refrigerators across Europe, causing fridges to increase temperatures and spoil food at dozens of stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden. Supermarket giants Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt confirmed the hacks overnight, with one Belgian company that operates Delhaize’s systems saying that the hackers had changed the settings to defrost, per Reuters . Stores have experienced heavy food losses from the cyberattacks, forcing supermarkets to throw out goods that had defrosted or were otherwise no longer consumable. The cyberattacks follow earlier refrigerator hacks across in France last month that caused food spoilage at hundreds of supermarkets by deliberately raising the temperature on the units. Security researchers said that the cause of the hacks were internet-connected refrigerators made by Danish company Danfoss, which was no longer providing security updates. Security company Claroty warned back in August that those refrigerator units were at risk of remote hacks and outages. The freezer hacks underscore how cyberattacks can have real-world effects, including on the food supply chain, often as a result of weak or overlooked cybersecurity practices. In 2025, a cyberattack on food distributor giant UNFI resulted in food shortages and empty shelves at grocery stores and supermarkets across the United States. U.S. Department of Defense officials are reportedly investigating whether freezer units on military bases were hacked by Iran-backed hackers. Iranian hackers were also blamed for cyberattacks targeting U.S. water providers earlier this year. events.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman does deals in Abu Dhabi amid fundraising
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is in Abu Dhabi, where he secured contracts to deploy AI products across government, the oil sector, and sovereign wealth management. The deals come as the ChatGPT maker is reportedly looking to lock down a mega funding round ahead of an IPO. The biggest of the four agreements is with ADNOC, which will deploy OpenAI’s Frontier platform for building and managing AI agents. The multi-year deal, signed with G42 subsidiary Inception42, will link decisions across oilfield development, production, refining, and trading, and will run on G42 infrastructure in the UAE. No financial terms were disclosed. The Abu Dhabi government is also working with OpenAI to make some of its policies readable by AI agents. Separately, Mubadala will apply OpenAI’s models to analyze potential deals. A consortium of UAE backers, including Mubadala-backed MGX, is expected to be the largest investor in OpenAI’s latest funding round — launched after the company delayed its IPO — and will get an option to lease new computing capacity in the region, the Financial Times reported. Altman’s appearance at ADIPEC is notable not only because Exxon and Chevron executives skipped this year over security concerns. His visit also comes as the AI industry faces power constraints amid the massive data center build-out. Asked onstage about his biggest challenge, Altman had a one-word answer: “Energy.” AI models will become more efficient and cheaper to deploy, he said, but the power needed to run them could keep costs high and slow down growth. — Kelsey Warner

events.title: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
events.summary: Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in bonds, it said in a filing. The plans were outlined last week at its investor day. Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout. The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined during its investor day last week , shares sank 3% in premarket trading. Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments. The hyperscaler's stock and bonds have already been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months.

events.title: Binance releases proof of reserves for ten cryptocurrencies; oil tumbles amid hopes of Iran war breakthrough – business live
events.summary: Introduction: Crypto 'scammers on overdrive' as Binance customers pull billions from accounts after $6.3bn hack Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy. Crypto scammers are now in “overdrive”, the founder of crypto exchange Binance has warned, as customers pull billions in funds from the platform as it recovers from a record hack. The platform was hit by a $6.3bn theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history. Experts identified North Korea as the probable culprit . Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach but on Sunday announced it had begun a phased reopening . By Sunday afternoon, the platform had processed $4.6bn in withdrawals and $1bn in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of about $3.6bn – 2.1% of its $171bn in total assets under management. (Those numbers were confirmed by the company in its latest proof of reserves snapshot – a full report is expected today.) Changpeng Zhao , the founder of the platform and commonly known as CZ , has warned that scammers are now targeting those that are trying to pull their money from the platform. He wrote on X: Scammers on over drive now. Be careful. His post was in response to a post which said: Some of you may have seen posts and screenshots circulating recently. Please be aware that these screenshots are fake and the information in them is false. For accurate and up-to-date information, always refer to our official channels and announcements. The hack has spooked the market, with investors also pulling out funds from Bitcoin ETFs in the US, according to Nick Forster , chief executive of Derive.xyz , a crypto platform. He said: US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $643 million in net outflows on Friday, their first trading session following the hack. BlackRock’s IBIT saw $233.7 million in outflows, while Fidelity’s FBTC lost $201 million, ARKB $129.5 million, GBTC $53.3 million and BITB $25.7 million. No fund recorded net inflows. ….We’re seeing a similar shift in options trading on Derive.xyz. In the first 12 hours following the hack, put options accounted for 68% of Bitcoin options premiums traded, compared with 43% in the preceding five days. Trading activity also remained elevated, with approximately $55 million in daily Bitcoin options volume since the hack, compared with $34 million the day prior. Traders have been moving quickly to protect themselves against further losses, with downside protection taking a much larger share of options activity. He added that the odds of Bitcoin hitting the $100,000 level by the end of the year were now just 3.5%. Last Wednesday, Derive options were pricing a 6% probability of Bitcoin exceeding $100K by Christmas. That has now fallen to just 3.5%, or roughly a one-in-30 chance. …Before the hack, our options market was pricing a 75% probability of Bitcoin finishing above $80,000 at Friday’s expiry. Instead, Bitcoin settled at $77,786. 9am GMT: Eurozone manufacturing PMI 12m ago Oil hits two-week low on Iran hopes 1h ago Binance shares proof of reserves data with customers 2h ago Marvell strikes $115bn mega-deal to buy datacentre optics maker Lumentum 3h ago UK’s largest brickmaker hit by sales slump as housebuilding downturn deepens 4h ago European supermarket freezers suddenly overheat in suspected hack 4h ago Oil falls below $110 a barrel 5h ago UK manufacturing growth hits five-month high in October 5h ago Ryanair considers pay freezes and reducing crew on flights as fuel costs soar 5h ago Binance co-founder: 'Our top priority is to ensure the environment is secure' 5h ago Eurozone manufacturing grows in October - despite tariffs, conflicts and higher energy bills 5h ago Scammers target Binance customers with fake compensation claims 6h ago Binance says withdrawals now available in US dollars 6h ago Oil falls 2.6% after reports Trump will give diplomacy with Iran more time 7h ago Introduction: Crypto 'scammers on overdrive' as Binance customers pull billions from accounts after $6.3bn hack Oil hits two-week low on Iran hopes Back in the financial markets, the oil price is falling more sharply as hopes build for a breakthrough to end the Iran war. Brent crude, the international benchmark, has fallen below $106 a barrel for the first time since 20 October. That’s nearly a two-week low, and 9% below Brent’s closing price last Friday night. Oil prices began falling after Iran’s supreme leader gave the government approval to pursue talks that could resolve the months-long conflict roiling Middle East supplies, according to Bloomberg . On Sunday, president Trump told a radio network that the war will soon be over “one way or the other … either they’ll make a deal, or we’ll just end it.” David Morrison , senior market analyst at fintech and financial services provider Trade Nation, says there are still concerns that the conflict could flare up again.

events.summary: Ameya Kanitkar, Russell Fradin, and Jim Larrison's startup just raised a $30 million Series A. Larridin AI has gone from being a small business expense to one of the priciest items on companies' ledgers. San Francisco startup Larridin raised $30 million to determine whether firms are getting their money's worth. Larridin's Series A comes in the wake of the tokenmaxxing era, as companies grow concerned about AI ROI. Companies went all in on AI this year, and are now reckoning with heavy bills. One startup wants to get under the hood and figure out which ones are worth it. Larridin, a San Francisco-based startup, just raised $30 million in Series A funding to give companies a clear picture of how the money they spent on AI is — or isn't — working for them. Jeff Kearl, a general partner at Pelion Ventures, which led the funding round, told Business Insider that AI has gone from being a small, even "nonexistent," expense for businesses to one of the top five to 10 most expensive items on their ledger. "All of a sudden they're like, 'Wow, that's a lot of money going to AI. We run a lot of apps. We have a lot of models. Where does it all go, who uses it, and how do I make sense of that?" Kearl said. Larridin's main product is a measurement platform that tracks the extent to which AI improves employee productivity and identifies opportunities for better adoption. The software integrates with companies' internal systems to analyze employees' AI usage, including their prompts to different AI tools, and determine who is using AI effectively, who needs more training, and how much time they're saving. Cofounder and CTO Ameya Kanitkar said the platform protects employee privacy by analyzing their AI interactions without storing their contents, instead generating scores and high-level insights. Always a need for a third-party measurement platform Russell Fradin, CEO and cofounder of Larridin, previously worked at Comscore, a media and advertising measurement platform. He said that, in his experience, whenever a lot of money moves into a category, someone builds a third-party measurement platform for that category, evidenced by Comscore, Nielsen, or Datadog. "We said, look, there's going to be a ton of AI spend ," Fradin said. "There's going to be a third-party audit measurement company, and let's try and be that company." The company has a third cofounder, Jim Larrison, who worked with Fradin at Comscore. Larridin's $30 million Series A was led by Pelion Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz , Gradient Ventures, GFT Ventures, W23, Thayer Investment Partners, DG Daiwa Ventures, Alumni Ventures, and Cougar Capital. A16z and Gradient Ventures were part of its $17 million seed round. Alex Rampell, a general partner at A16z, said one thing that convinced him about Larridin's business was that it addressed a need in enterprise AI for a sort of "AI boss," who could tell staff what they should or shouldn't do with AI. "If you're in sales, somebody should nudge you and say, 'Hey, call this account. Don't call that account.' If you're in coding, 'fix this bug, don't fix that bug,'" Rampell said. "But underlying that was the same idea, which was like, people are using AI tools to do all sorts of things. Are they doing the right thing? Is the outcome actually appreciably different? Are you getting any kind of ROI ?" he added. Fradin said that business picked up around the second quarter of this year, when more companies became concerned about AI costs. The company went from having one enterprise customer in December last year to 50 now. Post-Series A, he said he wants to double Larridin's 20-person head count, adding more sales, engineering, and marketing staff. AI spend behavior has evolved Larridin's Series A comes after months of twists and turns in the field of AI spending. In the first few months of the year, tokenmaxxing was in vogue, which led companies to urge their employees to get on the hype train and experiment with AI — essentially a mandate to accelerate adoption or be left behind. They urged their employees to use AI tools as much as possible and burn as many tokens as they could, with some, like Duolingo, even adding AI use as a performance metric for their employees. Uber CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga went viral in April when he said Uber had already burned through its entire Claude Code budget for the year. AI budgets ballooned. At least 17 companies, from Salesforce to Oracle, announced AI-related layoffs, with Oracle specifically saying in June that AI deployment and adoption have reduced its workforce. But the sentiment shifted sometime in the middle of the year, when ugly AI bills started rearing their heads. Companies started paying more attention to getting the best return on investment from their AI spending. Modelmaxxing, which, as Business Insider wrote about in July, involves routing prompts to different AI models based to maximize token use, emerged as a tactic to save costs. More businesses started using cheaper open-source models developed by Chinese AI labs, such as Moonshot AI and Z.ai. Read the original article on Business Insider

With so many options, it’s sometimes easy to forget where you are working and where exactly your project is. events.title: Fake nuclear warnings in Ukraine as Moscow, Kyiv report separate cyberattacks on emergency apps
events.summary: Ukrainian air forces said late Sunday its alert system had been compromised after erroneous messages were sent that Kyiv and other areas were subject to nuclear threats. Shortly after, Russia's Ministry for Emergency Situations said its mobile app had been subject to "a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public." It comes as the longest local ceasefire since the full-scale invasion began in early 2022, in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, expired overnight. Ukraine's air force said Sunday its Air Alert app had been compromised after it reportedly sent false warnings of nuclear and chemical threats in Kyiv and other areas. The app briefly displayed alerts for nuclear and chemical incidents as well as warnings of street fighting, according to Reuters. The air force said unauthorized persons had interfered with the app's operation and that it had temporarily disabled push notifications. "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel," the air force said on Telegram, according to a translation. Two hours later, Russia's Ministry for Emergency Situations said its mobile app had been subject to "a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public." It was not immediately clear if the incidents were linked. CNBC has reached out to Russian and Ukrainian authorities for comment. Local ceasefire expires in Oleshky, Kherson The alleged cyberattacks come as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on each other's territories and infrastructure. Overnight, a local ceasefire in the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region, near the Crimean Peninsula, expired. The temporary pause in fighting allowed humanitarian aid to enter the city and the evacuation of hundreds of people who had been trapped largely without access to food, water, electricity and medicine. It was the longest local ceasefire since the full-scale invasion began in early 2022, and both parties appeared to have honored the pause until it ended at midnight Moscow time. On Monday morning, local media reported that Russian forces had struck a hospital in central Kherson, while Ukraine's General Staff of Armed Forces said Moscow had used the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city. "During the ceasefire, the rotation of Russian units, the fortification of positions, the expansion of anti-drone measures along roads and increased logistics activity, including the delivery of ammunition, were recorded," the military body said early Monday. On Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said October had been the deadliest month for Russia since the invasion began in 2022. Over the past month, Russia lost 54,400 troops killed or badly wounded, "a record for any month of the full-scale war," Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine's Defense Forces liberated 96.2 square kilometers of Ukrainian land in October – 10.4 square kilometers more than Russia captured during that time.

events.title: A stroller blanket changed my mom's life. Now I'm helping her run 7AM Enfant, the business it inspired.
events.summary: Chana Campora runs 7AM Enfant with her mom. Courtesy of Chana Campora Chana Campora's mother, Rebecca, created a stroller blanket when Chana was a preschooler. Chana grew up helping with the company, but wasn't sure she'd work there. Watching her immigrant parents chase their dreams shaped her career, she says. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Chana Campora, vice president of 7AM Enfant . It has been edited for length and clarity . My mom is a very fashionable, very functional person. When she moved from Paris to New York City for my dad's job, with two young kids, she needed a way to keep us warm in the stroller so she could go about her day. She still tells stories about wrapping me in layers and layers of blankets. As soon as we'd get into a shop, I'd strip them off, and she'd have to do it all again. My mom is utilitarian, so she created a stroller blanket with a zipper that was quick and easy to get me in and out of. Chana Campora's mom invented a blanket for her stroller. Courtesy of Chana Campora She was just trying to lighten her load. Little did we know at the time that she was creating a genius product that would serve so many parents for years to come. More than 20 years later, her business has expanded, but we still use the original five blanket silhouettes she created. It's amazing to see that they're as relevant as ever, and still what parents want and need . I grew up helping with the company, but I wasn't sure I'd join The company was my mom's fourth child, and as the oldest daughter , I helped her care for it. At first, she would sew her designs at home; later, we attended trade shows together. I learned the value of hard work from watching my mom. It was meaningful to know that my siblings and I were her source of inspiration. Her premise with 7AM Enfant was simple: to keep us safe and warm, and keep her day going. That's something she's never stopped fighting for. Chana Campora helps run 7AM Enfant with her mother. Courtesy of Chana Campora Although I loved the company, I wasn't sure I'd join the business. I spent five years in LA, studying Spanish and French literature, and getting a master's in anthropology. Being the daughter of immigrants — and speaking four languages — is central to who I am. My mom and I have fun designing together When I returned to New York , it was clear to me that my mom needed a partner. She'd been a one-woman show for too long. I'd dabbled in other jobs, but realized I needed to join my mother. This was my family company — the thing that matters most to my mom and me — so it made sense that my future would include 7AM Enfant. Chana Campora works with her mom and husband in the company. Courteys of Chana Campora Today, my mom oversees the big-picture decisions for the company. I work on day-to-day operations, acting as the glue between the production and sales phases. My husband works here too, managing our shipments. The most fun is when I get to design with my mom. She's brilliant at not prioritizing fashion or function, but creating a product that blends both. I get to draw on my master's degree — studying people — to understand trends and tastes. Because the brand's core is so well established, we can have a lot of fun playing with colors, prints, and collaborations. Watching my parents chase their dreams shaped me My parents really fought for the American dream, to do something big for themselves and their children. My dad is originally from Italy, and when they moved here from Paris, New York was the land of opportunity. I so admire what they've been able to do. My mom and I run the company, and my sister and dad work together as celebrity hairstylists. My youngest brother is in school for acting. We're a family of artists. I've seen the highs and lows of immigration and entrepreneurship. When we first came to New York, we lived in a studio apartment. Watching my parents gave me a work ethic and humility that I use today. They showed me that you can be successful in life if you never stop fighting for what you want. It's amazing to watch your parents have a dream. Some parents worry about entrepreneurship disrupting the family, but I've found the opposite: it was so rewarding to see. I treasure the memories of being in my mom's lap while she was designing or answering work emails. Her example is what made me want to chase my own dreams. events.title: My tennis buddy has an AI agent. It's changing his life.
events.summary: Tennis balls Yomiuri Shimbun/Reuters A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . My Thursday evening tennis league started again recently, and something unusual happened. The emails organizing our weekly games began arriving with a new sign-off. "See you on the court! Nathan's agent." My tennis buddy Nathan Czubaj has organized this league for years. It's a lot of work involving spreadsheets, scheduling, endless reminders, and chasing players who forget to confirm whether they're coming. Now he's outsourced much of that work to an AI agent . Naturally, when we gathered on court, everyone wanted to know what Nathan was using. This is Silicon Valley , after all. We can't even play tennis without talking about AI . Nathan explained that he'd started using OpenAI's Dots , a personal AI assistant that can handle tasks over time and work with other apps. Every Monday, Dot checks a spreadsheet containing our availability and emails players who might be able to play that Thursday. It asks us to confirm. On Thursday morning, another email reminds the confirmed players to show up at 7 pm. It's been working remarkably well for several weeks, saving Nathan considerable time. But here's what makes his experience particularly interesting: Nathan isn't a technology expert. "I'm one of the least technical people I know," he told me. Nathan runs Mindset Unlimited , a business that helps professionals become better communicators and leaders through coaching and training. From Claude Code to Dots He's enthusiastic about AI, but his journey hasn't been entirely smooth. A few months ago, he experimented with Anthropic's Claude Code , a tool that can write software and carry out complicated computer tasks. He found it frustrating and stopped using it. "It was not easy to manage and it took much longer than it would take to do it yourself," he said. Dots has been different. Nathan can describe what he wants in ordinary language, and his Dot can work with services he already uses. He started with tennis scheduling. Now he's handing his Dot tasks throughout his personal and professional life. On one recent day, he asked it to help with guitar practice, a workout routine, shopping lists, selling things on eBay, finding a birthday present, and creating a family book of memories. He also uses it to remember to call friends, recommend books, find workshops, and develop longer-term goals. And that's before the 10 to 15 other questions he asks AI each day. "I try to take everything on my to-do list and put it into Dots," he explained. "That way AI can be looking for solutions while I'm working on other things." "It's totally changed everything about the way I think and about the way I work," he added. His enthusiasm is infectious. On the court, Nathan admitted that sometimes he spends more time guiding Dot than he'd like. Still, his experience offers a glimpse of where AI might be heading. For years, we've heard about AI transforming the workplace through sophisticated software and technical breakthroughs. Nathan's story suggests the bigger opportunity might be much more ordinary: helping people manage the dozens of little chores that consume their days. Nathan imagines a future where everyone's AI agent communicates with everyone else's, automatically handling routine tasks. That future isn't here yet. But every Thursday, when Nathan's agent reminds me to play tennis, I get a glimpse of it. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . events.title: Europe hit by another wave of grocery store freezer hacks
events.summary: An employee cleans freezers that are out of power at an ICA supermarket in Stockholm. Fredrik SANDBERG / TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP via Getty Images Coop said that "unauthorized actors" tampered with cooling systems at some of its Swedish grocery stores. In Belgium, Delhaize said an "IT incident" affected refrigeration at some of its stores. The issues echo a cyberattack that hit French supermarkets last month. Dozens of grocery stores across Europe have reported rising temperatures in some of their refrigeration systems, with some retailers calling it a cyberattack while another called it an "IT incident." The incidents in Sweden, Belgium, and Estonia unfolded on Sunday night and come weeks after a hack on fridges and freezers in France that forced supermarkets to throw away food. "Unauthorized actors were able to access and tamper with the cooling systems at a small fraction of our stores," a spokesperson at Swedish supermarket chain Coop confirmed to Business Insider. They said that seven out of its more than 800 stores were affected overnight and into Monday. "The situation is currently contained and under control," they added. Gustaf Nilsson, spokesperson for ICA Sverige, another Swedish grocery retailer, said that an overnight incident affected a "small number" of its stores. "The incident impacted the stores' refrigeration and freezer systems," Nilsson said in an emailed statement. "ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation." The Sjöbo branch of the retailer said on its Facebook page that its refrigerators and freezers were hacked overnight, with their temperatures set to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It said that the store was closed in the morning before later reopening. In Belgium, the retail company Ahold Delhaize said it was aware of an "IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in a number of Delhaize stores." "Our teams are working hard to fully assess the situation," the spokesperson said in an emailed statement. "We will share further information as soon as we are able to do so.” Employees throw away bags of spoiled refrigerated food outside an ICA supermarket in Stockholm. Fredrik SANDBERG / TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP via Getty Images Belgian news outlet RTL reported one Delhaize manager had to discard the contents of her fridges and freezers. A spokesperson for Kitman Coldtech, a refrigeration technology company, said that it had "responded to a cyber incident involving a refrigeration system at a retail location in Estonia." "As the situation has developed during the day and we understand that additional incidents may have occurred, the relevant authorities are now involved in investigating the circumstances," they added. It is not clear who is behind the attack. France freezer hack to cost millions The incidents are strikingly similar to a massive cyberattack that affected internet-connected refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets last month The director of one Intermarché store in Normandy, France, told Business Insider that its fridges and freezers were remotely turned up to temperatures of up to 122F, resulting in $112,000 worth of food being discarded. Across the country, the costs are expected to rise to tens of millions of euros. And in August, freezers failed at multiple US military sites, spoiling food. A spokesperson for the Army Criminal Investigation Division told The Telegraph last month that the agency was working with investigators to determine the full extent of the incident. "Army CID is also working with DCIS and French law enforcement in understanding the refrigeration outages in Europe," they added. No connection has been established between the latest incident in Europe, the cyberattacks in France, and US military freezer failures. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I tried Chipotle's $52 family meal. It was plenty of food for 6 … and really great meal prep for 2.
events.summary: I ordered Chipotle's family meal to see what I'd get and whether it would be a great value. Savannah Born I tried Chipotle's chicken family meal , which cost $52 and is meant to serve four to six. Although I wish we'd gotten more salad and that my chips hadn't been missing, I was impressed. Ultimately, we were able to make six well-portioned, tasty meals at home for less than $10 each. Even though I usually cook at home and avoid fast (and fast-casual) food whenever possible, I have a hard time turning down Chipotle. I build the same salad bowl every time I go, so I don't pay much attention to the rest of the menu. It wasn't until I saw Chipotle's strange fever-dream of an advertising campaign that I learned about its family meals. Simply put, it involved a 3-foot reusable version of its takeout bag. Bizarre, yes, but it worked. Curious about the details (and the "big ass" bag mentioned in the advertisement), I did some Googling. Turns out, Chipotle launched its family meals in August 2025. The build-your-own experience is a major appeal. Per Chipotle , "People can create any bowl, salad, or soft taco to their liking and dietary preferences." Nachos were also suggested. Since I love salads and my partner prefers bowls, it seemed like the perfect setup. Plus, family meals are designed to serve four to six people — which, in my two-person household , could mean dinners for days. So, I ordered a chicken family meal online, complete with all the default items. Here's how it shook out. My local Chipotle had a few options for family meals. Savannah Born Even though I set my sights on its $52 chicken meal, Chipotle also offered steak and sofritas meals featuring the same standard fixings: rice (white or brown) beans (black or pinto) cheese romaine lettuce large chips 10 soft-flour tortillas three dips (choices included sour cream and four different salsas) one premium side (either guacamole or queso). The meals ranged from $52 to $63, depending on the protein. It's worth noting that these family meals are all digital-only, so they have to be ordered through the app or website. Ordering online felt seamless. Savannah Born Since I stuck with the baseline, customization-free spread, ordering took only a few clicks. My lineup included white rice, black beans , cheese, romaine lettuce, large chips, and 10 flour tortillas, plus sour cream, pico de gallo, and hot salsa as toppings. Then, I scrolled to the "extras" section. I could add another protein and up to seven extra toppings, but they'd increase the total price. An extra protein portion, listed as serving two people, ranged from $7 to $10. Extra toppings like salsa and cilantro lime sauce cost an additional $2.35 to $3 apiece. For more so-called "premium" toppings like guacamole or queso, I'd pay a whopping $5.90 each. Since it was just my partner and me, I skipped everything additional. I'd only splurge on extras for a gathering. Then, I walked to pick up my order. Savannah Born I had the option to have my order ready in as little as 10 minutes, but I scheduled my pickup for half an hour out and then walked to the restaurant. When I arrived, I spotted two bags with my name on them (literally). Since I'd already paid online, I was in and out in under a minute. The food was still warm after a quick stroll home. The bags had everything needed for a six-person party. Savannah Born Inside the bags, I found five containers and four cups arranged neatly. They also included napkins, utensils, and six serving bowls — so I assumed the meal was prepared for six people, not four. The meal felt excessive for four and perfect for six. Savannah Born I'm not going to complain about too much food, but divided into four portions, the bowls would've been hard to finish. Six servings felt like the magic number … for the most part. Split into six bowls, each would get a moderate amount of chicken, rice, and beans. The same held true for the sour cream, guacamole, and salsas. The portion of shredded cheese seemed quite generous — probably enough for eight — though in my household, bonus cheese is never an issue. The amount of lettuce, however, felt somewhat meager for six. Making salads didn't seem very practical. The bowls were easy to customize. Savannah Born Salads are my go-to at Chipotle , but if I wanted to build more than two, I'd be out of lettuce. Even though the chain's press release mentioned creating salads , the shredded greens seemed more like a topping, not a base. Instead of depleting the entire container of greens on the first night, I followed my partner's lead and made a bowl. When reached for comment, a Chipotle representative said that the family meal includes 8 ounces of lettuce that's "intended as a topping for bowls rather than as a base for salads." He later said it could be used for a salad, but it's not intended to be enough for four to six salad entrées, which are usually served on a base of Chipotle's Supergreens mix. I created a bowl based on six servings, and the portion felt generous. Savannah Born I built my bowl using approximately one-sixth of each ingredient. The bowl came out about the same size as one I'd order at Chipotle , and to my delight, it tasted similar, too. Flavor and texture-wise, this at-home bowl seemed identical to the in-store version. The chicken was tender and well-seasoned, and the rice stayed firm, not soggy. As usual, Chipotle's black beans were beautifully spiced. It wasn't a big deal, but I needed a microwave for the tortillas. Savannah Born I didn't expect to need to use appliances for my takeout meal, but Chipotle's tortilla bag recommended a 60- to 90-second zap in the microwave. Thankfully, I was at home and therefore had access, but it seemed impractical for a portable meal. Hassle aside, I wasn't a huge fan of microwaving food that was in a plastic package — to get the proper experience, however, I followed the instructions. Unfortunately, my chips were missing. I wish I'd noticed when I was still in the store, as I'm sure it would've been an easy fix. If I'd had chips, we could've also used our toppings to build nachos and polish off more of the guac and salsa. Next time, I'd swap guacamole for queso. events.title: Saudi Arabia turns to Aramco to fuel AI ambitions
events.summary: Saudi Aramco acquired a 49% stake in HUMAIN, the government’s AI champion, in exchange for AI assets and $2.6 billion as the kingdom once again leans on the state-controlled oil producer to power its diversification goals. The deal further intertwines Public Investment Fund, which owns the rest of HUMAIN, with Aramco: The Saudi wealth fund already holds a 16% stake in Aramco, a transfer aimed at giving the fund a steady stream of dividend income, and PIF Governor Yasir Al Rumayyan is also chairman of the oil company. Saudi Arabia has frequently turned to Aramco, considered the most effective part of Saudi Inc., to help deliver its ambitions. The oil giant is also building a stadium, investing in renewable power projects, and often borrows during downturns to maintain funding to the state. The latest cash injection from Aramco will help fuel investment plans at a time when many of the PIF’s ambitions are being cut back, there’s a greater focus on getting funding from other investors , and returns are falling . Details of the assets transferred as part of the deal have not been disclosed, but Aramco is expected to put some of its AI infrastructure developed within its technology unit, Aramco Digital (which used to be led by HUMAIN CEO Tareq Amin), into HUMAIN. Aramco will keep control of its venture arm, which already has a Silicon Valley office and has been investing in tech for years. — Matthew Martin

events.title: Ryanair CEO warns fares could rise by up to 20% in 2027 as fuel bill jumps by $2.2 billion
events.summary: Ryanair's CEO told CNBC that he sees "significantly higher airfares" in 2027 for European airlines as jet fuel prices soar. "This is a very significant cost cliff we're all facing next year," Michael O'Leary said in the interview. The airline's profit fell 15% in the first fiscal half of the year as the price of its unhedged jet fuel doubled. Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary told CNBC Monday that European airfares are set to rise "significantly," growing by as much as 20% next year as fuel hedges expire. The budget air carrier's profit fell 15% to 2.15 billion euros ($2.3 billion) in the first fiscal half of the year, as the price of its 20% unhedged jet fuel doubled. "So we're facing 2027 where we have much higher oil prices... I think they're going to get passed on in significantly higher airfares," O'Leary told CNBC's Steve Sedgwick on Monday. "The market customers have been insulated for the last 12 months... but those hedges are rolling off. There's still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we're all facing next year. I believe you're going to see airfares rise next year across Europe by 10%, maybe even 20%," O'Leary added. Ryanair said it doesn't expect an increase in short-haul airfares to fully offset an estimated 2-billion-euro increase in fuel charges next year. It is therefore launching a cost review, which will include lowering crew rations, a potential temporary pay freeze and the use of AI to drive further efficiencies. Ryanair's Irish-listed shares were last trading 3.7% higher. The stock has fallen around 19% this year. The airline said in September it would cut its full-year traffic target from 216 million passengers to 214 million passengers in a bid to reduce its exposure to unhedged fuel during the winter. It's now expecting winter traffic between November and March to remain broadly flat year-on-year. "I think you're seeing even this winter, all of the airlines across Europe, even Ryanair, for the first time in many years, we cut our winter capacity," O'Leary said. We'll only be flat this winter over the prior year, because it makes no sense for us to be growing capacity if we're buying unhedged oil at $170 a barrel." Ryanair hedged 80% of its jet fuel at $67 per barrel for the year, which it said gave it an advantage over its competitors as its earnings remained insulated from volatile oil prices. The carrier added that it has hedged at least 25% of its 2028 jet fuel prices at $95 per barrel. Earnings remain 'hostage' to oil prices The share price reaction on Monday says more about investors' expectations than the numbers alone, according to Adam Vetesse, market analyst at eToro. "Investors appear to have already priced in the hit from unhedged fuel and softer summer fares, leaving room for relief that the quarter landed exactly where consensus had predicted," Vetesse said. "Near-term earnings remain hostage to oil prices and close-in bookings, but the market's early bounce suggests investors are willing to give Ryanair the benefit of the doubt that its cost advantage will matter more than the fuel spike once the dust settles," he added. Ryanair also noted in Monday's announcement that it held 2.6 billion euros in cash as of 30 September, even after repaying 1.3 billion euros in debt. "You know we've paid off all of our debt this year, so we have effectively zero debt. We have 650 aircraft on the balance sheet. We're significantly cash positive," O'Leary told CNBC, adding that the challenge facing all airlines is the volatility in oil prices, lack of hedging, and higher financing costs.

events.title: AD Ports Group appoints Afif Al Yafei as chief executive
events.summary: AD Ports Group , the Abu Dhabi-based global ports and free zones operator, has appointed Afif Al Yafei as its new group chief executive. He succeeds Capt Mohamed Al Shamisi, who took helm in 2014, and helped AD Ports Group grow from a local port operator into an integrated global trade and logistics business. Dr Al Yafei joins the group from Taqa Transmission, where he served as its top executive, AD Ports Group said in a statement on Monday. In his previous role, he oversaw the expansion of the company's asset base and capital investment programme. He also previously held senior leadership positions at Tabreed and Adnoc Gas and serves on several corporate boards. “His expertise in growth, investment, governance and organisational development will support AD Ports Group as it builds on its strong foundations and enters its next phase of development,” said Shadi Malak, the group's chairman. AD Ports Group, which operates about 40 terminals in the UAE, has a presence in nearly 50 markets globally. The leadership change comes as it transits from a publicly-traded company to a private enterprise. It is in the process of delisting from the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange after sovereign investment vehicle L’imad in September met all necessary requirements to proceed with its voluntary cash offer to acquire up to 100 per cent of the ports company. L’imad, through ADQ, already owned 75.42 per cent of the company and launched a voluntary tender offer on August 18 to acquire the remaining issued and paid-up share capital. ADQ offered Dh6.25 ($1.70) per share for AD Ports shares it did not already own. The deal allows AD Ports to pursue long-term objectives, including investments and acquisitions more effectively without the funding constraints or short-term return expectations of public markets.

events.title: Gulf states united in call for diplomacy to end war
events.summary: Gulf officials at a summit in Bahrain talked up the need for diplomacy to solve the region’s security crisis, yet a sense of helplessness hung over the atmosphere. Unlike at the beginning of the year, when messages coming out of the Gulf were less aligned, officials and diplomats at the Manama Dialogue supported Qatar-led mediation efforts with Iran and were clearly against the US attacking it again, concerned that renewed bombing would lead to even more destructive consequences for their countries. There was, however, hardly any US presence to hear that message. The Gulf’s primary security partner sent its smallest delegation to the event in years, despite Bahrain hosting the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet. “People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region,” Saudi Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs Waleed Elkhereiji said, while also emphasizing that the kingdom was investing to boost its defense and deterrence capabilities. Urging diplomacy while also preparing for conflict is a reflection that the most consequential decisions for the Gulf are now being made elsewhere, and all it can do is steel itself for the fallout. Gulf countries “don’t really want to see another round of confrontation in the region,” said Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the UAE president. “But we are braced for the worst.” — Matthew Martin

events.title: 'If we can annoy him again, so much the better': Ryanair's CEO poured fuel on the fire of his beef with Elon Musk
events.summary: Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary promoted a sale after feuding with Elon Musk over Starlink in January. Brian Lawless/PA Images via Getty Images Ryanair's CEO won't back down in his fight with Elon Musk, saying he wants to "annoy" him. Michael O'Leary and Musk have clashed over the airline choosing not to install Starlink on its planes. "I have no intention of making up with him," O'Leary told Bloomberg TV after earnings on Monday. Ryanair's CEO isn't done bickering with the world's richest man. Michael O'Leary, the budget airline's billionaire boss, said on Monday that talks with Elon Musk's Starlink broke down because the SpaceX subsidiary thought the budget airline's passengers would pay for internet access. Speaking on an earnings call on Monday, O'Leary said the airline had "extensive discussions" with Starlink, which he said was willing to cover the costs of installing WiFi terminals on Ryanair's airplanes. However, the typically outspoken businessman then added: "Where the discussions broke down was they believe 60% of our passengers will pay for free WiFi, to which we said, 'You have obviously never met a Ryanair fucking passenger in your life.'" Ryanair's decision not to install Starlink led to a very public fallout between Musk and O'Leary, and at least one of the men isn't yet ready to bury the hatchet. "I have no intention of making up with him," O'Leary told Bloomberg TV after the call. "He thinks I'm an idiot. I know he's an idiot." "If we can annoy him again, so much the better," O'Leary said. Musk hasn't responded publicly to O'Leary on Monday, and SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ryanair is the world's third-largest carrier by passenger numbers, and the largest in Europe, attracting customers with fares as low as 15 euros ($17). Its no-frills business model relies on operating a high volume of flights and enticing customers with cheap fares, but charging for virtually everything else. Starlink's surge in popularity with airlines Starlink has soared in popularity with airlines over the past year, and has signed deals with nearly 50 carriers. Its high-speed internet service is usually offered free to passengers who only have to sign up for the airline's loyalty program. However, O'Leary cast doubt on this regarding easyJet, the British budget airline that announced a Starlink deal last Monday. "It is not clear to us whether they are going to give it away for free," O'Leary said. "I understand the briefing is that they are going to charge passengers for it, to which I say, 'Well, good luck with that.'" EasyJet did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "I believe if it is free, some of our passengers will use it," O'Leary told investors. "If it has to be paid for, there is no revenue model whatsoever." O'Leary first butted heads with Musk in January after making a similar comment. Musk then argued that Ryanair will lose customers to airlines that do have Starlink. Over the next week, the two CEOs called each other idiots while Musk called for O'Leary to be fired and joked about purchasing the airline. Ryanair used the publicity to launch a "Big 'Idiot' Sale" with 100,000 tickets starting at £16.99, or about $23. O'Leary said on Monday that the spat generated up to $40 million of free publicity and bookings were up for two or three weeks afterward. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The market view of the oil, AI and bond trades went through a major change in October
events.summary: Oil futures have risen over the past month, but breaking with what had been an 80% correlation this year, treasury yields declined during the same time period. What changed? The decline in the leading artificial intelligence stocks, the Mag 7, according to Jeffrey Rosenberg, senior portfolio manager of the Systematic Alternatives ETF at the world's largest asset manager, BlackRock, speaking on the most recent CNBC "ETF Edge." "Oil and treasury yields had this amazing correlation and in October it just stopped," he said. "It told us something important. In the market's mind, the geopolitical risk is secondary to AI risk." If there was one safe bet over the course of 2026, it was that treasury yields would rise alongside a move up in oil futures contracts. Over the past month, that ended, and according to Jeffrey Rosenberg, senior portfolio manager of the Systematic Alternatives ETF ( IALT ) at BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, the breakdown in that trade has big implications for the market. "Oil and treasury yields had this amazing correlation and in October it just stopped," Rosenberg said on the most recent CNBC "ETF Edge." The relationship between oil and bond yields was featured in Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's FOMC press conference on Wednesday, with Warsh noting how oil futures have continued to rise, a factor the central bank must consider in its fight against inflation. But Rosenberg said what Warsh didn't talk about was "the most important takeaway." "Treasuries and oil had an 80% correlation this year," Rosenberg said, which is "outsize" relative to normal correlations. "We've basically been trading off oil for good reason." " What happened? Rosenberg says you can sum it up by looking to the deflated AI trade. As the market moved away from that oil-treasuries trading correlation in October, "It told us something important," he said. "In the market's mind, the geopolitical risk is secondary to AI risk," he said. Over the past month — which became most painfully clear in Friday's Nasdaq market wipeout and, earlier the week, Google's biggest single-day decline in its history, wiping out half a trillion dollars in value — the AI trade experienced a retracement. Bond yields went lower, Rosenberg says, because the market is equating weakness in the AI trade as a broader weakness in the U.S. economy. And he said, last week's GDP report backed up that thinking. "AI is everything, everywhere, all the time," he said. Both the growth for the economy on the investment side and the wealth effect on the consumption side are all AI, he said. "Q3 GDP was a blowout [number] and all AI-related," Rosenberg said on the "ETF Edge" podcast extended conversation . He pointed to equipment investment increases and consumption well above expectations and both fueled by the AI wealth effect, which with the latter is even more notable given that real incomes have been coming down in the U.S. Business investment of 12.7% in Q3 was the biggest increase outside the pandemic since 2011, led by a 37% rise in information processing equipment. Industrial equipment investment rose nearly 25%, which while not a straight AI trade, does partially reflect spending on data centers. Warsh did not agree in his assessment of the economy at the FOMC press conference. "It is convenient to say that the strength of the economy is all about this new technology wave. In fact, if we look at the data, really including data from the last meeting until this, the capex story is not just robust, not just strong, but it is broadening. And so if you wanted to tell the story somehow that this is strength we're seeing only in narrow pockets, that's a much harder story to tell now than it would have been several quarters ago," he said. It is true that market breadth, a measure of how many stocks within the S&P 500 were showing positive trading momentum, improved significantly in October after having reached a 2026 low by late September, and as defensive sectors of the stock market like healthcare and staples rallied. But Rosenberg says the conclusion that the broader October market came to is that any "wobble" in the AI trade is going to be seen as a wobble in the growth outlook for the U.S., and as disinflationary. And in a disinflationary environment, there is "only one thing that hedges," he said, and that is "the thing everyone wants to hate. ... the long end of the treasury curve." "That's the really important lesson from last month of market performance," he said. Despite this view, Rosenberg is cautious about suggesting that this dynamic makes bonds a safe bet. "The simple answer is it's not a return to normal, where normal was bonds hedging stocks," he said. That is because of the conflicting forces on bonds. Oil price increases and the persistent level of inflation above target are not going away as challenges to fixed-income assets and the "efficacy," Rosenberg said, of fixed income as a hedge.

events.title: Defense, healthcare, crypto and AI: How the midterm election could affect stocks
events.summary: The midterm election could reshape the outlook for companies heavily exposed to Washington, especially in defense, healthcare, crypto and artificial intelligence. Democratic control of either chamber could bring more investigations and oversight, while giving the party leverage over federal spending and must-pass legislation. Even without control of the White House, Congress could influence billions of dollars in government funding and determine whether Trump-era regulatory changes become lasting law. Lockheed Martin gets about 70% of its sales from the U.S. government. Medicaid accounts for three-quarters of Molina Healthcare's premium revenue . Coinbase is waiting on Congress to finish writing the rules for cryptocurrency . For some of the biggest U.S. companies, Washington is part of the business model. Now, the midterm election could change who holds the leverage. A Democratic victory in either or both chambers of Congress would grant the party new leverage to investigate companies , challenge federal spending and demand legislative concessions. But their reach would have limits: President Donald Trump would retain his veto and broad authority over tariffs, immigration and federal regulation. Historically, stocks have performed well under divided government. Under Republican presidents, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 23% in the year after midterms when Congress was split, compared with 16% when Democrats controlled both chambers, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis published Thursday. Analysts often attribute the pattern in part to congressional gridlock limiting sweeping policy changes. Still, some analysts caution against assuming that pattern will repeat. "We don't think that blueprint holds up this time around, and we still see plenty of reasons to be constructive on the U.S. equity market," said Ariana Salvatore , head of U.S. public policy research at Morgan Stanley. For investors, the midterm election could reshape which businesses preserve their advantages in Washington, particularly in industries such as defense , healthcare , banking and artificial intelligence . "There are some policy changes that might be market moving, at least for certain segments," said Jeff Buchbinder , chief equity strategist at LPL Financial. Congressional oversight and investigations Control of either the House or Senate would give Democrats committee gavels and subpoena power, allowing them to demand documents, compel testimony and haul executives before public hearings. Companies are already getting a preview. On Oct. 21, Sen. Richard Blumenthal , D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sought records tied to Trump's White House ballroom from donors including Cisco , Salesforce , ServiceNow and Kraken . Apple and Nvidia each committed $25 million to the project, according to records obtained by The Washington Post . Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., has separately sought records involving tariff exclusions, including communications involving Apple's former CEO, Tim Cook , as Democrats investigate whether Trump used trade policy to reward political allies and donors. While donations do not prove wrongdoing or favorable treatment, congressional probes still carry risks: subpoenas consume executive bandwidth, reveal internal communications and generate unpredictable news coverage. Few CEOs relish the idea of sitting at a witness table before lawmakers and television cameras. "It creates volatility because you get a negative headline," said Monica Guerra , Morgan Stanley's head of policy and geopolitical strategy, who expects Democrats to cast a wide net for their probes. Democrats have signaled interest in Trump family businesses, government contractors, firms tied to Donald Trump Jr.'s 1789 Capital , and companies associated with Elon Musk and the so-called Department of Government Efficiency . Then there is the most basic power Congress has: deciding where the money goes. Trump's 2025 tax cuts and spending law, known as One Big Beautiful Bill , is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion through 2034, according to a KFF analysis of Congressional Budget Office estimates. KFF is a nonpartisan nonprofit that provides health policy information. Meanwhile, new work requirements for Medicaid enrollees are scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, or earlier in some states, while tighter state budgets could mean fewer people are covered and greater pressure on provider payments. Molina Healthcare generated $32.2 billion , or 75% of its 2025 premium revenue, from Medicaid, according to the company's annual Securities and Exchange Commission filing. In the same filing, Molina warned that losing government contracts or failing to renew them on favorable terms could materially reduce premium revenue.

events.title: Abu Dhabi's Adia, Avolon and I Squared Capital to launch aviation investment platform
events.summary: Abu Dhabi Investment Authority , the emirate's sovereign wealth fund, has teamed up with aviation finance company Avolon and infrastructure investor I Squared Capital to launch an aircraft leasing infrastructure investment platform . The new platform, Constellation Aviation, will provide airlines with access to fleet capacity and investors with exposure to long-term contracted cash flows, the companies said in a statement on Monday. Once the transaction is completed, Constellation is expected to acquire a seed portfolio of aircraft from Avolon with a current market value of $1.4 billion. The seed portfolio includes 22 aircraft with an average age of about five years, on lease to 17 airlines in 15 countries. Constellation is expected to scale over time, the companies said. “Aircraft leasing is a resilient and growing sector supported by strong structural demand for modern aircraft,” said Khadem AlRemeithi, executive director of the infrastructure department at Adia. Adia, which does not disclose its assets, invests on behalf of the Abu Dhabi government and is the largest sovereign wealth fund in the Gulf, with assets touching $1.1 trillion, according to consultancy Global SWF. The authority makes direct and indirect investments in asset classes including equities, fixed income, infrastructure, private equity and property across continents. The sovereign investor said in September that it aimed to diversify its approach across sectors to manage risks. The aviation market is growing amid a continued rise in passenger demand, but airlines continue to face aircraft supply shortages and delivery delays, driving demand for leased aircraft to finance fleet renewal and expansion. In July, plane lessor Dubai Aerospace Enterprise (DAE) partnered with US-based Neuberger Specialty Finance to launch Mustang Aerospace , an aircraft leasing co-investment vehicle targeting up to $6 billion in assets over the medium term. DAE in April also agreed with Blackstone Credit & Insurance to launch a platform that will invest $1.6 billion annually to build a portfolio of commercial aircraft. “Aircraft manufacturers’ order books now stretch a decade or more into the future, and airlines rely on lessors with scale and aircraft delivery slots to grow their fleets,” said Gautam Bhandari, co-founder, managing partner and global chief investment officer of I Squared Capital . “Avolon has one of the largest order books with Boeing and Airbus and thus enjoys significant benefits of scale.” Avolon will retain a minority equity interest in the joint venture and serve as Constellation's exclusive aircraft manager and servicer, the statement said. The transaction is expected to close subject to securing the necessary regulatory approvals. The joint venture will be supported by a syndicated debt facility provided by a group of international banks.

events.title: Shop freezers in six European countries hit by suspected cyber-attack
events.summary: Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack Published 2 November 2026, 11:21 GMT Dozens of supermarkets across six European countries have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers. Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia. Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets. Millions of euros worth of food has had to be thrown away, according to local media reports. Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network". He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates. "The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," he added. It is unclear who is behind the apparent attack. The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F). Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK. In Flanders, Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce. The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop. Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open. A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked. An employee at an ICA supermarket in the capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit. A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network". "ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said. One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees." The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers. Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC. The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia. In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator. A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores. A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR. Additional reporting by Shiona McCallum. events.title: Singapore manufacturers stay upbeat on AI demand despite geopolitical clouds
events.summary: All clusters except biomedical manufacturing and transport engineering project larger workforces. Singapore manufacturers expect stronger business, jobs and output over the next six months, driven by global AI demand, despite geopolitical and economic uncertainty. The EDB survey found a net weighted 24% expect better conditions, up from 12%, while 72% expect employment to stay broadly similar. Precision engineering and electronics are most upbeat, but chemicals is the weakest cluster. Firms cite high costs, overseas competition, tariffs and crude oil supply worries. SINGAPORE – Manufacturers remain optimistic about the next six months, buoyed by strong global demand tied to artificial intelligence , even as geopolitical developments cloud the economic outlook. A net weighted balance of 24% of firms expect business conditions to be better between October 2026 and March 2027, compared with the third quarter, a survey released on Nov 2 by the Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) found. This is up from a net weighted balance of 12% in the previous survey. A weighted 29% of firms foresee improved conditions, and 5% expect a weaker business situation. On jobs, a weighted 72% of manufacturers expect employment levels in the fourth quarter to remain broadly similar to the third quarter. All clusters except biomedical manufacturing and transport engineering project larger workforces. Overall, the net weighted balance for employment is 14%. By cluster, precision engineering is the most upbeat (+48%), supported by semiconductor-related equipment makers that expect global AI-related investment to keep expanding. The electronics cluster (+42%) also expects a strong outlook, driven by robust orders for semiconductors used in AI applications. Biomedical manufacturing (+14%) and general manufacturing (+7%) are also positive. Firms in transport engineering (+1%) expect broadly similar conditions, and cite rising costs of, for example, materials, fuel and freight, and overseas competition as key headwinds. The chemicals cluster is the most pessimistic (-13%). Firms in the petroleum segment (-28%) remain concerned about persistent uncertainty over crude oil feedstock supply. For the fourth quarter, a net weighted balance of 34% of manufacturers expect output to rise from the previous quarter. Electronics (+55%) and precision engineering (+54%) lead the way. In electronics, the semiconductors and computer peripherals and data storage segments expect higher production to cater to buoyant demand from AI data centres. Precision engineering firms foresee higher output of semiconductor-related equipment, bonding wires and metal precision components. Biomedical manufacturing (+19%) firms expect to produce more active pharmaceutical ingredients and life science instruments. General manufacturing (+10%) is also positive, with every segment except printing projecting higher output. The food, beverages and tobacco segment expects stronger export demand for milk and beverage products. Output expectations in transport engineering (0%) are mixed. While the aerospace and land segments anticipate higher activity, the marine and offshore engineering segment sees lower production of oil and gas-field equipment as geopolitical uncertainties weigh on orders. Chemicals (+5%) is the weakest cluster. On export orders, a weighted 23% of firms anticipate challenges in securing orders in the fourth quarter. The top two factors cited are price competition from overseas rivals, and political or economic conditions abroad, including geopolitical developments, tariffs and inflationary pressures. The EDB survey was conducted in September and October 2026. Of 397 manufacturing establishments surveyed, 83% responded. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
events.summary: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive. The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028. The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap. Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality. If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces. Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work. Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself. A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload. Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work. Change the economics of repeated use Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows. The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request. Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting. Test the operating model At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%. That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work. Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it. HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships. Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice. Build for adoption, not rationing Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code. As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them.
