events.title: Greenpeace activists create ‘boulder barrier’ in North Sea to deter industrial fishing
events.summary: Action taken to prevent bottom trawling in the marine protected area and conserve porpoise populations Greenpeace activists have dropped boulders in the North Sea to snag the dragnets of industrial trawlers fishing in a marine protected area. Activists onboard the Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise dropped the giant stones to form an underwater barrier around the Southern North Sea marine protected area (MPA) – the UK’s most bottom-trawled MPA. The Southern North Sea is an area of importance for harbour porpoises , supporting nearly 20% of the UK North Sea population . But despite its MPA status, there are no restrictions on fishing in most of it. Bottom trawlers, dredgers and other industrial fishing vessels scour it daily. Bottom trawlers logged more than 37,200 fishing hours in the protected zone in 2025, an act akin to “a bulldozer tearing through a treasured national park”, Greenpeace UK said. “Hulking great ships prowl the sea day after day, stripping it of fish and killing precious wildlife like porpoises, sharks and sea birds,” said Will McCallum, the campaign organisation’s co-executive director. “With our ship and a movement behind us, we’re doing what the government isn’t: protecting our seas.” The “boulder barrier” had effectively closed 116 sq km (about 45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea MPA to bottom trawling, Greenpeace UK said. Over the coming days, the Arctic Sunrise will patrol the area to deter any other kinds of industrial fishing. The activists have declared the zone an “ocean park”, in the spirit of Britain’s national parks. The Southern North Sea MPA lies along the east coast of England, from north of Dogger Bank to the strait of Dover in the south. It is intended to protect porpoise populations, partly by ensuring the “availability of prey is maintained”. Greenpeace UK’s activists say intensive fishing in the area contradicts this objective. “We announced in June that if the government didn’t act soon, Greenpeace UK would take direct action,” McCallum said. The action coincided with the nationwide premiere of Blue Planet III , the latest BBC wildlife documentary narrated by David Attenborough to focus on the oceans and the human-made threats they face. In 2025 bottom trawlers and dredgers tore through a cumulative 55,600 sq km of MPA seabeds, an area 58 times the size of Dartmoor national park, according to a Greenpeace analysis. The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential A number of notable figures added their names to boulders tipped from the Arctic Sunrise into the North Sea. Among them was the Labour MP Kerry McCarthy, a former climate minister and a member of the all-party parliamentary group for the ocean, who said: “Industrialised fishing is having a hugely destructive impact on our marine environment, yet less than 1% of our seas are protected from it. “[Fishing boats] can legally tear through supposedly protected areas of the ocean, wreaking havoc upon the seabed, precious habitats and the sea life that lives there. Progress is too slow and nature can’t wait, which is why I’ve added my name to one of Greenpeace UK’s boulders. We need a ban on bottom trawling and properly protected ocean sanctuaries, both here in UK waters and right across the Atlantic Ocean.” The government has been contacted for comment.

events.title: The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts. This new era is being called the agentic web. It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process . —Grace Huckins Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide. They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults. Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits. But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes. Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign. Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths . —Sara Kiley Watson This story is the final part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Subscribe to read the other five instalments in our new Impossible issue . The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble Big AI bills and weak earnings have spooked investors. ( BBC ) + The Nasdaq 100 had its worst day since June on Friday. ( NBC News ) + OpenAI has cut its funding target by $10 billion. ( CNBC ) + What even is the AI bubble? ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Hackers have hit Ukraine and Russia’s emergency alert apps Kyiv residents were warned of “nuclear danger.” ( NBC News ) + Russia’s app said nuclear warheads had been launched. ( CNN ) + Ukraine has blamed Russia, which hasn’t yet accused anyone. ( BI ) + AI will transform cyber warfare. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Binance users withdrew $3.6 billion after the largest ever crypto hack The funds moved when the exchange reopened on Sunday. ( Guardian ) + Binance says it’s covered $6 billion of the stolen $6.3 billion. ( Reuters $) + But the industry’s response has undermined its “decentralized” image. ( Gizmodo ) 4 An AI agent injected drugs into a live mouse’s brain It chose the gene therapy and controlled the needle itself. ( Wired $) + We need real-time tracking of AI agents. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Data centres have made utilities a flashpoint in the midterms Americans are angry over rising electricity bills. ( Reuters $) + Virtual power plants could help. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Apple has overtaken Nvidia as the world’s most valuable company Investors are favouring its restraint on AI spending. ( Bloomberg $) + But critics say it’s entering its “slop era.” ( 404 Media ) 7 Supermarket fridges have overheated in a new wave of cyberattacks Stores in Belgium, Sweden, and Luxembourg were hit. ( Politico ) 8 The first chocolate bars made from lab-grown cocoa are here Startups are cultivating chocolate to tackle a cocoa shortage. ( WSJ $) 9 Hackers hijacked digital billboards in multiple countries to show porn They also criticized security flaws and Egypt’s government.( Gizmodo ) 10 A new 3D map reveals instability in interstellar space The discovery could help explain why stars form so inefficiently. ( Quanta ) Quote of the day “It would be great if all this was just a house of cards.” —Kevin Roose, a technology columnist at the New York Times, tells NPR that an AI investment crash would be preferable to the technology permanently upending work and society. One more thing Useful quantum computing is inevitable—and increasingly imminent Last year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang jolted the stock market by saying that practical quantum computing is still 15 to 30 years away. He also suggested that those computers would need Nvidia GPUs to function. But Huang’s predictions miss the mark—both on the timeline and the role his company’s technology will play.  Quantum computing is rapidly converging on utility. And that’s good news, because the hope is that they will be able to perform calculations that no amount of AI or classical computation could ever achieve. Read the full story . —Peter Barrett We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + A miniaturist has built a delightful diorama of the world’s creepiest living room . + The year’s best dog photos have been announced, and they’re very good boys and girls. + At the Green Zone golf club , you tee off in Sweden and putt in Finland, an hour in the future. + Astronomers say they’ve found the real celestial arrangement that inspired van Gogh’s The Starry Night .

events.title: I made it to the C-suite of a media company and was the picture of success. Inside, I was falling apart.
events.summary: The author was editor in chief at HuffPost but felt severe burnout. Courtesy of Danielle Belton My career was thriving, and I was the picture of success. However, I was struggling inside, experiencing extreme stress and burnout. When I was diagnosed with ADHD, a lot clicked into place. When I was hired for my last job as editor in chief at HuffPost, it made The New York Times . My family was thrilled. My old staff rallied around me and sent me off in style. It was a crowning achievement for someone who had fought so hard in their career to get to the next level. But as I ascended to the C-suite , I had a feeling of dread. I knew myself, and something was wrong. Working remotely was difficult for me Not with my job, which I would learn was staffed with bright people who just needed to be supported and empowered. And not with my desire to lead the team to the best of my abilities. The problem was, it was 2021, and the pandemic was still in full swing. All my interviews had been virtual, and I would start the role remotely . My staff, my leadership team, and my bosses were just little boxes on a screen. The first year was rough, but we managed to make the site profitable. Then, I focused on building trust with my team. Things got better, but I never felt secure. Of my woes, I thought, "That's just me." I'd always needed outside pressure to get work done and had trouble with procrastination. I chalked it up to my bipolar disorder, which I was diagnosed with in December 2005. However, I also had plenty of coping skills that helped me mask some of these issues. I kept a strict schedule to fix my time-blindness. I wrote everything down to avoid forgetting important dates and meetings. I did most of my work in the mornings to avoid afternoon brain fog . But other things I couldn't hide — my inability to focus and lack of attention to detail, for example. My disinterest in things that "bored" me or that were rote and repetitive. If I received a document or email longer than a few paragraphs, my eyes would glaze over, and I'd struggle to get through it. I also hated interacting with people solely through video chat because I was easily distracted by alerts on my computer — emails, social media pings, Slack notifications all seemed urgent, and I couldn't differentiate between the importance of the conversation unfolding on Google Meet and the 15 messages flying at me at any given moment. And while I was struggling, I also felt like I couldn't ask for help. Work felt stressful and surreal. I left my job, and the time off made some issues even more apparent Then, in 2024, after countless advertisers started to stray away from news, disrupting the industry's revenue models, I knew my company, like so many others, was in trouble. After our parent company announced layoffs in January 2025, I walked away from the team I had led for four years, hoping to save jobs. With time off for the first time in nearly a decade, I rested. And in that rest, the wheels completely came off. No more meetings. No more people calling. No more pressure prompting me to act. It was all on me to decide if I would do anything, and my brain, suffering from burnout and depression, wanted to do nothing. Unable to function, I found myself looking for distractions from how I felt. For months, the only time I felt good was when I was away from home — whether abroad or just at a party — because home was a constant reminder that I was stuck in the same place. I traveled a lot. I went to events and parties. I made and lost friends. I did everything but talk to a doctor. None of this was new; I'd always had brain fog. I'd always struggled with executive dysfunction. This was my "normal," I reasoned. I saw myself as simply flawed and kept telling myself I just needed to try harder. And yet, I couldn't focus on writing and rewriting cover letters for jobs. I couldn't finish the sample chapters for my memoir that I'd been working on for nearly three years. I wasn't getting better. I was mired in sadness until I remembered an old, dusty notion — Do I have ADHD ? Thinking more deeply about ADHD changed things In my 20s, before I was diagnosed with bipolar, I went in and out of hospitals for years, trying to find a treatment that worked. Then in 2009, after my last hospitalization, I learned a little about how ADHD manifests in women — more hidden, not always as agitated or fidgety, not always as physically disruptive — but rather than dig deeper, I stopped. Though I wondered if I might have ADHD , I had also heard that the medications most commonly prescribed for it could sometimes cause swings into mania for bipolar sufferers. I couldn't risk it. So I didn't ask my doctor about it and, in fact, forgot about ADHD altogether as I focused on building my career. However, earlier this year, I started seeing more successful women talk online about the same symptoms I had. The brain fog, the memory issues, the lack of focus, and at the end of each post, the women said the same thing — they had ADHD. So in July, I saw my doctor. After a short test, he confirmed what I believed — I had ADHD . He then prescribed me a low dose of Ritalin. After taking it, it was like someone turned the lights on in my mind. I felt … normal . These days, I'm busy writing, running my own digital media consultancy , and relaunching my old news blog as a podcast. I'm no longer burned out, and my stress is manageable. But, ADHD meds aren't a cure-all. I still sometimes struggle to start things, and I remain very "pressure-prompted." Thankfully, I already had years of helpful coping skills in my arsenal. But I now know that just because I had these skills didn't mean I didn't need help. Even with medication, executive dysfunction will sometimes creep in, but I now realize it's OK to reach out. It's OK to get help and find a way to thrive, and not just survive. And there was no need for me to continue to suffer from my own success. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Getting a big head start on holiday shopping can benefit retailers and consumers alike
events.summary: Does it make sense to wait until late December to wrap up, like these California shoppers did in 2023? Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Amazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales as early as October . But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping. As a finance professor who studies how people and companies make financial decisions , I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping. Why retailers get such an early start Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about US$1 trillion to $1.7 trillion in the U.S. Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the Bank of America Holiday Spending survey . But many people like to shop for holiday gifts early – meaning before Halloween . Some do this out of necessity : They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks. For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually . In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping. Retailers are adjusting by getting an early start on holiday sales and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more people to join the early birds . And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season. A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics , since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs. Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory gives retailers more opportunities to sell those items. However, an earlier shopping season does not necessarily increase consumer spending overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October. Early birds could buy these Christmas decorations at a discount on Oct. 17, 2026. Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images Beware of some early-shopping pitfalls To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should read vendors’ fine print and research their return policies . Many big retailers are making their return policies more restrictive by shortening the length of time you can return purchases and adding return/restocking fees. In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, Best Buy’s extended policy takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. Target similarly restricts its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1. Amazon extended its holiday return policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas. The timing of holiday shopping varies whether you buy gifts online or in brick-and-mortar stores. Anchiy/E+ via Getty Images When buying early makes financial sense Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary. For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price. But that doesn’t mean you necessarily need to rush to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out. And you should do some comparison shopping to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items. Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The key is to have a budget , recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping. events.title: Elon Musk says 'unsustainably high' costs are the reason for Grok Bot usage limits
events.summary: SpaceX said last month that Grok Bot now has over 800,000 paid weekly users. Illustration by Cheng Xin/Getty Images Elon Musk said that the cost of providing SpaceX's Grok Bot was "unsustainably high." Musk was responding to users complaining that they'd maxed out their usage limits for the AI agent. Agents like Grok Bot and Muse are Silicon Valley's next big thing, but they're still burning through cash. Elon Musk says an age of AI abundance is coming. For now, that doesn't include unlimited Grok Bot. The SpaceX CEO wrote on X on Sunday that the cost of serving the company's AI agent was "unsustainably high relative to revenue," after some users complained that their weekly allowances were running out faster than usual. SpaceX launched Grok Bot , an AI agent that uses a virtual computer to perform tasks on behalf of humans, like shopping, in August. It's available in a series of tiers ranging from free to $200 a month. All of those tiers come with varying usage limits that refresh weekly, a tactic employed by SpaceX and other AI agents, such as  Meta's Muse, to prevent users from racking up massive AI bills. Numerous Grok Bot users posted on X over the weekend, saying they had maxed out their usage sooner than expected, prompting Musk to weigh in. "Upgrade to higher usage plan cost increase is too high?" the billionaire wrote in response to one user, adding in another X reply that reducing allowances and communicating it to users was "just being sensible." Upgrade to higher usage plan cost increase is too high? — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 1, 2026 SpaceX said that Grok Bot had 800,000 paid weekly users in its earnings last month , with Musk telling investors the AI agent had "the fastest growth of a product that I've ever seen in my life." "I think Grok Bot may end up being what uses most of our Super Intelligence compute," he added. SpaceX recently announced it would roll Grok Bot into a new $8-a-month "X subscription" that also includes X premium and Cursor, the AI coding platform it acquired earlier this year . In October, Musk said that the AI agent would also use AI models other than Grok , including Claude Opus 5.5, MidJourney, and Suno. 23:59: saving money is pointless 00:00: we need to save money https://t.co/Q4bFtjZLm5 pic.twitter.com/uIyyAr9ZDB — Bruno Lemos (@brunolemos) November 1, 2026 AI agents have become the tech industry's hottest new trend, but there are still questions about how they will make money. Meta has not said how much Muse, which has been a major hit for the company and now has over 10 million users, costs to run, but CEO Mark Zuckerberg told investors last month that the agent is "very compute-intensive" and is not yet profitable . Musk's admission that Grok Bot is burning a hole in SpaceX's wallet sparked mockery from some X users, who pointed out his recent comments suggesting saving money is "pointless" due to a fast-approaching age of AI abundance. events.title: Unions gain access to thousands of Google workers after UK employment rights overhaul
events.summary: Prospect to hold workplace sessions and recruit members under agreement with tech company Trade unions are expected to make further inroads into big tech companies in the UK after new rights for unions to access workplaces came into force , with Google UK signing an agreement on Monday. The Prospect union has reached an agreement with Google to begin organising among about 7,000 workers across its UK operations, including YouTube but excluding DeepMind . Google DeepMind is expected to strike a separate agreement, with the Communication Workers Union seeking recognition there. The deal follows a similar agreement between Prospect and Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram and employs about 5,000 people in the UK. The agreements will allow unions to communicate with non-unionised workers and encourage them to join. The union, which represents more than 160,000 UK workers across several sectors, will now be able to run sessions inside Google’s workplaces, including the flagship headquarters in King’s Cross, London. Prospect’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, said: “Prospect has been organising tech workers for many years, and this access agreement is a powerful signal of intent that we can successfully negotiate agreements with even the biggest global tech companies. “Tech workers deserve a stronger voice at work, whether that is over bread-and-butter trade union issues like pay and flexibility, AI deployment or workplace culture. I am pleased that Google has struck this agreement with us, and hope it sends a clear signal to other tech companies that having a relationship with trade unions is the new normal in the sector.” He said workers would have a stronger voice as more employees at Google and Meta joined trade unions. “With our track record of delivering wins for members, I am looking forward to seeing what we can achieve together.” Google said it had signed the access agreement to comply with the new UK workplace legislation, although it maintained that it already had good internal employee relations. “This step builds on our established work with internal employee representative groups, allowing us to fulfil these new requirements while preserving the respectful, direct dialogue our culture is built on,” a spokesperson said. Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary, said last week that he expected a wave of union recognition deals in the private sector over the next year as the “transformative” rules on accessing workplaces came into force. The Employment Rights Act gives unions the right to enter workplaces to meet workers or communicate with them electronically. From January, employers will be required to inform workers of their right to join a union. Previously, unions seeking recognition have sometimes had to organise workers from outside their workplaces – as was the case with the GMB’s thwarted effort to gain recognition at Amazon’s warehouse near Coventry two years ago.

events.title: Singapore factory activity grows at slower pace in October after accelerating since March
events.summary: Singapore’s purchasing managers’ index remained in expansionary territory while falling to 51.4 points in October. Singapore factory activity kept growing in October, but the PMI fell to 51.4 from 51.7 in September. Electronics sector, which accounts for 40% of manufacturing output, also saw its PMI ease. Analysts said there were no signs of a sharp downturn in the manufacturing industry, with AI demand expected to keep supporting exports and investment. SINGAPORE – Factory activity here continued to expand in October but at a slower pace because of factors including a slight decline in new orders. Singapore’s purchasing managers’ index (PMI) – a barometer of the manufacturing industry’s overall health – fell to 51.4 points in October, from 51.7 points in September. The electronics sector, which accounts for 40% of Singapore’s manufacturing output, recorded a PMI of 52.5 points. This was lower than the 52.9 points it posted in the previous month. A PMI reading above 50 indicates growth, while one below that signals contraction. Although the benchmarks remain in expansionary territory, they represent the first pullback in the broader PMI reading in seven months and in the electronics PMI since October 2025, OCBC chief economist Selena Ling noted. Still, she said: “Growth momentum may be taking a breather rather than flagging an outright and imminent reversal of the global artificial intelligence-related capital expenditure boom.” Meanwhile, input prices saw slightly faster growth, and finished goods inventories contracted at a slower rate. The supplier deliveries index contracted much more slowly, indicating that delivery delays have eased. Stephen Poh, executive director at the Singapore Institute of Purchasing and Materials Management, which compiles the monthly survey, also said the readings pointed to a manufacturing sector that was “cooling from a high base, not losing momentum”. He said: “Strong exports, AI-linked orders and elevated backlogs keep electronics the main pillar of manufacturing growth. “However, output still lags orders, and higher input costs weigh. Easing supplier delays help, but renewed Middle East shipping disruption could constrain output.” Other analysts agreed that it was premature to conclude that the manufacturing sector was set for a prolonged slowdown. The moderation in October was driven by slower growth in new orders, with an index tracking the measure declining by 0.1 points from September. However, the new export orders index rose by 0.1 points over the same period, indicating that demand remains robust, said Maybank economist Brian Lee. For the electronics sector, the 0.3-point fall in the output index and the 0.5-point decline in the stocks of input purchases index were more significant, as they “could point to supply constraints”. In China, a recent government survey showed that factory activity contracted in October, marking the third contraction in four months. The reading was weighed down by soft domestic demand for goods and signs of weakness in Chinese exports. Manufacturing activity also slowed while continuing to expand in October in Japan, South Korea and ​Taiwan, according to private surveys. This has raised concerns that the persisting Middle East conflict may be offsetting the benefits from the robust global demand for chips and AI-related goods. Oxford Economics senior economist Sheana Yue said she will be watching developments across the regional electronics supply chain, particularly export performance in Taiwan and South Korea, and global semiconductor sales, in the months ahead. “These provide useful signals of underlying demand for electronic components and semiconductors, which have been an important source of strength for Singapore’s manufacturing sector,” she said. Yue added that she expects AI-related demand to continue to support Singapore’s exports and investment. “We have raised our GDP growth forecast to 5.7% for 2026 and expect growth of 4.3% in 2027. A sustained slowdown in electronics demand would pose a downside risk to this outlook, particularly if it also feeds through to investment and hiring,” she said. Jonathan Koh, senior economist and FX analyst for ASEAN at Standard Chartered, noted that manufacturing activity may continue to moderate over the coming months, as it had a strong run-up so far in 2026. Even so, he added: “We do not currently see signs of a sharp downturn. Electronics new orders remain strong, while finished goods inventories are still contracting, suggesting that underlying demand remains healthy, and that some inventory rebuilding may still be required.” Annabelle Liang is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, where she specialises in trade and macroeconomics.

events.title: Ryanair faces clash with unions as it mulls pay freezes amid soaring fuel costs
events.summary: Airline also weighs up reducing crew on flights and increasing use of AI as part of cost-cutting measures Ryanair has said it is considering implementing pay freezes, setting the scene for a confrontation with unions as the airline tries to offset soaring fuel costs driven by the Middle East conflict . The airline is also considering reducing crew numbers on flights and increasing the use of AI, in a cost-cutting drive. Europe’s largest low-cost carrier said it expected European airlines to raise ticket prices by up to 20% , with its own jet fuel costs forecast to rise by about €2bn (£1.6bn) in its next financial year, which ends in March 2028. “Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair . “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.” Oil prices hit a six-month high on Friday before falling to about $110 a barrel on Monday. Ryanair expects European short-haul fares to “increase materially” next year, as fuel hedging deals taken out by airlines to reduce costs expire. “To help address this, we’re reviewing all costs across group airlines with a particular focus on airport churn negotiations, maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes), lower crew ratios and increased use of AI,” O’Leary said. He said the company had several pay deals that would come up for renegotiation from March. However, the Unite union said it had a multiyear pay deal in place that covered 2027, and in any case was not linked to company performance. “Unite hasn’t been advised of any such proposals and we have a multiyear pay deal in place which covers next year,” said Oliver Richardson, a national officer at the union. “A number of unions across Europe have the same. Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured.” O’Leary also said Ryanair was “slowing down hiring meaningfully” for new pilots, cabin crew and across its training courses. The company said its increased use of AI would focus on improving productivity in operations and back-office and support functions. O’Leary said AI had already been used to increase capacity by 4%. “When you’re running 650 aircraft, it’s too big for a human to be able to do it,” he said. “The machines can actually design the schedules better than we know [how to do], so we are getting more productivity out of the aircraft.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ryanair said 80% of its fuel requirements until the end of March were hedged at $67 a barrel. Twenty-five per cent of its fuel requirements for the subsequent 12 months are hedged at $95 a barrel. “It’s beginning to dawn on everybody that we [the industry] are not well hedged,” O’Leary said. The Irish airline, Europe’s largest by passenger numbers, said average fares fell by 2% year on year in the quarter ending in September. Ryanair added that fares in the final three months of the year were trending “modestly ahead” of the same quarter last year. “The booking window remains closer-in which reduces visibility,” the company said. “[The current quarter’s] fare outcome will heavily depend on the strength of close-in October-November school midterm [holiday] and Christmas bookings.” The airline reported a post-tax profit of €1.61bn in the quarter ending in September, a fall of 6% year on year but in line with analyst expectations. Passenger numbers grew 5% year on year to 64.5 million during the quarter. Ryanair has taken delivery of about 30 aircraft annually over the last two years, but the delivery rate is set to drop to 15 annually for the next few years. The airline said it was to take deliveries of the Boeing 737 Max 10 aircraft in January, which has about 20% more seats but burns a fifth less fuel than its current fleet.

events.title: S&P’s negative outlook on Meta underscores the risks of the AI spending boom
events.summary: Good morning. After last week’s tech earnings, Wall Street is increasingly questioning the sustainability of the AI spending boom. Late Friday, S&P Global revised its outlook on Meta to “negative” from “stable,” citing negative cash flow and uncertainty around its capital expenditure plans, Fortune’s Jason Ma reports . The agency affirmed Meta’s AA- credit rating but warned that the company’s leverage could exceed 1.0x as early as 2027. That’s the threshold for Meta’s current rating. Leverage is up from about 0.1x in 2025, largely because of Meta’s strategy of leasing data-center capacity, rather than relying solely on traditional debt financing. S&P projects Meta’s capex will reach $140 billion this year, exceed $225 billion in 2027 and hit $252 billion in 2028 before flattening out. It expects free operating cash flow to remain negative: -$22 billion this year, -$71 billion in 2027 and -$39 billion in 2028. Other hyperscalers are also running cash deficits. According to S&P, what sets Meta apart is its ability to monetize its investments. Rivals can lease compute capacity to frontier model labs and enterprise customers. Meta is betting on better advertising tools and new revenue streams from agentic apps like Muse. But S&P said it is “unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs.” Meta disagrees. A spokesperson said in a statement to Fortune that its AI investments are already delivering stronger engagement and greater returns for businesses. The broader backdrop is shifting, too. OpenAI reportedly cut its latest fundraising target to $20 billion from $30 billion. And Alphabet had its worst day on record after reporting negative free cash flow for a second consecutive quarter. Read more here . For CFOs, the lesson extends beyond Big Tech: lease commitments count toward leverage, and the market wants a credible timeline for turning AI spending into revenue. Not everyone sees a bust, though. Market veteran Ed Yardeni argues that constraints on capital, power and politics could actually make the boom last longer. events.title: ‘Bragawatts’ and why all data-center investing isn’t created equal
events.summary: The News For all the talk of AI bubbles and market crashes, Scandinavian private-equity giant EQT says it’s making a bet that regardless of what happens with the frontier labs, AI is still going to need a massive amount of power, energy, chips, and data centers. “All of a sudden, we find ourselves with $100 billion of energy assets, which are really the limiting factor for AI right now,” said Jean Salata, global chair of EQT, which has $400 billion in assets under management. “A lot of people went out and signed tons of contracts with anybody — they call them ‘bragawatts.’ But signing something and delivering it on time, and with power connected, are two very different things,” Salata said. “Sophisticated investors understand that, but there’s a lot of things happening in the public markets where people are investing in things that they really don’t understand.” EQT is a unique animal in an industry where exits have dried up, a generational bet on software companies looks vulnerable to AI, and higher interest rates have broken the math of cheap leverage and multiple expansion. Since 2018, PE firms have asked their investors for $1.5 trillion more capital than they’ve given back, and the industry is sitting on nearly $4 trillion worth of businesses it can’t sell. EQT has largely stayed out of the private credit and insurance boom that has turned its US rivals into asset-gathering giants — a “beta business,” said Salata, an artisanally crafted Wall Street dig. And it has an unusual backstop: The Wallenbergs, Sweden’s most powerful business dynasty, helped found EQT in 1994 and remain its largest shareholder. The family’s patient approach to ownership is close to the long-hold model that much of private equity is now trying to reinvent. Q&A Liz Hoffman: For a long time, private equity firms could borrow cheaply, ride a rising market, and look like geniuses. It feels like the jig is up, and I know you have some thoughts on that . Jean Salata: Our industry needs to remember what we are meant to be doing, which is delivering returns for our clients. If we’re not doing that, we’re going to end up in a very difficult place. There’s been a lot of attention on the growth in assets under management, a business model that has really benefited from the tailwinds of the private credit run of the last five years. But we’re in an environment where the tide is going out and that means you’re going where there is real value being created. There are something like 10,000 private-equity firms out there. What should that number be? The industry already is consolidating and that will accelerate. This year the top 10 firms in the world have raised 50% of the capital. When you raise smaller funds, people don’t see the carry coming in and so they leave and you get zombie funds. EQT has chosen not to chase those credit tailwinds you mentioned. It doesn’t have the big lending business that Apollo, Blackstone, and others have ridden to huge AUM piles. Do you feel good about that decision? I think there’s a role for private credit, but the question is who’s best positioned to deliver that? We’re good at being an equity investor, being really close to the sectors that we invest in, bringing the best operational talent, bringing the technology and the AI capabilities that we have to the company. None of those are really relevant to the credit business. It’s an origination business. It’s a beta business. Best case scenario, you make 8% return on your money. So, the answer is yes, I think we are happy with the decision. But how do you resist the pressures to be a one-stop shop? Eventually there is a feedback loop. Second-quartile [performance] is, maybe, good enough. But when you start talking about third- and fourth-quartile returns, clients will either stop or reduce the amount that they invest with you. It’s hard to take anything public right now that isn’t a giant AI company and private equity’s track record on returning capital has been abysmal . How does the industry get out of this funk? There are a lot of assets for sale that need to find a home and there aren’t that many buyers. At EQT, we’ve been able to take advantage of where there are pockets of opportunity and liquidity. We had $33 billion of distributions to our investors in the last 12 months, and as a result, we’re continuing to attract capital. There’s this strange incentive structure in our industry, where you sell businesses that you otherwise wouldn’t want to sell because of this finite [fund] life. There’s a bit of frustration on the part of sellers that have sold assets because they need to go fundraising, only to see the buyers make like another 3x on it, which is why you’re seeing these longer-hold vehicles like evergreen structures, open-ended structures, continuation vehicles. But then isn’t the market saying that the 10-year closed-end fund is outdated and should probably go away? One of the reasons we bought [secondaries firm] Coller is we think there is a convergence happening between the primary market and the secondary market. There’s a case to be made for the secondary market essentially becoming the private equity market, as it is in the world of listed equities. Remember, the stock market is a secondary market. Yes, you have some IPOs, but the vast majority of the trading is in existing shares. Where we’re heading in private markets is not quite that extreme, but it’s going to be a much bigger part of the industry. There were $250 billion of PE secondaries deals last year. That’s doubled in the last three or four years and it’s probably going to double again in the next five. One other tension in PE right now is that everyone seems to be in the same trade — the AI trade . Are you worried about correlation? There’s no patents in finance. We’re all moving in a similar direction and it’s going to boil down to execution. A lot of this is about talent. There’s a shortage of really good talent that understands technology and AI, and the ability to attract, to afford, that talent becomes a question of scale. Tell me why all this AI investing is not going to end terribly. There’s a lot of noise right now about data centers — ‘it’s a bubble, the market’s crashing.’ But if you look at the fundamentals of what’s going on in the AI buildout with power, energy, chips, data center demand, we think it’s very fundamentals-based and a very, very attractive opportunity. I don’t want to say we stumbled onto it — the team deserves more credit than that — but we found ourselves in the middle of this in a big way because we were investing in power assets and in data center assets for cloud migration. The pre-AI generation of data centers. Yes. So all of a sudden, we find ourselves with $100 billion of energy assets, which are really the limiting factor for AI right now. Now we are building the industrial AI core for the next generation of data centers, but we’re still only working with the hyperscalers. This is an important point; 92

events.title: Blackstone-backed data center operator tests AI debt fears
events.summary: The Scoop Wall Street is finding out just how expensive things can get in a matter of months. For a look at how much investors’ jitters are reshaping AI-related debt financing, look to QTS, an investment-grade Blackstone-backed data center operator, that just six months ago was weighing a deal to borrow $800 million at a rate of 1.7 percentage points over Treasurys. That deal never went through. And now, that same debt is being shopped to investors at 2.2 to 2.50 points above comparable Treasury yields for a nearly identical offering, according to people familiar with the matter. Both offerings involve the same company, same blue-chip Wall Street backing, and the same collateral — just for a lot more money. Blackstone declined to comment. As debt jitters spread and borrowing gets more expensive, it’s a lesson in just how much sentiment has shifted in such a short amount of time. Know More On Friday, the Financial Times reported that Blackstone told investors it no longer expected Anthropic to get an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its IPO, a reversal of previous guidance about the frontier lab, which is raising billions of dollars to finance its AI buildout. And investment-grade SpaceX’s $40 billion debt launch saw its pricing widen out — reaching an expected 8.75% yield for the riskier portion of its recent debt deal, up from where pricing was discussed just a week earlier, Semafor reported .

events.title: Binance will survive the $6.3 billion hack—but this is the start of a terrifying new era
events.summary: It’s been more than 72 hours since North Koreans robbed Binance in the biggest hack in crypto history and, by all indications, things will be fine. The company’s executives, who went days without sleep to evict the hackers, have gotten the exchange up and running again—all without imposing a haircut on their customers. That’s the good news. The bad news is that the Binance incident is just part of a scary new wave of hacking that cyber experts are calling Black October —and that could be just a preview of a coming wave of attacks against the broader internet. Before turning to the bigger picture, it’s worth recounting just what happened at Binance. A simplified version goes like this: The vile North Korean regime, which relies on crime to keep Dear Leader in power, got into a laptop belonging to a Binance engineer and installed so-called sweeping tools that moved crypto from the company’s wallets to ones controlled by the hackers. The operation was sophisticated enough that it not only locked out Binance’s security team, but ripped up log records that provided clues to how the hackers broke in. Binance’s co-CEO Yi He, who is seven months pregnant, and other execs reacted quickly. They unplugged part of the exchange, halting all withdrawals—but not before the North Koreans stole $6.3 billion. This is a staggering amount, but the Binance team caught a break in the form of a lightning response on the part of longtime rivals Tether, Circle, and Coinbase, which froze around $2.5 billion of stolen USDT and USDC stablecoins. But the rest of the stolen funds—consisting of Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and various off-brand currencies—are gone for good, and will soon be buying more weapons for the DPRK. All of this went down on Thursday afternoon and evening, New York time. By Saturday, as Halloween went into full swing, Binance had turned on withdrawals again for Bitcoin and other major currencies. Meanwhile, the company has reassured customers their funds are safe and that it will be able to offset the roughly $3.8 billion in net losses. Binance is doing this in part by raiding reserve funds set up to stabilize volatility at its derivatives business. The company will presumably scratch together the rest by tapping into its operating income and, possibly, arranging a short-term loan or two. All’s well that ends well—sort of. Binance put on a masterclass in crisis management with regular and candid updates, helping reassure customers and the markets that the situation was contained. But there’s still the question of how the hackers could pull off a robbery of this magnitude in the first place. It’s easy to accuse Binance of failing to implement adequate safety protocols but, by all accounts, the North Koreans displayed extraordinary skill and knowledge in order to circumvent the company’s layers of permissions. There’s also the question of AI. There’s no evidence AI agents directly carried out the attack. But the speed at which it was executed, and subsequent steps to drain the funds to thousands of wallets suggest the North Koreans are, at the least, using AI to hone their tradecraft—in the same way that many of us have used tools like Claude to be more productive at our jobs. This is the frightening bit: AI is helping hackers get better at every stage of their crimes. That includes making deepfakes of employees in order to get into a company’s system, to writing hyper-polished code capable of stealing as much as possible. Even more sinister, there are reports of criminal syndicates gathering data related to hacks like the one on Binance, and using it to train LLMs that specialize in cybercrime. It may be tempting to think all of this as a problem that will only afflict crypto. Indeed, some news reports painted the Binance hack as a 2020-style crypto bro escapade, but the broader threat is much greater. The North Koreans and others will almost certainly employ the techniques they honed in the Binance hack to go after traditional Fortune 500 companies. What’s more, unlike certain industries, crypto companies are typically excellent at security—employing serious people with deep backgrounds in military intelligence and computer science. In the case of Binance, the company has already launched joint investigations into the hack with the Secret Service and the FBI. If the North Koreans can rob Binance, it’s a safe bet they can also find targets among banks, credit unions, government agencies, and nearly anyone who is online. The web is going to become a lot more dangerous. Jeff John Roberts jeff.roberts@fortune.com @jeffjohnroberts This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Jordan’s King Abdullah promises to confront ‘terrorists’ after Karak attack
events.summary: King tells parliament attackers ‘are not of us’ and warns that Israeli expansionism is greatest threat to the region. Jordan’s King Abdullah II says the kingdom would not be shaken by a deadly attack on a church in the southern city of Karak last month. Opening a new session of parliament in the capital, Amman, on Monday, Abdullah said “the treacherous hand of terrorism” had reached out “to test the resilience of our state and the resolve of our people”. list 1 of 3 Syria-Jordan border reopens amid probe into deadly air strikes list 2 of 3 Victims of Jordan’s air strikes in Syria list 3 of 3 Damascus, Amman contradict each other on attack that killed civilians “They are not of us,” he said of the attackers. “There is no place for them among us, not today and not tomorrow.” The attack about two weeks ago killed nine people and wounded dozens. The king asked lawmakers to stand for a minute of silence for the victims, whose relatives attended the session. Al Jazeera’s Ahmed Jarrar, reporting from Amman, said Abdullah made clear that Jordan would confront “terrorism and extremism” by relying first on national unity and public awareness, backed by the army and security services, which would strike “with an iron fist”. Abdullah also addressed regional tensions, warning that Israeli expansionism is the greatest threat to the Middle East. “Israeli expansionist ambitions are the greatest threat to the future of the region and its security,” he said, adding: “The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza continues, and successive assaults persist in the West Bank and Jerusalem.” The king also pledged to protect Jordan’s scarce water supplies, Jarrar said. “We will not allow the thirst of Jordanians to be held hostage by any party,” he said. Jarrar said this reflected concerns that Israeli projects threaten the kingdom’s water security. Jordan, a close United States ally, signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994, and millions of its citizens are of Palestinian origin. Jarrar said the king’s third message was directed at lawmakers as he stressed that the nation is the source of authority and debate in parliament is healthy as long as it serves the national interest. “Your differences of opinion are a strength so long as Jordan’s interest is the goal,” Abdullah said, urging the government to improve living conditions. He also warned officials against abusing their positions. “The law knows no name, no position and no influence,” he said.

events.title: Wholesale marketplace Faire survived the ‘fog of crazy valuations.’ Now, it’s eyeing an IPO
events.summary: Phil Wahba here. Faire, the online wholesale market, is eyeing a potential IPO in the next 12 months, after surviving the perils that come from pressure on Bay Area tech darlings to grow, grow, grow.  “It was like the fog of war or the fog of crazy valuations, and the tech industry collectively losing its mind,” co-founder and CEO Max Rhodes tells Fortune . “We got a little addicted to vanity metrics to pump growth.”  Now, Faire has re-engineered itself with a healthier business model for the long haul. Faire was mostly recently valued at $5.2 billion last November in a $100 million tender offer. That’s less than half its peak valuation of $12.6 billion in May 2022, when its heady rise attracted eager investors. (The company had been valued at $1 billion just 18 months prior.)  The problem Faire ran into, Rhodes recalls, is that the pursuit of fast growth was causing questionable decision-making that could have jeopardized Faire down the road. The company, whose name means “to do” in French and evokes trade shows, operates as a digital marketplace to connect independent retailers and independent brands. Its platform is similar to Shopify in that it powers smaller businesses’ ecommerce, and democratizes technology once reserved for larger retail players. The brands that list goods on Faire—in categories such as decor, food, beauty, jewelry and apparel—pay a commission on items sold to retailers, which typically have one or two locations, like New York’s Strand bookstore chain or Washington, D.C.’s National Archives Museum. About 500,000 retailers and 100,000 brands now use the site. Small, independent retailers still largely get their inventory by going to trade shows. Indeed, the idea for Faire, founded in 2017, came from Rhodes’ prior experience selling high-end umbrellas. (He later entered the tech world, including a stint as an early product lead at Square, where he worked on Cash App.) He remembers being deflated after attending a trade show at New York’s Javits Center; he’d paid a $15,000 fee to sell his wares with only $2,000 worth of orders to show for it. Early on, Faire lined up brands at breakneck speed, which eventually led to retailer churn and high marketing costs to regularly recruit new buyers.  Faire felt like a runaway train. The only way to slow it down to a sustainable speed was to focus on “high-quality supply,” Rhodes said. In 2022, Faire gave many brands the boot and deliberately shrunk the company. It cut jobs and introduced technology aimed at retaining customers long-term.   “Reorder rates for the products retailers are buying have gone way up and that’s leading them to come back,” says Rhodes.  In its most recent quarter, Faire earned $750 million in annualized revenue, up 49% from a year earlier. More crucially for Wall Street, Faire broke even on an EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) basis for the first time. Faire’s finance chief Jason Lee said he is readying the company for an IPO without committing to a specific timeline. The company’s goal for an IPO and beyond is to maintain the discipline it found in 2022.  “The No. 1 thing on the path to durable success in business is solving problems for customers,” says Rhodes. “Retailers don’t care about how much they’re buying, they care about the quality of what they are buying and whether it actually sells.” See you tomorrow, Phil Wahba X: @philwahba Email: phil.wahba@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . events.title: Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy has stroke and is in the hospital, office says
events.summary: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., was hospitalized on Saturday after having a stroke, his office said. Murphy is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate and had been campaigning for Democratic candidates ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections. Murphy's office said he is "awake and alert," after being transferred to Johns Hopkins. Sen. Chris Murphy , a Connecticut Democrat , was hospitalized Saturday after suffering a stroke at his son's hockey game, his office announced on Sunday. Murphy is "awake and alert," according to a statement from his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt. "Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment," Herwitt said. Johns Hopkins Hospital's main campus is in Baltimore, though it has other locations in and around Washington. "The doctors are encouraged by his progress," Herwitt said. "We are optimistic he will make a full recovery." events.title: Ryanair warns that high fuel costs will likely mean more expensive flights and frozen staff pay
events.summary: Ryanair expects its fuel bill for the next financial year to cost an extra $2.4 billion. Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images Ryanair reported on Monday that profits were down 15% year-on-year. It also expects its fuel bill to increase by more than 2 billion euros. The budget airline is planning to raise airfares and freeze staff pay. Surging fuel costs are eating into Ryanair's profits, which it has warned could lead to more expensive tickets and frozen pay for staff. Ryanair reported on Monday that its post-tax profits were down 15% to 2.15 billion euros, or about $2.4 billion, for the six months preceding September 30. As the world's largest budget airline , Ryanair is known for its cheap fares, bolstered by a strong fuel-hedging strategy that uses financial derivatives to lock in future prices. However, the Iran War has kept fuel prices high. While Ryanair has hedged more than 80% of its fuel costs at around $67 per barrel until next March, the remaining fifth has doubled in price to roughly $130 per barrel, the airline said in its earnings report. It added that it expects its fuel bill to increase by 2 billion euros ($2.2 billion) for the next financial year. The airline said it believes airfares will rise due to higher jet fuel prices, but that won't be enough to offset all its additional costs. "We need about a 20% increase in airfares, or about 10 euros per passenger, to fund all of that," CEO Michael O'Leary said on the earnings call. "While I do think there will be a significant boost in airfares next year, I am not sure we will see 20%. Therefore, we do need to close that gap." The airline said it is therefore "reviewing all costs," which may include temporary pay freezes for staff. Ryanair also suggested lowering the crew-to-passenger ratio on its flights, and increasing its use of AI to boost productivity in operations and support functions. To reduce the impact of unhedged fuel costs, Ryanair has also cut its traffic target from 216 million passengers to 214 million, which would result in no year-over-year growth for the coming winter season. Next year, it hopes to boost growth by 3% by expanding its fleet with 16 new Boeing 737 Max 10 aircraft. The Max 10 has room for an extra 20 passengers than the Max 8. The Max 10 was certified by the Federal Aviation Administration last month after years of delays, with European regulators likely to grant certification soon. As of 7 a.m. ET, Ryanair shares were up about 2% in Europe, and 2.75% in pre-market trading on the Nasdaq, as it also announced a share buyback of 800 million euros ($896 million). events.title: The ANC set to lose South African cities
events.summary: The News The African National Congress is on course to lose control of most of South Africa’s major cities in Wednesday’s local elections, according to polling data, potentially disrupting power dynamics in the national coalition government. Several polls suggest the party’s remaining support is increasingly concentrated in smaller towns and rural provinces as opposition parties make deeper inroads in the biggest cities that drive Africa’s largest economy. The local government vote will decide who runs 250-plus municipalities responsible for basic service provision including water, sanitation, and refuse collection. It is the ANC’s first nationwide test since falling support forced it to share power in 2024 after losing its parliamentary majority — unprecedented in the democratic era. The latest Ipsos poll , conducted between Sept. 12 and Oct. 13, put the ANC’s national support at an “all-time low” of 30%, reflecting just how far its backing in urban areas has fallen. Roughly 30% of respondents in Johannesburg, the nation’s commercial hub, and Tshwane, home of the capital Pretoria, said they would vote for the ANC. And that figure fell to just 10% in the port city of Durban, where the populist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (or MK), which is pressing for sweeping state control of the economy and built around former president Jacob Zuma, is comfortably ahead in polls. Support for the ANC, the party once led by Nelson Mandela, remains near 60% in Limpopo and the Eastern Cape, vast provinces of villages, small towns, and dispersed settlements that remain far less urbanized than Gauteng or the Western Cape, an earlier Ipsos poll showed. “After 30 years of democracy, voting patterns are changing and we are moving into a completely new reconfiguration of the political spectrum,” said Andre Duvenhage, a political analyst at South Africa’s North-West University. The Ipsos survey and several other polls — if replicated on voting day — indicate that most metropolitan municipalities would require coalition governments after the local elections. This broadly matches the assessment of think tank Oxford Economics, which has predicted that voting in six of the eight metros would fail to produce an outright winner, creating the need for coalition negotiations. A poor ANC showing would “upend the power dynamics” inside the national coalition government, said William Gumede, a political analyst and governance professor at the Johannesburg-based University of Witwatersrand. He argued that if the ANC’s share of the vote was close to or fell below the Democratic Alliance, it would force the former liberation movement to treat its junior partner “as an equal power” in policy-making and government decisions. The two parties became governing partners after the 2024 general election for the first time, bringing ideological rivals into the same government where the ANC remains committed to state-led economic transformation policies while the DA has pushed for bigger private investment. Know More Political parties have entered the final stretch of campaigning with failures of local government providing much of the ammunition. Unreliable water supplies, deteriorating roads, corruption, and mismanagement of municipal finances, have left many councils struggling to provide basic services. Companies are increasingly paying for the failures, said Busi Mavuso, CEO of lobby group Business Leadership South Africa, whose members account for nearly a third of the country’s $490 billion GDP. She said businesses are investing in backup water storage, private security, and road repairs to remain operational. “Capital is not sentimental,” she said, warning that investors can redirect money when infrastructure and municipalities fail. That makes the quality of municipal governments formed after the election important to investors, according to Awongiwe Booi, a fixed income analyst at South African lender Investec. “The alignment and performance of the coalition post the election will matter more than the poll results themselves,” she said. South Africa’s eight metros house about 40% of the population and account for an outsized share of economic activity. Tiisetso’s view The theory from an investor’s perspective is that a weaker ANC is better for public finances. That deserves testing. For starters, there is a risk over what the party does to win voters back or retain those largely rural areas, where official data shows that these countryside towns accounted for nearly 60% of the country’s poor in 2023. Under such circumstances the ANC, in its effort to recover voters and shore up support, would have every reason to demonstrate that the government can deliver more on its campaign promises to expand public employment and automatically enrol grant-receiving households for free basic services. The spending pressure is hardly hypothetical, with Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana saying government departments have asked for more than 700 billion rand ($41 billion) in additional spending over the next three years, more than a third of everything the government expected to spend this year. “That money simply doesn’t exist,” he told a local radio station last month. Even so, an electoral decline makes saying no politically harder, creating a longer term political risk. It might just embolden those arguing that a post-President Cyril Ramaphosa ANC should move toward MK Party and Economic Freedom Fighters, a radical left movement advocating for nationalization of mines and banks, and ditch the market friendly DA, which has long struggled to shake off its image seen by many Black voters as a party of white interests. There’s nothing irrational about voters demanding more from a state where a third of the work force is unemployed and ranks highest in the World Bank inequality index. The problem is that political need does not create fiscal space. Room for Disagreement David Omojomolo, Africa economist at research house Capital Economics, said fears about the coalition government stability after the election are overdone, and expects the macroeconomic impact of the vote to be limited, with borrowing costs constraining the recovery remaining on track. His comment rests on the DA, rather than MK or the EFF, picking up the ANC losses, which the polls support in Gauteng. “That should compel the next ANC leader to continue to follow business-and-investor-friendly policies, including the commitment to fiscal consolidation,” he said. Notable Unpaid bills owed to municipalities have grown more than seven-fold since 2011 to nearly 500 billion rand ($30 billion), Investec noted, a measure of the fiscal hole new councils will inherit.

events.title: Snowball fight: Cadbury owner in trademark row over festive chocolate treat
events.summary: Mini Snow Balls’ maker Mondelēz is demanding vegan brand Moo Free remove its White Choccy Snowballs from shelves Toblerone owner sues British vegan chocolate brand over chunky shape The owner of Cadbury and Toblerone has demanded that a small vegan chocolate brand remove its products from shelves in a trademark dispute over the use of the word snowball. Mondelēz International has written a legal letter to Moo Free accusing it of trademark infringement by selling its White Choccy Snowballs – gluten-free biscuit-flavoured rice balls covered in dairy-free white chocolate. Cadbury Snowballs first launched in the UK in 1966, and have been sold in their current form as packs of Mini Snow Balls since 2023. The brand registered use of the word Snowball and Snowballs for use in chocolate confectionery as a trademark in 2001. Its Mini Snow Balls are made from Dairy Milk chocolate covered in a crispy shell of white icing sugar. The legal fight has emerged just days after Mondelēz launched legal action against another small vegan chocolate brand, Catherine’s Originals, accusing it of copying the famous chunky shape of Toblerone with its O’bar. Moo Free, which has products stocked in several major supermarkets and online, said it had been selling its Snowballs for about two years before Mondelēz demanded it immediately remove the items from sale just ahead of the busy Christmas period. Mike Jessop, who co-founded Devon-based Moo Free in 2010 when he and his wife could not find allergen-free chocolates for Easter or Christmas, said they began selling online before being picked up by Waitrose and then other supermarkets. He said he had “never even heard of” Cadbury Snow Balls and was lactose intolerant so couldn’t try one. He was surprised Mondelēz had been so “heavy-handed” in its letter and questioned whether it could be possible to trademark an apparently generic term. “It’s a snowball, it is not like we are making a Freddo,” he said, referring to Cadbury’s famous frog-shaped bar. In a letter to customers, Moo Free wrote: “Moo Free takes intellectual property concerns seriously. However, we do not accept that any infringement has been established and have responded accordingly … We are disappointed to find ourselves in this position, and we stand in solidarity with Catherine’s Originals as it addresses its own situation. We hope to resolve these matters appropriately.” A spokesperson for Mondelēz International said: “ Cadbury Snow Balls are one of our most popular Christmas products, enjoyed by households across the UK. No legal action has been taken, but we have been in touch with Moo Free to make them aware of our trademark. We are open to reaching an amicable resolution.” It is not the UK’s first snowball fight. Tunnock’s and Lees of Scotland won legal action against HMRC in 2014 after proving they did not have to pay VAT on their coconut-covered confections, as they were deemed sufficiently similar to a cake for an exemption. Snowballs made by these two suppliers – defined as “a dome of marshmallow coated in any combination” of chocolate, sugar strands, carob, cocoa or coconut – were subsequently given their own VAT-free status .

events.title: Ryanair says it may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares
events.summary: Published 2 November 2026, 08:06 GMT Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran. The airline said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict. Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be €2bn (£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and its boss, Michael O'Leary, said airfares would have to rise by "double-digits" to help cover the cost. But the firm said that was unlikely to be enough and it is looking into pay freezes. Unite, the union representing Ryanair staff, said it had not been told of "any such proposals". O'Leary also said the company would slow down hiring as airline's costs rise. The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to €2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to fuel costs jumping by 15%. The company said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" – in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices – the cost of the remainder was elevated. O'Leary reiterated forecasts from earlier this year Ryanair would "need a 20% fare increase" to cover the cost of jet fuel. "I'm not sure we'll get to 20%," he said. "But we're certainly looking at double-digit fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027." Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere. Ryanair also said it was weighing up freezing pay as "maturing labour agreements" – multi-year wage deals with unions – come to to an end and the policy could be implemented from April next year. Oliver Richardson, national officer at Unite, said the union "hasn't been advised of any such proposals and we have a multi-year pay deal in place which covers next year. A number of Unions across Europe have the same". He said: "Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured." Ryanair also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions. Meanwhile, Ryanair has cut back on winter flights and said on Monday there would be more to come. It said this was happening across the airline industry, particularly with short-haul carriers. O'Leary said: "We believe those cuts will continue into the summer of 2027. Over the medium term, we expect short-haul capacity will remain constrained out to the early 2030s." events.title: UAE oil exports surpass prewar levels despite Hormuz disruption, energy minister says
events.summary: UAE oil exports surpassed prewar levels “at a certain time” as the Arab world’s second-largest economy continues to work as reliable supplier to the world, despite Hormuz disruptions. “At a certain time, we did better than prior because of our continuous work,” UAE’s Minister of Energy and Infrastructure Suhail Al Mazrouei told delegates at the Adipec conference in Abu Dhabi on Monday. He did not disclose the timelines or the volumes the UAE exported, but said [we] "did our best to make sure that the prices of commodities do not go very high”. The Emirates shipped 3.94 million barrels per day of crude and condensate in June, the highest monthly total in the past year, and a sharp reversal from March, when the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz cut exports to a record low of 2.13 million bpd, Kpler data showed. “We feel the pain on those consumers, and we understand that if prices go too high, that's going to strike the demand in years … the pipeline helped us a lot over there. Our readiness through the fleets and the ships have helped us tremendously," Mr Al Mazrouei said. The UAE's Habshan–Fujairah pipeline, often referred to as the West–East crude oil pipeline, has the capacity to transport up to 1.5 million bpd of crude oil, representing a substantial share of the country’s total oil exports. In May, the UAE announced the expansion of the West-East crude oil pipeline to be completed by 2027, with the project expected to double export capacity through Fujairah . Mr Al Mazrouei said the UAE was able to “fill in the supply gap” as supplies from other countries reduced due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. “Sometimes even we have filled in the gap ... we managed to oversupply to those countries because there was a significant reduction from many countries.” Oil prices volatile Oil prices have remained volatile since the Iran war broke out on February 28, with prices rising to more than $120 per barrel in March as the Middle East war escalated, with Iran hitting energy infrastructure in the region and ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz coming to a virtual halt. Prices fell in subsequent months amid peace talks between the US and Iran to end the conflict and reopen the strait, but surged again amid concerns that the US is preparing to restart the Middle East war and attack Iran. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, is trading close to $110 per barrel, with West Texas Intermediate at about $100 per barrel on Monday. “When I think about what happened over the last eight months, it's really quite stunning the level of disruption to the global energy system. Crude oil, natural gas, products have all been disrupted. The thing that stood out is how resilient the system has been,” Meg O’ Neill, chief executive of BP, said in a separate panel discussion at Adipec. “If you went back to the start of the conflict, people would have said that oil should have been $150 a barrel by June, and that didn't happen. People said that natural gas prices should have spiked, and they really didn't until the last month or so.”
