events.title: Sales slump at UK’s largest brickmaker as housebuilding downturn deepens
events.summary: Ibstock, which has cut production by a fifth, criticises government for delay in help for housing sector Sales at the UK’s largest brickmaker plunged by more than a fifth over the summer, as it criticised the government for not introducing fresh help for the housing sector faster. Leicestershire-based Ibstock said on Monday that sales slumped by 22% below its expectations in the three months to the end of September, prompting it to slash production levels by a fifth. Ibstock issued its second profit warning this year and said UK brick market volumes declined by 17% year on year in July and August, with weak market conditions continuing through September and October. “Trading conditions deteriorated sharply during the third quarter, with weakness continuing into October,” said Joe Hudson, the chief executive of Ibstock. “We have responded by reducing production to manage inventory, taking further cost action and maintaining tight control of cash. These production decisions create an additional near-term earnings headwind but are necessary to align output with demand.” The warning by the company, which now expects full-year profits to be “materially below” previous expectations, comes days after the Office for Budget Responsibility cut its forecast for the number of new homes that will be built by 2031 by 190,000. Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, has said there is only a “slim chance” the government will meet its goal of building 1.5m new homes this parliament, amid estimates that the target could be missed by a third. Ibstock also criticised the government’s decision to delay the start of a support scheme that is designed to help first-time buyers in England buy a newbuild home with a 2.5% deposit. “The introduction of the Your First Home support scheme represents a welcome and potentially meaningful intervention for the UK housing market, with the potential to improve affordability, stimulate new-build demand and strengthen confidence in future housing supply,” the company said. “While the announcement reinforces confidence in the group’s medium-term market outlook, the delay to its introduction until April 2027 is disappointing and has put additional pressure on near-term demand.” Ibstock said it now expected full-year profits to be in the mid-£40m range, well down on analysts’ previous consensus of £59m. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The company said its cost savings and cash management initiatives were focused primarily on overhead and discretionary spend. “Domestically exposed building stocks like Ibstock continue to face very challenging industry conditions,” said Clyde Lewis and Sam Cullen, analysts at Peel Hunt, in a note to investors. “The new Your First Home programme should be modestly helpful next year but lower interest rates remain key to a pickup in sector activity and share prices.”

events.title: Al-Jawf becomes new hotspot in Yemen war between government forces, Houthis
events.summary: Recent military advances by Yemeni government forces highlight the geographic and strategic significance of Al-Jawf Governorate. Al-Jawf has become a new focal point in the conflict between forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis, highlighting the strategic importance of the northern governorate. A major counteroffensive has been launched by the Yemeni government army and forces loyal to it to capture the strategic heights east of the provincial capital, al-Hazm, from the Houthis. list 1 of 3 New Yemen fighting displaces 290,000, says UN, with pregnant women at risk list 2 of 3 Yemeni government forces seize strategic positions in al-Jawf list 3 of 3 Saudi-led coalition intercepts a missile as fighting rages in Yemen’s al-Jawf The operations are part of Operation Dawn of Yemen, launched by the government last month to reverse Houthi territorial gains and restore state control in the country. Al-Hazm has become a central part of this operation, with the city a potential launchpad for government forces against the Houthis. They have controlled the capital Sanaa and most of northern Yemen since the war broke out in September 2014. During the 12 years of war in Yemen, control over al-Hazm has shifted several times, with the Houthis seizing the city in March 2020. The governorate remains highly coveted due to its expansive border with Saudi Arabia and its direct geographic links to five pivotal governorates: Hadramout, Saada, Sanaa, Amran and oil-rich Marib and close to the capital, Sanaa. Al-Jawf also acts as a vital defensive shield for Marib, controlled by government forces, preventing the Houthis from advancing into the eastern regions. It is also a gateway to major Houthi strongholds in northern Yemen. Field Commander Colonel Rabie Al-Qurashi said government forces have been able to win complete control over the strategic Huwaishan mountain range, east of al-Hazm city. He said it is the first line of defence for the Houthis in the eastern axis and control over the rugged region would give government forces the ability to disrupt rebel supply routes. “Government forces succeeded in breaking that defensive format with partial control over the Al-Alam front road,” Al-Qurashi said. “The government advance represents a beginning to tighten the noose on the Houthis in the upper al-Labanat camp,” which is regarded as a vital eastern gateway to Sanaa. Ali Al-Dahab, a military and strategic affairs researcher, said there are immense tactical benefits from holding this elevated terrain. “The recent advances of government forces in Al-Jawf are a military transformation that serves the course of future operations for their arrival to al-Hazm city,” Al-Dahab told Al Jazeera. “The government forces’ recovery of a number of heights there provides a military and psychological morale advantage and confuses the Houthis’ decisions, in addition to granting government forces monitoring, movement, and observation of Houthi supply lines and securing their own lines.” Military spokesman Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaili said on X that recent military operations against Houthi positions in al-Jawf were “inflicting losses on the militia’s capabilities”. The government dominates the vast eastern desert district of Khabb wa ash Sha’af, representing 82 percent of the governorate’s total area. The Houthis control the provincial capital, al-Hazm, and 10 other districts. Security and political affairs researcher Brigadier General Ahmed Al-Awadhi stressed the importance of “continuous but not rapid” government advances in the area. “The advances of government forces in Al-Jawf cannot be ignored or their importance underestimated,” Al-Awadhi told Al Jazeera. “Control over heights or mountain ranges in the desert Al-Jawf governorate represents points of military strength regardless of their proximity to or distance from the governorate capital.” The government forces advances in al-Jawf highlight a historical vulnerability for the Houthis, having suffered repeated defeats in battles in desert and open areas, he added. The developments coincide with the Presidential Council’s appointment of Major General Amin Ali Al-Akimi as governor and military commander of al-Jawf. “[His] reappointment… comes within the context of restructuring the theatre of operations and unifying the front,” Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst told Al Jazeera. “Hailing from Dhu Hussein, a branch of the Daham Bakil tribe, Al-Akimi possesses tribal and military influence that could help mobilise tribes, overcome divisions and bolster momentum on the ground. However, translating this influence into sustainable gains remains contingent upon unifying command and control, coordinating operations across all battlefronts, securing military and logistical support and strengthening anti-corruption efforts to improve the efficient management of military resources.

events.title: Demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments
events.summary: We have seen demands being made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries as a way to avoid tax. HMRC has sought to tackle this tax avoidance through what has been termed the loan charge and published guidance for those affected.Questions have been raised about the regulatory status of these loans and whether they were ever intended to be repaid.Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they’re unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.Some consumers are, however being sent legal letters threatening potential court action and asking for immediate repayment of the loan. Repayment is being sought after these disguised remuneration loans were sold by the original provider to a third party.Those seeking payment may ask the FCA to agree to a Validation Order. This is the formal permission needed before the loans could be enforced. We would consider any request carefully and our agreement is by no means guaranteed. If a Validation Order is required and not granted, the debt would remain unenforceable.Anyone who receives a demand for repayment of a disguised remuneration loan, and is unsure whether they are liable for the amount claimed, should consider carefully whether to make any payment. We’d encourage them to look at the HMRC guidance and consider taking legal advice.Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.If you are experiencing any difficulties, whether they are health, money or other difficulties, or if you don't understand what is happening, you should raise this with those contacting you.

events.title: Supermarket fridges in Sweden, Ireland overheat amid suspected cyberattacks
events.summary: Suspected cyberattacks trigger supermarket fridge failures across Europe Temperature increases have been reported in the cooling systems of dozens of stores across the continent, weeks after a similar attack in France caused fires and food losses. Suspected cyberattacks have triggered temperatures to rise in grocery store refrigeration systems in a growing number of countries across Europe. Overnight temperature spikes were recorded in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden. On Monday, retailers and authorities pointed to alleged cyberattacks that underscored the vulnerability of systems that once largely operated mechanically. list 1 of 4 Hundreds of supermarkets in France hit by ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack list 2 of 4 How Israeli firm’s ‘zero-click’ malware attack poses global security risk list 3 of 4 Cyberattack on French supermarkets causes fires, millions in losses list 4 of 4 Experts defer to AI in decision-making, Anthropic study finds The head of ⁠⁠⁠⁠Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, confirmed on Monday to the Reuters news agency that the centre ⁠⁠⁠⁠is responding to ⁠⁠⁠⁠multiple incidents affecting store cooling systems. “We have in recent weeks … identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” he said. The temperature of freezers in several Swedish stores rose suddenly overnight, store operators ICA and Coop said, while Swedish retailer Axfood said freezers at a distribution centre for home delivery of groceries in the Gothenburg area were hacked. SuperValu, Ireland’s third-largest supermarket chain, ⁠⁠⁠⁠said a specific model of refrigeration systems has been affected by a “cyber incident” at 13 of its 223 ⁠⁠⁠⁠stores. The Belga news agency reported overnight temperature increases at dozens of ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg. They were blamed on a cyberattack, according to the chief ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠executive ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠of refrigeration company,⁠ ⁠⁠⁠Sabcobel. Stephan Moelans said the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode. Also in Belgium, five Spar shops had their fridge systems attacked, said a spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates the franchise system. In Estonia, at least one supermarket chain was affected, technology supplier Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR. “This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” Kitman CEO Jann Mutso said, without naming the affected chain. Ahold Delhaize reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month. The cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets in France raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F), spoiling food and causing fires at several stores. One Swedish store said in a social media post on Monday that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been set to the same temperature as during the cyberattack in France. “We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems,” a spokesperson for privately held ICA told Reuters in an email. Kitman’s Mutso also said that temperatures at the Estonian chain were set to 50 degrees Celsius (122F). Privately-held retailer Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents. There has been no claim of responsibility for Monday’s attack, nor the one earlier in France. However, the incidents help to increase concern regarding hybrid warfare stemming from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran-United States war. European states have blamed Moscow for a growing number of incidents affecting infrastructure, including via cyberattacks, in recent months. Russian has repeatedly denied involvement in any sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. “These incidents show that cyberattacks ⁠can disrupt services, affect ⁠businesses and directly affect citizens’ ⁠daily lives”, a ⁠European Commission spokesperson ⁠said, stressing the importance of strengthening ‌cybersecurity across the bloc.

events.title: I’m a wealthy Californian. The billionaire tax is a win for everyone | George Zimmer
events.summary: I’m a wealthy Californian. The billionaire tax is a win for everyone The measure would ease inequality and bolster healthcare – without draining our coffers or triggering a billionaire exodus On Tuesday, California voters will decide whether to enact Proposition 40 , a one-time, 5% tax on the net worth of about 250 California billionaires . In recent months, a number of California billionaires and their apologists in the media and in government have come out swinging against the ballot measure. I’m not a billionaire, but I’m a Californian wealthy enough to know that they have no valid reason to fight the proposition. For multimillionaires like me, paying a 5% tax would not change our lives materially, and if we can afford this as people well below the billionaire line, certainly those at the very top can too. Prop 40 would enact the first tax on billionaires anywhere in the world, with organizers estimating it would raise roughly $100bn in revenue, most of which would be directed to healthcare to make up for federal cuts from Trump and Republicans’ 2025 tax bill. Six Nobel Prize-winning economists said it would “kickstart a movement to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals in other states – and eventually at the federal level and in other countries”. Opponents’ primary objection to Prop 40 is that it will spark an exodus of the state’s billionaires, who would run for the hills of lower-tax states. They further claim this would blow a hole in the state’s tax base and kill the Golden state’s “ golden goose ”, or its trove of innovative minds. For one thing, numerous studies have failed to find evidence that wealthy people flee en masse when their taxes are raised, which suggests that Prop 40 critics’ fears of a billionaire exodus are overblown. After Massachusetts and Washington state raised taxes on high earners in 2022, both states actually experienced an increase, not a decrease, in their millionaire populations. A 2023 study also revealed that, despite being a relatively high-tax state , since 2011, California has had the second lowest out-migration rate among households earning more than $200,000. As a person of wealth, I can choose to live wherever I want, no matter the tax rates. Like so many of my rich counterparts, I choose to live in California because I love it here. I don’t intend on leaving anytime soon. I will never be able to get enough of our beaches, our forests, our piers, our cable cars, our universities, and everything else in between. I’m willing to pay higher taxes than I would elsewhere to maintain (and improve) all of these wonderful things that make California the Golden state that it is. To avoid the tax, billionaires would have had to move by 1 January 2026; from what we know, only six of them did. Between 2019 and 2025, California billionaires’ wealth grew an average 15% per year, but they paid just 0.26% of it in state income taxes. They pay so little in taxes as it is that, even if they were all to leave, it would take 25 years under current California law for the loss of their tax payments to exceed the $100bn that Prop 40 would raise. Taxes should be based on the principle that our government should be financed based on one’s ability to pay. When 250 billionaires have the means to pay more, it is their civic duty – just as it is mine – to do so. There is also no reason to believe innovation in California will end if Prop 40 passes. Wealthy entrepreneurs like me are the brains behind a lot of products and services that have enhanced countless lives, and our state has become the place to be for aspiring industry leaders. California’s industries attract top talent and intelligence. A 5% one-time tax will not deter people from pursuing a livelihood in entrepreneurial epicenters. So far in 2026, amidst all the buzz about the ballot measure, no less than 80% of all new venture capital funding found its way to California. In short, Prop 40 will not trigger a billionaire exodus, it will not drain our coffers, and it will not spell the end of Golden state innovation. What it will do is add some progressivity to our state tax code , put a check on the power of the richest among us, and raise significant funds that will prevent hospitals from closing, millions from losing their healthcare coverage, and thousands of healthcare jobs from being cut. I want less inequality because my family and I will be better off in a society with less inequality. That should be a win in every Californian’s book, rich and poor alike. George Zimmer, a member of Patriotic Millionaires, is the chairperson, CEO and founder of Generation Tux, an online rental platform for tuxedos and suits. events.title: Could the US midterms cause a surprise stock market rally?
events.summary: Investors have a lot on their plate. Oil, inflation and interest rates are climbing, while tech stocks are volatile amid growing fears of an AI bubble . Throw in US President Donald Trump's unpredictability, mounting government debt, regional wars and stretched stock valuations, and it’s all getting a bit much. Now comes another challenge: Americans go to the polls on November 3 for the midterm elections , which will determine control of Congress and the direction of Mr Trump's presidency. Yet here’s a curious twist. History shows that midterm elections have typically been followed by a strong run for Wall Street. JP Morgan Asset Management’s analysis shows the S&P 500 has risen in the 12 months following every midterm since 1950. Might history repeat itself? If so, stock market bulls have plenty to look forward to, says Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell. “The past is no guarantee, but the third year of a presidential term is, on average, the best one for the US stock market.” The average third-year gain across postwar presidencies is a stellar 16.1 per cent. No other presidential year averages a double-digit gain, he says. One theory is that presidents have an incentive to boost the economy ahead of the next election. Another is that the midterms often deliver a lame-duck president who struggles to pass legislation, allowing businesses to operate without interference from Washington. Markets are often volatile before the vote, but when the result is known, investors can focus on policy rather than polling, says Jason Hollands, managing director at Evelyn Partners. Gridlock could boost stocks Mr Trump looks on course to lose control of both the House and Senate. If that happened, it could actually help stocks. “A divided Congress would make major new legislation harder to pass. That could limit the prospect of sweeping changes to areas such as tax and regulation,” Mr Hollands says. But investors shouldn’t assume divided government means quiet government. Aliasgar Tambawala, co-chief investment officer at Klay Group, warns that political gridlock brings problems of its own. “A divided legislature may lead to greater disruptions around issues such as the debt ceiling and government funding.” Mr Trump's executive powers, including tariffs, would remain largely intact, while the President retains his veto. Mr Tambawala expects political volatility to persist, but says GCC investors face bigger concerns, notably the situation in the Strait of Hormuz . “A durable resolution would augur well for the region.” Despite recent volatility, the S&P 500 and tech-focused Nasdaq are up around 12 per cent this year, says Tony Hallside, chief executive of STP Partners. Further gains depend on earnings. “Getting the election out of the way helps sentiment, but it does not create earnings growth. If inflation persists or profits fall short of expectations, the historical election pattern will offer little protection.” AI is another concern. Can the technology justify the huge sums being invested by generating sustainable revenue and profits? “Political clarity will not compensate for disappointing commercial results,” Mr Hallside says. Reality checks for investors Madhur Kakkar, chief executive of Elevate Financial Services, warns that markets face formidable headwinds. Brent crude has hit $117 a barrel, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September and may do so again in December, while 10-year Treasury yields are approaching 5 per cent. “Higher Treasury yields give investors a competitive income alternative at a time when US equity valuations remain demanding,” Mr Kakkar says. The S&P 500's Shiller price-to-earnings ratio ended October at 40.88, a level exceeded only during the dot-com boom. On October 29, Alphabet shares plunged 13 per cent, wiping $500 billion off its value after heavy AI infrastructure spending contributed to negative quarterly free cash flow of $9.1 billion. Yet the US economy remains resilient, with third-quarter GDP growing at an annualised 3.4 per cent. Mr Kakkar urges investors to maintain balanced portfolios rather than chase a post-midterms rally. Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial, believes AI and interest rates, rather than politics, will determine whether markets finish 2026 strongly. “Easing inflation and a successful Anthropic IPO could still fuel a year-end rally.” For the GCC, the outlook is firmer than headline figures suggest, he says. The IMF expects Gulf output to shrink 4.8 per cent this year because of the Iran war, before rebounding 9.1 per cent in 2027. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are shipping substantial oil volumes around the Strait of Hormuz, while high crude prices bolster revenue. Non-oil activity remains strong, but a full recovery depends on the strait reopening, which the IMF assumes will begin in March 2027. Mr Mould remains cautious. Inflation is sticky, interest rates may rise, the Middle East war could drag on, oil and equity valuations are high, and the AI boom could end in an investment bust. History suggests the midterms could unleash another Wall Street rally. But with so many risks stacking up, investors may discover that this time, history really is bunk.

events.title: Resilience of Gulf oil infrastructure has its limits
events.summary: Amena’s view The drums of war are beating again, and the oil-exporting states are bracing “for the worst,” as the UAE’s presidential advisor Anwar Gargash recently put it. Eight months into the US-Iran war, one lesson is clear: There is no amount of operational resilience that can shield energy infrastructure from an unresolved political conflict. Renewed strikes will put more of the region’s oil supply at risk. Saudi Arabia and the UAE have demonstrated exceptional levels of resilience, activating contingency plans, carrying out repair works in record time, and keeping customers supplied. Their bypass pipelines have proven the value of planning for the shift from the “just in time” model to the “just in case” approach. The UAE’s 1.8 million-barrel-per-day (bpd) pipeline from Abu Dhabi to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman was once questioned as an investment. Its cost was recovered after just one month of conflict, according to people familiar with the matter. A second link with similar capacity is expected to be completed by July 2027. Saudi Arabia is considering expanding its larger East-West Pipeline and may bring in countries like Iraq and Kuwait that don’t have shipping outlets outside the Gulf. Within the industry, there’s a growing consensus that the pre-war oil flows will not return. More investment will be earmarked for contingencies, reflecting in part the view that reaching a diplomatic resolution to the Iran war is unlikely anytime soon. So far, the global energy system has performed better than expected. Gulf exporters kept their oil flowing despite the risks faced in Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, inventories were released, and some demand was curtailed, all of which combined to limit the oil price spike. But this resilience should not be mistaken for future security of supply, especially as this potential escalation comes at a time when global inventory levels have been drained by around 1 billion barrels. Brent is trading above $110 a barrel, of which perhaps $40 could be attributed to geopolitical risk. While much of the focus is on guessing what US President Donald Trump is planning, the reality for the oil industry is that higher prices may have eroded around 3 million bpd of demand, according to energy industry executives. This assumption is even more pessimistic than the IEA’s forecast of demand declining by around 2.6 million bpd this year. Another rise in prices, or oil prices sustained at this level, will only lead to even more demand destruction. This week, ahead of Abu Dhabi’s flagship energy conference ADIPEC, senior executives and CEOs from the energy industry gathered to discuss the challenges facing the industry under the Chatham House Rule. There was frustration about the lack of policy support, especially from European governments, for investment in the upstream sector and the construction of refineries. Over the past two decades, around 25% of Europe’s refineries were shut down, mainly as a result of policies related to the energy transition. Today, energy executives from European oil majors are pressured to address rising prices of oil products without having the facilities needed to deliver the energy to consumers. If there’s one silver lining from this crisis, it’s prioritizing investments in new supply and abandoning the dichotomy between the concepts of “old energy” and “new energy.” At the opening of ADIPEC on Monday, Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, was asked what the biggest challenge facing his industry is. He replied with one word: “energy.” Another round of war will make that energy costlier, and less abundant. Notable The UAE’s race toward its “Zero Hormuz” strategy runs through Fujairah, where investments can be seen in all directions intended to move the fossil fuels and products that would otherwise be trapped in the Gulf, Semafor reported.

events.title: Current price of oil as of November 2, 2026
events.summary: As of 6:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil sold for $112.60 per barrel (using Brent as the benchmark, which we’ll get into momentarily). That’s $3.26 lower than yesterday morning and approximately a $47 rise over the past year. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $115.86 -2.81% Price of oil 1 month ago $106.84 +5.39% Price of oil 1 year ago $65.77 +71.20% Will oil prices go up? It’s impossible to predict the future of oil prices. Several factors determine the movement of oil, but it ultimately boils down to supply and demand. Again, when threats of economic downturn, war, etc. are high, the oil trajectory can turn rapidly. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices When you pay for gas at the pump, you’re paying for more than just the crude oil itself; you’re also springing for links along the chain, such as the refineries and wholesalers—not to mention taxes and local gas station markups. Still, the crude oil aspect affects the final price most dramatically, as it typically accounts for more than half the price per gallon. When oil prices spike, so do gas prices. And frustratingly, when oil prices drop, gas prices tend to take their time drifting down to the lower price (sometimes referred to as “rockets and feathers”). The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks. It’s not a long-term answer—more of an immediate relief to assist the consumer and keep critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Oil and natural gas are both major energy fuels. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible—which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil When examining oil’s performance, there are generally two major benchmarks: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Between the two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s brought the first big oil shock when the Middle East cut exports and imposed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices dropped in the mid-1980s for reasons such as lower demand and more non-OPEC oil producers entering the industry. Prices spiked again in 2008 with increased global demand, but it soon plummeted alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before—bringing prices below $20 per barrel. All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: As Trump eyes new attack, Iran vows to retaliate beyond the Mideast While Americans turn against data centers, Brazil offers tax breaks and cheap power Chevron speeds ahead in Venezuela while Exxon urges caution with a ‘little pinch of salt’ Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: Business Insider's 2026 Rising Stars of Wall Street
events.summary: Ray Dak Lam for BI A lot of what's happening on Wall Street right now is unprecedented. Record-breaking sums are being raised to fuel the artificial intelligence boom, geopolitical uncertainty and technological disruption are shaking up markets , and more blockbuster IPOs that could shatter records are on the horizon. For the industry's up-and-coming talent, it's been a moment of enormous opportunity. As one of this year's rising stars, Morgan Stanley managing director Maya Venkatraman, put it: "The most interesting work happens when there isn't a ready-made template." Business Insider's Rising Stars of Wall Street is celebrating its 10th class of young professionals making a substantial impact in investing, trading, and dealmaking. The process begins with nominations from bosses, colleagues, recruiters, and other industry insiders. To be considered, nominees must be US-based, 35 or younger, and stand out among their peers. Business Insider's editors make the final selections. Several of our stars are investing billions in the companies building AI and inventing new ways to finance the infrastructure that will support it. Others are pioneering new trading strategies, building businesses from the ground up, and advising on consequential deals. Maya Venkatraman Courtesy of Maya Venkatraman; Ray Dak Lam for BI Maya Venkatraman is helping create the blueprint for Wall Street's data-center debt boom. Venkatraman, a managing director, played a leading role in structuring a novel $3.2 billion bond for data center developer TeraWulf, with credit support from Google. "There wasn't really a playbook that existed," said Venkatraman, Morgan Stanley's US head of transportation and infrastructure leveraged finance. Traditional project financing couldn't meet the industry's enormous capital needs alone, so her team developed the structure last fall, which has since served as a template for a market she said has generated roughly $45 billion in high-yield bond issuance over the past year. Venkatraman also had to educate investors and ratings agencies about the emerging asset class, swapping traditional roadshows for visits to data-center project sites, steel-toed boots and all. The deal was "really defining" for Mumbai-born Venkatraman, who joined Morgan Stanley in 2013 and was promoted to MD in January 2026. She's led the structuring and execution of more than 110 transactions throughout her career. It also wasn't the first time dealing with unconventional financing solutions. Newly promoted to vice president when COVID-19 brought travel to a halt, she worked with her team around the clock to help airlines and cruise operators secure liquidity, including raising billions for Royal Caribbean. "People were asking, are we ever gonna get on an airplane again? Are we ever gonna take a cruise again?" she recalled. The crisis accelerated her career, giving her "multiple times the reps" of others at her level. Venkatraman discovered finance and her analytical side at the University of Virginia. She credits her love of literature and history with helping her translate complex financial concepts into compelling stories for investors. Outside work, the longtime distance runner finds that her best problem-solving happens on runs, sometimes accompanied by her 4-year-old daughter in a stroller. She's expecting her second child in the coming weeks. Theo Saarinen Courtesy of Theo Saarinen; Ray Dak Lam for BI Theo Saarinen's career path is more akin to that of a high-flying tech founder than a hedge fund researcher. The 27-year-old is the chief research officer for Bridgewater's AIA Labs, the internal AI research unit run by the $102 billion Connecticut-based hedge fund giant. The unit's AI-powered fund is up nearly 16% through September this year, outpacing the S&P 500 and the average hedge fund over the same period. While Saarinen is checking his fund's performance "returns all the time — it's a very important piece of feedback," he approaches his role with an almost academic mindset, befitting his background. He joined the AIA group in 2023 while pursuing a doctorate in statistics from the University of California, Berkeley. He became one of the group's first hires, thanks in part to a relationship with his academic mentors Bin Yu and Jasjeet Sekhon, the latter of whom co-founded AIA Labs at Bridgewater with the firm's co-CIO Greg Jensen. Now, Saarinen is focused on connecting "the frontier of AI" with markets. He spends a lot of his time deconstructing the decision-making of the strategy — "peeling back the machines' thoughts to understand why they're doing what they're doing," he said. And, on top of his role, he's kept a foot in academia — he's writing his dissertation and plans to complete his doctorate soon, while keeping tabs on new developments across the AI space. He's also a player in the hedge-fund talent war, saying they're always looking for talented people at rivals, but also at Big Tech companies and high-flying startups. He believes the firm is doing just as interesting work as the frontier labs, with a much more concrete goal — generating returns. "Markets are an extremely hard problem — the ultimate challenge," he said. Diana Liu Courtesy of Diana Liu; Ray Dak Lam for BI People might think Diana Liu had some foresight when she started working on financing data center deals 12 years ago. But really, she was just starting out in structured finance at Deutsche Bank and found that because data centers didn't fit neatly into traditional real estate or infrastructure portfolios, they created an opportunity to earn "excess returns" relative to the risk. More than a decade later, Liu said the sector still offers outsized returns — not because there aren't investors, but because hyperscalers can't stop growing. In her role as a Principal at Blue Owl, she helped develop the novel JV structure behind the financing for Meta's $50 billion Hyperion data center in Louisiana, dubbed Project Beignet. Conversations about the deal began when Liu was still at IPI Partners, the data center specialists that Blue Owl acquired in 2025, and she had been at since 2021. The deal, financed 80% by Blue Owl and 20% by Meta, raised more than $27 billion and pioneered the use of 144A bonds in data-center financing at an unprecedented scale. The approach gave them access to a wider pool of institutional investors without requiring them to register the securities. While some may have criticized the deal for taking some of Meta's AI computing costs off its balance sheet, she said it is "the most public deal ever done in data centers" because of the novel use of public bonds. "It's always been a progression of trying to become a mainstream asset class and be recognized and be able to access traditional forms of markets," Liu said. events.title: French school protests resume on small scale as students return from break
events.summary: Education ministry says 41 schools blockaded as students return after holiday break. High school students in France have resumed protests on a much smaller scale than in previous weeks as pupils returned from their two-week holiday break. The Ministry of Education said 41 high schools were blockaded on Monday, about one percent of the country’s 3,700, according to the French public broadcaster Franceinfo. list 1 of 3 No, France is not ‘burning’ list 2 of 3 Photos: Youth-led rallies sweep Germany list 3 of 3 France opens ‘attempted murder’ probe into petrol bomb attacks on police Students attempted to blockade schools in Paris, Marseille and Rennes, the Reuters news agency reported. Hundreds of schools were blockaded in the weeks before the break. “In terms of blockades, or attempted blockades, the phenomenon is very marginal. We’re talking about a handful of units, a few individual schools,” Education Minister Edouard Geffray told France Inter radio. He said protests were allowed, but preventing access to schools was illegal. “The school year is now at risk for several hundred thousand pupils and we can’t allow that,” Geffray said, according to the state public news service Franceinfo. The protests began in the Paris suburbs in September and spread across France. Last month, the focus of the anger broadened beyond education to the cost of living, drawing in trade unionists and activists. In a test for President Emmanuel Macron’s minority government, some protests turned into violent clashes with police and riots in several cities, with shops looted. Students are demanding the renovation of ageing schools, more teachers, more university places and an end to a university admissions system they see as socially unfair. Last week, the government announced a gradual replacement of the Parcoursup admissions platform by 2028, cancelled planned education job cuts, promised 500 additional posts and a cap of 28 pupils per class in the first year of high school, Franceinfo reported. It also pledged 4 billion euros ($4.47bn) to renovate schools and 15,000 new places in higher education. Student representatives said the offers were not enough and vowed to continue protesting. “Of course we’re calling for a blockade,” Pierre Sourzat, president of the student organisation Les Lyceens!, said on Sunday, according to France 24. The Union Syndicale Lyceenne and Student Union have called for further blockades on Tuesday and Thursday, while the UNEF student union said Tuesday should be a “black day” for universities, with blockades across the country.

events.title: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
events.summary: Chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg say fridge temperatures rose overnight, similar to hack of French stores Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have said the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers in dozens of stores rose overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of food losses in France. Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet on Monday that six of ​its stores ‌had been ​affected, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”. The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​cybersecurity ‌incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said an “IT incident” ​had hit fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg. A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the supermarket chain had established that temperatures in the cooling systems had increased, adding that the incident was being investigated. Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets were affected, including five Spar outlets, multiple Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations, and a number of smaller Proxy Delhaize minimarkets. “We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which specialises in refrigeration system installations, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid.” French ⁠police said in October that hackers had seized control of cooling units at ⁠up to 700 supermarkets in a large-scale attack that led to heavy losses of chilled and frozen foods and underlined the vulnerability of internet-connected systems. Hackers had remotely overridden the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C. The Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains were among those affected. Stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products, with many suffering losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). Two stores in Alsace reported a combined loss of €270,000. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss. A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day They disabled alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours. Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates. The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigatiion into the French attack, saying damage included “food losses and fires”, and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, to investigate. ANSSI subsequently confirmed that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted in the attack.

CEO Sam Altman met with Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, crown prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, as the artificial intelligence lab secured arrangements for a number of sectors to use its models, the Abu Dhabi Media Office said on Monday. OpenAI and Anthropic have turned to Middle East investors as they've looked for ever-larger pools of capital to fund growth. MGX, an Abu Dhabi-based investment firm, has backed both labs, including co-leading Anthropic's $30 billion raise in February and OpenAI's $122 billion raise in March. OpenAI is currently seeking to raise $20 billion in a new funding round co-led by investors from the United Arab Emirates, CNBC reported on Saturday. "Abu Dhabi and the UAE are setting a bold, global standard for AI integration across both the public and private sectors to make sure the benefits of AI reach everyone," Altman said in a statement. "We are proud to support the UAE's ambition, anchored in a shared commitment to safety, accessibility and responsible innovation." Sovereign investor Mubadala, Inception42 and OpenAI signed an agreement to apply advanced AI capabilities to investment analysis. The Abu Dhabi Government announced an initiative with the AI lab to translate government policies and regulations in machine-readable form. Inception42 and OpenAI also signed a five-year agreement to enable the adoption of frontier AI across government, enterprise and education.

events.title: Prediction market bettors are the new political pundits. Why are we listening to them? | Judith Levine
events.summary: Prediction market bettors are the new political pundits. Why are we listening to them? Sites like Kalshi and Polymarket offer faux populism as elites reap the benefits – and voters risk being misled Online betting is a bit like Donald Trump. The prediction markets – platforms where users bet on whether events will occur – pretend to be populist, pushing the nabobs aside and representing the “wisdom of the crowd”. “This data is bottom-up, not elites-driven,” a Kalshi ​spokesperson told Reuters . But in fact, the markets are controlled by a few, skillful traders. Their users are led to believe they can strike it rich. But like gamblers everywhere, most of them lose most of the time, while enriching the casino and bankrolling the winner’s takings. The markets pretend honesty and transparency, but they open the door to fraud and insider trading. Like opinion polls, they affect voters’ expectations of the outcomes of elections but make them no smarter about whom to vote for. Fundamentally, the assumptions projected by the prediction markets are Trumpian. The companies suggest that their results are improved by the financial stake customers have in them. “Prediction markets are a way to see what people are saying when there’s money on the line,” said the Kalshi spokesperson. When money talks, in other words, its message is more authentic and valuable than mere political speech. The prediction markets made a better collective call on the 2024 elections than conventional polls and pundits, particularly in the swing states. But why? The authors of a much-cited 2025 study from Vanderbilt University infer that their results – that Polymarket was more accurate than polls – were “in alignment with research on the ‘Wisdom of Crowds’ theory, which suggests a large group of people are often accurate in predicting outcomes, even if they are not necessarily experts or closely aligned with the issue at hand”. But more recent analyses suggest that the betting masses are not so wise after all. A new working paper from scholars at the London Business School and Yale University looked at publicly available trading data from Polymarket. Whereas almost every wagerer’s outcomes were no better than chance, they discovered, the “accuracy comes from a minority of persistently skilled traders, around 3% of accounts”. The crowd “generates most of the volume but little of the information”. The crowd also furnishes most of the cash but reaps little of it. Analyzing 1.6m Polymarket accounts, or “wallets”, traded since November 2022, the Wall Street Journal found: “Casual traders are bleeding cash while a small number of sophisticated pros – including trading firms with access to vast streams of data – eat their lunch.” What skills do these pros employ? They react quickly to public and financial news, say the London and Yale authors. They gather poll data and buy access to big data streams, which can cost $200,000 annually . They analyze the data using “algorithms to predict price movements and manage risk”, says the Journal, “faster than any human”. Operating at scale and speed, with commensurate information and discipline, the pros can make tens of thousands of trades a day. And the more they trade, the more they earn. In the Journal’s analysis, three-quarters of the profits went to 0.1% of the accounts. Of at least 2.3 million accounts on Polymarket’s site, just 2,000 netted a total of almost half a billion dollars. Meanwhile, the median Polymarket user placed 46 trades across 10 active trading days in 2026, according to Pew Research . And because the few have the skills to trade against the mistakes of the many, the losses of the many bankroll the profits of the few. The traders steering the prediction markets are not PhD pollsters and PBS talking heads. But they are elites nonetheless – the same elites who dominate Wall Street and make economic policy, whichever party is in office. If it were a simply a matter of some people’s money squandered or increased, the problems of the traders would remain with the traders. But the press and the public are listening to them more and more. “Prediction market odds shift voters’ expectations substantially,” a study funded by the Brennan Center found. The same features that rig the markets in favor of the few can distort what we think we know about coming elections. Explained CoinMarketCal , a newsletter serving crypto traders: “A market price reflects trades, liquidity, and available capital, not a representative poll. A well-funded trader can move a thin contract without any change in voter sentiment.” And it’s not just expectations that prediction markets influence. They can also change voter behavior. “Elections have the property that what one believes is going to happen can actually affect what happens if a candidate is thought to be losing momentum or the campaign is flagging,” the Barnard College economics professor Rajiv Sethi told NPR .

events.title: This Wharton professor says becoming a plumber won't save you or your kids from AI — but these 4 things could
events.summary: iStock; BI If you're not freaking out about AI and what it means about your job — or your kids' jobs … you should. But that doesn't mean AI will make you unemployable, says Wharton management professor Ethan Mollick. Mollick thinks experienced workers have skills and attributes AI can't replicate, like "taste." But what happens to young people just starting out? You can't make AI go away. How can you live with it? Or more precisely: How can you make a living in an AI world? Here are a couple standard answers: "Learn to use AI." Or figure out an AI-proof career, one that can't be automated away. Maybe something with your hands . Ethan Mollick doesn't think that will work. Mollick is a Wharton management professor who has become one of the more influential guides to what AI can already do — and what it will mean for people who have to work alongside it. His new book, " Co-Existence ," argues that the models are improving much faster than most people understand, and the only way to deal with their rapid acceleration is to learn how to live with them. That means acknowledging that a lot of what you can do today will be less useful in the future, and concentrating on the attributes you already have that AI can't replicate. I talked to Mollick about what AI means for your job, your kids' future, and what happens when the systems that train workers start to break down on my Channels podcast. The following is an edited excerpt of our conversation. Peter Kafka: People worried about their jobs, or their kids' jobs, are being told to become AI experts — or to find lines of work that are AI-proof, like plumbing or nursing. Is that useful? Ethan Mollick: I don't think it's very useful. First of all, that's great until PlumBot 6000 comes along. I'm not a robotics expert, but the robotics experts I know went from, "LLMs will never … this AI boom is completely unrelated … robots are hard" to, "Actually there's a thing here." I don't know what the future holds. I don't think anyone does, which is either comforting or very upsetting to hear from somebody who's an AI expert. Look at the most changed field, which is coding. We already know coding is changing. [But] we aren't even clear whether there are going to be more or less jobs in coding. We know what you do as a coder is going to change and keep changing. Writing error-free code is now less important than conceiving of what you want to have built. A lot of coders are happier than they've ever been before. Some are sadder. These are evolving jobs. In the book, I talk about four things that give you at least some advantage. Deep knowledge : knowing an area really well, because that expertise lets you outcompete the AI. Wide knowledge : knowing about lots of different things. One thing I see in companies is they say, "Our coders are doing design work, our designers are doing coder work, and the marketers are doing business plans." The more you know about a lot of little things, the more AI can help you. Then there's taste . AI produces a lot. What prevents it from being slop? Your taste about which things to pick. And finally, agency . I don't think "learning to use AI" means very much right now. We've been testing all the methods we use to teach people how to use AI. None of those tricks work anymore. Prompting has started to look a lot more like managing. You don't have to do magic words anymore to make the AI do something. Instead, you specify: Here's the product I want, here's how I know it's good, here's how you should test it, here's what you show me partway. Give me five different mockups that I can pick among. That seems like good news for someone mid-career, who has experience, taste, and has gotten good at their job. But if you're starting out, how do you develop that stuff in a world where AI says, "I'll do the research. I'll write it for you." There are two problems. One is people as individuals, and the other is the institutions we have for teaching people. As individuals, we love to cognitively offload stuff. That's what we're built to do. Technology has always been about replacing annoying labor. No one pines for washing dishes by hand once they have a dishwasher. No one wants to churn their own butter. My kids don't learn cursive. I don't know how to use a slide rule. But we're bad at picking which things we want to offload. That's a problem with everyone cheating on homework. And then there are the institutions. There are two sets of learning institutions for learning how to do a job. One is college and high school education. They're screwed up right now, but we'll figure that out. AI is actually a really good tutor, and we know how to test people without AI: You put them in a classroom with a blue book or have a conversation. We'll have better education as a result, with AI tutoring outside of class and active learning inside of class. What I'm worried about is the other method, which is apprenticeship. I send people to a bank, consulting company, audit firm, or car dealership, and they learn the same way everyone always has. They do grunt work, poorly paid. They might get abused a little bit. The trade is that they learn skills and contacts, and they learn how to do stuff because we force them to do it. And middle managers get somebody to do their crap work. Even if you're a bad mentor, people still learn the ropes. If they show they can do a good job, they advance. You get the next generation of good employees. It has worked out wonderfully for a few thousand years. That all broke because the incentives are no longer aligned. As a junior employee, your best bet is to use AI for everything because it's better than you. Junior people are much worse at using AI because they dump everything into Claude and give you Claude's results. How could they tell you whether it's a good report or bad? They haven't built taste. And managers realize: "Why would I go to an intern when the AI will solve the problem for me, at a better rate?" And company leaders say: "Why would I want to slow this train down? Why would I want worse work from interns?" The training mechanism was this virtuous cycle, and it is completely shattered. Either we will have to make more formal education happen — a lot of light, white-collar work will have to look more like welding or plumbing, with a trade-school aspect—or companies are going to have to get serious about mentorship as a real thing they do. It takes time and costs productivity, but you gain the benefit of having junior people. My fear is that companies will say, "We'll just hire senior people." That's the dangerous area. The talent pipeline ends. There are no replacements. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: With homeownership expensive, parents are saving for their young kids' down payments
events.summary: A new survey found that 82% of parents with young kids are thinking about or already saving for their child's down payment. The Good Brigade/Getty Images Many parents with young kids are thinking of or already saving for a down payment. Parents may have recently become homeowners and seen how costly it is. Fourteen percent of parents in a Coldwell Banker survey said they've already begun saving. It's never too early to set your kids up for future life milestones , new survey results suggest. An emerging trend includes parents prepping their kids for homeownership years in advance, said Mary Lee Blaylock, president of Coldwell Banker Affiliates. Coldwell Banker's September survey found 82% of parents with kids 5 and under are already saving or considering saving for their child's down payment. Fourteen percent of surveyed parents have already done so, compared to 20% who have already stashed money away for their child's college. Affordability is the key driver . Blaylock said young parents who have just achieved the American dream of homeownership realize exactly how expensive owning a home can be. Most Gen Z and millennial parents surveyed said they've either considered or already have begun saving. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate has risen over the past few months, and remains above 7% for the week ending October 29. The Atlanta Fed tracks how much qualified income is needed in order for homeownership to make up no more than 30% of annual income, a standard affordability measure. As of August, that number is $126,849. Median household income is 32% lower. "Historically, if you made the median income or you made below the median income, you could still be a homebuyer," said Domonic Purviance of the Atlanta Fed's Supervision and Regulation Division. "Well, that's less likely today." We're looking to hear from people about their time on the housing market. Have you given up looking for a home, can't sell your home, got multiple offers, or moved back in with parents? Reach out to this reporter to share your housing story at mhoff@businessinsider.com If you have the money, now can be a good time to look for a home , as there are more sellers than buyers and some deals available. Redfin data shows about 20% of active listings in September had a price drop, up 0.4 percentage points from a year prior, and that there were 929,000 buyers compared to 1.5 million sellers. The number of buyers has been trending downward, so sellers might not have a lot of offers. "Builders are offering $10,000 or $20,000 in concessions, buying down mortgage rates and throwing in appliances," said Amanda Peterson, a Redfin Premier agent, in a news article. "I had clients walk away from a home they loved because the pantry was too small and they didn't like the laundry room — even after the sellers offered to alter the floor plan. There are so many homes for sale that buyers are holding out for one that checks every box." Older family members could also set their adult kids or young grandkids up to achieve the American dream of homeownership , Blaylock said. The Coldwell Banker survey showed 15% of homeowners received money for their home down payment from family or friends. Seventy-one percent of those who received family money said they expect to pay it back. While people can get help from others, Blaylock said people still need to save for a down payment and "can't just rely on pennies from heaven." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ford launches a ‘privacy promise’ and explains how and why it uses customer data
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. As Ford prepares to launch a new generation of connected cars, the automaker is making a public promise about how it will handle that information. The company unveiled on Monday what it calls a “privacy promise” — an “explicit commitment” to keep customers’ vehicle data safe and give them control over what they share. Ford also launched a website designed to educate customers about how, where, and why the automakers uses their data, and to show them how to change those settings. While those controls have existed for years now, Ford wants to communicate more clearly with its customers about them, especially ahead of the launch of new, more connected vehicles like the ones being built on its upcoming “universal electric vehicle” platform. “I personally think that it’s super important for us to be making it very clear to our customers what our data practices are, and not only that, but making a commitment to them about it,” Ford’s chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I also see this as a great opportunity to educate our customers about how they share data.” This new privacy push comes as automakers are making their cars increasingly connected. While some polling shows U.S. customers want the kinds of features enabled by this connectivity , such as remote start, navigation, and driver-assistance software, only 14% said they fully understand what data their vehicle collects. That has left room for some companies to quietly sell that data to third parties — a practice that got General Motors in trouble with the Federal Trade Commission, and also resulted in a $220 million settlement with 36 states last week . This lack of consumer awareness around data collection and sharing has also opened the door for other companies to market themselves as better stewards of customer data. Slate Auto, the EV startup backed by Jeff Bezos, has made that pitch ahead of the expected launch of its minimalist pickup truck later this year. “We did a survey of 1,000 consumers, and 91% of them said that data privacy was a key consideration for them. Realistically, it’s not something they engage with every day, but they want to know that they’re, again, in control, and that they have access to the information they need there,” Jones said. “I wouldn’t comment on what our competitors are doing, or anything that’s sort of been in the news there, but certainly it’s something that people don’t trust companies to take care with their data, and we really want to make sure we’re building that trust relationship with them.” Jones, who joined Ford in 2024 after nearly two decades of working on privacy in the legal, financial, and healthcare fields, said the effort to improve how the automaker communicates with customers about data sharing has been in the works for a while. “It’s been a journey for, frankly, most of the time I’ve been at Ford,” she said. Ford’s new website will feature a mix of content that explains what data the company collects, how it uses that information, and how customers can opt in or out. Opting out of sharing some data will naturally make some modern features inaccessible, Jones said. For example, turning off “connected services” in a Ford vehicle will disable features like real-time navigation and the built-in access to roadside assistance. But one of the goals of this “privacy promise” push is to better justify why Ford is asking for access to this data and make it clear that the information won’t be used for purposes such as targeted advertising. Giving Ford access to data about a vehicle’s health, for instance, will provide an owner with better real-time information about whether their car needs maintenance. But it will also “support research and development for future technologies,” Jones said. “We also do not share information about how our customers are driving their vehicles to data brokers,” Jones said. “I just want to kind of reiterate that we’re not in it to try and monetize data in some way. We’re trying to offer products and services that customers derive value from.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane.

events.title: “Chaos” in the Air: Five Ways Voting Could Be Disrupted on Election Day
events.summary: Election workers in Los Angeles County process ballots for the state’s primary in June. Mario Tama/Getty Images As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out. Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting . The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters , an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants. The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats. Help Us Report on Key Election Issues ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something? Send Us a Tip Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens. The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines. Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system. “The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.” “Paper Trail” Podcast Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “ Paper Trail .” In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.” The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.” Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm. Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said. Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds: People arrive to vote early on Oct. 27 in Coral Gables, Florida. Lynne Sladky/AP Images 1. Will There Be Federal Interference? An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls. Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this. He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage . “Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said. It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places. Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots. “We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.” A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.” It’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers said they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.” Workers prepare ballots to be scanned for counting in Orange County, California, on Oct. 28. Apu Gomes/Getty Images 2. What Effect Will Noncitizen Voter Challenges Have? The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday. Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud. On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.” This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls , which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data. In a court filing , California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. events.title: The paths to Wall Street success: Where 25 rising stars went to school and started their careers
events.summary: iStock; Tyler Le/BI Business Insider's Rising Stars of Wall Street list of 25 future leaders has landed. We've broken down their college years, first jobs, and paths to Wall Street success. They attended 20 different schools, but 11 graduated from Ivy League universities. While there's no single route to the top of Wall Street, some paths are more well-trodden than others. Of the 25 rockstar professionals on Business Insider's Rising Stars of Wall Street , 11 attended Ivy League universities — more than double the five in last year's class . And nearly half began their careers at four financial powerhouses: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, and Bank of America. Though that's not to say there are not some who took less conventional routes . We analyzed the alma maters of this year's class and their career trajectories to gauge how they broke into finance. Here's a snapshot of the next generation of Wall Street leaders. Meet the class: The 25 rising stars range in age from 27 to 35 , with an average age of 32 . Three are under 30 , including the youngest, Theo Saarinen, 27 , who is the chief research officer of AIA Labs , which sits within hedge fund Bridgewater Associates. Twelve work at investment banks, seven at hedge funds, six in private equity and other private markets, and one at a market maker. New York is still the dominant office location, as 20 of the 25 work in New York City. Two work in Houston, two in San Francisco, and one in the Wall Street of the South, Miami. Where they went to school The class hails from 20 different universities for their undergraduate years. It's a mix of large research universities, top business schools, and elite liberal-arts colleges. Eleven attended Ivy League universities for their undergraduate degrees, up from five in 2025. The University of Pennsylvania was particularly well represented, with five graduates . Economics, finance, and business were popular choices, but others pursued degrees in engineering, mathematics, and the humanities. ExodusPoint portfolio manager Ben Atlas studied philosophy at the University of Cambridge, while Bank of America's Cody Kiechle majored in applied mathematics at Harvard. Two pursued graduate degrees. Goldman Sachs managing director Bridget Chaudhry earned an MBA from Harvard Business School, while Balyasny portfolio manager Sahil Singhal earned a master's degree in applied mathematics. List of schools Amherst College Boston College University of California, Berkeley Columbia University Cornell University Dartmouth College Duke University Franklin & Marshall College Harvard University Middlebury College Princeton University University of Cambridge University of Chicago University of Dayton University of Florida University of Pennsylvania University of Virginia University of Warwick Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University Wesleyan University How they got their start Wall Street's biggest banks remain a popular launching pad. Twelve members of this year's stars began their careers at Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, or Bank of America. Goldman and JPMorgan each account for four, while Morgan Stanley and Bank of America each account for two. Seven made the popular leap from banking to investing. Apollo principal Daniel Borkenstein started at PJT Partners before moving into private equity, while TPG's David Bessel got his start at Morgan Stanley. At least nine have spent their entire careers at one firm. Blackstone's Jake Epstein joined the alternative asset manager straight out of college. Morgan Stanley's Maya Venkatraman and Goldman Sachs' Bridget Chaudhry have climbed the ranks at the firms where they started.
