Jim Tilson played defensive end at Middlebury College, while Alex Winrich played soccer at the University of Dayton. events.title: I'm a sports medicine doctor who works with NFL players. I wish more people would stop following 'no pain, no gain.'
events.summary: Aaron Mates works with teams in the NFL and MLB. Courtesy of Aaron Mates Dr. Aaron Mates is a team doctor for the Denver Broncos. He says that stretching is instrumental to maintaining mobility, and high-impact exercises have limited benefit. You should leave workouts feeling good, not pushed to the brink, he says. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Dr. Aaron Mates . It has been edited for length and clarity . You know the adage, no pain, no gain? Well, it's time we all drove that from our minds. I'm an orthopedic surgeon and sports medicine doctor . I currently work with the Denver Broncos and the Toronto Blue Jays. I also have an active community practice, so I see professional athletes and community members each week. Professional athletes have an emphasis on healing and maintaining their bodies, which I wish more community members would understand. Whether you're chasing longevity in your NFL career or your day-to-day life, here's how to approach it. Ditch no pain, no gain When you leave a workout, you should feel good. You shouldn't be in any pain. That's a change of perspective for many people, and it's an important one. You don't want to push yourself so hard that you break down. Modify exercises, and skip high-impact There's no shame in modifying exercises . In fact, it's often a smart choice. High-impact, repetitive exercises increase your risk for injury. Maybe instead of doing 20 burpees, you do a sprint on the rower, getting a lot of the same benefits with less risk. Even my pro athletes modify all the time. If someone is recovering from a rotator cuff injury, we remove the bench press from their workouts, opting for pulling rather than pushing. Often, those modifications become permanent. If you have a history of herniated disks, for example, it's unlikely I'll ever recommend you do deadlifts again. Stretch throughout the day Stretching is one of the most important yet overlooked parts of being able to move well in the long term. As we age, we become deconditioned in the areas where our ligaments attach to the bone. This increases the risk of enthesopathy, or injuries to these areas — such as Achilles tendonitis or plantar fasciitis . It's especially important to stretch your hamstrings and calves throughout the day. People who sit (most of us, these days) become very tight through their posterior chain. This tilts the pelvis forward and puts strain on the back. Just a few minutes of stretching while you're waiting in line, pumping gas, or sipping your coffee can make a difference. Skip the pills and potions There's a ton of marketing around health supplements, and it confuses people. The truth is simple: the healthiest diet is one full of whole, clean foods. If it's bagged or boxed, you shouldn't be eating it. That's not always easy — I know that as a busy surgeon — but it's something to aspire to. For the most part, you can skip the potions that promise better gut health, faster recovery, and anything else. The best way for your body to get what it needs is from clean, whole foods. Scrutinize new treatments There's a lot of junk science in longevity medicine. Patients are often sold big promises, with more hype than hope. The future is bright for treatments like stem cells. And yet, for now, the science just isn't there to know about the best use cases. We need to continue to scientifically interrogate these technologies to know when they're appropriate to use. Unfortunately, many practitioners can provide treatment without understanding the full scope of the science. There's typically no quick fix for pain or injury. But getting back to basics — like stretching, eating well, and adapting your workouts — will help you recover and continue moving well into old age. Don't rely too much on trackers Health monitoring technology — like smart rings and bracelets — is a mixed bag, in my opinion. Professional athletes can provide reliable data for tracking performance over time. But for community members, they're largely unnecessary. Sometimes, they cause anxiety or give a false sense of security. You don't need a ring to tell you whether you slept well; your body already has that information. In general, the more we can step away from technology, the better we'll be. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I started going to Disney with my kids 6 years ago. Now that they're teens, the expense is still worth it for one unexpected reason.
events.summary: The author (center) said she and her two daughters return to Disney annually to experience the magic. Courtesy of Alana Dawson. My daughters are 16 and 19, but I still spend thousands to take them to Disney World every year. Instead of trying a new destination, we return to one that we know will give us the escape we need. At a Disney park, we can all forget about the worries of life and focus on fun. That's priceless. Earlier this year, my daughters and I returned from our sixth annual visit to Walt Disney World . Of course, we had a great time. I've spent thousands of dollars on these trips over the years, and I will continue to spend it. Why? For one unexpected reason: me. I can be a kid again when I'm at a Disney Park. While I'm there, I'm able to forget the worries of the world, which are many. For a few days every year, I don't have to think about cooking, cleaning, and the logistics of life . All I have to worry about is navigating an app and whether we'll start our day at Epcot in Mexico or France. The author said she likes that trips to Disney parks are fully planned in advance, so she can focus on having a good time with her family. Courtesy of Alana Dawson. We keep going back In 2021, I was a military spouse solo-parenting my two daughters during the pandemic. My spouse was stationed on an aircraft carrier in the middle of the ocean. And like everyone else in our country — and world — I was tired. Online learning, juggling isolation on my own, and missing my spouse were taking their toll. My daughters and I needed some fun. "What's more fun than the 'Most Magical Place on Earth'?" I thought to myself. So I booked a spring break trip to Walt Disney World. That one trip became a tradition. This year, coming off Tiana's Bayou Adventure soaking wet and hair dripping, both girls turned to me at the same time and said, "That was awesome." My oldest is now 19, and her sister is 16. They still want to come. Disney has become not just a tradition, but a part of our family fabric. Disney Adults have their place I hear and see a lot of people disgruntled about Disney. From politics to price increases , it seems every year you have to spend more for the same experience. I get it. There are so many places to travel, and with the cost of living increasing, it can be hard to justify returning to somewhere you've already been. This is exactly why the rise of the Disney Adult makes complete sense to me. Life has gotten heavier, and not just for adults. Kids and teens are carrying more than ever. Expectations, pressure, the pace of it all. The to-do list is never done. Disney is one of the very few places designed entirely around joy. And when joy starts feeling scarce, people will pay for it. I know I happily do. As a busy mom, the decreased mental load alone is worth it for me. And not having to drive on the trip also helps. All the planning is done upfront, dining reservations included. Add in the ability to connect with my daughters, dress up in cute Disney-themed attire, and make more memories I'll never forget, and the price of the trip becomes completely irrelevant. The author said that over the years, she has learned to embrace being a Disney Adult and all the fun being one entails. Courtesy of Alana Dawson. I cherish these magic moments I know Disney gets eye rolls from some; I used to give them, too. But I've learned that joy doesn't need justification. My girls and I will keep going back as long as they want to go with me, and I'll keep showing up as the mom who believes in and happily participates in the magic. events.title: I didn't realize how much I missed my childhood. Then I saw my parents with my daughters.
events.summary: The author, shown with her dad in the 90s (left), said seeing him with her daughter (right) helps her connect with her past. Courtesy of Alex Vance. Watching my parents with my kids has given me glimpses into parts of my childhood I can't remember. Their small gestures of affection have made me realize how deeply I was loved. Now I find myself showing my daughters love in many of the same ways. I hadn't heard my mom sing in years. The memories were there, of course, her singing along with the car radio or lulling us to sleep with a song from the latest Disney movie . But the actual sound of her voice had faded with time, slipping away somewhere between teenage angst and newfound adulthood. So when I heard it again as an adult — gentle, melodic, familiar — it was an unexpected jolt of nostalgia . I watched as she cradled my months-old firstborn, gently nuzzling nose to nose, softly singing the chorus to "You Are My Sunshine." My daughter looked up, her giant blue eyes fixed on my mother's face. Did she sing that to me as a baby? I couldn't remember. But in that moment, it struck me that what I was witnessing wasn't just a grandmother with her granddaughter, it was my mom with me. As I watch my parents with my kids, I get glimpses of my own childhood Like most people, I remember bits and pieces of my childhood. The bigger moments are the easiest to recall: the summer road trips to my aunt's lake house, the giant plate of nachos my mom made on Friday nights, or the summer evenings we rode our bikes until the streetlights came on. It's those little everyday moments in between that remain elusive. But now, watching my parents with my girls, I can almost feel them. The author said seeing her mother (shown) and father with her three children helps her see glimpses of her own childhood that she hasn't thought about in years. Courtesy of Alex Vance. In a way, I'm transported back to my earliest days, catching brief glimpses of a time I was too young to remember. My toddler begs my dad for tickles, and my mom can't hold the girls without a playful flurry of kisses. I watch her patiently coach my oldest through making a peanut butter and jelly sandwich , or softly stroke the back of my 2-year-old's hair as she sits in her lap. My dad uses a playful "baby" voice that I'm sure he once used with me, and they both created Louvre-level displays of the girls' artwork in their offices. Their smallest gestures make me realize how loved I was Of course, things like putting on the girls' shoes or wiping crumbs from their mouths aren't exactly life-altering gestures. But the forehead kisses from my mom after zipping their jackets or the random, silly nicknames my dad gives them add a deeper layer, the tiniest insight into the tokens of affection I was too young to notice. At times, my parents even call the girls by my name without realizing it, catching themselves mid-sentence. It's subtle proof that those little gestures were once reserved for me. I never expected it all to be so bittersweet. I've become homesick for a part of the past I hadn't realized I missed. I understand now that childhood isn't shaped only by what I can replay in my mind, there's also the vague yet reassuring awareness that my parents loved me in a way I can still feel to this day, even if I can't remember it. I'm sure they never realized those small moments were shaping my childhood at the time. My mom is the first to admit that, at age 22, she wasn't exactly an expert on raising kids. (Take the time, for example, that she said she was informed that, yes, she actually needed to wash my hair as a newborn.) Yet, long before parenting advice filled our social media feeds, they didn't just figure it out, they unknowingly created the kind of childhood that would stay with me long after the memories faded. Now I'm creating those same memories for my daughters In turn, my parents set the blueprint for how I raise my own girls. I doubt they will remember the quick pecks on the head as I walk by, or the way I tuck their hair behind their ears while we watch TV. They'll likely forget that I sing "You Are My Sunshine" the way my mom did. But I know these seemingly insignificant gestures will somehow resonate with them the way they did with me — they just might not realize it until they have kids of their own. The author said she has enjoyed remembering parts of her own childhood by watching her parents with their grandchildren. Courtesy of Alex Vance. It turns out that the clearest window into my childhood isn't memory alone. It's the privilege of watching it play out with my own kids, where past and present blend together. The kisses, songs, tickles, and silly voices stick with us somehow, even when the memories themselves don't. To my girls, they're Maw and Pops. To me, they're Mom and Dad. And seeing them together is all the proof I need that I don't have to remember every moment of my childhood to know how deeply I was loved. Sometimes it just takes growing up, and a little perspective, to finally see it. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Pharma's next cash cows could be specialized treatments
events.summary: Pharmaceutical companies facing a steep patent cliff are concluding the key to future profits may be customized treatments tailored to patients' genes and lifestyles — not blockbusters aimed at large patient populations. Why it matters: The pivot could influence which diseases get treated in the decades to come, and how much the health system pays. The stakes are huge. More than $500 billion in brand-name drug sales is potentially at risk from generic competition between 2026 and 2032, according to the consulting firm Evaluate. The latest: The race is on to find new treatments that each generate at least $2.4 billion in global sales, a new Iqvia Institute report finds. They're increasingly specialty treatments, biologics and rare disease drugs — with a small group of flagship products accounting for an outsized share of industry sales. GLP-1 drugs like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Zepbound now define that elite category. The next wave could include "biological missiles" that combine antibodies with chemotherapy to target specific cancer cells. "As precision medicine continues to advance, similar approaches may extend beyond oncology into areas such as immunology, metabolic disease and neurology," the report states. Reality check: It's not clear whether all of the innovation will cure more people, or just make health care more expensive. Novel RNA drugs and cell and gene therapies are expensive, hard to make and target small groups of patients. Challenges identifying eligible patients and getting insurers to pay for treatments have already revealed a disconnect between promising R&D and patient benefit. Widespread concern over high drug prices will force manufacturers to find more unmet needs and build sales more quickly after a drug's launch, according to the report. Context: Top-selling drugs historically were aimed at large patient populations with chronic conditions like high cholesterol. The ulcer drug Tagamet became the first to exceed $1 billion in sales in 1986. Over time, cancer and immunology drugs became major drivers of growth, followed by GLP-1s, which are sparking huge demand for conditions beyond obesity and diabetes but also driving up health costs. Iqvia found that blockbusters on average maintain a dominant market position for 12.1 years before losing market exclusivity, or nearly 80% of their commercial life. Specialty drugs for rare or complex diseases lasted even longer. Yes, but: A substantial number of top-sellers will lose patent protection and face potential competition from generics between 2028 and 2036. Bristol Myers Squibb's blood thinner Eliquis and Merck's cancer blockbuster Keytruda, which are both due to lose market exclusivity in 2028, accounted for a combined $65 billion in global sales in 2024. Follow the money: The search for new blockbusters is playing out in a highly charged environment. Drugmakers and biotechs not only have to figure out how to grow outside of crowded categories but also how much payers value new classes of drugs, Evaluate says . There's also uncertainty over China , where Western drug giants have invested tens of billions of dollars to bolster their product pipelines. Evaluate predicts that only autoimmune disease drugs will come close to rivaling GLP-1s, because of their potential to treat dozens of conditions. One example is AbbVie's injectable Skyrizi for plaque psoriasis, arthritis, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, which could find more uses and generate more than $33 billion in sales in 2032. Iqvia identifies RNA therapeutics as a potentially important middle ground between traditional "small molecule" drugs for chronic diseases and highly specialized genetic treatments. These drugs can target disease-causing mutations across many genes and conditions, with applications for central nervous system, cardiovascular and kidney disease, as well as rare conditions. The bottom line: The success at innovating while also making sure patients have access to the new treatments "will ultimately determine whether the growth in blockbuster medicines observed over the past 25 years can continue at its extraordinary pace," Iqvia concludes.

events.title: Sudan files complaints against Ethiopia with UN over deadly drone spree
events.summary: One-way drone attacks have killed or wounded 484 civilians since February, Khartoum says. Sudan has lodged a complaint against Ethiopia with both the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council after a series of deadly drone attacks this year. In a statement late on Sunday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group of using Ethiopian territory to launch “brazen aggression” against “civilian sites and power stations” in Sudan, resulting in hundreds of casualties and disruptions to essential services. list 1 of 4 RSF senior commander defects, accusing Sudan group’s leadership of nepotism list 2 of 4 Drone attacks across Sudan escalate, 160 people reported killed list 3 of 4 Tigray resumes daily life amid fears of wider war list 4 of 4 Tigray rebels urged to disarm as commander vows to fight Ethiopia’s gov’t The string of incidents “places Ethiopia before international law”, the ministry added. Sudan’s military has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of aiding the RSF, which it has been fighting in a civil war since April 2023. Ethiopia, meanwhile, has accused the Sudanese military of backing rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front , a charge Khartoum denied. The ministry’s statement came alongside a report from Sudan’s army-led Transitional Sovereignty Council that alleged 70 assaults from February 15 to October 27 involving 187 one-way attack drones. The attacks killed or wounded 484 civilians and killed 176 Sudanese soldiers, the report said, with another 200 soldiers wounded. “Since February 2026, armed drones have taken off from Ethiopian soil … to strike Sudanese cities and civilians,” the report said. The report identified launch sites at Asosa Airport in western Ethiopia, the Kurmuk-Gizen border area and Bahir Dar airbase in northwestern Ethiopia’s Amhara region. Last month saw 28 attacks carried out by 97 drones, the report said. It cited an October 9 attack on displaced families in Wad el-Mahi, located in Sudan’s Blue Nile region near the Ethiopian border, which it said killed 30 civilians – 26 women and four children – and wounded 100. A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Saturday that he was “appalled” by the impact of drone strikes in Sudan, days after another strike on a market in RSF-controlled territory in Darfur killed more than 100 people . The secretary-general “strongly condemns the escalating drone attacks in Sudan by the parties to the conflict and the catastrophic toll these attacks are inflicting on civilians”, the spokesman said, adding that the strikes constitute violations of international humanitarian law.

events.title: Jailed PKK founder Ocalan moved to new section of Turkish island prison
events.summary: Improving prison conditions for Abdullah Ocalan has been a key Kurdish demand in push to end PKK-Turkiye conflict. Turkiye has moved the jailed founder of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), Abdullah Ocalan, to a newly-built section of the island prison where he has been held for 27 years, pro-Kurdish legislators said as they urged Ankara to speed up the stalled peace process. Mithat Sancar, a member of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM) delegation that regularly visits Ocalan, confirmed the transfer on Saturday in an interview with the Kurdish television channel Medya Haber TV. list 1 of 3 Turkiye approves pardon-like bill for thousands of PKK fighters list 2 of 3 Turkiye passes law giving thousands of PKK members chance at amnesty list 3 of 3 As SDF disband in Syria, Kurds ponder how to secure their rights He said the move “necessitates an acceleration of the (peace) process”, which he said had been paused for two months. “The process cannot proceed with unilateral expectations and demands,” he said. Fellow DEM politician Pervin Buldan said on Sunday that Ocalan himself had announced the transfer, but played down its significance. “This new facility is part of the prison; it is not somewhere outside the prison,” she said, according to the AFP news agency. “The question of status cannot be defined solely by Mr Ocalan having moved to this location.” Erbil-based broadcaster Kurdistan24 described the facility as a new house built for Ocalan on Imrali island. It said the move was seen as part of preparations to give him a more active role in the peace process. Better prison conditions for Ocalan have been a key Kurdish demand. The PKK was founded in 1978 by Ocalan and others, initially fighting for an independent Kurdish state, before shifting its demands to autonomy and greater rights for Turkiye’s Kurds, who make up an estimated 15 to 20 percent of the population. The group launched an armed campaign against the Turkish state in 1984 and is designated a “terrorist” organisation by Turkiye, the United States and the European Union. The conflict has killed more than 40,000 people . Ocalan has been held on Imrali, in the Sea of Marmara, since his capture in 1999. In February last year, Ocalan called on the PKK to disband and disarm and the group announced its dissolution that May. Turkiye’s parliament adopted a law offering limited amnesty for PKK fighters in August and the PKK leadership has repeatedly demanded Ocalan’s release as part of the process.

events.title: JP Morgan boosts UAE presence with wealth management branch at DIFC
events.summary: JP Morgan Chase has expanded its private banking offerings in the Middle East with the opening of a dedicated wealth management branch at Dubai International Financial centre . Regulated by the Dubai Financial Services Authority, the DIFC branch will enable JP Morgan Private Bank to better serve clients across the UAE and the wider region, it said in a statement on Monday. In the 12 months leading up to the final DFSA approval, JP Morgan more than tripled the size of its Dubai-based private banking team to build capabilities before launch, it said, without specifying the number of bankers added. The team in Dubai is led by Selim Elgen, UAE market head and senior executive officer, and Karim Rekik, regional head, Middle East at JP Morgan Private Bank, the lender said. “JP Morgan Private Bank’s expansion into DIFC reinforces Dubai’s position as a global hub for private wealth,” said Arif Amiri, chief executive of the DIFC Authority. JP Morgan is the latest among major global financial institutions that have expanded in the UAE this year despite Iran war-driven uncertainty and economic headwinds. HSBC, Barclays as well as several Swiss wealth managers have also boosted their operations in the country to leverage the rapid growth of domestic wealth as well as the migration of global capital into the UAE. In October, Dubai and Abu Dhabi were ranked among the top 10 destinations for next-generation wealth despite the fallout from geopolitical tension. Dubai was ranked eighth and the UAE capital was 10th among favoured cities for the $84 trillion of wealth expected to be transferred between generations over the next two decades, consultancy Savills said in a report. Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility, according to Boston Consulting Group data. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at an annual growth rate of 10.6 per cent, the consultancy said in a report last month. Long-term relations JP Morgan Private Bank said its dedicated money management branch is the latest chapter in the bank’s five-decade relationship with the UAE. Over the past 20 years, the company has also used DIFC as its regional base for corporate and investment banking and, more recently, broadened its activities with authorisation to provide asset management services through JP Morgan International Advisers. "The UAE and the broader Middle East represent a significant and growing opportunity for us as a business and for our clients,” said Mr Rekik.

events.title: "Arrogance": 3 GOP Senate candidates blasted over costly red-state rescues
events.summary: Republicans are burning tens of millions of last-minute ad dollars to try to rescue three red-state senators who they say ignored months of warnings that their campaigns were in danger. Why it matters: Senate races in Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi are normally GOP layups. This year, Republicans have diverted resources from swing-state battles to defend them. The frustration with Sens. Roger Marshall (Kansas), Darline Graham (South Carolina) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (Mississippi) comes amid broader GOP finger-pointing as polls show a nationwide backlash against President Trump . "Democrats may win these seats in a wave ... but not a blue wave. It's the wave of arrogance [and] laziness ... that washed over these GOP incumbents and made them think they were invincible," said a national GOP operative involved in several key Senate races. By the numbers: National Republicans have spent $33 million in Kansas, $21 million in South Carolina and $2.4 million in Mississippi, according to data compiled by campaign finance expert Rob Pyers. Trump also has spent valuable campaign time in all three states. Behind the scenes: Republicans say the three senators ignored warnings to raise more money and build stronger campaign operations. National Republican Senatorial Committee chair Tim Scott warned all GOP senators in February 2025: "We do not need to spend time and money in places where races should not be competitive." Trump's political operation also warned Senate Republicans that they would need to pull their own weight. The most complaints center on Marshall, who has raised just $7.5 million compared with $19 million for his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton. Republicans blame his strained relationship with the banking and credit card industries — major GOP donors — and a lack of outreach to K Street. Republicans describe Marshall's campaign as overconfident. About a month ago, his team told aides to other GOP senators that the race would be effectively over within 10 days once it released opposition research on Hamilton. It wasn't. Strategists blame chief of staff Brent Robertson for Marshall's weak campaign operation. The campaign only recently tapped veteran Trump operative Chris Grant as part of a last-minute rescue effort. Alex DeGrasse, another veteran strategist recently hired to help Marshall, pointed to millions in spending by national Democrats and said the senator has made "hundreds of stops across all 105 counties in Kansas" and continues to "work hard for the people of Kansas." In Mississippi, Republicans have long viewed Hyde-Smith as a political underperformer. In 2020, she ran six points behind Trump. She has raised just $6.5 million despite warnings that Democratic megadonors, including George and Alex Soros, were preparing to spend heavily against her. Democratic groups have poured $13.7 million into the race. Republicans also fault Hyde-Smith for holding too few campaign events and underestimating her Democratic opponent, district attorney Scott Colom. Hyde-Smith's campaign did not respond to a request for comment. In South Carolina, Republicans fault Graham for failing to tap her late brother Lindsey Graham's donor network and showing little interest in soliciting contributions. In the first two weeks of October, Democrat Annie Andrews outraised Graham $4.2 million to $570,000. Graham spokesperson T.W. Arrighi said the senator "has faced unprecedented headwinds since losing her brother three months ago, and has risen to the occasion." Some Republicans are sympathetic to Graham, a political novice thrust into the Senate after her brother's death who faced a grueling primary and little time to campaign. They blame Trump for pushing her to run. Yes, but: Republicans point to Idaho Sen. Jim Risch, whose campaign required no spending from national GOP groups, as an example of an incumbent who took the political environment seriously. What they're saying: Representatives for the NRSC and the pro-GOP Senate Leadership Fund super PAC didn't respond to requests for comment. What's next: Top Republicans say the party needs to rethink how it deals with complacent incumbents in 2028 — and make clear that its campaign organizations can't be treated like a charity.

events.title: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it
events.summary: Exclusive: Gap between NHS claim and trusts’ comments described as ‘very misleading’ by senior health official More than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited from Palantir’s medical data platform are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology, the Guardian can reveal. The 29 hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as “realising benefits” from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official. It comes as the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, which aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements. Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”. The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”. NHS England has previously faced scrutiny over how it has used data to defend the Palantir contract, which began in 2024. It claims 117,539 more operations were carried out by trusts using the FDP in a year , but this summer it conceded it could not prove cause and effect, and the Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) watchdog ran an investigation. Asked about the claim of NHS Trusts “realising benefits”, the OSR said it will now be “taking this forward under our casework function”. The contrast between the number of hospitals the NHS claims realise benefits from Palantir’s technology and the statements of the hospitals themselves emerged from more than 100 freedom of information requests. NHS England states on its website that 137 trusts are “live” with the FDP, but of those described as “realising benefits”, 29 responded that they were either not using the system or its apps. Epsom and St Helier said it was “not using FDP at the moment”, Kent and Medway said the trust “has been focused on other priorities … the FDP is not currently live”, Mersey Care said they had “not yet gone live with the FDP”, Nottingham University Hospitals said “no implementation timeline has been agreed”, and University Hospitals of North Midlands said: “FDP is not live. We do not intend to roll it out in the future.” Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology committee, said: “If many NHS trusts don’t see the value of the FDP, serious questions need to be asked about whether the hype surrounding Palantir’s products matches reality.” She called on the government to activate the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s contract and launch an open competition for a UK-owned and based supplier to handle patient records. The Commons health select committee is also calling for ministers to pull Palantir’s deal. The FOIs were obtained by Medact, a medical charity campaigning for Palantir to be ejected from the NHS , and shared with the Guardian. Medact spokesperson Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne said: “Our NHS institutions are meant to work in the interests of public trust and evidence-based healthcare, not use creative accounting to justify a deeply controversial contract. There is no good reason for the government to continue this failing project. We now have to ask, if ministers are using these flawed claims to make their decision, are they being misled?” Asked to respond, NHS England insisted nearly 140 trusts “have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform, helping staff join up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.” It has previously said that its list of hospital trusts reporting benefits includes those using the tools for back office data analysis and submission rather than to support patient care. It is understood trusts that say they do not use the FDP may use a small part of its functionality to help calculate treatment costs. For example, Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust said it is “not currently operationally using the FDP” but NHS England records it as “live” because infrastructure is in place “to support data submission, rather than active operational use of FDP apps.” Palantir has been hitting back against criticism of its deal and last month hired Labour’s former deputy leader and member of the House of Lords Tom Watson as a full-time senior lobbyist. Watson this week has been posting videos on X aiming to debunk “myths” about Palantir, including concerns that public services will become “locked in” to its systems.

events.title: Steven Strogatz is doing OK
events.summary: Steven Strogatz, a professor at Cornell University, said he's beginning to accept AI's impact on mathematics. Christopher Michel/Contour RA by Getty Images Steven Strogatz cried on "The Daily" in October. Now, however, the math professor at Cornell told Business Insider that he's doing OK. Strogatz said he's starting to accept AI's role in mathematics. Steven Strogatz has good days and bad days. Recently, though, the math scholar and professor at Cornell University has been feeling more positive about AI's brusque entrance into the field to which he's devoted his life. "I think I'm pretty far along into the acceptance phase ," he told Business Insider on Wednesday. Strogatz, 67, has become a kind of de facto spokesman for the math community since he shed tears last month on " The Daily ," the popular New York Times podcast, while talking about the fleeting nature of human life. "I may end up doing it with you," he told me about crying in front of a reporter. (He didn't.) In the last two months, Strogatz said hundreds of people have sent him emails, from curious students to ministers asking to pray with him. Among the more notable figures hitting him up were OpenAI engineers responsible for the company's math operations. Before the AI colossus released hundreds more solutions on October 6, for instance, Strogatz received a phone call from bigwigs at the company, who, he thinks, wanted to gauge his reaction before the dump. "I think the subtext was: 'Are you gonna badmouth us tomorrow?'" he said. As it turned out, though, Strogatz, who has a book coming out this month in part about AI, didn't have much badmouthing to do. In an X reply to OpenAI's post that day, Strogatz highlighted one solution he called "particularly amazing." "This leap in progress is like Bob Beamon's long jump," he wrote, referencing the athlete's famous 1968 feat that shattered the previous distance record by nearly two feet. Part of Strogatz's fortitude has to do with his position as an educator, he said, where on most weekdays he orates at a lectern before dozens of wide-eyed undergraduates looking to him for answers in a turbulent time. If he stood before them and, like some have in his field, freaked out — or sullenly declared mathematics over — he'd be doing something of a disservice to his students. It's also not what he believes. "I want to give a message of happy optimism, but not stupid optimism," he said. "Like, let's keep our eyes open and figure out what we need to do to stay strong." So during a recent class at Cornell, after he'd spent over an hour discussing quantum mechanics and the Schrödinger equation — if a cat in a box has a 50% chance of kicking the bucket, at the moment before you open the box, the feline is both alive and dead — a tricky question came up. And instead of clearing some space on the blackboard and picking up the nub of chalk, Strogatz said he broke out his computer. "I said, 'Let's just see what the AI thinks about this,'" he recalled, adding that AI is a useful tool to enhance understanding after students wrestle with the concept in their minds. "In other words, I find all kinds of ways to use AI to improve my class," he said. To be clear, though, all is not fine and dandy in the world of math. Mathematicians everywhere are reckoning with reams of AI-generated solutions to problems that once animated their dreams and chalkboards. Jeering from math geeks quickly turned to astonishment, and then soul-searching, after OpenAI in September published solutions to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize question, a famously thorny mathematical question about whether the equations governing fluid motion can break down. Now, AI programs are at solving levels analogous to or superior to those of grad students, Strogatz said. And without a doubt, the intoxicating satisfaction of finally cracking a problem after suffering over it for years may be getting lost in the flux. Strogatz recalled one remarkable episode from his youth, in which, after spending years mulling over a mathematical explanation for how systems sync up — like fireflies flashing on a summer night — he experienced a bona fide epiphany. In what he described as a "psychedelic dream," the solution came to him in the form of "swirling colored fluids." And when he woke up, he immediately checked the answer. It turned out to be right. "It was the first correct way to formulate this problem," he said. "That was a big happy time." But now, Strogatz says somewhat blithely that with AI doing the solving, future generations likely won't have similar dreams. "Unless you struggle like that and suffer, you won't think of anything deep," he said. "You'll just be superficial, and you'll miss that marvelous human experience." "But I don't want to make too much of it," he added. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: As aid situation worsens, displaced Sudanese worry about warnings of famine
events.summary: Sudan’s displaced people now face a mounting food crisis, with warnings of famine. The sound of gunfire forced 50-year-old Aisha Adam to flee her home in the al-Kalakla neighbourhood of Khartoum days after war erupted in Sudan between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on April 15, 2023. She went to the neighbouring city of Omdurman, but fighting followed her and in May 2023, Adam had to find a new refuge. It brought her to a camp for internally displaced people (IDPs) in Port Sudan, on the country’s Red Sea coast, where she lives with her orphaned grandson and nephew. list 1 of 3 Drone strike in Sudan’s Nyala kills at least 21, injures 40 list 2 of 3 Strikes on Darfur market in Sudan killed more than 100, rights group says list 3 of 3 RSF senior commander defects, accusing Sudan group’s leadership of nepotism “Amid the clashes, I left with my grandson for the bus station, intending to travel to Wad Madani in Gezira state, south of Khartoum. But I found a bus heading to Port Sudan and boarded it, even though all I knew about the city was that it was safe,” she told Al Jazeera. The fighting between the SAF and the RSF has killed as many as 200,000 people, according to aid workers. The war has also displaced 13 million people and led to famine in parts of the country. After Adam was forced to move to Port Sudan, she initially stayed at a shelter for IDPs in the centre of the city. In June, she and others were relocated to a displacement centre on the outskirts of the city. Accommodation was allocated according to household size. Adam was given a tent to share with the two children under her care, and shared a boundary with two other families. “At the first shelter, I received some assistance from organisations, other agencies and even ordinary people. But things are different here. The aid we receive has decreased significantly, so I had to try to find work to avoid starving to death,” she said. Adam’s struggle to feed the two children comes as Sudan faces deepening food shortages. In a joint statement released on October 27, the United States Department of State warned of the deterioration in food availability and the risk of famine in the coming months. “Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security. The risk of famine in the coming months, as warned by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, needs urgent action,” the statement said. Fatima is experiencing the real-life consequences highlighted in the report, as finding food becomes a daily struggle. Humanitarian assistance over the past six months has been limited, and she recalls receiving aid on only three occasions. Once, she received 550,000 Sudanese pounds ($59.13) in cash. Another time, she was given 12kg of flour. At the last distribution, she received personal hygiene supplies for women. “I have no choice but to work. There is no one I can rely on. My two sons are missing, and I do not know where they are, while my other son died before the war began,” she said. Adam leaves her accommodation early in the morning and heads to a nearby market, where she makes and sells zalabia, a traditional Sudanese fried pastry, alongside tea and coffee. Some days she makes a profit; on others, she loses money. “I do not know how to calculate my profit. But as soon as I finish selling the zalabia, I go to buy the ingredients … for the next day: 3kg of flour for 21,000 pounds ($2.25), 2 litres of oil for 22,000 pounds ($2.36) and three bags of charcoal for 9,000 pounds ($0.97),” she told Al Jazeera. Adam says the money left after buying these supplies is often insufficient to provide a meal for herself and the two children in her care. A kilogramme of lentils, one of the cheapest food items available to her, costs 16,000 pounds ($1.72). Meat is no longer on her shopping list, and her diet now consists mainly of lentils and rice. “Fortunately, aid organisations have been providing water for the past five days. Before that, I used to buy 18 litres for 1,500 pounds ($0.16). Sometimes I did not have the money and had to borrow it,” she said. Adam says her priority is to keep her small business running. It helps her put food on the table while helping her cope with the pain of not knowing what happened to her two missing sons. “The important thing is that we eat, even if it is only lentils and water, with nothing else. But my greatest fear is that we will fall ill, because we have no money for treatment,” she said. Her struggle reflects the wider food crisis facing millions in Sudan. On October 22, 2026, the World Food Programme (WFP) announced that funding shortages had forced it to cut monthly food assistance to displaced people, affecting about 900,000 people. Meanwhile, some 19.5 million people across the country face acute hunger, including five million experiencing emergency levels of food shortages.

events.title: America's changing power grid faces a powerful El Niño
events.summary: A powerful El Niño could bring major shifts in electricity supply and demand across the U.S. this winter, posing new challenges for utilities. Why it matters: The U.S. power grid has far more solar, wind and battery storage than during the last major El Niño, and the ongoing event could reveal whether that changing energy mix has made the grid more resilient or left it vulnerable in new ways. Driving the news: A very strong El Niño is strengthening in the tropical Pacific and is expected to continue into spring 2027, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says. NOAA's latest outlook favors wetter-than-normal conditions across California , the Southwest and much of the southern U.S. this winter, while the northern Rockies and parts of the Great Lakes lean drier and much of the northern U.S. leans warmer. The intrigue: El Niño doesn't affect every electricity resource the same way. A March study found that previous super El Niños were associated with reductions in potential solar power output of nearly 5% in parts of California over 12 months — and more than 10% in the state's north during winter. Vincent Tidwell, chief scientist at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, says a wetter California winter could boost hydropower, while reduced precipitation or snowpack in the Pacific Northwest could cut generation there. Erik Smith, a climate scientist at the Electric Power Research Institute, tells Axios the Southeast is another region to watch for reduced solar generation as El Niño favors cloudier conditions. California now has more than 21 gigawatts of battery capacity , giving the grid another tool to manage fluctuations in electricity supply — one it barely possessed during the last very strong El Niño. The Columbia and Snake river basins accounted for roughly 62% of Western U.S. hydropower generation between 2001 and 2020, according to a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory analysis . Tidwell tells Axios that the Western grid is accustomed to shifting electricity between regions when hydropower conditions differ, helping compensate for shortages. Federal water managers, states and utilities use seasonal forecasts to plan for potential hydropower availability at Hoover and Glen Canyon dams on the Colorado River, Tidwell says. Zoom in: Tidwell expects natural gas to play a larger backup role if El Niño reduces Pacific Northwest hydropower and California solar generation this winter. Other resources, including wind, geothermal and nuclear power, provide additional options, though he says El Niño's effects on wind generation remain poorly understood. The big picture: A very strong El Niño could actually ease some pressure on the electricity system, Smith says. Warmer-than-normal conditions across the northern U.S. could reduce winter heating demand, potentially offsetting some of the pressure from changing electricity supplies elsewhere. Yes, but: Even a very strong El Niño doesn't guarantee specific weather impacts. A severe cold outbreak could still stress the grid despite a warmer-than-average winter, while a few major storms could radically alter regional rainfall and snowpack, Smith says. The bottom line: "We have a lot of confidence in how the averages are going to play out, but we don't have a lot of confidence in the day-to-day, week-to-week, particular weather events that could drive those averages," Smith says. events.title: 3 job seekers over 50 share how they navigated ageism, AI, and not giving up hope after rejection
events.summary: Jennifer Mannix ultimately launched her own company. Chona Kasinger for BI Some job seekers in their 50s have had to make career pivots after facing countless rejections. One person we spoke to landed a job via her network, without submitting a single online application. Other 50+ job seekers found new opportunities in consulting, part-time work, or entrepreneurship. Finding a job in this market has become a struggle for many professionals, no matter their age or years of experience. But for job seekers in their 50s , the challenges can be unique. For the Still in the Game series, Business Insider has been speaking with 50-something job-hunters about the unique encounters they've had while pivoting careers and looking for new work. Some have mentioned feeling that ageism, AI, and their seniority have worked against them. Others have found ways to successfully move into new roles or find new paths by using their age and experience to their advantage. The 50-and-older workers who are successfully navigating rejection and moving forward share three things in common: they used their network, sold their experience, and didn't wait to be hired. Here's what they shared. In Still in the Game , Business Insider is chronicling the realities of job hunting in your 50s — from overcoming age bias and navigating career transitions to rebuilding confidence, updating skills, and finding new opportunities in a competitive job market. Read more stories here , and share your own experience here . Use your personal and professional network Nicole Cicero, 54 , is one of the job seekers we spoke with who managed to leave her old job and land a new one. Most impressively, she did this without submitting a single job application online. Cicero told Business Insider she applied to fewer than 10 companies while still in her old sales job, and exclusively used her network and a professional recruiter she's known for decades. "Ultimately, I went with a company where I actually knew somebody from the past," Cicero said. "It felt like a comfortable choice, as though I could go in there and just breathe." Similarly, 56-year-old Michael Shmarak built relationships through his retail job, teaching, and sharing his ideas on Substack. While those connections haven't gotten him to a full-time role, they've led to interviews and new consulting opportunities. Consider your age and experience as an advantage, not a hindrance Shmarak also shared how he shifted his mindset to embrace his age and reframe his experience after being ghosted countless times. "When you're 50, you have to look at all the things that you have that are advantages ahead of younger people," he said. "What can I do to teach them? What can I do to bring that experience to the table? That's more forward-thinking, instead of saying, 'I have 25 years of experience in an industry.'" Cicero said she came into her interviews with that same confidence. She focused on her years of experience and what she brought to the role, instead of worrying about her age. Even when switching industries, as 56-year-old Jennifer Mannix did, leaning on past experience has been an asset. Mannix is transitioning from the world of risk management to women's professional sports. Although she sought entry-level positions, she said that her 30 years of work experience have given her many transferable skills that put her at an advantage. Take control of your career and don't wait to be hired While networking and using age as a sign of experience can be helpful, they don't always lead to a secured full-time role. In Shmarak and Mannix's case, they were still job searching when Business Insider last spoke with them. However, they both found ways to continue working. Shmarak developed a bob-and-weave strategy to keep himself encouraged in his search. "The idea of bobbing and weaving is that, as different challenges come at you, you don't let them stop you," he said. "Like in dodgeball, you're not letting that be the thing that tags you out. You continue to dodge and keep going." While he'd prefer one full-time role, he has several fractional jobs, works in retail part-time, and teaches once a year. Mannix, on the other hand, is building her own business. "This year, I started building a business that curates events surrounding women's sports. I figured, if I can't get hired, why don't I make something for myself?" Are you navigating a career change in your 50s? events.title: ‘No room for debate’ over human control of AI, says Sam Altman
events.summary: People, not artificial intelligence, must stay in control of the future, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said on Monday. “There are a lot of other things we can debate, but on this one, we think there must be no room for debate,” he said in conversation with The National 's Editor-in-Chief Mina Al-Oraibi. Speaking at the opening ceremony of Adipec in Abu Dhabi, Mr Altman said there “should not be a handoff to AI” and that the technology “needs to be a tool built for people and needs to serve people, not the other way around”. “I can’t believe that this differentiates us from other AI companies, but it does,” he said. “This is a value that we intend to really go fight for. And I wish it didn’t need to be said.” The remarks followed OpenAI's agreements with Abu Dhabi, covering energy, education, investment and government. These include a deal with Adnoc and Abu Dhabi technology group G42 to use OpenAI’s most advanced models on the energy industry’s hardest problems. Mr Altman’s message was that AI has crossed a threshold. By his account, it has gone from trailing the world’s best scientists at the start of the year to mostly outperforming them. Its demand for power is growing just as fast, he said. “AI was mostly not as smart as our smartest scientists, and now it’s mostly smarter than them,” Mr Altman said, adding that AI could now do “a lot of parts” of many white-collar jobs. He said he believed society would “navigate through this all fine”. But he warned that the industry must show it can prevent harm as its systems become more capable. “How do we guarantee, and how do we give the world comfort with that guarantee, that we are going to avoid serious safety and alignment incidents?” he said. “I think that’ll be increasingly important for our industry to demonstrate.” Energy challenge In a quick-fire round, Mr Altman was asked what challenge he faces today. He answered with one word: “Energy.” He said the energy needed for each AI query had dropped sharply, but demand kept climbing . Six years ago, OpenAI’s heaviest internal user consumed about 100,000 tokens a month. Today, that figure is roughly the global per-capita average, and the top user consumes about 500 billion, he added. Costs could fall “in almost every way, except, you know, atoms are still atoms”, Mr Altman said. He called power “the very dominant factor” in how much AI the world can use. He said he hoped AI would deliver “a net gain for energy availability in the world”. Mr Altman also said OpenAI had solved one of the Millennium Prize problems, a set of unsolved mathematics problems. He said the work used 10,000 agents running an upcoming GPT model for about four days, collaborating with “no hierarchy”. The claim could not immediately be verified independently. He praised the UAE as “consistently the most forward-looking country in the world for AI adoption”, saying about 80 per cent of young people in the country were using ChatGPT .

events.title: I quit my job after accepting a new one. Then the company rescinded the offer.
events.summary: Alexandra Plainte is looking for a new role after her job offer was rescinded. Courtesy of Alexandra Plainte Alexandra Plainte recently signed an offer for a new job and gave two weeks' notice at her old one. The technical-support leader told family and friends and treated herself to a new iPhone. About a week and a half before she was due to start, the company rescinded the offer. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Alexandra Plainte, a technical-support leader whose job offer was rescinded. Plainte, 36, who lives near Sarasota, Florida, shares how the experience has changed the way she thinks about job security. Business Insider has verified her identity and job offer. The following has been edited for brevity and clarity. The role I was in until recently wasn't going to give me the growth that I wanted. I found a role as a senior manager of technical support. The interview process was thorough : There were four rounds over about two months, with five people, all the way up to the CTO. By the time the offer came, I felt like they really knew me, and I really knew them. It didn't feel like a "maybe" at that point. It felt like I was embarking on the next chapter in my career. I've spent almost 10 years in senior management, building and running teams that help customers when software breaks. Most recently, I've been building AI-backed tools to make support teams faster and less burned out, which is work I love doing. Because I'm the main provider for my family, the job search wasn't something that happened casually. I was going after those senior manager and director roles at software companies. The job that came through felt like the perfect next step. When the recruiter called with the offer , I accepted it on the spot. Not only was it a senior manager role, but it also reported directly to the CTO, which, to me, signaled enormous growth opportunities. I was so excited. I told my husband right away. When the verbal offer came through, I thought, "With the state of the economy and from what I've seen people posting about offers being rescinded, don't do anything until you have it signed." The company sent me the formal offer letter. We both signed it. I filled out my onboarding paperwork, picked my laptop preference, and submitted my background check and I-9. With all of that done — because it felt so concrete — I gave two weeks' notice at my prior job. I told other family members and friends, and we celebrated. I had a five-year-old iPhone at the time that was having battery issues, and to treat myself, I bought a new one. A missed call from the recruiter About a week and a half before my start date, I saw that I had missed a call from the recruiter . I called back right away. She told me that because of organizational changes and budget realignment, they'd eliminated the role and were rescinding the offer. The recruiter was clear that it had nothing to do with me, my interviews, or my background check. By then, I had already given notice at my job . I was devastated. I had already told my family and friends, and now I had to effectively un-tell everyone. My mind immediately went to the what-ifs. Luckily, I have some savings, but I know how hard the job market is. I was scared of potentially being out of work for a long time and watching that cushion slowly disappear. I had treated myself to the iPhone, and it was "Oh wow! Now I regret making that purchase." There's really no going back When I gave notice, my employer posted a requisition to backfill my role . When I later checked, over 700 people had applied. I thought to myself, "Well, there's really no going back." At that point, I had made my decision. I was going to focus on moving forward, whether that's seeing if I can build something of my own or trying to join another software company. If I'm ever again in a position where I receive an offer while I'm still in a role, I would try to negotiate something so that if they rescind the offer, there would be some sort of exit package or some contractual guarantee that the role isn't going to suddenly be eliminated. Since then, what I've done is start applying, tried to network, and looked at options for how I can start my own venture. It's about having as many options as possible open. It's getting to the point where I feel like we can no longer depend on just a single W-2-style job, because we've all seen how quickly those can come and go. events.title: 10 pieces of job-search advice I give my daughters, as the former governor of Massachusetts
events.summary: Jane Swift. Courtesy of Jane Swift Jane Swift, former governor of Massachusetts, shares the job advice she's given to her daughters. Swift advises them to employ personalized applications and impactful communication in interviews. She also suggests asking about the office dress code before an interview and not bringing iced coffee . This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jane Swift, the 61-year-old former Gov. of Massachusetts and the CEO of the national work-based learning nonprofit Education at Work, based in Boston. It has been edited for length and clarity. I've always loved leading organizations and finding ways to make a positive impact on younger generations. I was elected lieutenant governor of Massachusetts in 1999 and served as acting governor from 2001 to 2003. My family moved to Vermont while I was CEO of Middlebury Interactive Languages, a role I held from 2011 to 2017. Now, I'm the CEO of Education at Work, a nonprofit that helps students become financially independent by providing paid, flexible opportunities with companies that need the talent students offer. I understand what employers and job seekers need today Today's job market is competitive, and AI has made it easier for applicants to submit a high volume of applications. That can make it harder for employers to identify the right candidate. Some employers use automated screening tools, making tailored, clearly written applications especially important. Elizabeth is my oldest daughter, who earned her master's degree from Emmanuel College. She handled security for the Red Sox and also has a math degree from UMass Amherst. Lauren has a degree in psychology from Northwestern and worked for the Northwestern football team. Sarah holds an integrative education degree from Trinity College and a master's degree in social work from Case Western Reserve University. Lauren and Sarah are twins. Currently, Elizabeth is a video operations engineer at KISWE, Sarah works as a business analyst for Education at Work, and Lauren is a consultant at Echo Group and Edmentum. I've been guiding them since they were in elementary school. I gave them the option to come with me on one of my business trips each year. They've grown up seeing me talk during board calls in our minivan and drafting RFP responses at the kitchen table late at night. I'd say they've been preparing for the job market since childhood without realizing it. Here are some crucial suggestions and job search coaching I've given my daughters. 1. Prepare for each and every conversation You don't know when you might make an impression outside a formal interview, which could help land a job. Try showing up to any and all opportunities as if they could help your career. That's what I asked Elizabeth to do, as she wanted to work for MLB. During an online informational group session, about 20-30 people attended, most of whom had their cameras off and were unprepared. Elizabeth dressed professionally with questions ready, and the host remembered her. When a position at MLB Replay became available, she was chosen from a pool of candidates on that Zoom call. 2. Before the conversation comes the application email You can use AI, but make sure you're personalizing each job application. Avoid generic, identical email copy, and include specific details about your experience that relate to the job to show hiring managers you've put in some effort. Keep it readable and scannable. You can add a short "why you" paragraph that includes an example or mentions a recent update the company has posted. If it's an online application, look for a warm connection, which can often get more attention than a cold email. Instead of sending emails to a generic inbox, reach out to a named person at the company, such as a recruiter. 3. Highlight your "win themes" I've taught my daughters to identify their "win themes" — the two or three strengths and accomplishments they want an interviewer to remember. Use specific examples to show how you achieved results. Before an interview, choose your three win themes and rehearse examples that illustrate each. Transferable skills can be part of that, too. Lauren and I often attend events with donors to sports programs, and she makes a point of explaining how her experience translates to the work she wants to do. 4. We all make mistakes at work Create a journal dedicated to your career and profession. If you have a bad day or make a mistake, work on solving or correcting that. Journal how you turned your worst day into your best day, and how you resolved an issue eventually. Add a star next to that journal entry and use these star entries as examples during your interviews. Writing it down helps you memorize it faster and more effectively in the long term. Ask yourself: Did I rush? Should I have asked for clarification? Build a strategy so you don't repeat the same error. 5. Dress appropriately for both video and in-person interviews Whether you're on screen or in person, interviewers notice how you show up and engage. Reach out to the organizer and ask, "What is the standard dress code for the office?" so you don't have to guess or arrive completely out of place. Try to level up. For example, if they say the office is business casual, interpret that as your baseline, not your final outfit. 6. Lots of full-time job opportunities get advertised as paid internships Try applying for those roles as well, and keep your perspective open. You may think a position or an internship is below your level, but don't always apply for the title; if possible, apply based on the description. Even if it's not the right fit, it can still be a valuable experience. At an event I managed in 1996, a Williams alum said, "You will learn the most about the job and career you want from the job you hate," and that quote has been with me ever since. Knowing what you don't want to do is equally as important as discovering what makes you happy. 7. Improve your problem-solving and communication skills every day These are skills you never stop building. Ask for feedback and adjust your approach based on it. No one can be perfect, but employers value professionals who incorporate feedback and grow from it. events.title: The midterms are a referendum on public trust
events.summary: In today’s CEO Daily: What’s at stake in tomorrow’s elections. The big leadership story: The AI boom hits a wall. The markets: Stocks rebound globally. Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . Good morning. The midterms are tomorrow, and the outcome will determine more than which party controls Congress. If Democrats win back the House, the Senate, or both, President Donald Trump will have a harder time securing the policies, people, and funding needed to carry out his agenda, and the right could push back. If the GOP retains control, there could be outrage on the left, some over the record $12 billion in projected campaign spending tracked by OpenSecrets, including almost half a billion by Elon Musk alone. Either way, the results will test public trust in three areas:  Trust in capitalism. Americans put up with a lot when they think they have a shot at the prize, but that sentiment is fading in this winner-take-all economy. This Fed chart shows how a rapidly increasing share of U.S. household wealth has gone to rich white Boomers since 1989. Gen Z in particular is seeing signs that the system is rigged : from record oil company profits amid rising energy prices to the unaffordability of housing, health care, and education. They’re worried AI will take their jobs. Hundreds of thousands of anti-government protesters marched across Europe over the weekend. I hear a lot of concern about more unrest here. Trust in politics. I’ve interviewed several hundred CEOs over the past year, on and off the record, across a range of platforms and settings. Publicly, many cheer the Republican agenda on taxes, deregulation, and putting American business first. Privately, far more tell me they’re rattled by the $40 trillion national debt , the government taking ownership in large companies, the vilification of allies and immigrant talent , and the perceived need to show loyalty . And I’ve yet to meet one who’s not shocked at the alleged level of personal enrichment by the president and his family. As one CEO said at a recent dinner: “Everything good gets forgotten when there’s grift.” (A recent AP-NORC poll found 6 in 10 U.S. adults believe Trump is profiting off the presidency in unethical or illegal ways.) Trust in business leaders. We know from the Edelman Trust Barometer that people trust their employer more than any other institution. But they don’t trust business leaders in general, especially when it comes to tech and AI. Shearwater Strategies gave me an exclusive look at their new survey on tech leadership and public trust, which polled a demographically representative sample of 1,563 Americans. When asked what they think tech leaders prioritize, 58% of participants chose “making money for themselves and shareholders.” A distant second was “creating exciting new products” at 34%. When asked what those leaders should prioritize, 58% said “protecting user safety and privacy,” while 12% cited making money. If people don’t trust that tech leaders care about safety and privacy, they’ll vote for politicians who promise to protect those interests instead. events.title: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer
events.summary: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires We cannot let the billionaire class take unprecedented risks with our future A merica is a divided country in crisis. Despite the sunny economic forecast coming from the Trump administration, millions of Americans are struggling to find and keep jobs, getting crushed under the rising cost of living, and losing health insurance when they need it the most. Meanwhile, via corporate consolidation and political corruption, the billionaire class is getting richer faster than ever before: a 40% increase in wealth in just the last two years. Today, the combined wealth of nearly 3,000 global billionaires equals one-fifth of the entire world’s yearly output . Nearly 1,000 billionaires live and do business in the United States. The tools of their domination are tax loopholes, corporate mergers and, in the tech world where many of these billionaires exist, IPOs . When a company goes public, its founders and investors win the capitalist lottery. And instead of paying their fair share of taxes and redistributing resources back into society, most turn around and fund even more corporate consolidation and political corruption to extend their dominion. Elon Musk became an instant trillionaire when SpaceX went public earlier this year, on the backs of workers’ pensions – and is bankrolling the Republican midterm campaigns with a small percentage of his egregious gains. Oracle’s Larry Ellison – currently seventh on the Forbes billionaires list – backed the Paramount-Warner Brothers merger that is destroying the film industry and the livelihoods of the Americans who labor in it. Google’s Sergey Brin spent $100m opposing California’s Prop 40 , a one-time wealth tax that would put the funds toward healthcare and other public services. To pay for essential services, we must tax billionaires, and pass legislation to do so starting in California and New York, but that is clearly not enough. We cannot allow more billionaires – or trillionaires – to be made in this country, further expanding the inequality chasm that’s turning a dignified life into a luxury in this country. We must also block the impending tech IPOs and preserve what’s left of our economy and our society. The Trump administration and tech investors have positioned IPOs as market success stories: when a company goes public, US investors could gain from their valuations. But regular Americans also shoulder a company’s risks – and risk their own futures when that stock ends up in their retirement accounts without consent. Problems with a private company or its products become problems for everyone invested in that company once it goes public, whether they’ve made the choice or not. And when the speculative investment bubble pops – such as with the 2008 crisis – regular people end up holding the bag. It’s no secret that the AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI are intending to go public in the near future. Both of these players also had major security flaws exposed recently, and openly acknowledge mind-bogglingly huge amounts of debt. If these companies are allowed to go public, their cofounders and investors – some of whom are already billionaires – will rise to whole new strata of private wealth. Americans, meanwhile, will be financially crushed if the technologies fail or if these companies prove unable to make good on their extravagant financial promises. Already, the 10 most valuable public companies are in tech, which means the country’s economy depends on the stability of a single industry, one with an undeniable history of bubbles, crashes and, in extreme cases like Theranos, outright fraud. June’s highly contentious SpaceX IPO already carries great risk for regular investors. If more speculative tech companies with staggering risk profiles are allowed to follow suit, the results will become too much for the market to bear. If and when the AI bubble bursts, it will take all of us with it, investors or not. Recessions level lives indiscriminately, and globally. The one exception will be the billionaires, who will have sufficient resources to walk away from the wreckage relatively unscathed. We cannot let the billionaire class take these kinds of risks with our future. To stop these reckless IPOs we must stand together, take collective action, and push for real change. We must find legal and legislative avenues to stop the new tech IPOs from minting new billionaires and transferring the AI industry’s enormous risks onto us. The first step is passing wealth taxes on billionaires to keep them in check. Today, let’s send a message to the billionaires that Americans will not lie down and let them bulldoze working people and the environment on their way to the bank. Tax the billionaires. Block the IPOs. Naomi Klein is a Guardian US columnist and contributing writer. She is the professor of climate justice and co-director of the Centre for Climate Justice at the University of British Columbia.
