events.title: ‘They assume the man next to me is the owner’: four women doing business in Africa in their own way
events.summary: From feeding schoolchildren to recycling tyres, these entrepreneurs are challenging stereotypes while solving social and environmental problems A frica is thought to have a higher proportion of female entrepreneurs than any other continent and yet many still struggle to access financing . Four business leaders from Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya and Malawi tell us about the inspiration behind their success – and the challenges women still face. Ifedolapo Runsewe, Nigeria: giving waste tyres a new life On the outskirts of Ibadan in south-west Nigeria , thousands of discarded tyres are fuelling an industrial experiment. They arrive at Freee Recycle’s factory where they are sorted, shredded and reduced to rubber granules. Some will become playground surfaces. Others will be turned into gym flooring, paving blocks and interlocking tiles. Ifedolapo Runsewe, the company’s founder, is building an industrial recycling business in a sector where women rarely own factories or lead manufacturing operations. In Nigeria, women own about 40% of small businesses , but 56% of female entrepreneurs’ last loan applications were denied , compared with 17% for men, according to the World Bank. In capital-heavy fields such as recycling, this financing gap may prevent female entrepreneurs becoming factory owners. Runsewe has made that leap. She has built a factory that turns one of Nigeria’s most intransigent waste problems into products. The factory employs about 62 people, collecting tyres from four states in Nigeria: Oyo, Lagos, Osun and Kwara. Nigeria produces millions of waste tyres each year. Many end up in dumps or are burned to recover scrap metal, releasing hazardous pollutants. “Burning tyres releases a complex mix of toxic chemicals – it’s not just pollution, it’s a direct public health threat,” says Oladele Ogunseitan, a presidential chair at the University of California, Irvine. After more than 12 years in banking, Runsewe became interested in tyre recycling after seeing first-hand the impact of burning tyres. What convinced her there was a business opportunity was the fact that almost every part of a tyre can be recovered and reused. She started Freee Recycle in 2020. The challenge has been to convince people that waste can be a business. Recycling tyres requires substantial capital. Turning the recovered rubber into finished products requires another layer of machinery, expertise and investment. And unlike collecting waste, manufacturing depends on finding customers willing to buy what comes out of the recycling process. “People view recycling as more of an informal, small-scale activity rather than a serious business capable of generating substantial returns,” she says. “And that is absolutely not true.” Early on, she encountered another obstacle: the assumption that an industrial recycling business was a man’s domain. “I’d go into banks and boardrooms, and investors would assume the man next to me is the owner. As soon as I spoke, the question came up: why should we give a woman millions, hundreds of millions?” Yet she does not want her business reduced to a story about gender. “I don’t think organisations choose to work with us because we’re female-owned,” she says. “They see a brand that is good, transparent, credible and ethical.” Freee Recycle has secured partnerships with organisations including Michelin, Save the Children and the International Committee of the Red Cross. And she is looking into expanding beyond tyres. “There are plans to set up what would be the first in Nigeria dedicated to recycling aerosols, like insecticide cans and spray containers,” she says. Through the company’s Freee art residency programme, launched in 2025, discarded tyres have been transformed into large-scale artworks inspired by African history and culture, including the Bata drum, Ikom monoliths and Benin bronze traditions. The symbolism is deliberate: materials that would otherwise be thrown away are being given another life. Valentine Benjamin Kyokushaba Shine, Uganda: building solar-powered irrigation systems As a little girl, Kyokushaba Shine would watch her mother get up before dawn, labouring hard all day to tend to the acres of onions she had planted near their house in Kabale, southern Uganda . Often her mother’s harvests – the family’s only source of income – would fail. A lack of water or degraded soil could leave them with almost no yield, making it difficult to put enough food on the table. Now, as a water engineer and entrepreneur, Kyokushaba, 31, has made it her mission to help farmers like her mother. “I started my company with the goal of designing small and affordable irrigation systems for smallholder farmers. When I started the business in February 2025, I had neither staff nor capital, but I had a goal in mind and I wanted to work towards it,” she says.

events.title: ‘Just the beginning’ for Antonelli, F1’s prodigious, charismatic new king
events.summary: Kimi Antonelli, F1’s youngest world champion at 20, has become the life and soul of the paddock with his personality. Kimi Antonelli has sparked affectionate tributes from all quarters of the Formula One paddock after becoming the sport’s youngest world champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix. The 20-year-old Italian finished third for Mercedes on Sunday behind Red Bull’s four-time champion Max Verstappen and Ferrari’s seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton – who then hoisted him aloft as a carnival of celebrations began. “It’s a very special day,” said Antonelli’s race engineer Peter ‘Bono’ Bonnington, who has worked with seven-time champions Michael Schumacher and Hamilton and regards the new champion – Italy’s first since 1953 – as another generational talent. list 1 of 4 Hamilton calls for Palestine and DR Congo freedom as Rwanda takes F1 spotlight list 2 of 4 Dakar Rally 2027 moved out of Saudi Arabia amid conflict in Middle East list 3 of 4 Mercedes no longer have the fastest car in F1, says leader Antonelli list 4 of 4 F1 leader Kimi Antonelli wins Italian GP after epic charge from the back “I feel privileged to work with him and to put up with his pranks and tricks, including the water pistols and the rest. It’s him all over.” Antonelli said it was “truly incredible” to share the podium with multiple champions Verstappen and Hamilton. “I’m looking forward to more battles with them in the future,” he said. “This is just the beginning. This win is just going to mark a beginning, a new point to build on and keep improving and keep trying to win a championship.” Lived and breathed motorsports his whole life The sound of engines and smell of exhausts have been part of Antonelli’s life since he was a child. The Mercedes driver was barely 10 when he sat on his father Marco’s lap behind the wheel of a competition Lamborghini, changing gears and guiding the car around a racetrack while his father operated the brake and accelerator pedals. He was eight when his racing driver dad smuggled him into the Formula One paddock for the first time inside a stack of tyres with an umbrella on top. “Sometimes we may look like lunatics because we just talk about racing,” Antonelli said of his close relationship with his father and the passion they share. “We like to analyse things together. Racing is always in our minds. We have a lot of fun together, and racing is our passion. It’s what I live for.” The son of Elisabetta, who stays out of the spotlight, and Marco, a former driver and team principal, Andrea Kimi Antonelli started karting at seven although his father, surprisingly, opposed a career in the sport. “He didn’t want me to become a driver because motorsports can be very cruel at times, especially financially, since it’s very hard to succeed without the support of the right people,” the younger Antonelli said before the US Grand Prix last month. “He taught me everything he knew, first about racing and now about life. It’s really important to have him by my side during races.” Prodigy picked up by Mercedes at 11 Antonelli was spotted and, at the age of 11, recruited by Frenchman Gwen Lagrue, head of the Mercedes junior driver programme, where Hamilton was his mentor. “He’s incredibly impressive and deserves to be world champion,” said the Englishman, whose record of seven world titles may one day come under threat from his protege. Antonelli began in karting, dominating the sport in 2020 and 2021. He was Italian and German F4 champion in 2022 and champion in Formula Regional in F3 cars in 2023. He skipped F3 and went straight into F2 in 2024. Although he finished only sixth, another leap followed when Hamilton left Mercedes for Ferrari. There were a few bumps and brushes in his rookie year in F1, but he still managed a second place in Sao Paulo and two other podiums, finishing seventh in the championship. “I said from the start that he had tremendous talent and a great personality but that he would need a season in F1 to grow and learn through both great moments and setbacks,” Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said. “He was catapulted into F1, and it wasn’t easy, even though he had always driven very well. He had to handle the pressure, the media and the expectations.” Always cheerful, smiling and full of jokes, Antonelli has become the life and soul of the paddock. Every news conference is laced with humour with other drivers joining in the fun. Congratulations from across the world poured in for the new champion, including from Italian compatriots, such as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, football clubs and multiple-time Grand Slam champion Jannik Sinner, who teamed up with Antonelli to give Italy several victorious weekends as the duo triumphed concurrently in their sports. Six races that made Antonelli world champion Not only did he become the youngest driver ever to take pole position, but Antonelli, still only 19, went on to win his first grand prix, becoming the second youngest F1 winner behind Verstappen.

events.title: I tested Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo. It's a fascinating experiment, but the price is hard to justify.
events.summary: I've spent the past week trying to figure out whether Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo is the future of smartphones or just an expensive way to do things I could already do on my regular iPhone. The answer, unsurprisingly, is a bit of both. Why it matters: Apple wasn't first to the folding smartphone party. Samsung, Google and others began making them years ago. But Apple's arrival in a category has a way of reinventing it. The big picture : The most exciting thing about Apple's first foldable iPhone isn't necessarily what it can do today but what it can become. Already, it's inspiring developers to explore possibilities that could reshape how we use our devices. Old habits die hard One of my first surprises was how little I initially used the Duo's biggest selling point: its folding screen. While other reviewers talked about endlessly opening and closing their devices, I found myself mostly using the smaller outside display. After years of conventional iPhones, it was a mix of instinct and muscle memory. Zoom in: Over time, though, I found reasons to unfold it. Watching sports was one of the clearest advantages. I pulled out the Duo at Starbucks to watch the 49ers with my son and later followed a tied World Series game in a doctor's waiting room. At the WNBA Finals, having forgotten my laptop, I managed some quick edits to a story about Anthropic's IPO . I wouldn't want to write a full article that way, but it was reassuring to have the option. Playing the New York Times' Spelling Bee alongside its Spelling Bee Buddy helper was a small but delightful example of multitasking without constantly switching apps. Between the lines: The Duo's advantages aren't always about more screen space. Sometimes they're about what you can physically do with a phone that bends. I tried watching Netflix with the phone unfolded, propped up like a tent and partially folded into a miniature laptop. I also used the Duo's ability to stand on its own to capture wide shots of the WNBA Finals from a press-box ledge without needing a tripod. Other experiences were less seamless, including getting the orientation right when trying FaceTime's option to use multiple camera views. The developer wild card Perhaps the biggest difference between the Duo and the Android foldables is the enthusiasm Apple's device has sparked among independent developers. Zoom in: Some of the early experiments are more entertaining than useful, including apps that turn the Duo into a virtual cassette player or a grilled cheese toaster . My favorite was Tiny Computers , which let it simulate a semi-functional 1984 Mac, Windows 95 PC or candy-colored iMac. Nearly two decades after the App Store debuted, we aren't all using our iPhones as virtual cigarette lighters. And I doubt we'll all be making imaginary grilled cheese sandwiches on our phones 20 years from now. Zoom out: But these early experiments offer glimpses of what might be possible when developers start thinking beyond a conventional rectangular screen. The question isn't whether today's novelties become hits. It's whether all this experimentation eventually produces genuinely new ways of using our phones — the kind of breakthroughs that make today's smartphones feel indispensable. The $2,000 question For all the fun I've had with the Duo, its price is an insurmountable obstacle. At $2,000, it's simply not a purchase I could justify for myself, much less recommend broadly. The catch: There are other compromises. I missed Face ID, occasionally fumbling for the side-mounted Touch ID sensor until I started wearing an Apple Watch to make unlocking the phone easier. And when I needed to accomplish something quickly, I often instinctively reached for my familiar, traditional iPhone. What I'm watching: On Friday, I tried putting the Duo away to see if I missed it. I didn't find myself longing for it the way I sometimes felt when I only had the Duo only and missed having a better camera. The bottom line: The Duo is a fascinating glimpse of where smartphones could go next. But early buyers are paying a steep premium to participate in an experiment whose biggest rewards may still be years away.

events.title: Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right.
events.summary: Quitobaquito Springs, a rare Sonoran Desert oasis imperiled by border wall construction, is located within 200 feet of the U.S.-Mexico border in Organ Pipe National Monument outside Ajo, Arizona. Anna Watts Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors. “People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said. Fifteen days later, her fears were realized. ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors. The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said. The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted. “The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural practices.” Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe, and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will disturb more sites. “​​Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.” Hia-Ced O’odham elder Lorraine Eiler stands in the shade of a giant saguaro cactus in Organ Pipe National Monument in 2022. Roberto “Bear” Guerra Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a saguaro cactus that was still standing. In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this location to date.” The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as the Las Playas Intaglio , that was believed to be at least 6,500 years old. (CBP said the incident was accidental .) Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica recently reported, DHS has responded by deploying masked federal agents as escorts for its work crews and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border.” Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it was necessary. “When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members — whose remains are being desecrated.” U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.” James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the field. While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.  Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained, and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the land.” “Work in the immediate discovery area must remain suspended for at least 30 calendar days,” he wrote, while the park service consults with tribal representatives “to determine the disposition and physical treatment of the remains.” Workers clear desert flora to make way for construction of a double border wall in Organ Pipe National Monument. Anna Watts In a region as rich with archaeological sites as the American Southwest, the inadvertent disturbance of Native American remains occurs with some regularity. What sets the discovery in Organ Pipe apart are the extraordinary powers the Department of Homeland Security wields to expedite wall construction in the borderlands. Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Real ID Act, which included a provision empowering the secretary of DHS to waive any law that might slow border wall construction. In the two decades since, DHS has invoked its powers 66 times, with 60 of those instances occurring under President Donald Trump’s two administrations. events.title: Banking on innovation for a more connected future
events.summary: At Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026, Hang Seng Bank will showcase AI-enabled innovation and partnerships designed to enhance customer experiences while supporting Hong Kong's development as an international innovation and technology centre [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Hang Seng Bank will bring AI-powered wealth management, digital banking, investment innovation and an interactive table tennis experience to Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026 as it makes its debut with a dedicated exhibition booth at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre on November 2 and 3. Six interactive experiences will showcase innovation across Retail Banking and Wealth Management, Commercial Banking, Markets and Securities Services, Hang Seng Indexes and the bank's partnership ecosystem. One example is Hang Seng's e-Passbook, Hong Kong's first service of its kind, launched in April 2026 with the needs of elderly customers in mind. Another demonstration is a Proof of Concept exploring the potential of bond tokenisation to make fixed-income investments more accessible to retail investors. Tokenisation holds the potential to enable fractionalisation of an underlying bond into smaller digital tokens, lowering the minimum investment required. It may also help streamline transactions and enable faster settlement. Visitors can follow a simulated demonstration investment journey, to experience the conversion of traditional bond into digital tokens. Elsewhere at the booth, visitors can take on a humanoid table tennis robot as part of an AI-wealth management experience. The game introduces visitors to AI-powered personalisation already available through the Hang Seng Mobile App, which provides tailored financial insights and suggestions based on customer profiles and preferences. Its Wealth Overview page and Goal Planner also help customers review their finances and plan ahead. The table tennis connection draws on Hang Seng's more than 35 years of support for local sporting talent. Supporting businesses and investment decisions Hang Seng will also showcase digital services designed to support businesses at different stages of development. An interactive installation takes visitors through an SME owner's journey, with three steps triggering videos covering remote account opening and daily operations, business expansion and wealth management. The bank's capabilities include digital payment solutions, a cross-bank cashflow analysis platform, Hang Seng SME Business Loan, Hang Seng TradePay, alternative data-backed financing and business mobile investment trading.Investors, meanwhile, can explore ThemeFinder, a Gen-AI-enabled solution co-developed by Hang Seng Indexes with an AI innovator from Cyberport's community. The technology identifies thematic investment trends and accelerates index development, improve the efficiency of identifying listed companies and processing relevant data by up to 5 times. The solution also helps maintain consistency across index operating processes and supports data traceability. Visitors can experience how thematic investment themes can be identified in the markets, create simulated personalised indexes and compare their performance against the Hang Seng Technology Composite Index. The showcase will also feature the Hang Seng Technology Index Family and HK-US index series, which combines Southbound Stock Connect-eligible Hong Kong tech stocks with major US-listed tech companies. Connecting Hong Kong's innovation community Its Living Lab programme with HKSTP, for example, launched a second cohort in April 2026 focused on AI applications in retail and commercial banking, providing technology ventures with opportunities to test solutions in banking environments. Such collaborations can move ideas from exploration and pilot programmes towards safe deployment, turning technological advances into solutions that can benefit customers at scale. With deep roots in Hong Kong, Hang Seng is connecting people, ideas and expertise to make banking more accessible, personalised and responsive to changing customer needs.

events.title: Election ‘war rooms’ enter the AI age
events.summary: Both OpenAI and Anthropic will have “war rooms” dedicated to ensuring their platforms provide accurate information about the midterm elections, a first for both companies. The concept of a tech platform “war room” dates back to 2018, when Meta stood one up for the first time amid concerns about the proliferation of election-related misinformation. The AI age has supercharged those threats, which now include deepfake videos and AI-powered search results spreading incorrect information. Case in point: Last week, Google’s AI Mode wouldn’t respond to a query about who won the 2020 election, which the company said they were working to fix . “Teams across the company work year-round on strengthening our election-related safeguards and enforcing our policies. Ahead of the election, we have a dedicated war room monitoring our platform for misuse and ready to quickly respond to any incidents,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Semafor. These efforts will be made more difficult by AI’s unpredictable nature, recent cybersecurity issues, and the tendency of AI search tools to reflect back results users want to see. Former Meta director of public policy Katie Harbath told Semafor that war rooms are “built for dealing with the things we can’t necessarily predict going wrong and you need a quick, established process in terms of triaging.”

events.title: Leading progressive wants Democrats to think big post-midterms
events.summary: A leading progressive lawmaker says his party colleagues need to think big and dare President Donald Trump to veto Democratic bills if they take the majority. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, is pushing for votes on bills to tackle “price gouging, that crack down on utility rates going up, that crack down on politicians profiting off their jobs” — and though he acknowledged some might become law, “if Donald Trump vetoes them, then that’s exactly the platform upon which we beat JD Vance or whoever else in 2028.” House Democratic leaders have sketched out some early priorities for their potential majority, like restoring lapsed health insurance subsidies or reversing cuts to Medicaid; the path beyond that is fuzzier. But the scope of House Democrats’ ambitions will depend on how many seats they pick up, and on Senate control, too. Casar bristled at recent comments by Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who said that Democrats should table bigger policy questions until the 2028 campaign, since Trump is still in the White House and likely to veto their legislation. He argued that pushing the envelope was necessary for Democrats to prove to voters they care. “I don’t want to waste our majority by negotiating down to Trump’s level,” Casar said. And if Democrats take the Senate as well on Tuesday, party-line legislation to circumvent the filibuster should be on the table, Casar said. “We should do a reconciliation bill, or multiple reconciliation bills, and dare Trump on those issues. We should also push for policies that are 80% popular across the country and dare Senate Republicans to vote against them,” Casar added. Some incoming progressive lawmakers have threatened to withhold votes for Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries in a speaker election unless he commits to progressive policy goals. Casar sidestepped a question on that prospect. “I’ve worked very regularly with Leader Jeffries, and I am a supporter,” he said. “Everybody’s vote, of course, is their own, and I would let each member speak for themselves on that question.”

events.title: How Trump's iron grip on the Republican Party put the Senate in play
events.summary: The News Americans are angry about war and prices, and a president’s second midterm is always difficult — but a series of decisions by President Donald Trump has made Republicans’ Senate majority ever-more vulnerable. The mark Trump made on the midterms began in the summer of 2024, when he selected former Ohio Sen. JD Vance as his running mate. Since then, the president’s personnel and political decisions have reshaped the Senate battleground from what looked like an impenetrable red wall into a toss-up. His decision to pick Vance opened up a special election in Ohio that will by the end of this week cost the GOP hundreds of millions of dollars and potentially a Senate seat. Trump’s party-boss mentality in North Carolina, Texas, and South Carolina has further contributed to the yawning battleground. He endorsed Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia’s Senate race against Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff — a contest that never really got off the ground after Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, whom Trump tried to take down in a primary in 2022, passed on the race. Ossoff is favored to win. And party insiders blame Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran for creating a volatile Senate map that has left seats in red states like Nebraska and Kansas vulnerable. Republicans could hold the chamber — or lose as many as a half-dozen seats on Tuesday. “Every negative for the GOP this cycle is a downstream effect of Iran,” said a person close to the White House. Republicans can lose up to three seats and still keep Senate control. Trump’s zeal on the campaign trail is undeniable and he helped direct huge sums of money into the midterms, albeit later than many Republicans would have liked. He spent the last weekend capping off a breakneck fall campaign schedule stumping in Iowa and Kansas, two places where the GOP was strongly favored to win a few months ago but now is struggling. “President Trump has a 97% endorsement record and he remains the best turnout machine for our base voters,” said Republican National Committee press secretary Natalie Baldassarre. Trump is hosting nearly 20 tele-rallies in the last days of the campaign, in addition to his almost-daily travel for rallies over the past month. The White House has sought to emphasize the administration’s accomplishments on issues like the border, crime, and US investment and manufacturing, as they look to encourage low-propensity voters to turn out for Republicans. “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle said. But his moves to reshape the party in his image over the past two years also often showed little regard for conventional political risk assessment. Trump created two special elections with decisions to put Vance as his vice president and Marco Rubio, a popular former Florida senator, as his secretary of state. On Tuesday, Democrats are underdogs in Florida after nominating democratic socialist Angie Nixon to face appointed GOP Sen. Ashley Moody. The race is more competitive than expected but not a five-alarm fire like Ohio, where Vance’s replacement, Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is in a precarious position. The longtime preference of Husted, a former lieutenant governor, was to run for governor, according to multiple people familiar with internal party deliberations. He was instead appointed to the Senate and Vivek Ramaswamy ran for governor; Ramaswamy now trails Democrat Amy Action. A campaign spokesperson for Husted said that he “is completely focused on retiring Sherrod Brown once and for all this Tuesday.” “Public polls in the national media have gotten Ohio wrong every election cycle since 2016,” one Ohio GOP operative argued. drama in the south A year after selecting Vance, Trump tangled with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., over healthcare cuts included in the tax cut law, prompting Tillis to retire. Tillis told Semafor afterward that Trump’s backing might not have helped anyway: “I’m not sure that his endorsement would have helped me in a general election in North Carolina next year, to be quite candid.” Trump quickly cleared the field for former RNC Chair Michael Whatley, avoiding a costly primary, but Whatley’s candidacy crumpled against his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said in an interview last summer that Tillis was “established” and “knew how to run and win in North Carolina,” while also praising Whatley as a candidate who could win with Republicans united behind him. In recent weeks, however, Republicans essentially ceded the race as the battleground map expanded to places like Texas. Thune and many sitting GOP senators had hoped to convince Trump to back Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas. But Trump gave Cornyn the cold shoulder after the Texas Republican’s remarks questioning Trump’s viability heading into the 2024 election cycle. Trump instead backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who won the nomination. Paxton is trailing in most polls while receiving the most air support of any candidate. “Texas was an unforced error, I think, on the part of the president,” Cornyn told Semafor in previously unreported comments earlier this year. “We spent a lot of money trying to win the nomination, but the promise was that if I won the nomination, then that would be a layup in November. That’s all off the table.” Had they been nominated again, Cornyn and Tillis may have had tough races too, but most Republicans now believe they would have been closer. Paxton could still win, but the race undoubtedly opens up a shocking vulnerability in Republicans’ red wall. So too in South Carolina. After the death of his longtime ally, Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., Trump backed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who most senators thought would be an interim senator. Instead, Trump helped launch Graham’s run for a six-year term, even as several other prominent Republicans mounted their own campaigns. Graham defeated conservative Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., in the primary runoff this summer with Trump’s help, but Graham is now in a toss-up race with Annie Andrews, who is outraising her by astronomical margins. Norman barely lifted a finger to help Graham and the race has gotten closer and closer, prompting intervention from the Senate Leadership Fund, a GOP-aligned super PAC. “There’s an incredibly divided Republican Party in South Carolina,” Andrews told Semafor in September. She added that polling clearly showed “that Darline was going to be easier for me.” Room for Disagreement Republicans say some of Trump’s impact has been positive. Trump helped draft top GOP recruits like Michigan Senate nominee Mike Rogers, directed tens of millions of dollars into battlegrounds, and gave Sen. events.summary: Houthi-affiliated media report that seven people were wounded in strikes on the city of Hodeidah. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen says air defences intercepted a Houthi missile, while fighting continues to rage along key fronts between the armed group and forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government. Defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile” targeting Saudi Arabia’s southern region, said coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki in a statement on Monday. list 1 of 4 New Yemen fighting displaces 290,000, says UN, with pregnant women at risk list 2 of 4 UN demands investigation after staffer’s death in Houthi custody in Yemen list 3 of 4 Yemeni government forces seize strategic positions in al-Jawf list 4 of 4 UN staffer’s death in custody exposes Houthi ‘political extortion’ in Yemen Earlier, he said defences destroyed a drone launched toward the southern region on Sunday evening. Also on Monday, the Saudi Civil Defence authority issued and then lifted alerts warning of “potential danger” in the city of Abha, as well as the provinces of Khamis Mushait, Taif and Najran. The authority warned residents against “filming, publishing or sharing information” related to missile and drone attacks. In Yemen, a media outlet affiliated with the Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), reported that seven people were wounded in Saudi-led coalition air strikes on Hodeidah on the Red Sea coast. Four people were wounded in the attacks on Ras Isa port dock, while three others suffered injuries in a strike on an oil company site in the governorate’s Bajil district, Houthi media reported. There was no comment on the reports from the Saudi-led coalition. The latest clashes come as Yemeni government forces keep up their campaign to regain positions from the Iran-aligned Houthis in the strategic northern governorate of al-Jawf. Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said on Sunday evening that government forces conducted 1,272 “targeting operations” against Houthi fighters, fortifications and weapons supplies over 24 hours. Operations are ongoing in al-Jawf, neighbouring Marib and al-Bayda to the south, added al-Nazili. Government forces killed roughly 500 Houthi fighters and destroyed or disabled nearly 170 vehicles, equipment or heavy weaponry. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims. In southwest Yemen, the Houthis continue to besiege the city of Taiz, blocking the entry of food, fuel and medical supplies, in what authorities warn is a mounting humanitarian crisis. Taiz Governor Nabil Shamsan has called for urgent help for the city’s deteriorating health facilities. He said 120 health centres have stopped operating and another 66 are close to shutting down since the Houthis cut off supply routes to the city in early October. Nour al-Din al-Mansouri, a member of the committee facilitating the work of the Taiz Siege Affairs Office, told Al Jazeera that at least 23 trucks were damaged or overturned in the past two weeks while seeking alternative routes to Taiz. The city is Yemen’s third-largest and home to about one million of the country’s roughly 43 million people. Full-scale fighting reignited in Yemen in September, when the Houthis made crucial gains that tightened their grip on the Red Sea coast. Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched a campaign called Operation Dawn of Yemen last month to regain Houthi-held sites and restore government control over other territories held by the group, which seized the capital Sanaa in 2014.

events.title: ‘Long gone are the days where we just provided numbers’: The CFO-to-CEO pipeline is growing but does a finance background always make a good leader?
events.summary: When Toyota needed a new chief executive this year, it looked one seat over. Kenta Kon, the carmaker’s chief finance officer, took the top job in April. Kon joins a long list of CFOs that have risen to the CEO role, including ConocoPhillips CEO Andy O’Brien, CME Group’s Lynne Fitzpatrick and Unilever’s Fernando Fernandez.  In Europe, 21% of CEO appointments at the continent’s largest listed companies last year were previously CFOs—second only to divisional chiefs, according to data published by executive search firm Spencer Stuart .  “Long gone are the days where we provided the numbers and asked somebody else to tell the story,” says Darren Ellis, CFO for Europe, Americas, Africa, and the Middle East at Standard Chartered . “The CFO now needs to be able to tell that story.”  Ellis believes that there is now much more crossover between the CFO and CEO role, including setting strategy, allocating capital, steering technology investment, navigating geopolitical risk, and speaking with investors. “The CFO and CEO career paths don’t necessarily diverge anymore,” he adds. “I think they converge.”  Mark Thumser, chief financial and strategy officer for the Americas at Japanese financial services company MUFG, says AI is accelerating this shift. As automation takes over reconciliations, reporting, and analysis, the value finance leader’s provide changes from producing numbers to interpreting them.   “The number crunching, facts, and research, is all going to be done by models,” he says. What’s left is judgment: “Does it make sense? Is this a good risk-return trade-off? Is there a return on capital? That cannot be modeled out.”  This is reflected in the skills sets boards now expect CFOs to exhibit. Uvashni Raman, CFO at online travel agency Booking .com, says boards want commercial, strategic, and technology skills in a future CFO.   Nurturing CFOs into future leaders Companies seeking to develop CFOs into future CEOs must adapt how they identify and develop senior talent. Flatter organizational structures have reduced the number of middle-management roles where employees traditionally gained leadership experience. At the same time, AI is taking over some junior tasks that have historically helped employees develop basic financial and analytical skills.  In response to this challenge, MUFG rotates entry-level hires through four finance functions in their first six months and is working “more intentionally” to move mid-level staff across the business. As AI takes on routine work, Thumser says, the bank is hiring for different traits. “We need critical thinking skills. We need people who’ve got some technology experience. We need people that can think about change management.”  Ellis reviews succession plans for his senior roles twice a year, while Thumser says MUFG is planning for “the next, next CFO.”   Despite the frequency with which CFOs are promoted to CEO, they do not necessarily excel in the role. In an analysis of 1,300 CEOs by Spencer Stuart, f ormer CFOs were the least likely to rank in the top quartile ffor CEO performance .  Finance chiefs are also most at risk of being replaced. Nearly 60% of the 645 CEOs surveyed by Boston Consulting Group said they planned to make changes to their senior leadership team within the next six months, with finance chiefs the most frequently cited targets.   Raman’s advice for remaining resilient is to build experience beyond finance. “You will not be as effective a leader if you just stay within finance,” she says. Before Booking.com, she worked across operational finance, procurement, IT strategy, M&A and transformation, in several different sectors. “It was less about moving up,” she says, “and more about increasing the tools in my toolbox.”  The CFO seat has become one of the most reliable routes to the top. But success as a chief executive depends on the breadth of experience and leadership skills finance chiefs develop before taking the job.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Nuclear radiation in Russia, Ukraine? No, just hacked warning alerts
events.summary: Warnings startle people in Ukraine, but authorities say they cleared up the confusion in under an hour. Ukraine and Russia have accused each other of hacking into systems used to send out emergency alerts to citizens, raising fears of a new escalation of digital and psychological warfare tactics. The systems’ apps sent out radiation alerts on Sunday and Monday to civilians before officials issued public clarifications. list 1 of 4 Russia, Ukraine air raid alert apps hit by cyberattacks after truce ends list 2 of 4 Kherson braces for return of war as localised Russia-Ukraine truce ends list 3 of 4 US greenlights $2.1bn Patriot missile sale to Ukraine list 4 of 4 Dead dolphins, naval mines: Russia-Ukraine war destroys the Black Sea The fake threats began on the same day as a localised ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Kherson region came to an end on Sunday. The truce, which the United States said was brokered by first lady Melania Trump, is the longest so far in Russia’s more than four-year war on Ukraine. The ceasefire lasted for six days, during which humanitarian aid and evacuations were allowed in the Russian-occupied town of Olekshy. Al Jazeera’s Audrey Macalpine, reporting from Kyiv, said many people in Ukraine now expect renewed fighting along the front lines. Here’s what we know about the fake notifications: Ukraine’s Air Force said late on Sunday that users of its Air Alert app, which warns people of incoming air attacks, received fake warnings of nuclear and chemical threats to areas in and around Kyiv. Users were also warned of potential street combat and told that Russia’s hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed. “The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the Ukrainian Air Force said on Telegram. “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.” Ukraine’s Center for Strategic Communications blamed Russia. In a post on X, the agency pointed to the use of the Russian language in one of the fake messages. The Ukrainian government said a separate app created for the capital city was working normally. The fake alerts came just after 10pm (20:00 GMT), startling a lot of people, Macalpine reported. “Even the speakers here in the centre of the city rang out warnings of these attacks,” she said. “But most people here understood within at least half an hour that this was some kind of hacking attack.” Hours later on Monday morning, similar announcements came from Russia’s Ministry of Civil Defence, Emergencies and Disaster Relief, which said its warnings app came under a “massive cyberattack” and wrongly warned users of imminent drone attacks. The ministry did not name any suspects but said the alerts spread “false information”. Media reports said the hackers warned Russians that “nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [Ukrainian drones] had been launched on all regions” of the country. The alerts also instructed people to “urgently” stock up on food for three weeks and to hide. This appears to be the first time either Ukraine’s or Russia’s official alert apps have been hacked. However, cyberwarfare has long been a major part of the countries’ previous confrontations. Russian hackers have attacked Ukraine’s election systems in the past and in January 2022 attacked Ukrainian government and banking sites. Cyberwarfare tactics have only intensified since February 2022 when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In late 2023, the Russian hacker group Sandworm took the private telecommunications network Kyivstar offline, disrupting notifications for days. Ukrainian groups have also launched multiple cyberattacks on Russia. The country’s volunteer-based IT Army of Ukraine was founded in the wake of Russia’s invasion specifically to engage in cyberwarfare against Russia and has reportedly targeted the Moscow Stock Exchange, Russia’s power grids and several government websites. In 2022, the Reuters news agency reported Ukrainian attackers used facial recognition software to scan the faces of dead Russian combatants and notified their families of their deaths. Why is the threat of nuclear radiation in Ukraine significant? Ukraine is particularly vulnerable because it has already suffered one nuclear disaster and it remains at risk due to fighting around another major nuclear plant. In April 1986, the Chornobyl nuclear power plant , located in the then-Ukrainian Soviet Republic, exploded, releasing radioactive material. Scores of people died from the explosion itself, but thousands later developed severe health issues as a result, including thyroid cancer. Radiation was detected as far away as Sweden. It’s regarded as one of the two worst nuclear accidents in history along with the 2011 Fukushima disaster in Japan. Chornobyl remains a ghost town after its inhabitants were evacuated. Ongoing fighting in the Ukrainian region of Zaporizhia has raised fears that the tragic story could repeat itself.

events.title: The agentic web is here
events.summary: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book a physical therapy appointment for their mother, making sure it would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.  At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent and OpenAI’s Dots are logging record downloads and being given access to people’s bank accounts and email inboxes, and Anthropic launched a research preview of its own Claude Duet agent in October. And in a worrying incident, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their badly protected sandbox and caused havoc on the open web.   Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, an associate professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place for humans that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus.  They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse hundreds of sites in just a few seconds, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight.  As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the 1990s and early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as the sites and creators we now favor struggle to survive the shift. And as last summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents themselves could even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not. How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.” Building a web for agents There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers. When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces. The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are great at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not. PINGNAN LU So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do.  Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. events.title: Asian shares are mixed and US futures advance, while oil prices retreat
events.summary: Asian shares are mixed ad oil prices have retreated, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran HONG KONG -- Asian shares were mixed and oil prices retreated Monday, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran. U.S. futures advanced after U.S. stocks fell Friday to their worst day since June as investors dumped technology- and artificial intelligence-related stocks. Japan’s Nikkei 225 gave up early gains, slipping 0.3% to 63,081.86 as some major technology companies fell. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index rose 2.2% to 5,859.08. Samsung Electronics added 1.8%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 3.8%. Technology stocks have been volatile as investors worry that the AI buildup may prove to be a bubble. Apple is due to report its latest earnings results later in the day. Last week, earnings reports from Google parent Alphabet Inc. and Amazon rattled markets and raised fresh questions over whether their massive AI-related spending will bring profitable returns as quickly as hoped. While recent developments do not necessarily mean that the AI boom is beginning to unravel, the debate is entering another phase, Sunil Tirumalai at UBS Global Research wrote in a recent note. Investors have become “distinctly more nervous about a handful of companies with weaker balance sheets or bigger financial commitments,” he said, rather than the technology sector as a whole. “Some cracks have appeared,” said Tirumalai. “Increasingly, the question will be whether all the money being spent on it can generate adequate financial returns.” Over the past month, the Nikkei 225 has fallen more than 7% and the Kospi dropped more than 16%. Taiwan’s Taiex was 0.7% lower, with leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., shedding 1.7%. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.5% to 23,411.49. The Shanghai Composite index was up 1.1% to 3,638.03, despite China reporting over the weekend that its factory activity returned to contraction territory in October indicating that the economic momentum may have slowed. China’s central bank and its securities regulatory body met with financial institutions Monday to discuss ways to support the markets, according to Chinese media reports. The Shanghai Composite index has fallen 14.6% in the past year. In Australia, the S & P/ASX 200 lost 0.6% to 8,856.50. On Friday, Wall Street’s benchmark S & P 500 fell 1.8% and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite declined 2.9%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 1.1%. Investors are watching for the outcome of Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections . Voters across the political spectrum have shown increasing concerns about AI and data centers , along with inflation and other key issues. Oil prices dropped more than 2% early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, down 2.8% to $110.24 per barrel. Benchmark U.S. crude gave up 3.1%, to $100.85 a barrel. Iran’s top diplomat said in an interview shared on his Telegram channel over the weekend that Iranian negotiators were in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. meets several conditions. However, he said no direct talks were being held with the U.S. The final outcome of the diplomatic efforts to avoid a return to all-out war depends on answers provided by the United States to the “Iranian questions,” he said. In other dealings early Monday, the U.S. dollar rose to 157.83 Japanese yen from 157.49 yen. events.title: Asia’s factories lose steam as AI glow meets war’s economic chill
events.summary: Manufacturing activity slowed in China, indicating the drag from Iran war may be offsetting gains from robust global demand for AI chips. Asia’s factory growth slowed in October, especially in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, even as chip and AI demand stayed strong. The Middle East war is lifting fuel and food prices, hurting spending and confidence, while China’s price competition is also pressuring exporters. The IMF warned Asia’s growth may ease in 2026 and 2027, and Japan’s central bank said an AI slump could hit exports, production and financial markets. TOKYO – Factory activity across Asia continued to expand in October, but growth slowed in major chip exporters, private surveys showed on Nov 2, suggesting the AI boom may be losing momentum as markets start to question the sector’s profitability. The data points to growing strains on export-led economies, as prolonged conflict in the Middle East keeps fuel and food prices elevated, hitting consumption and business confidence, even as demand for chips and artificial intelligence-related goods remains resilient. Manufacturing activity slowed in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, the surveys showed, indicating the drag from the US-Israeli war on Iran may be offsetting the benefits from robust global demand for chips and AI-related goods. “Strong chip and AI demand had masked soft spots in Asian and global economies. But that’s becoming hard to sustain with the Middle East war dragging on for so long, pushing up fuel and food prices,” said Toru Nishihama, chief emerging market economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute in Tokyo. “High inflation is hurting Asian consumption. Intensifying price competition from China is also weighing on rival exporters like Japan and South Korea,” he said. The RatingDog China general manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI), compiled by S&P Global, stood at 52 in October, exceeding the 50-mark that separates growth from contraction but falling from 52.1 in September. The reading followed official data released on Oct 31 showing China’s factory activity shrank in October, marking the third contraction in four months. “The PMIs suggest that China’s economic activity lost momentum in October following September’s pick-up. Manufacturing softened a touch, but foreign demand still looks resilient,” said Nguyen Hoang Nam, China economist at Capital Economics. “More worrying was the sharp reversal in construction activity and expectations, suggesting that firms have become less confident that fiscal support will provide a substantial boost over the rest of the year.” Japan’s PMI eased to 53.3 in October from 54.1 in September, a survey by S&P Global showed, marking the slowest expansion in seven months as output and new orders lost momentum. South Korea’s factory activity grew in October at the slowest pace in eight months on weaker output and demand, with the PMI falling to 51.3 from 53.9 in September. Taiwan’s PMI stood at 54.9 in October, down from 56.7 in September. Other economies showed factory activity expanded in October at a faster pace than the previous month, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia. India’s manufacturing growth slowed in October as domestic demand eased and hiring weakened, though a surge in export orders helped cushion the slowdown. Asia has outperformed many other regions as manufacturers benefitted from brisk demand for chips and AI-related goods. But the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected Asia’s economic growth to moderate in 2027 , and warned of heightening risks from the Iran war-induced energy shock and a potential correction in the AI boom. The IMF said it now expects Asia’s economy to grow 4.8% in 2026 and 4.4% in 2027, higher than projections made in April but still slowing from a 5% expansion in 2025. While Japan has been among the beneficiaries of the AI boom, the central bank warned the technology also poses risks to the country’s long-term economic outlook. “If growth expectations for AI decline substantially, a tightening of global financial conditions, accompanied by a rapid repricing of stocks and a sharp slowdown in the race for AI development, could significantly hurt Japan’s economy through a plunge in exports and production,” it said. events.title: Al Habtoor Group board approves sale of all assets and investments in Lebanon
events.summary: Dubai-based Al Habtoor Group said its board of directors had approved the sale of the company's assets and investments in Lebanon , after it ceased operations there. The company, which has hotels, commercial and residential properties in Lebanon, said in January that it was ceasing operations and would terminate its employees in the country due to "prolonged instability" and an investment dispute. The conglomerate, which made investments across hospitality, retail, leisure, real estate and banking-related activities in Lebanon, said at the time that it suffered losses exceeding $1.7 billion. "Following careful consideration, the board has determined that the complete divestment of the group’s Lebanese assets represents the most appropriate course of action, consistent with its commitment to responsible investment management, capital allocation, and the protection of its interests," Al Habtoor Group said on Monday. The company said it intends to undertake the divestment "through a structured and commercially driven process, with each asset evaluated on its individual merits and transactions pursued in accordance with appropriate market conditions and valuations". In February, Al Habtoor Group said it also appointed law firm White & Case to begin arbitration proceedings against Lebanon in the US. The case is based on the dispute resolution mechanisms provided under the UAE-Lebanon bilateral investment treaty, Al Habtoor Group said at the time. The group established its presence in Lebanon with the opening of its first hotel in 2001. It said it "has made substantial investments" since then and has remained committed to the country through successive periods of economic and political uncertainty. The board’s latest decision "reflects a considered shift" in its investment strategy and its plan to concentrate resources on markets "offering greater long-term stability, investment certainty, and sustainable growth opportunities", it said. Al Habtoor Group will announce further details regarding the divestment process, it added. Lebanon has been mired in an economic crisis since 2019, one of the worst in modern history, according to the World Bank. The lender expects Lebanon's economy to contract by 6.4 per cent in 2026. The country, which is heavily reliant on imports, is also struggling from the fallout of the Iran war, as it is more exposed to shocks such as the disruption to shipping and energy supplies. The International Monetary Fund said last month that it was advancing discussions with Lebanon as part of broader efforts to support vulnerable countries in the Middle East and North Africa.

events.title: Apollo launches $11 billion private credit platform, backed by Abu Dhabi
events.summary: Apollo has launched European Credit Company, a 10 billion euro ($11.2 billion) private credit platform. The platform will lend to companies and finance assets across corporate, asset-backed, infrastructure and real estate markets. Its backers include the Abu Dhabi Investment Council, marking a further push by Apollo into Abu Dhabi's huge wealth pool. Apollo Global Management has launched a European private credit platform with more than 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) of lending capacity, backed by several blue-chip investors, including the Abu Dhabi Investment Council (ADIC). The European Credit Company will invest in performing credit across the large and mid-market sectors, including corporate and asset-backed lending, as well as lending to real-asset owners in infrastructure and real estate. The venture is led by Giacomo Petrobelli, serving as chief executive officer, and Christian Meissner, its chairman. Petrobelli said Apollo's ECC aims to capitalize on a "generational opportunity" to finance Europe's long-term growth agenda using global pools of capital. The venture's backing from ADIC comes a week after Apollo agreed to buy a nearly 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Mubadala Investment Co., Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund. Other strategic partners in the new platform include European insurance group Athora, Japanese lender Norinchukin Bank, Standard Chartered and Aranda Principal Strategies, a U.S. credit investor, Apollo said in an announcement. "We aim to build ECC into a premier pan-European credit platform, focused exclusively on the region, with deep local relationships, differentiated sourcing and flexible solutions that span all credit types," said Petrobelli. "The Global Industrial Renaissance is creating tremendous financing needs around the world that are acutely felt in Europe, whether it's energy transition and transmission, defense, or digital and traditional infrastructure," added Apollo president Jim Zelter.

events.title: US midterms: 1 day to go – Democrats rally around El-Sayed amid attacks
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms Democrats slam Haley Stevens over her endorsement of a Republican candidate a day before the polls. With one day to go before the United States midterm elections , campaigning has reached a fever pitch with Democratic and Republican leaders pulling out all the stops to mobilise voters. Democrats are hoping to flip control of both chambers of Congress, which is currently controlled by US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party. list 1 of 3 US midterms: What to know about independent voters and candidates list 2 of 3 Trump leans into Islamophobia and conspiracy in last-ditch campaign rallies list 3 of 3 Write-In Ralph: South Carolina Republicans challenge Trump’s Senate pick All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are up for grabs on Tuesday. Voting will also be held to elect governors in 36 of the 50 US states. With the cost-of-living crisis, exacerbated by the US-Israel war on Iran, becoming one of the key talking points of these elections, here’s where things stand as of Monday: What’s happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours? In a dramatic political development on Sunday, Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens threw her support behind Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her own party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan – one of the most closely watched races of the US midterm elections. Stevens had lost Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary in August to El-Sayed. Her announcement followed weeks of tension with El-Sayed over US support to Israel, which has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza. El-Sayed has opposed military support to Israel, arguing that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed the US into the Iran war. Stevens has accused El-Sayed of anti-Semitism for his criticism of Israeli actions in Gaza. El-Sayed said a vote for his rival Rogers “is going to be a vote for Donald Trump” as his campaign reportedly saw a fundraising surge after Stevens crossed party lines. Democratic leaders have rallied behind El-Sayed, who has faced Islamophobic attacks during the campaign. The chairman of the Democratic Party in Michigan criticised Stevens. “She does not speak for that larger community,” Curtis Hertel said in an interview with CNN. The leader of the Democrats in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, slammed Stevens over her endorsement of the Republican candidate. “This is a despicable betrayal from Representative Stevens,” he posted on X. “Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors.” Meanwhile, the advocacy group Michigan Jews for Democracy has backed El-Sayed. “Haley Stevens does not speak for Michigan’s Jewish community,” it said in a statement, which rejected her “attempt to divide our community” two days before the election. While Democrats have been angered by Stevens’s action, Trump celebrated her decision. During a rally in Iowa later on Sunday, the US president said he would “love” it if Stevens joined the Republican Party. “Haley said what few people are willing to say,” Trump added. “It’s a thing called bravery.” The question now is whether Stevens’s endorsement could persuade some of her supporters to back Rogers or discourage them from voting altogether. Polling suggested El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support, according to the Reuters news agency. Judge dismisses Trump’s Alaska election lawsuit Meanwhile, a ⁠federal ⁠judge has thrown out a Trump administration ⁠lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from ⁠certifying a loss by Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The administration has argued that a rival on the ballot with the same name could change the outcome. Sullivan pledged to accept the election outcome, days after the US Department of Justice filed a lawsuit seeking to decertify the results of the Senate race if he loses. “I’m going to accept the election results,” Sullivan, an ally of Trump, told CNN on Sunday. Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-up races that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in the upper chamber of the US Congress. How many Americans have already voted? This year, out of about 210 million registered voters, 54.5 million had voted early as of 10am US East Coast time (15:00 GMT) on Sunday, according to a University of Florida analysis. This includes 30 million in-person votes and 24 million mail-in ballots. In the 2022 midterm elections, 46 million people voted early. Early voting enthusiasm has been higher among Democrats this year with more than 11 million registered Democrats having voted early, compared with about 8 million registered Republicans, according to the university’s analysis. Early voting has particularly surged in the state of Texas, a key battleground, where more than 7.7 million people have voted early.

events.title: MLB ‘spot-fixing’ trial set to begin in US court
events.summary: MLB pitchers charged with conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery go on trial in New York. Former Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz go on trial on Monday on charges of accepting bribes after colluding with gamblers who made hundreds of thousands of dollars by betting correctly on individual pitches in Major League Baseball (MLB) in the United States. Their careers and possibly their freedom are at stake in the jury trial expected to unfold over the next month in New York’s Brooklyn federal court. According to an indictment, the pitchers accepted thousands of dollars in payoffs to help two gamblers from their native Dominican Republic win at least $460,000 on in-game prop bets on the speed and outcome of certain pitches. Prosecutors allege that Clase began providing the betters with information about his pitches in 2023 and recruited Ortiz into the scheme in 2025. Ortiz’s lawyers unsuccessfully sought to have him tried separately from Clase. Judge Kiyo A Matsumoto said at a conference last Friday that she hopes to complete jury selection quickly enough that lawyers can deliver relatively short opening statements in the afternoon. Clase, 28, is a three-time All-Star and two-time American League Reliever of the Year who had completed his fourth season of a $20m, five-year contract when charges against the pitchers were revealed in November 2025. Ortiz, 27, had earned $782,600 as a starting pitcher for the Guardians during the 2025 season. The pitchers have been charged with wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy and conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery. Defence lawyers are expected to argue that the pitchers did not collude with gamblers and instead were varying the placement of pitches strategically to fool batters. On Friday, the judge ruled that prosecutors cannot show the jury proof that Clase owed $500,000 in US taxes because they had only provided the evidence to defence lawyers several days earlier and long after a deadline had passed to turn over evidence to their adversaries. A prosecutor had argued that the government wanted to put the evidence in the trial to offset any claim by Clase’s lawyers that he had no incentive to collude with gamblers because he had several million dollars in financial accounts in the Dominican Republic. MLB and the Guardians have said they have fully cooperated with authorities. MLB said it contacted federal law enforcement when it began investigating unusual betting activity.
