events.title: Anthrax outbreak kills hippos in DR Congo’s Virunga National Park
events.summary: Drought and conflict compound the threat to wildlife in eastern DR Congo. Vitshumbi, DR Congo – While the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to grapple with the deadliest Ebola outbreak in its history, another disease is taking a heavy toll on wildlife in Virunga National Park in the country’s east. Over the past four weeks, hippopotamus carcasses have been discovered in the Semuliki River, west of Africa’s oldest national park, raising concern among communities living along its banks. list 1 of 3 Fears grow in DRC as former President Joseph Kabila joins rebellion list 2 of 3 Hamilton calls for Palestine and DR Congo freedom as Rwanda takes F1 spotlight list 3 of 3 Ebola death toll in DR Congo passes 5,000 “It was in mid-September that we began to notice the mass deaths of hippos in the Semuliki River. We have started to fear this situation, which is unfolding whilst we are in the midst of the Ebola outbreak,” Michael Kambale, a resident of the Vitshumbi enclave, about 100 kilometres (62 miles) north of Goma, the capital of North Kivu province, told Al Jazeera. Following laboratory tests, Virunga National Park confirmed that anthrax, caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis, was responsible for the wildlife deaths. According to park officials, 28 hippos died over approximately one month. “This disease can be transmitted to humans through contact with a dead or sick animal or by consuming its meat,” Virunga National Park said in a press release sent to Al Jazeera. Anthrax threatens wildlife and local communities Joel Mbusa Mapoli, an expert in ecology and veterinary medicine, said the deaths represented a significant loss for Virunga National Park and called for urgent action to contain the outbreak. He explained that hippos act as ecosystem engineers, altering nutrient flows and the ecological conditions of their habitats. Virunga National Park said it was focusing on surveillance, the safe management of carcasses and reducing risks to wildlife and local communities. “Teams are monitoring the affected area, recording new cases of mortality and coordinating the safe handling and disposal of carcasses,” the park said. “People living in the affected area and its surroundings are being informed about the outbreak; they are advised not to touch, skin or consume animals found dead, and to report any carcasses or suspected cases to the relevant authorities,” the park added. Founded in 1925, Virunga is Africa’s oldest national park and is renowned for its biodiversity. Olivier Ndoole Bahemuke, a Congolese environmental activist and head of Alerte Congolaise pour l’environnement et les droits de l’homme, a nonprofit organisation operating in the DRC, said the armed conflict that has persisted in the country for nearly three decades had fuelled poaching and deforestation. The park says it has lost control of a significant part of its territory over the past four years because of the ongoing conflict between the Congolese army and M23 fighters. The M23 armed group says it is helping protect the area from poachers and other potential human threats. Drought and recurring anthrax outbreaks Park officials said anthrax outbreaks had previously been observed among hippos and other wild animals in the ecosystem during periods of drought. According to Mapoli, several factors contribute to recurring anthrax outbreaks in Virunga National Park. These include the persistence of the bacterium in the environment, deteriorating ecological and climatic conditions, the concentration of animals around aquatic habitats and difficulties in monitoring wildlife health. “When vegetation becomes scarce, herbivores may graze closer to the ground and congregate around the few remaining grazing areas and water points, thereby increasing their exposure to contaminated soil,” Virunga National Park said in a statement sent to Al Jazeera, adding that the situation was being monitored “closely”. The park’s February 2026 census estimated the hippo population at more than 2,700, distributed across 171 groups. In 2025, an anthrax outbreak killed 65 hippos in Virunga National Park, according to the park’s February 2026 population update. Park staff mobilised excavators to retrieve the carcasses from the water. According to park officials, anthrax can survive for decades in the soil in the form of spores. Protecting hippos means protecting the ecosystem Mapoli said the response to anthrax should combine conservation measures with public health interventions, in line with the One Health principle, an approach that recognises the links between human, animal and environmental health. events.title: Alstom shares plunge after it cuts guidance, plans overhaul in second warning
events.summary: Alstom’s anticipated positive free cash flow was revised to an expected cash burn of €1.5 billion (S$2.1 billion). Alstom cut full-year guidance after delays in German projects hurt margins. It now expects about 1% adjusted Ebit margin and a €1.5 billion cash burn. Problems in Coradia Max orders caused penalties and a “domino effect” across other projects. Chief financial officer Bernard Delpit said the project’s gross margin is now negative. The company will review its organisation, cut costs, and seek about €2 billion of debt reduction through more asset sales. It reports full results on Nov 17 and a capital markets day in 2027. Alstom cut its full-year guidance and announced a deep overhaul after delays in key German projects led to penalties and hurt margins, plunging the French train maker into a fresh crisis. Its stock slumped as much as 27% in early Paris trading on Nov 2, after the company slashed its profit margin, cash flow and train car production targets for the fiscal year. The shares have lost more than half of their value in 2026. Alstom now expects an adjusted Ebit margin of about 1% for the fiscal year, down from 6.5% previously, it said on Nov 2 . An anticipated positive free cash flow was revised to an expected cash burn of €1.5 billion (S$2.1 billion). Alstom also downgraded its train car production target for the period to about 4,000 units from as many 4,500. The latest warning is tied to the Coradia Max orders, a series of projects including regional trains ordered by German states such as Baden-Wurttemberg and Lower Saxony that were meant to be the company’s biggest ramp-up in 2026 . The delays in one of the Coradia Max projects, caused by problems in the final development phases, had a “domino effect” on other German projects, leading to penalties that weighed on margins, chief financial officer Bernard Delpit said on a media call. The Coradia project’s gross margin is now negative, according to Delpit. The problem was detected after chief executive officer Martin Sion, who took the helm in April, sent out teams to deal with struggling projects, Delpit said. The CEO found that “not only were there engineering issues, but the organisation surrounding project management was neither efficient nor effective”, Delpit said. Alstom is now tackling a broader review of its organisation to improve execution and accountability, to lower costs and to make processes simpler. It also will carry out a new plan to slash debt by about €2 billion, which will include further divestments. “We have identified the assets and are beginning the process,” Delpit said on the call, when asked about the group’s possible future divestments. He declined to elaborate on details, saying it was too early. The company already stunned markets in April by withdrawing its financial guidance due to slow progress related to various projects, prompting a share slump. The group has been seeking to shore up its balance sheet after the troubled US$5.5 billion (S$7.03 billion) acquisition of Bombardier’s rail business in 2021. The group’s former CEO, Henri Poupart-Lafarge, had completed a previous €2 billion plan to slash debt. Alstom is due to report full fiscal results on Nov 17 and hold a capital markets day in the second quarter of 2027. BLOOMBERG

events.title: China’s top three airlines head for full-year losses as fuel costs rise
events.summary: China Southern Airlines, which returned to the black in 2025 for the first time since 2019, is set to slip back into the red. China’s top three airlines are heading for full-year losses as surging jet fuel costs, weak domestic fares and typhoon disruptions hit third-quarter results. Air China, China Eastern and China Southern all posted sharp profit falls, with China Southern swinging to a loss and all three losing money in the first nine months of 2026. Analysts said airlines remain under heavy pressure because fuel costs have more than doubled, competition is intense, and profits may stay weak into the fourth quarter. BEIJING – China’s three biggest airlines are on track for full-year losses after posting far weaker third-quarter results than in 2025 as surging jet fuel costs, weak domestic fares and typhoon disruptions hit what is normally their most profitable period. Air China and China Eastern Airlines are heading for a seventh consecutive annual net loss since the Covid-19 pandemic, according to analyst estimates compiled by LSEG. China Southern Airlines, which returned to the black in 2025 for the first time since 2019, is also set to slip back into the red, the estimates showed. Air China’s third-quarter net profit fell 92.6% from a year earlier to 270.6 million yuan (S$52 million). China Eastern posted a net profit of 64 million yuan for the quarter, down 98.2% from 2025. China Southern swung to a third-quarter net loss of 609 million yuan from a net profit of 3.84 billion yuan in 2025. All three airlines reported losses for the first nine months of 2026, a period in which they were profitable in 2025. The third quarter, which covers the peak summer travel season, is traditionally the strongest for Chinese airlines and set a high base for year-on-year comparisons. But all three carriers said the steep rise in jet fuel prices had a negative impact on their results. The price of jet fuel has more than doubled since the United States and Israel launched a military campaign against Iran in late February. Chinese airlines hedge far less of their fuel than many Asian and European peers, leaving them more exposed to swings in oil prices. Domestic fares were weak in the third quarter amid intense competition, including from high-speed rail. Huatai Securities estimated Air China’s yields, a proxy for airfares, fell 5% during the period, leaving it unable to recoup higher fuel costs. “Chinese airlines are expected to remain in net loss into the seasonally weaker fourth quarter given the impact of spiking jet fuel,” said Nathan Gee, head of Asia-Pacific transport research at BofA Global Research. Gee said third-quarter earnings had come in slightly better than “very low expectations”. Checks suggested domestic fares were rising at double-digit rates year-on-year after the October Golden Week holiday, as airlines kept a lid on capacity. But fuel “remains the big headwind”, he said. “Chinese airline margin remains under extreme pressure from spiking jet fuel and soft consumption demand,” Gee added. Airlines are trying to boost flying hours per plane to control costs, but big cost cuts will be difficult, he said.

events.title: The ‘haunted’ housing market’s real problem may be too few people, not too few homes, says J.P. Morgan’s David Kelly
events.summary: “The housing market is haunted,” according to David Kelly, the chief global strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. He lists the ghosts in his widely read Oct. 26 research note: more than a decade of too-easy money, tariffs, and immigration policies that raise the cost of building homes while limiting the number of people who need them, and a Fed whose rate swings hit housing harder than almost anything else. The one that should get the most attention is the people who aren’t showing up. Kelly said he expects U.S. population growth of just 800,000 a year over the next few years. With an average household of about 2.5 people, he writes, that “implies a demographic need for just 320,000 new housing units per year,” compared with roughly 1 million per year in the first two decades of this century. That cuts against the story most Americans have heard about housing: that the country simply hasn’t built enough. Zillow estimated in July the U.S. was about 4.7 million homes short as of 2024, based on how many families are doubled up with unrelated people compared with how many homes sit vacant for rent or sale. Kelly’s read is that the country is “still in a situation of net excess supply.” Thursday’s GDP report bore that out, Kelly told Fortune by email. Homebuilding fell again in the third quarter, “marking the 8th decline in residential construction in the last 10 quarters.” But “the homebuilding decline is still relatively modest compared to the very fast increase in AI-related capital spending,” he said. Where the people went In the first 20 years of this century, Kelly wrote, the U.S. population grew by an average of 2.4 million people a year—about 1.5 million from births minus deaths and about 900,000 from net immigration. The natural increase peaked at 520,000 in 2025, he writes, and has likely resumed a steady decline as the population ages and birth rates fall. Immigration swung harder. Net international migration fell to 1.3 million in the year through July 2025 from 2.7 million a year earlier, and the Census Bureau projected it would be about 321,000 by July 2026 if trends continued. Kelly estimated that deportations are now almost canceling out legal net immigration, which is still positive but smaller. He said he expects that to hold “regardless of the outcome of the midterm elections,” because enforcement is largely up to the administration, and Congress and the White House are unlikely to agree on an immigration reform bill. The empty-house signs Kelly pointed to vacancies. Over the past four years, he writes, the rental vacancy rate rose from 5.6% to 7.3%, and the homeowner vacancy rate from 0.8% to 1.2%. Census figures released Wednesday put rental vacancy at 7.6% in the third quarter, up from 7.1% a year earlier. Between the second quarter of 2024 and the second quarter of 2026, he writes, the housing stock grew by about 2.8 million units. Buyers have thinned out. The National Association of Home Builders’ measure of buyer traffic fell to 18 in October, its lowest level since April 2012 excluding the start of the pandemic, and 43% of builders cut prices. Kelly expects housing starts of 1.32 million this year, the weakest since 2019, falling to 1.24 million in 2027. Others see demand cooling, too. Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies said in June that household growth “has slowed sharply” and that reduced immigration is expected to dampen housing demand further. A Mortgage Bankers Association white paper projects 8.6 million new households from 2025 to 2035, down from 10.1 million in 2010 to 2020. The anomaly Fewer buyers haven’t meant cheaper mortgages. The 30-year fixed rate averaged 7.32% last week, according to Freddie Mac . Kelly notes that’s below its 50-year average of 7.68%. From January 2008 to December 2021, the rate averaged just 4.15%. “It is important to recognize that this period was the anomaly, rather than today,” he writes, and there’s “little reason to believe that mortgage rates will fall much below 7.0%” without a recession. Kelly said he expects the Fed to raise rates in December and thinks weak housing could make that the last hike of this cycle. What would change his mind, he told Fortune , is if “wage growth suddenly picked up,” or if inflation expectations priced into Treasury inflation-protected securities “were to rise significantly.” Builders are squeezed from both sides. Construction workers are hard to find, Kelly writes, and wages in the industry are rising faster than elsewhere, partly because of the swing in immigration and partly because data-center construction is competing for the same workers. Tariffs and the same infrastructure boom have pushed up the cost of materials. Kelly told Fortune it’s hard to put a number on how much the AI boom is adding to the cost of building a home. But spending on data centers rose 73% in the year through August, to an annual rate of $85 billion, he said, and “it is likely that the resource squeeze from data centers will intensify in 2027.” The ghosts are hardest on the young. Homeownership has fallen since 2022, Kelly writes, “with a much sharper recent decline for those under age 35.” He calls it a decline that is “postponing the reasonable aspirations of young people to be able to marry, settle down and build a family in their own home.” Asked whether that drop is mostly about mortgage rates, Kelly pointed elsewhere. “I think it is a combination of tougher lending standards and the reality that older households have had more of a chance to accumulate a bigger down payment,” he said. His forecast in the note: Housing “remains haunted for now with many personal housing nightmares to be endured.” Generative AI was used for research assistance and/or transcription of this article. events.title: Shift Left Is Becoming A System-Level Problem
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Shift left is pushing beyond verification to system-level validation. Fragmented workflows with disconnected tools and models are allowing bugs to escape even though individual components have been verified. AgenticAI may improve coordination across disciplines, identify bottlenecks, and optimizetool usage, but it cannot replace fundamental processes such as simulation and emulation. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss why shift left is pushing beyond verification to system-level validation, and where AI can and cannot help, with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys ; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one of this discussion, click here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv. SE: The focus of shift left in design has largely been about verification. But increasingly it’s also about validation, right? Darbari : Yes, and it’s influencing huge decisions that could make small companies go bankrupt if they get it wrong. We’ve seen meetings with architects, designers, UVM leads, emulation leads, FPGA and software leads, and VPs, where they’re all looking at bug escapes and asking, ‘Why did this happen?’ The architect is saying, ‘It’s supposed to be this.’ The designer is saying, ‘We didn’t know that.’ The software team says, ‘It’s supposed to be this.’ And we’re sitting there as formal verification people thinking about communication and the model not being accurate, and I don’t know how well we’ll be able to solve this unless we bring the software into the development cycle. Schirrmeister : It’s not only software. It’s all the other aspects, like multi-physics. EM, thermal, and mechanical, which all have to be integrated. To look at this differently, there are hurdles that I cannot fix in this project. But perhaps I can fix it in the next one. It’s a labyrinth. We have models that are digital twins that are irrefutable, because we’ve measured them against the real thing. We can’t overcome those. We are dependent on the application. It may be more vertical, it may be more horizontally stacked to fit into a certain form factor, like a phone or a data center. But it’s like a video game where you have these things popping up. I want to package it this way, but the packaging guy says we can’t do that, at least not today. Maybe a year from now. All of this needs to be taken into consideration as part of your model. Dabari : Absolutely correct. Laviv : Shrinking times for packaging or power estimation or simulation, or even emulation — isn’t that something we could look at? We’re shifting left using AI in order to do stuff earlier. Berg : Verification traditionally has been the longest and most expensive part of doing a design, and it would be nice to say we can take everything and shift it all left. There are chunks that are being shifted left and verified, and that’s good. But how to shift everything left is something we’re still learning. Darbari : If we pick up historical data from packaging and thermal, why can’t we start building models to say, ‘This happened last time. This time it could be done better.’ Berg : You can do that based on inference. Darbari : But we don’t have a tool that ties everything together in one frame. ‘This is the model of functional safety, security, power, packaging, thermals. Go build it.’ Berg : We have different aspects of that, and we, as an industry, are working slowly but surely to integrate all of those. But we don’t have a single workflow that does that. And it really is a workflow, not just a single tool. Laviv : Nowadays, with AI knowing everything with its skills and touching everything, there is kind of a common database for verification and emulation and all the physical stuff. It might benefit customers if they have access to everything is there to be used, potentially even cross-companies. Schirrmeister : There are certain things you can shift left, and others you have to wait for. Certain things are irrefutable. Yes, you can make them faster, but you can’t bypass them. You can be smarter about how you use them. You can figure out which things should be done in emulation, which should be done in simulation, and which should be done with FPGA-based prototyping. We have customers telling us that if they find something in simulation that should have been found in formal, or simulation beforehand, they’ll review why that happened. Laviv : Why not look at bottlenecks in formal, in verification, in emulation, and see if you can handle those bottlenecks in a way that would open the flow for faster AI? Schirrmeister : There are two views here on this whole AI stack. I’m a firm believer that the underlying portions of the stack will still be required. They will be used in different ways by the AI objects, but you don’t take away the characterization, the simulation, the emulation. You get smarter about how to use them. But at the end of the day, you need to build the emulator. That takes some time. You need to get the design into it. And there is a certain number of things which you cannot overcome. You can make the tool flow more productive, but the underlying engines still need to execute, and there are limits to how fast they can become. Darbari : We need to put all of these things in a singular context because if the manufacturing, or the physics, the heat, or the functional, are all sitting in separate context windows, and the software is sitting somewhere else, then you don’t have a complete picture of what this whole device will look like. I was coding for one project and I remember asking a designer, ‘What would happen to this processor if there was more than one outstanding transaction? Could you discard the later ones?’ And he said, ‘We’ll just discard them.’ Everything was exhaustively proved, and while I was taping, the software teams were running their own stuff. But a bug got missed. The software team had a completely different understanding of how they were going to drive the SoC. So they found a trace, and they said, ‘We are losing transactions.’ There was a complete misalignment between what the architect and the designer thought they were building, so they had to patch it at the end of the day. events.title: Putting AI To The Test
events.summary: There are an increasing number of new EDA companies these days, and this is great news. The industry needs some new vitality, new thought leaders, people willing to take risks. The same goes for established companies that cannot go outside their existing comfort zone while meeting next quarter’s financial goals. But sometimes, new startups forget the risks associated with semiconductor design. While they may be able to point to an improvement in time to market, or meeting better performance goals, they fail to understand how small that particular step is in the whole process. Today, a number of companies want us to believe that AI can do everything. Some point the way to automating design, others to verification, and some even claim it can do both at the same time, from the same source material. No, it can’t. While some of it may be possible in the future, it is far from that point today. What many of them fail to do is show proof. One example, one design, one piece of IP is not proof. When verifying any new tool or methodology, you always need to hold back a test set to apply at the end. In this case, with AI, it has to be something it has never seen before, never been trained on. That is the only thing that can provide a fair, unbiased result. As soon as you tweak your tool to do well on that test case, it is no longer a true test. This is why I was delighted to receive communications from Vikash Kumar, senior verification architect at Arm. He has 15+ years of semiconductor industry experience and is the author of the book “AI-Assisted Hardware Verification: Cognitive Verification Architecture with the VEGA Framework.” What he shared with me was his independent work on the quality of existing LLMs for the creation of testbenches. More than 20 years ago, Certess introduced the industry to mutation analysis. If you inject a bug into the design, does the testbench find it? They used the traditional stuck-at fault model and sophisticated statistical analysis to reduce the total number of faults required. The results were a slap across the face to many companies that thought they were doing a good job, only to find out how poor their testbenches were. Vikash’s approach is different. “The setup was simple — hand AI a spec and the RTL, tell it to verify and report back when it is confident the design is clean, and check what it actually found. I hand-seeded realistic, design-representative functional bugs, which keeps the ground truth clean. I know exactly which bugs were planted, so detection is measured against a known set rather than an impression.” I asked Vikash why he chose to insert bugs rather than using the stuck-at model, which has been the industry go-to since the ’80s. “The whole question with AI verification is whether it comprehends design intent well enough to catch the subtle, intent-level bugs, and that is exactly where it struggled — the misses clustered in data-path, encoding logic, and functional corners, not in anything a stuck-at pattern would have flagged.” He started with 25 hand-coded designs spanning bus protocols, DMA engines, ECC memory, control and peripheral logic, and concurrency scenarios. The RTL has never been made public. Into those he inserted 806 bugs. The models were given a specification based on published protocol standards. Three frontier AI models were chosen: Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.4, and GLM-5.2. “Without human intervention or predefined time limits, each model generated testbenches, developed coverage goals, executed simulations, identified and corrected RTL defects, and iteratively refined verification until independently declaring sign-off. All defects were seeded upfront, although some became observable only after earlier corrections.” Here are his key findings: Claude Opus 5 detected 79.2% of seeded defects, GPT-5.4 detected 76.2%, and GLM-5.2 detected 62.8%. Even the highest-performing model missed 20.8% of seeded defects, which is approximately 168 bugs. All three models reached 100% of their self-defined verification goals and declared sign-off despite remaining functional defects. In this audit, particularly high miss rates were observed in ECC memory, GPIO, and AXI DMA designs. Some missed defects involved ambiguous specifications. The agents proceeded without requesting clarification and ultimately declared verification complete. Even the best model, Claude Opus 5, did not detect roughly 168 defects. GPT-5.4 missed about 192, and GLM-5.2 missed close to 300. Perhaps even worse is that Vikash ran each model three times, and each run produced different results. But he is very optimistic about the results. “The impressive part is how much AI caught on its own,” he says. “The important part is how much it missed, and that’s where the engineer still matters.” In a similar manner, ChipAgents just released its new build-a-chip-bench tool. It goes from a workload specification to GSD. The company ranked five models. The best, Claude Fable 5.1 achieved a score of 16.6%, whilst the bottom of the pack was GLM-5.3 with a score of zero. These results look dire, but the biggest failure was their lack of understanding of performance constraints. I believe this will be an even bigger problem when it comes to writing software that has to be cognizant of the underlying hardware and its performance beyond raw speed. Real-time systems deployed within physical AI need predictable latency, at low power, over a broad range of operating conditions. None of this data is available for training today. I will finish with another comment Vikash made: “You can automate the work of verification. You cannot automate the responsibility for it.” The post Putting AI To The Test appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: Investor scrutiny of the AI spending boom is rising, but Big Tech is unlikely to give up
events.summary: Given that the bulk of chip manufacturing capacity is in Asia, the AI boom’s fate has the potential to redefine the region’s economic outlook. Investor scrutiny is rising over Big Tech’s huge AI spending. Alphabet fell 13% after reporting US$51.4 billion capex and negative free cash flow, despite 25% revenue growth. Big Tech says it must keep buying compute and chips to stay competitive. Scaling Laws, custom silicon and lower compute costs are driving more data centre and chip investment. Asia’s chip exporters are watching closely because AI demand supports trade and growth. Analysts say spending should stay high, with supply still tighter than demand and more sell-offs possible. SINGAPORE – As tech titans continue pouring massive amounts of money into data centres and equipping them with ever more expensive chips, growing investor scrutiny on the AI build-out is pulling down stock prices and pushing up borrowing costs. The selling pressure isn’t just pounding hard on Big Tech; their most consequential partners in the global AI supply chain, semiconductor chipmakers, have also suffered. Hence, investors and policymakers in Asia’s top chip-exporting nations, including Singapore, are watching Wall Street’s attempt to reset the AI trade with measured trepidation. The International Monetary Fund recently noted that global trade rose 8.3% between 2023 and 2025 – a figure that would be closer to 4.6%, or nearly half, without AI-related products. The Monetary Authority of Singapore’s latest Macroeconomic Review said Singapore’s technology-related sectors accounted for around 75% of overall year on year GDP growth in the third quarter of 2026. On the face of it, the question investors are asking seems plain: Can Big Tech can afford the AI buildout? The market evidently doesn’t think so. Google’s parent, Alphabet, for instance, saw its stock drop by as much as 13% , erasing US$500 billion (S$639 billion) in market capitalisation, following its third-quarter 2026 earnings report released on Oct 28. Even as Alphabet posted strong revenue growth of 25% and a doubling of Google Cloud revenue, its stock was hammered after it reported US$9 billion in negative free cash flow, driven by a massive US$51.4 billion in capital expenditure, mostly on AI infrastructure. Free cash flow is the money left with a company after paying day-to-day operations and maintaining or expanding physical assets. So why aren’t companies that are leading the charge on AI giving in to the demand for fiscal discipline? For tech firms investing in AI infrastructure, including computing and memory chips, sufficient compute capacity is a must. This capacity is the single most important driver of AI capability, speed and competitive advantage. In the tech world, the concept is known as Scaling Laws. A framework of predictable mathematical relationships in AI that shows how a large language model’s performance improves – it gets smarter and makes fewer mistakes – as the resources driving it increase over time. According to the Center for Governance of AI, a non-profit research organisation, compute capacity is also the primary gatekeeper of AI diffusion, acting as the bridge that transforms elite lab research into affordable, ubiquitous commercial tools. Economic experts refer to this process as compute deflation, which reflects the rapid, sustained drop in the cost per unit of processing power, memory and AI inference. As the falling cost of compute replaces the cost of labour and production, it exerts downward pressure on the general price of software and tech-enabled services. That’s why some AI hyperscalers are also designing their own high-performance AI accelerator chips – specialised semiconductor hardware designed to process AI, machine learning, and deep-tech learning workloads much faster and more efficiently than standard chips. Big Tech is also investing in chips The shift towards custom silicon is reshaping the entire cloud computing industry. To break free from Nvidia’s hardware monopoly and drastically lower operational costs, all major cloud hyperscalers – including Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure – have aggressively built out their own proprietary chips. Alphabet disclosed in its third-quarter earnings report that more than 100 significant Google Cloud customers – including Anthropic and Apple – are now running AI using Google’s own tensor processing units, an alternative to Nvidia’s AI chips. Consumer tech platforms are also designing custom silicon – Meta’s MTIA, or Meta Training and Inference Accelerator, chip family, for instance – to power their internal AI tools and ad engines. This competition in semiconductor chips and devices aims to break old hardware monopolies and force down pricing.

events.title: Nine big oil firms on track to share more than $95bn profit two quarters in a row
events.summary: Windfall for oil corporations such Saudi Aramco and BP comes on back of soaring fuel prices driven by Iran war The world’s biggest oil companies are on track to amass profits of more than $95bn (£71bn) in the third quarter as the war in the Middle East drives up the price of fossil fuels. The windfall war profits have sparked calls for oil corporations such as Saudi Aramco and BP to pay for environmental damage and help the world transition towards renewable energy. Analysis by the investment broker AJ Bell has found that nine of the biggest listed oil producers are on course to make more than $95bn in the three months to the end of September. The windfall came seven months after the US-Israel war on Iran caused a surge in global oil prices to highs above $126 a barrel , and followed a second quarter in which the same businesses made $96bn in profit. The companies have used the biggest disruption of fossil fuel supplies in the market’s history to bolster their profits, with campaigners warning that millions of households are left to pay the price in higher bills and climate chaos. Saudi Arabia’s state-owned Aramco is expected to top the profits chart for the third quarter. Analysts anticipate the $1.7tn company to report a 7% increase in its quarterly net income to $30bn, even though it was targeted by Iran-backed Houthi forces. Aramco’s fossil fuel production has made it responsible for more carbon emissions than any company in history , according to the database Carbon Majors, followed by Chevron and ExxonMobil, with Shell and BP also in the top 10. The London-listed BP published its results for the July to September period last week, reporting quarterly profits of $8.46bn – its biggest since 2008. The industry’s profits have been driven higher by refining divisions, which have capitalised on higher prices and made up for a supply shortfall after the Iran war in hit shipments through the strait of Hormuz. The big oil companies “are raking in enormous profits while millions of people struggle to afford their energy bills and the planet burns”, said Mike Childs, of the campaign group Friends of the Earth. “Instead of investing in cheap, homegrown renewables that would drive down bills, strengthen energy security and create new jobs, the fossil fuel industry is fighting for permission to extract even more oil and gas. This would further lock us into a polluting energy system that is driving climate breakdown and exposing communities to extreme heat, flooding and storms.” Childs added: “We need an energy system that works for people, not one that rewards polluters and leaves the public footing the bill. Ministers must act now to decisively accelerate the transition to renewables, make our homes more energy efficient and end our reliance on volatile fossil fuel markets. And those polluters making billions from the current system must be forced to contribute more to build the cleaner, cheaper energy system we urgently need.” Robin Wells, the director of the climate activism organisation Fossil Free London, questioned why the UK government continued to subsidise an industry that was making billions in profit each quarter. “The oil lobby is pushing hard right now for more drilling, even adopting the tactics of grassroots campaigners by holding banners in Parliament Square,” he said. “As they rake in billions they want billions more in tax breaks to develop Rosebank – an oilfield that won’t lower our energy bills by a single penny, because the oil will be exported and sold for the profit of a select few shareholders.” The UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is weighing up whether to allow drilling in the Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea after approving a licence for the less controversial Jackdaw gasfield in October. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Experts estimate Rosebank could emit 1m additional tonnes of carbon dioxide a year by 2042, against an overall projected UK target of 90m tonnes. A decision to approve the oilfield would be met with dismay from climate campaigners and some Labour backbenchers who view it as a step away from prioritising net zero. Shell and Saudi Aramco declined to comment. A spokesperson for BP pointed to comments from its chief executive, Meg O’Neill, at an industry event this year, in which she highlighted the company’s role in responding to the global energy crisis, ensuring supply of diesel and jet fuel. A spokesperson for Eni said: “[Its profits are a result] of an effective operational and financial management model that first of all enables the company to develop new hydrocarbon resources to meet global demand, which continues to structurally rely on oil and gas to ensure energy security and affordable energy for households and the industries.” They added that Eni had expanded its energy transition business, including renewables.

events.title: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack
events.summary: Published 2 November 2026, 00:26 GMT Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history. The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets. Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack . The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack. Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion." There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added. Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance. The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack. Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed. Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back. "We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme. "The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added. AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened Published 22 October The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them. The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets. Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions. The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue. Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said. Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices. Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally. events.title: MAS sets aside $30m to help insurers build expertise in funding major projects
events.summary: MAS is also proposing changes to the capital insurers must set aside against investment risks, reducing requirements for investments where the risks justify this. MAS will set aside $30 million to help insurers build skills in financing major projects such as power grids and data centres, using funds from the Financial Sector Development Fund. It also plans lower capital rules for some project investments, if risks are lower. The public consultation runs from Nov 2 to Dec 18. At the Singapore reinsurance conference, industry players launched a data centre insurance scheme and an AI risk handbook, showing new growth areas and new risk concerns. SINGAPORE – The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will set aside $3 0 million to help insurers build expertise in investing in major projects such as power grids and data centres. The central bank is also proposing changes to the capital insurers must set aside against investment risks, reducing requirements for investments where the risks justify this. Minister for National Development Chee Hong Tat announced the measures o n No v 2 at the 2 2nd Singapore International Reinsurance Conference at Sands Expo and Convention Centre. The event, organised by the Singapore Reinsurers’ Association (SRA), drew more than 4, 300 delegates representing 85 countries and territories, according to the association. Reinsurers provide insurance to insurance companies. Chee, who is also MAS deputy chairman, said insurers could play a bigger role in financing Asia’s growth, alongside protecting businesses and communities against risks. The $30 million, from the Financia l Secto r Development Fund , will help defray the costs of building dedicated investment teams, training staff and engaging professional services to establish and expand these investment activities in Singapore. Across ASEAN, more than U S$200 billion (S$256 billion) is needed annually for projects ranging from roads and ports to renewable energy and telecommunications networks, Chee said. Yet, past studies put such investments at only around 1 % to 2% of insurers’ assets, although this share has been growing. “High-quality infrastructure assets can generate stable, long-term cash flows that align well with insurers’ long-dated liabilities, particularly those of life insurers,” Chee said. This means income from these projects can help insurers meet payments owed to policyholders years later. MAS proposes extending lower capital requirements to qualifying debt investments in these projects that have credit ratings, subject to conditions. Investments with features that reduce risk, such as stable contractual revenues, could qualify for further reductions. MAS also proposes lower requirements for certain rated investments backed by pools of assets, subject to conditions including repayment priority, ease of trading and structural safeguards. The public consultation runs from Nov 2 to Dec 18. Chee said industry players are developing a Singapore-based insurance facility for data centres, with US $200 million in initial capacity. An insurance facility is a pre-arranged agreement where several insurers join their underwriting ability to cover particular types of risks. Participants include MSIG, Gallagh er Re, SCOR, Samsung Re and the Cybersecurity Association Singapore. The facility is expected to cover construction, operational, supply chain, design and cyber risks. Separately, SRA launched a handbook at the conference to help reinsurers assess risks associated with artificial intelligence. The guide addresses issues including the reliability of data and AI decisions, dependence on external providers, and how AI affects decisions on insurance coverage and claims. Minister for National Development and deputy chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore Chee Hong Tat speaking at the Singapore International Reinsurance Conference on Nov 2. SRA ch airman Glen Rid dell said: “AI is creating new opportunities across the insurance value chain, while also introducing new considerations for the risks insurers and reinsurers assume.” Reinsurers need to understand how AI affects the risks they cover and claims outcomes, he said. “This handbook provides practical, principles-based guidance to help reinsurers assess these considerations and incorporate them into reinsurance decision-making.” The conference runs until Nov 5, with discussions covering geopolitical and economic shifts, disaster protection and the skills needed as technology changes the insurance industry.

events.title: What to look for if you’re buying a smart lock in the UK
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . More people are fitting keyless devices to their front door – but are they worth it and do they affect your insurance? A s the nights draw in, thoughts turn to home security. A growing number of British homeowners are choosing to upgrade their front doors with tech-enabled “keyless” smart locks, which allow them to be opened by phone, fob, fingerprint or a number pad. But you need to make sure you have the right lock for the door – and that your insurance isn’t invalidated by installing it. They allow you to get into your home without a key, instead using a code, a phone, a fingerprint, a voice assistant such as Siri or facial recognition to give you entry. Some can be operated remotely via wifi so that if a tradesman calls to do work, you can let them in wherever you are. Many offer a combination of several options. In South Korea, and some Scandinavian countries, they are becoming the norm, says Steffan George of the Master Locksmiths Association (MLA), a UK trade body. In the UK they are more common on offices, but interest is increasing. The types vary in complexity. Some have the smart feature and a handle in one unit that fully replaces an existing door handle. Others are made up of a small unit which can be fitted on an existing lock, sitting on top of it, opening the door when activated. This type essentially turns a traditional lock into a smart one. And there is a third type where the existing mechanical lock cylinder is swapped for an electronic one, which opens the lock once activated. Some allow for a physical key to be used in an emergency. They range from less than £100 to well over £1,000. Shane Hales, of HalesLocks in Sidcup, Kent, puts the starting price for a good quality version at between £200 and £250 for the unit. Getting a professional to fit them will add to the cost. Look out for the Kitemark on the faceplate to ensure that it meets security requirements set by theBritish Standards Institution. Sold Secure, an agency which judges the performance of locks, has a certification called SS504 . To qualify, locks are tested for physical security, technical performance and cybersecurity. Hales highlights the Black X (about £200) and the Ultion Nuki (£339) as two well-regarded units. George says that a smart lock is unlikely to last as long as a traditional one, which “will last 20 years easily with just a little bit of lubrication”. Hales adds that, in his experience, smart locks will last for five to six years before they need to be replaced . In the UK front doors are made from a variety of materials, including UPVC, timber, and a composite of different types. Checking the lock works with whatever type of door you have is vital. Many US imports will be unsuitable for British doors because of differences in the locking cylinders. Lots of lockmakers have guides on their websites so you can check whether their product would work for your home. For example, Yale has a “smart lock compatibility checker” which uses a visual guide on what your lock looks like to recommend options. You can email in pictures of your existing fitting and door to some installers and manufacturers, and they will advise what is suitable. Retrofit smart locks are usually installed on the inside of the door and work with the existing cylinder – the barrel in which you insert the key. They have a motorised unit inside which connects to the lock and turns it open. To install one yourself, you will need basic tools. Most people will also want to choose a lock that has been designed to be easy to install, with no modifications needed to the door itself. Things get more complicated when wiring, drilling or carpentry is needed to get the lock to fit properly, or if the door you have is UPVC, composite or non-standard. Checkatrade, the tradespeople’s recommendation site, says installation costs vary; it puts the labour at between £63 for a basic keypad lock and £210 for a Z-wave-enabled lock, a communication system similar to Bluetooth and wifi. If you are considering getting a smart lock, it is important to run it by your home insurer to be sure that what you buy adheres to its standards. The Association of British Insurers (ABI) says you should check the terms of your policy before making any changes. “Some home insurers have specific requirements for the type of lock you use to protect your home, and your provider will be able to advise you,” says its general insurance policy adviser, Charlie Inwood. Your insurer may also require that the lock is put in by a professional. Hales says people should always get professional advice. “There is no one size that fits all doors. For that lock to be compliant, it needs to fit properly, and if it’s not fitted properly, then you know you could leave yourself open to problems.”

events.title: Billionaire Sergey Brin is building political infrastructure that will last beyond his $102 million fight against Prop 40
events.summary: Google cofounder Sergey Brin spent much of his career on the sidelines of electoral politics. But a proposed California wealth tax has turned the billionaire into one of the state’s most powerful political financiers, prompting him to build an organization that can continue shaping state policy long after voters decide on the measure that initially mobilized him. Brin has contributed $102 million to Building a Better California, a political organization that has become the central vehicle for Silicon Valley billionaires seeking to influence California’s political direction. The group has raised hundreds of millions of dollars from wealthy tech executives, venture capitalists and business leaders—channeling money into ballot measures that extend beyond the immediate fight against Proposition 40 . Of that amount, approximately $118.5 million went toward opposing Proposition 40, while the other $186 million supported Propositions 41 and 42, according to Capital & Main .  Proposition 41 would bar the state from exempting new taxes from its spending limit and require state audits of programs funded by new special taxes, making it harder for the state to use funds raised by the billionaire tax. Proposition 42 would outlaw retroactive taxation, directly countering Proposition 40. The strategy gives the ultrawealthy opponents multiple opportunities to defeat the measure: If either one gets more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, the Legislative Analyst’s Office says, the wealth tax could be stopped even if a majority of voters approve it. And according to an analysis by Politico , more than 70 current and former California billionaires had directed a record $612 million into state elections during the 2026 cycle. Nearly half of that money went toward groups working to defeat Proposition 40 and at least 30 billionaires had contributed more than $293 million specifically to the wealth tax fight, according to the analysis. Building a Better California also endorsed Propositions 1, 3, 37, 41 and 42, according to its policy platform. It also put $10 million behind Proposition 45, a separate measure addressing California’s environmental review process, and $6 million behind Proposition 37, which would create a $25 billion homebuyer loan fund, according to Capital & Main . The ballot measure that awakened the billionaire beast The immediate catalyst for the ultrawealthy movement was Proposition 40, a proposed one-time tax on the wealth of California billionaires that will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot. The measure would impose a 5% tax on the assets of individuals and certain trusts worth more than $1 billion who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026. The proposal is designed to raise money to offset federal healthcare funding cuts, with 90% of the proceeds allocated to healthcare and the remaining 10% directed toward education and food assistance. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the tax, spread across several years. The proposal was sponsored by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which argued that California needs additional funding to protect its healthcare system as federal cuts threaten coverage for residents. The ballot measure is also backed by progressive leaders Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). For Brin, whose fortune is estimated at $231 billion by Bloomberg, the potential financial exposure is substantial—and he has been particularly vocal about his opposition. In an interview with The New York Times in April, he compared the proposal to the socialism he experienced growing up in the Soviet Union—saying he did not want California to end up in the same place. He also relocated to Nevada in December, ahead of the Jan. 1 cutoff date that determines which billionaires would be subject to the proposed tax. But rather than leave California’s political fight behind, Brin organized a coordinated campaign to prevent the measure from becoming law. Sergey Brin did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune . In January, Brin established Building a Better California—contributing an initial $20 million. By August, his contributions had reached $102 million, according to campaign finance filings. The organization has since become a major coordinating point for wealthy tech executives. Other major contributors include Kleiner Perkins chairman John Doerr, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison and former Sequoia Capital partner Michael Moritz. events.title: AI is coming to construction sites. But does it make workers safer?
events.summary: AI is cutting paperwork and flagging hazards on construction sites, but researchers say evidence that the technology prevents injuries remains limited. Software firm FYLD says customers have reported reductions of up to 48% in serious worksite injuries and incidents. But researchers say evidence that AI prevents workplace injuries remains limited, even as Britain’s construction death count fell last year. When Shelley Copsey was appointed by the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan, one of the world's biggest infrastructure investors, her job was to find ways to use technology to solve problems across its portfolio. She quickly learned that there were persistent problems facing front-line workers. Four years later, Copsey is CEO of FYLD, a London-headquartered software company that uses artificial intelligence to support workers in construction, utilities and infrastructure. It comes as AI plays an increasingly important role in some of the most physically demanding jobs, from maintaining roads and railways to working on construction sites. The aim is to reduce both paperwork — and accidents. According to Copsey, when fieldwork goes wrong, attention usually turns to budgets or cash flow. "We always go to the back office and we're like: oh, if we could help them forecast the job better, maybe this wouldn't be a problem," she told CNBC. "I think that what nobody ever did was just sit and say: well, what goes on in those field workers' lives and how do we make the life of the front line easier?" FYLD uses AI to predict which permits a project will need, helping workers avoid delays. Previously, workers often arrived at a site without all of the information they needed, Copsey said. The system can also help crews plan around the weather, for example, rescheduling heavy lifting from a day when strong winds are forecast. Workers record short videos describing their day's tasks and safety concerns. AI analyzes the information to help workers and managers anticipate potential problems. An additional benefit is a reduction in paperwork, according to Copsey. Field workers can spend around 20% to 25% of their time on site on administrative work, she said, whereas now, photos, video and job information can be used to generate draft reports, reducing a task that previously took around half an hour to two or three minutes. Infrastructure services provider Amey announced in March that it would roll FYLD out to 2,500 field workers as it looks to improve safety and give supervisors real-time visibility of work on the ground. Copsey said FYLD case studies have reported reductions in incidents and injuries of as much as 48%. AI is also being used to reduce the need for physical infrastructure inspections. Nathan Marsh, London-based senior vice president for Europe, the Middle East and Africa at U.S. software company Bentley Systems, told CNBC that the company's road maintenance platform, Blyncsy, analyzes images captured by drivers to spot problems, including damaged guardrails, overgrown vegetation and debris. "Applying AI to existing imagery provides complete asset coverage in a fraction of the time a conventional survey would take," Marsh said. Steven Elsham, U.K.-based CEO of Dutch maintenance software company Ultimo, told CNBC its AI tools can flag safety incidents that might otherwise go unreported. The system scans work orders and shift logs for signs of incidents, then drafts a report for a person to review. Elsham gave the example of a warehouse door with damage that suggested it had been struck by a forklift. "People should still report things themselves," he said. "This is there for what gets missed." Waleed Umer, an assistant professor at Northumbria University, England, told CNBC that many studies so far have focused on what models can detect, rather than whether they prevent harm. Construction sites change constantly, making it difficult for cameras to capture every hazard, he said. He also warned that false alarms can lead workers to ignore warnings, while overreliance on AI can create a false sense of security. Billy Hare, a professor of construction management at Glasgow Caledonian University, Scotland, told CNBC that research projects and pilot studies have primarily focused on productivity gains, often assuming that less exposure to hazards means lower risks. Bentley Systems, for example, said one rail project it supported cut physical site visits by 50% and manual surveys by 70% using a digital twin, a virtual model of a physical asset. It's reasonable to assume that less time spent in hazardous environments could reduce risks, Hare said, but establishing whether technology actually prevents accidents needs further investigation. According to the U.K.'s Health and Safety Executive (HSE), the number of construction workers killed in work-related incidents in Great Britain fell to 25 in 2025/26, down from 35 the previous year and below the five-year average of 37. ( Supplied: Environmental Protection Authority Tasmania ) Tasmania's EPA says it has "disrupted an interstate waste tyre operation" it alleges unlawfully collected an estimated 4,000 to 5,000 tyres from local businesses. The operation posed as legitimate controlled waste transporters, making $50,000 in 10 days. The EPA says investigators have located six shipping containers filled with the tyres collected from businesses under false pretences. Tasmania's Environment Protection Authority says it has disrupted an interstate waste tyre operation that unlawfully collected thousands of tyres from Tasmanian dealerships and mechanics. The EPA's investigation began last year, after it received reports that an unlicensed company was approaching businesses posing as "legitimate registered controlled waste transporters" approved by the EPA and Tyre Stewardship Australia. At least 30 instances of unlawful tyre collection involving around 20 Tasmanian businesses were identified. The unlawful operators made approximately $50,000 in 10 days. Investigators located six shipping containers filled with waste tyres, four in Bridgewater and two in Launceston. ( Supplied: Environmental Protection Authority Tasmania ) Investigators uncovered a tyre network that had been operating in various Australian states over recent years, using rented vehicles, short-term shipping container leases and false credentials to collect the waste tyres. In June, six shipping containers filled with waste tyres, four in Bridgewater and two in Launceston, were located, with an estimated 4,000 to 5,000 tyres having been collected and stored across the state. The EPA said the investigation resulted in enforcement action against one operator, with warning notices issued to "retailers who should reasonably have recognised and acted on suspicious activity." Call Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 Report anonymously via the Crime Stoppers website Evidence gathered across the investigation included alleged breaches of the Environmental Management and Pollution Control (Waste Management) Regulations 2020 and potential fraud offences. EPA chief executive and director Catherine Murdoch said the investigation would assist other jurisdictions in tackling the unlawful activity. "The EPA undertook its largest proactive industry-targeting exercise in response to organised environmental crime to date. events.title: 'Impossible to get ahead': Canberra inflation rate rises above national average
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Small businesses feel the pinch as ACT inflation rate rises above nation's average Casey Johnston said her business had been avoiding passing on costs to consumers. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Household inflation has risen to 4.7 per cent in the ACT, with the national average being 4.3 per cent. Canberrans are continuing to curb their spending, with small businesses seeing declining foot traffic. An economics lecturer says inflation is not expected to come down anytime soon, with another rate increase on the horizon. The ACT's inflation rate jumped to 4.7 per cent in the 12 months to September this year, and now sits above the national average of 4.3 per cent. And with the RBA expected to lift the cash rate again tomorrow to 4.85 per cent — the highest rate since the 2008 global financial crisis — many households are doing all they can to curb their costs. But for some Canberra business owners that means sales are down, with no end in sight. "Nobody's out and about eating and obviously that hurts us," Casey Johnston, who runs a burrito business in Tuggeranong with her partner, said. Ms Johnston said she was used to business "fluctuating" in the hospitality sector, but sales were "a lot lower" than past years. "I feel like our foot traffic, people walking along the street just to find somewhere to eat for dinner or lunch, is definitely declining," Ms Johnston said. As the cost of living continues to bite, Canberrans are cutting back on their discretionary spending. ( ABC News: Mark Moore ) Ms Johnston said they were also absorbing rising business costs including products and rent, rather than passing those costs onto customers. "[It] is a hard battle because we can't increase our prices for our consumers, but we're definitely taking the hit of our products being more expensive ourselves," she said. "We can't always afford wages and that kind of thing. "If people aren't here then the employment is not necessarily needed all the time, and that can make things really tricky." Interest rates projected to rise again Dr John Hawkins said interest rates were predicted to continue rising. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Senior lecturer in economics at the University of Canberra Dr John Hawkins said global oil prices were the main driver for rising inflation rates. In the ACT specifically, the biggest drivers were fuel, electricity, childcare and school fees, new housing builds, and furniture, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. "You get these variations that are quite random," Dr Hawkins said. "Our inflation's lower than Hobart, Darwin, and Adelaide, but it's a bit higher than Sydney and Melbourne." Dr Hawkins also warned the Reserve Bank of Australia was likely to once again hike up interest rates. "There's an 80 per cent chance that [homeowners] will probably be paying 0.25 per cent more on their mortgages from tomorrow, and the financial markets think if the Reserve Bank doesn't move tomorrow, they'll probably move in either December or early next year," he said. "Raising interest rates will lower inflation because it will slow down the economy. Hairdresser Elanor said people tended to spread out their appointments these days. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Elanor, a hairdresser, said she has personally already cut down "literally everything" when it comes to discretionary spending. "So no coffees out, no more expenditures," she said. "Holidaying, going away, just being able to eat out — so not going out to restaurants, even though we've got all these beautiful restaurants and everything around us — no, I don't spend on that anymore." Elanor said her workplace's clientele base had largely remained the same, but people were booking hair appointments less frequently than they normally would. "It is impossible to get ahead at the moment, especially here in Canberra," she said. events.title: Christmas donations gift demand up, charities say
events.summary: The Christmas Sparkle appeal said demand for toys has gone up in recent years Charities giving Christmas presents to struggling families say more children need their help - but they are getting fewer donations this year. The Chard Christmas Present Appeal said it was having to deal with a high-than-normal demand this year, and blamed the problem on more people struggling financially. Martyna Lee, founder of the appeal, said a lot of families were worried about affording presents for their children due to the cost of living crisis and have "tears in their eyes" when the charity can help them. She added: "We are getting more referrals and less donations because of cost of living, so we do struggle. Cost of living is going to get harder and harder." Song urges builders to talk about mental health Published 7 hours ago MP facing voice loss after surgery shows recovery signs Published 1 day ago Bid launched for 410 new homes near motorway Published 1 day ago Lee started the appeal by herself in 2019 from her living room as part of the Lord's Larder food bank in Chard. They rely completely on donations and do not receive any funding. The Chard Christmas Present Appeal said more families need their help this year "With one family, the social worker asked the children what they would like for Christmas and they asked for pencils and a colouring book," Lee said. "That broke my heart. They weren't asking for expensive gifts. "So I made sure they had a large gift package, including board games." She added that another family she remembers had a fire at their home just before Christmas and they lost "nearly everything". "We managed to get them fantastic gifts and a Christmas tree and decorations," Lee said. Meanwhile, Taunton's charity appeal Christmas Sparkle said their demand has risen sharply over the last couple of years, with 500 presents given out in 2015 to 10,000 last year. They said they are expecting even higher demand this year. Gill Harrison, founder and manager at Christmas Sparkle, said she believes the cost of living crisis is increasing the demand for their services. "When we started the project in 2015, we gave out 500 individual gifts. Last year, it was around 2,300 parcels, that's about 10,000 individual gifts," Harrison said. "We are expecting possibly even more requests this year. That's mostly because of the cost-of-living crisis." Harrison said they work with schools, social services, police, women's refuges and community nursing teams, which have all increased their referrals to Christmas Sparkle over the last few years. events.title: Christmas shoebox appeal launches to help children
events.summary: The boxes will be available in supermarkets for shoppers to pick up and pack before they are passed on to school and charities for distribution. Children across Staffordshire who might otherwise go without a Christmas present are set to receive gift-filled shoeboxes through a new appeal encouraging residents to donate locally. The initiative, organised by World Give, is asking people to pick up empty shoeboxes from supermarkets, fill them with gifts and return them for distribution to families through schools, charities and Staffordshire County Council. Trustee Adam Contoret said the appeal was launched after the charity recognised growing levels of hardship closer to home. "We look around the shops, we see everyone going about their business, but you don't see the people that aren't there," he said. School children gave feedback on what sort of items could be included so that a list could be prepared to help shoppers understand what to put in the boxes. "There's people that would be buying Christmas presents, but they can't because they haven't got the money." Over the past 20 years, the charity has helped more than 100,000 children across the world by sending shoeboxes full of gifts. This year, however, it has turned its attention to supporting children and families in Staffordshire. "It's apparently one in seven children who won't get a formal gift-wrapped Christmas present under the tree at Christmas," Contoret said. "This year we're turning around. Charity begins at home. The boxes are being done in Staffordshire for Staffordshire kids." People will be able to collect empty shoeboxes from participating supermarkets, fill them while doing their shopping and return them to be distributed through schools and local charities. The appeal comes as a Family Action survey of 2,000 parents and carers found one in five had considered cancelling Christmas because they could not afford it, while one in nine said they would not be able to afford a Christmas present for their child. Adam Contoret has previously sent shoeboxes over the world but this year after seeing the statistics, wants to shift the focus closer to home Contoret said schools and local charities were best placed to identify families who could benefit from the scheme and ensure gifts were distributed discreetly. "The schools know the families and they're the best place to hand those gifts over at the right time in a discreet and respectful way," he said. Students supporting the campaign said the shoeboxes could have a significant impact on children at Christmas. Noah said he would include practical items alongside gifts. "I think it's good to give things to everyone and relate it to the age groups," he said. "I would give them notepads, pens, calculators and a stationery set, for example pencil cases, rulers and protractors." Steven said the appeal could help children enjoy the festive season. "Christmas is a festive season of merriness, so if you don't have any presents, you don't feel that giving and love and you won't feel that much merrier," he said. Isabelle said receiving a gift-filled shoebox could help children feel valued. "They might feel special because they know someone actually put thought into putting stuff in the box for them, so they know that someone cares for them and they feel loved," she said. events.title: Dr Sultan Al Jaber urges energy security overhaul as nearly billion barrels drawn from oil markets
events.summary: The disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has drained nearly one billion barrels from global oil inventories, exposing the need for a fundamental rethink of energy security, the Adipec conference in Abu Dhabi heard on Monday. “Simply put, the world has eroded its supply buffers,” said Dr Sultan Al Jaber, UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc. “But, trust me, supply is only half the story. The other half is delivery." During the event's opening ceremony, Dr Al Jaber called for greater investment in supply infrastructure and artificial intelligence to help the energy industry withstand future shocks, warning that securing production was no longer enough to guarantee that supplies reach consumers. Referring to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, who attended the ceremony, Dr Al Jaber said, “Sam, from the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI. And now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy.” He spoke as Adnoc announced an agreement with OpenAI and G42 to become the world's first energy company to deploy OpenAI's Frontier platform, with plans to transform the Abu Dhabi energy company's field development, well management and commercial operations. The partnership, guided by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, would make Adnoc's systems smarter, safer, more secure, more resilient and more productive, Dr Al Jaber said. The Iran war severely disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz and exposed weaknesses in global supply chains, he added. “For years, our industry optimised for just in time,” Dr Al Jaber said. “And to tell you the truth, we got very good at it. This year we got the bill for just in case.” Diesel stocks in some markets have fallen to their lowest seasonal levels in 35 years, while others face a 600 billion cubic feet gap in LNG supplies, he said. Shipping and logistics costs, which accounted for less than 5 per cent of the cost of a barrel before the disruption, now exceed 30 per cent. “Energy security is not only measured at the point of production. It is now also measured at the point of delivery,” Dr Al Jaber said. He outlined five priorities for strengthening energy security: accessible supply, routes to market, operational intelligence, investment confidence and people. He also called for intelligent energy systems capable of anticipating risks, improving performance and reducing costs. On investment, Dr Al Jaber said: “Capital follows confidence. Policy must create it … finance must accelerate it … and insurance must keep trade moving.” He said the UAE would continue to advocate dialogue, diplomacy and political solutions to support stability in energy markets and the global economy. “Talent stayed. Capital stayed. Investment kept coming … and the economy kept moving,” he said. “That is the UAE model, pressure-tested and proven by results.” Dr Al Jaber said Adnoc's preparedness had been developed years before the disruption. “We did not write our resilience playbook during this disruption. We wrote it years before,” he said. “Energy leadership is not measured by what you produce in good times. It is measured by what you deliver in hard times.” “Because when it counts the most. You can count on the UAE,” he added.
