events.title: South Korea targets 'world's highest performance' sovereign AI model in record new budget
events.summary: South Korea plans to raise total spending for 2027 by 12.8% to 820.9 trillion won, with a major investment push for semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers. Lee pledged 4.7 trillion won for a sovereign AI model and plans to train 2,000 specialists in semiconductor design and regional chip industries. South Korea is within reach of $1 trillion in annual exports, citing strong performance in key industries including semiconductors. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung unveiled the country's largest ever budget on Monday, pledging to "boldly invest in AI and future growth engines." Speaking to the National Assembly on Monday, Lee said total spending for 2027 would rise 12.8% to 820.9 trillion won ($610.14 billion), including 21.3 trillion won for semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers — nearly double the 2026 level. A separate 4.7 trillion won will go toward developing a sovereign AI model with what Lee described as the "world's highest performance." The government also plans to invest heavily into talent, including training 2,000 specialists to "lead semiconductor design and the regional semiconductor industry," while expanding AI education for students, job seekers and existing workers. South Korea has set up university "contract departments," where students can enroll in company-linked degrees that offer pathways to jobs at firms like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix before graduation. Companies help design courses, provide financial support and recruit qualifying graduates. The record spending plan comes as the International Monetary Fund forecasts South Korea's economy will grow 3.3% in 2026, its fastest pace since the post pandemic rebound in 2021. Lee said the higher spending would result in "virtually no net increase in government debt," with newly issued bonds used to repay existing debt. The budget also increases spending on defense and social security spending for the youth. Defense expenditure is set to rise 8.2% to 73.3 trillion won. "We will rapidly transform into a smart, elite, and powerful military by establishing a hybrid manned and unmanned system based on AI, robots, and drones," Lee said. South Korea's strong economic growth has been driven largely by semiconductor exports as global demand for computing power rises with the AI boom. Exports surged 93.7% from a year earlier to a record $115.3 billion in October, according to data released Sunday by the Korea Customs Service. Shipments totaled $930 billion in the first 10 months of 2026, surpassing the $900 billion mark for the first time. The country posted a $42.5 billion trade surplus in October, with imports rising 36% year on year to $72.8 billion. Lee said South Korea was within reach of $1 trillion in annual exports, citing strong performance in key industries including semiconductors.

events.title: Millions in UK brace to remortgage on worse deals as rate rise looms
events.summary: More than 2.3m households face jump in payments in 2027, after expected increase in Bank of England rate this week More than 2.3m UK households face a sharp rise in mortgage payments as they come off fixed-rate deals in 2027, with the Bank of England expected to begin raising interest rates this week. The Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC) is widely expected to increase the base rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November after UK inflation rose further to 3.5% in September. It could be the first of four quarter-point rises over the next 12 months, according to financial market expectations, which would exacerbate the financial pressure on households grappling with higher energy and food bills. Thousands of borrowers are due to come off fixed contracts in the final months of this year, with 700,000 having been forecast to switch over to new rates between July and December. A further 2.3m households will reach the end of their fixed rates next year, according to data collected by UK Finance, a banking industry body. There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets – triggered in part by energy prices and inflation fears linked to the war in the Middle East – has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages . An increase in the Bank of England rate could drive those rates, and wider household costs, even higher. Data released last week showed that mortgage approvals in the UK fell to a near three-year low in September as potential buyers were deterred by the jump in borrowing costs. Alongside last week’s budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) warned that household disposable incomes would fall by 0.6% next year after taking account of inflation. The downgrade compares with the 0.6% increase in disposable incomes the watchdog had forecast in March – an outlook the OBR’s David Miles described as “a pretty grim picture”. That income squeeze is also being driven by the energy price shock, which the OBR said would push consumer inflation to 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March. Ofgem’s energy price cap, which determines household bills, is expected to rise by more than £400 in January, according to the latest forecast from EDF . John Healey, the chancellor, made a £100 payout to 20m households the centrepiece of his budget , saying he wanted to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”. His cost of living package – which also included cancelling fuel duty rises planned by Rachel Reeves and extending a VAT cut on electricity bills – was paid for by tax rises on banks, savers and landlords. The Bank of England has taken a wait-and-see approach to rising inflation since the start of the Iran war, in contrast to other central banks, including the US Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and European Central Bank, which have already raised borrowing costs this year. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Andrew Bailey, the governor of the Bank of England, has made clear that the MPC is watching closely to see if rising prices are being passed through into higher wages for workers – evidence of the so-called “second-round effects” that can lead to inflation becoming embedded. Before the war in the Middle East, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates several times this year, with inflation expected to drift back down towards its 2% target. But an extended period of historically high oil prices, affected by the closure of the strait of Hormuz choking off supplies, has instead fed through into high and rising inflation. The Bank will publish updated forecasts for economic growth and inflation alongside its interest rate decision this week. The UK economy beat expectations to be the joint fastest-growing in the G7 in the first half of 2026, which the Office for National Statistics said was partly driven by AI-related sectors. But official forecasts for next year have been cut sharply amid fears that the higher cost of energy will eventually start to weigh on economic growth. Although money market pricing suggests the Bank will raise interest rates four times by next July, many City economists suggest two rate rises are more likely .

events.title: Land of the free, home of the bill shock. This is life in Trump's America
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rising cost of living to hit heavily at US midterms as bill shocks rattle Americans The decaffeinated coffee beans at a US cafe sum up how its customers feel about the rising cost of living. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) It's a quiet Sunday morning in Lansing, Michigan. The low autumn sun lights the interior of the Hob Nob cafe, illuminating a table of young regulars, including the flat-cap-wearing Nicholas Kolacz. He's just bought his weekly coffee. "After a tip, because I always like to tip, it's $US10," Nicholas says. "I used to come in here … probably three or four days a week. Now I come in once every Sunday because I don't have the money to spend," he says. Nicholas Kolacz rarely buys coffee out now due to the higher prices. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) Nicholas makes $US17.50 per hour as a delivery driver. After rent and bills, there is no spare cash. He stopped buying beer long ago and looks at every discretionary purchase through the prism of his wage. "When I do buy things, I look at like, 'Oh, how many hours am I working to get this?'" Once, America felt affordable. Now, the land of the free is also the home of the bill shock. I felt it myself at a bagel cafe on New York's Upper West Side. Twenty years ago, when I lived in Manhattan, my regular breakfast was a bargain: coffee, orange juice and a bagel with lox for $US5. This week, at a no-frills diner, the same breakfast cost me $US31 ($44). The owner of the Hob Nob cafe in Lansing, Trisha Kosloski, says her expenses have gone through the roof. She estimates her delivery costs have increased 50 per cent as shippers pass on fuel costs. But her biggest expense had nothing to do with petrol, or the US and Israel-led war with Iran. The price of coffee beans shot up just after Donald Trump was elected and announced a suite of tariffs on a number of nations where coffee was grown. The average price of coffee in the US is now $US9.33 ($13), the federal minimum wage is $US7.25 ($10.22) . "I'm an import business. We do not grow a lot of coffee in America, as much as we want to pretend that we do," Trisha says. "When we saw those first round of tariffs, that were just like blanket tariffs when he first got into office, all of my coffees went up at least 30 per cent. Trisha Kosloski has passed on the cost increases to her customers. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) In July, Donald Trump announced 50 per cent tariffs on goods from Michigan's neighbour, Canada — which also hit the coffee industry . "A large amount of the beans roasted in America … are actually roasted in Canada. So we had to pay those tariffs to get them," Trisha says. All the extra costs have put pressure on her business. "There is no profit margin," she says. Coffee might be a discretionary purchase, but for many Americans there has been no way to avoid the most painful price increase. Petrol — or "gas" as it's known the US — is hovering at about $US4.30 per gallon ($6.10 for 3.8 litres), about $US1 more expensive than it averaged in 2025. That is still cheaper than Australian prices, but Americans aren't used to paying anything like this. Big cars are standard, and long journeys are unavoidable in sprawling mid-western communities like Lansing, Michigan. The city is the home of the Michigan State University Spartans college football team, and for many, a lively Saturday morning tailgate begins before dawn. The parking lots around Spartan Stadium are filled with gleaming, oversized SUVs and "trucks", like Ford F150s and Chevrolet Silverados. It's costing Americans more to fill up the tank of their big cars. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) "Gas is the number one thing that used to not be so much," MSU student Samson Sprague says. It's not only students feeling the pain. It's Parents' Weekend at MSU, where there are two and sometimes three generations of Americans here today. "My daughter goes to University of Kentucky, so when we drive down to see her, gas is a lot more expensive. It's almost more reasonable to fly to Kentucky than drive to Kentucky right now because of the price of our gas," Michelle Krebill says. Michelle Krebill (right) says it's costing her more to visit her daughter interstate. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) Tara Lukaart is another struggling with the cost of filling up tanks. Her husband operates a plumbing business with several trucks on the road. "For a small business to be able to afford that kind of increase in gas price has been a big deal," she says. Elizabeth Madigan believes the current situation should lead to political change.

events.title: Sheng Siong shares continue last week’s slide, fall over 9% to hit one-year low
events.summary: Sheng Siong reported a modest 1.9% year-on-year increase in Q3 net profit. Sheng Siong shares fell as much as 9.4% to a one-year low after Q3 net profit rose only 1.9% to S$44.6 million, despite revenue growing 6.2% to S$441.5 million. Management said fierce supermarket competition, heavy promotions, rising labour costs, and the upcoming RTS Link could pressure sales and margins, so the group will adjust its strategy. DBS expects slower earnings growth in Q4 because of a high base, the Thomson Imperial Court store closure, higher utility prices, and staff costs; it kept a hold rating and S$3 target price. SINGAPORE – Shares of supermarket operator Sheng Siong continued to fall, dropping as much as 9.4 per cent on the morning of Nov 2, after the group reported a marginal 1.9 per cent year-on-year increase in third-quarter net profit on the evening of Oct 29. The stock had closed down 4.6 per cent or 13 cents at $2.67 on Oct 30. The counter opened on Nov 2 down 7.1 per cent at $2.48 as at 9.01am, before slipping to $2.46 as at 9.16 am. It fell further to $2.42, down 9.4 per cent, as at 10.44am. This is the lowest level the stock has reached since Nov 3, 2025, when it hit S$2.33 in intra-day trade. Some 7.4 million shares changed hands as at 10.44am on Nov 2. No married deals were reported, according to data from ShareInvestor. The mainboard-listed supermarket operator reported a net profit of $44.6 million for the three months ended Sept 30, up from $43.7 million in the corresponding year-ago period. Revenue for the quarter rose 6.2 per cent to $441.5 million, from $415.5 million a year earlier. The group attributed the increase to a larger store network in Singapore, as well as improvements in comparable same-store sales. The stock’s decline also comes after management said during its third-quarter results briefing that the grocery retail landscape remains competitive, with sustained promotional activity potentially putting pressure on revenue and margins. Competition could intensify further with the upcoming Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link, which is expected to begin operations in February 2027. The link could encourage more cross-border shopping and heighten price competition for selected packaged groceries and household products. Sheng Siong said it would adapt its strategies as developments surrounding the RTS Link unfold, in order to address the potential impact on its business. Beyond competition, the group also flagged rising labour costs as another challenge. These include wage increases under the Progressive Wage Model and the National Wages Council’s guidelines for 2026 to 2027. The group had raised the salaries of its retail workers in September last year to meet Progressive Wage Model requirements for the retail sector. DBS analyst Chee Zheng Feng said in a note on Friday that he expects Sheng Siong’s earnings growth to moderate further in the fourth quarter, as it comes down from a high base boosted by SG60 vouchers. Another potential factor is the full-quarter impact of the Thomson Imperial Court store’s closure on Sept 25, while higher utility prices and rising staff costs could also weigh on the supermarket chain’s profitability, he added. The brokerage maintained a hold and unchanged target price of $3 for the counter. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Adnoc becomes first energy company to deploy OpenAI Frontier
events.summary: Adnoc has signed an agreement with OpenAI and G42 , to become the first energy company to deploy OpenAI’s Frontier technology as it seeks to expand AI use across its operations. Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, met OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman on Monday and witnessed the agreement, signed by G42 through its subsidiary Inception42. “Abu Dhabi and the UAE are setting a bold, global standard for AI integration across both the public and private sectors to make sure the benefits of AI reach everyone,” said Mr Altman, who is in Abu Dhabi to attend Adipec . “We are proud to support the UAE’s ambition, anchored in a shared commitment to safety, accessibility and responsible innovation.” The project will integrate advanced AI capabilities across Adnoc’s operations, enabling more connected operational, investment and commercial decision-making to improve efficiency and productivity. The technology will run on OpenAI’s GPT models using inference infrastructure based in the UAE. OpenAI launched Frontier on February 5 as an enterprise platform for building, deploying and managing AI agents. HP, Intuit, Oracle, State Farm, Thermo Fisher and Uber were among its first adopters. The Frontier deal is one of four agreements signed between Abu Dhabi-based entities and OpenAI, spanning the government, energy and investment sectors. The Abu Dhabi government and OpenAI also launched what they described as the world’s first AI native Machine-Readable Government initiative , part of the emirate’s goal to become the world’s first fully AI-native government. The initiative converts government policies and regulations into a format AI systems can read, to help officials carry out routine compliance assessments, such as issuing permits and certificates. Officials retain oversight of the processes, and accountability for final decisions. Led by the Department of Government Enablement, its first pilot is already running with the Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority and focuses on food imports. Mubadala , Inception42 and OpenAI signed an agreement to apply AI to investment analysis, opportunity identification and risk assessment. Inception42 and OpenAI also signed a five-year agreement to support the adoption of frontier AI across government, enterprise and education in the UAE. Adnoc has been building its AI capabilities for several years. In 2019, it agreed with G42 to set up a joint venture to develop and commercialise AI products for the oil and gas industry. The venture, AIQ , was 60 per cent owned by Adnoc and 40 per cent by G42. The agreements build on OpenAI’s long-standing ties with the UAE. G42 and OpenAI first partnered in October 2023 to apply the US company’s generative AI models in sectors including financial services, energy, healthcare and public services. In May last year, the two companies announced Stargate UAE , OpenAI’s first international deployment of its Stargate AI infrastructure and the start of its OpenAI for Countries programme. The 1-gigawatt cluster is being developed by G42’s Khazna Data Centres within the 5-gigawatts UAE-US AI Campus in Abu Dhabi, with OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco and SoftBank as partners. OpenAI said at launch that the first 200 megawatts were expected to go live in 2026 . Abu Dhabi has also invested in OpenAI, with MGX among the co-leads of OpenAI’s $122 billion funding round, which closed on March 31 at an $852 billion post-money valuation.

events.title: Binance sees $3.64 billion in net outflows as withdrawals resume after massive hack
events.summary: Binance said it processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits on Nov. 1. The net outflows amounted to 2.1% of Binance's $171 billion in total assets. The exchange said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount following the $6.3 billion hack. Binance said it recorded $3.64 billion in net outflows after reopening withdrawals on Sunday following a $6.3 billion hack, as customers rushed to move funds off the platform. The exchange processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits between 6 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. UTC on Nov. 1, Binance said in a post on X. The resulting net outflows represented 2.1% of Binance's $171 billion in total assets, based on its latest available proof-of-reserves data as of Oct. 28. Binance said withdrawal volumes had declined and were stabilizing following an initial spike, while deposit volumes remained substantial. The exchange began restoring withdrawals in phases at 6 a.m. UTC on Sunday, with services resuming across all 15 networks and assets included in the initial phase by 12:36 p.m. UTC. It said testing was continuing for the remaining networks and assets. "Circle activated its incident response procedures and coordinated with law enforcement to freeze more than $1.1 billion in USDC associated with the incident," a spokesperson for the stablecoin issuer told CNBC in an email. The company said the investigation is ongoing. The updated figure follows a Friday post from Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire, who said at the time that more than $800 million in USDC linked to the incident had been frozen. Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao sought to reassure users following the breach, writing on X that "98% choose to stay!" He said most of the net outflows occurred within the first couple of hours after withdrawals resumed. "Trust isn't earned by what you say in good times. It's earned by what you do in hard times," Zhao added. The withdrawals followed a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance last week. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korean hackers, identifying the operation as TraderTraitor. The exchange has said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than pass the losses on to users. Binance said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount, up from 90% in its previous update. The exchange said the remaining 5% consisted of less liquid tokens that would take longer to source in the quantities required.

events.title: UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
events.summary: Commons committee says lack of coherent strategy is hampering business and leaving national security risks unaddressed The UK is making up policy on China “as it goes along” and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, a parliamentary report has concluded. An investigation by the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee said Labour’s failure to formulate a coherent strategy since 2024 “combined the worst of both worlds” for the UK in relation to China. Liam Byrne, Labour MP and chair of the committee said the UK’s policy on China meant it was also endangering its business with the EU with the risk of being “cut off” from big manufacuring contracts. The government could neither deliver commercial opportunities to British businesses nor control the “increasing exposure to unquantified, managed risk” in relations with China, it found. The report said: “In 2024, the new government promised a strategic, long-term, consistent UK approach to China. It has not delivered on this. “Britain must shape its own relationship with China or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.” The UK’s relationship with China has been marked by a lack of engagement in the last 10 years, with Keir Starmer making the first official visit in January since Theresa May in 2018. That trip was billed as an effort to end the “diplomatic ice age”, but since 2018 China has benefited from an export boom that is now fuelling fears about deindustrialisation, adding to deep-seated existing concerns about cyber espionage and national security. The MPs acknowledged the advantages of trading with Beijing in their report, noting that British businesses have profitable operations in China and “are ambitious to grow” and learn from the country’s “world-leading” innovations. At the same time, consumers benefit from low-cost imports when household incomes are squeezed, with electric vehicles being a case in point. However, Byrne sharply criticised the government’s piecemeal approach. “Britain’s businesses cannot plan for the future when the government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along. “Ministers promised clarity and consistency. Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the 11th hour.” The committee cited the decision in March to block the Chinese firm Ming Yang from building a £1.5bn wind energy plant in Scotland after years of negotiation because of unspecified security risks. Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, has called on Andy Burnham to reconsider Starmer’s decision. That decision, along with the emergency takeover of British Steel from its Chinese owners, “has been characterised by reactivity, inconsistency and opacity”, the report said. Work on a new strategy, the committee said, should be combined with official preparations for new trade remedies to counter unfair competition, including potential tariffs on EVs, something Downing Street has not ruled out. The report calls for “clear new rules of the game” and recommends the designation of a “red zone” for industries that would be off-limits for Chinese investment and a “green zone”, where trade should be encouraged. Byrne said a China strategy was an urgent concern as “Europe is changing fast” and “proposing new trade protections as it gets bolder with Beijing and warier of Washington”. The new laws “may trap Britain outside EU trade walls, cutting us off from our largest market”. Byrne said the government “should be prepared to consider dynamic alignment” with the EU include tariffs on EVs “as the price of securing British firms a place in the EU’s Made in Europe project” and to help guard against China dominance. The UK is already under pressure to align with the EU on tariffs on EVs, but the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, has said he will make a decision in the best interests of the UK. The EU has already imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs, capped the number of hybrid cars that can be imported from China and is now considering a Franco-German proposal for a “kill switch” to block imports if China weaponises trade – as it did last year with curbs on exports of rare-earth minerals and chips. “The UK’s partners are moving further and faster,” the report noted. China is now on track to surpass last year’s record $1.19tn trade surplus with the rest of the world. Its latest five-year plan, covering 2026 to 2030, gives a glimpse of where China is going next in prioritising the strategic expansion of high-value green exports such as EVs, batteries, wind turbines, hydrogen and solar panels. A government spokesperson said it did not accept the committee’s verdict. “We recognise the committee’s work on this report, but we disagree with its conclusion.” They added that the government’s approach was “consistent” - it cooperated where it could and challenged where it must.

events.summary: Oil prices fell on Monday morning amid hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough between the US and Iran , easing concerns about further supply disruption. US President Donald Trump reportedly said he wants to give diplomacy with Iran more time before considering renewed military strikes after Tuesday’s US midterm elections. The two key benchmarks slid more than 3 per cent in morning trading. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's crude, was trading at $110 a barrel at 7.55am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, dropped to $100.90 a barrel. Mr Trump reportedly told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a phone call that he wanted to give diplomacy with Tehran more time before considering further strikes, Axios reported, quoting sources. CBS News reported that Mr Trump said he believed the US would soon end the war with Iran, "one way or the other". The US President was speaking to Right Side Broadcasting Network before a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday, according to the report. "We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other," Mr Trump was quoted as saying. "Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it … The job we've done is amazing." On Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said no decision had been made on renewed strikes and that Mr Trump preferred a diplomatic resolution. On Sunday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said it received a report that a ship had been struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz , after an attack on a liquefied natural gas tanker on Friday. The UKMTO also reported a vessel was struck east of Ras Al Khafji, along Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast. An Iranian delegation was in Qatar for discussions with mediators on Saturday, according to a Bloomberg report. Fears of US strikes on Iran have maintained upward pressure on crude, keeping supply risk premiums elevated. Oil prices started sliding on Monday after hitting a six-month high last week on Hormuz strikes and a US threat to hit Iran. Over the past week, both Brent and WTI increased by about 0.8 per cent. On a monthly basis, the benchmarks surged by about 15 per cent and 12 per cent, respectively, to hit their highest levels since April. Meanwhile, Swiss lender UBS said in a report recently it expected Brent crude prices to remain elevated, near $110 a barrel at the end of the year, as Middle Eastern supply remains volatile and geopolitical uncertainty persists. "Record freight costs, constrained tanker capacity, and recovering Chinese imports are other factors likely to keep oil prices high," UBS commodity analyst Giovanni Staunovo said.

events.title: Borrowed reading: stories from our extended colleagues
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Readers don’t typically care who owns what media property, we realize, but last year, we became part of a broader portfolio , a move that has come with some decided benefits, including what amounts to a bigger extended family with cool cousins. Now, in addition to our TechCrunch channels in Slack, we can talk with the writers and editors of CIO, Computerworld, and PCWorld, among other outlets. We also find ourselves reading more of their work and figured you might like it, too. Here’s a handful of pieces I was just enjoying while watching the Warriors-Clippers game, which, as I type, is a little too close for comfort: Apple recently put a faster chip into the iPad mini and gave it an OLED screen, improving its color reproduction and also allowing it to slim down the display panel, and still, Macworld’s David Price isn’t entirely convinced it matters. In his view, Apple has built the “world’s fanciest horse and cart,” just as a Tesla Roadster with SpaceX thrusters has appeared on the scene in the form of the new foldable iPhone Duo. In short, he sees the mini as a Duo you can’t close. It’s a fun read, one that ends with a surprisingly practical plan to save this product. Google has a new laptop platform, the Googlebook, and Mark Hachman of PCWorld spent time with the Lenovo Googlebook 15 specifically, so you don’t have to. Hachman’s verdict on this one is a hard pass, with cons that include “I hate the keyboard,” which he means so literally that he gave up writing the review on it, “webcam biometrics work sporadically,” and, for good measure, “battery life isn’t great.” (He does like the $479 Chromebook at less than half the price.) If you’ve been wondering whether this is the laptop you’ve been waiting for, wonder no longer ! You shared your secrets and insecurities with a chatbot, and now its parent company has gone belly up. Bloop. In Computerworld, Mike Elgan looks at what happens to your confessions when the AI company that absorbed them announces Chapter 11. (Yes, this is largely centered on Character.AI, which filed for bankruptcy last month, and whose privacy policy, in particular, turns out to be “ spectacularly vague ,” notes Elgan.) He also reminds readers why deleting your chats may not delete them from the model. (Of course, the safest advice may be to channel the late Andy Grove, Intel’s longtime chief, who famously said only the paranoid survive. Grove was talking about the chip industry, but some would argue that’s solid advice generally.) PCWorld’s Ben Patterson built a security-minded AI agent to keep his data safe, then, surprise, the agent snitched on its own loophole. More specifically, BenBot, Patterson’s homemade Raspberry Pi assistant, wrote a blog post announcing that one of its tools was “accidentally acting as a jailbreak,” though it turned out the claim was only partly true. Patterson’s coding bots confirmed the hole was real and worse than advertised, and that BenBot had also slipped past its own fact-checker to publish the post. It’s an instructive read about vibe coding; Patterson readily admits BenBot hallucinated in the absence of information it needed. It’s also an interesting look at how AI agents turn into tattletales . Over at CIO, Sarah White looks at how AI is reshaping tech hiring, noting it’s a complicated picture right now. Companies are hiring again and paying a premium for AI skills, with the average AI job listing offering around $177,000 compared to $80,000 for non-AI roles, according to LinkedIn. But burnout among tech workers has doubled as daily AI use has quadrupled, and women are seemingly being left behind; they accounted for just 26% of AI hires in the U.S. last year, versus 50% of hires in non-AI roles. events.title: Canada-India $5.5 billion bank takeover attracts opposition from workers, politicians
events.summary: Employees of Indian state-owned lender IDBI have called for a two-day strike opposing the takeover by Canada's Fairfax. Fairfax won a bid in October to acquire over a 60% stake in IDBI Bank for $5.5 billion. Once approved, Fairfax deal to acquire the majority share in IDBI will become the largest foreign direct investment in India’s financial sector. Canadian firm Fairfax Financial Holdings' proposed $5.5 billion takeover of IDBI Bank is facing pushback from employees of the Indian state-owned lender and political parties in the country. On Sunday, the United Forum of IDBI Officers and Employees called for a two-day "nationwide" strike against the sale of the bank to Fairfax. The workers' union also expressed " grave concerns " about the transparency of the sale and valuation process, according to a post on X. It is demanding that the government "cancel the privatization process" and instead focus on strengthening the bank while protecting public investment and employees' interests. Last week, Rahul Gandhi, India's leader of the opposition, extended support to the IDBI Bank employee unions opposing the takeover by Fairfax. "Public banks are not assets to be sold off, they are tools to build the nation," Gandhi said in a statement on Thursday. He added that the sale of over 60% stake in IDBI Bank to Fairfax goes against the commitment of previous governments to hold a 51% stake in the state-owned lender. Nirmala Sitharaman, India's finance minister, in her response said the public sector bank was handed to the government in " poor shape " and was revived through "professionalism, prudence" and recapitalization of more than 250 billion rupees ($2.6 billion). "The IDBI Bank is now poised for its next phase of growth," the finance minister said. The government has previously said that the next phase of growth will be driven by a strategic investor. The Indian government on Oct.14 said the sale of over 60% of the share in IDBI will mark the largest foreign direct investment transaction in India's financial sector. Fairfax made a bid to pay 81 rupees per share for IDBI against the average fair value set at 75.99 rupees apiece. On Monday, shares of IDBI opened at around 79 rupees per share. However, Indian media outlet Businessworld on Thursday reported that government officials had suppressed the valuation of IDBI to make Fairfax's offer seem attractive. The Ministry of Finance has defended its procedure , adding that the bidding process was a "double blind" as the bidder did not know the valuation and the valuators did not see the bids. The Indian government has been divesting stakes this year as it pushes to keep the country's growth engine running amid deepening fiscal pressures. It sold shares in several companies, including Cochin Shipyard , Indian Railways Finance Corp , NHPC and Coal India . In August, it got $3.3 billion for a 6.5% stake in the country's top life insurer, Life Insurance Corporation of India .

events.title: Alterra's investments designed to hedge against AI bubble, says chief executive
events.summary: Alterra, the UAE's $30 billion climate vehicle , has designed its artificial intelligence investment strategy to protect it against a much talked about bubble in the sector, its chief executive has told The National . The fund's focus on investing in energy systems powered by AI and not directly into the technology is serving as a “hedge” against any potential bubble that may burst in the booming industry, Majid Al Suwaidi said. “We're investing in the only place that our portfolio touches the AI story – through the energy systems. What is great with our investment thesis is that we don't invest directly in AI infrastructure,” he said in an interview. “Those energy systems, regardless of whether it's powering AI or powering a factory, homes, schools, or hospitals, that power will still be needed. So, in a way, Alterra and the investments we make are a really good hedge against a bubble in AI.” Mr Al Suwaidi's comments come as Abu Dhabi-based Alterra gives a vote of confidence to the technology by partnering with one of Europe's biggest sovereign AI companies. On Monday, Alterra announced that it had partnered with Milan-based Domyn to develop a proprietary climate intelligence system that the former will own and control, which will pave the way towards becoming an AI-native company, Mr Al Suwaidi said. “Once we've built that core system, we can then extend that to other aspects of the business and truly become an AI-native organisation,” he said. The system, which will be developed in phases, will “come into the fore” next year, he added. “To pick up these technologies and apply them very early in our development means that we will be able to use AI or our analytics to … take advantage of the power of this technology.” Alterra did not disclose the value of its partnership with Domyn, which was formerly known as iGenius and founded by former Apple employee Uljan Sharka. Domyn has raised $1.1 billion in debt financing over the past two years and is valued at about $2 billion. In June, the European Commission chose Europa, a project led by Domyn, to develop an open-source AI model covering all 24 official languages in the EU. “The way we're designing the system is that it can be evergreen in the sense that as new models are being built or as new developments happen within the technology that they can be plugged in immediately and we can upgrade our system,” Mr Al Suwaidi said. The partnership with Domyn mirrors his confidence in the AI sector, where the bubble debate is hot. Recently, two of the biggest names in asset management, Citadel chief executive Ken Griffin and Blackstone president Jon Gray, gave negative and positive views, respectively. Mr Al Suwaidi acknowledged that there is a bubble “in some ways”, but managing expectations and doing due diligence to make sound investment decisions will help contain potential ill-effects. “Any time you have a new asset class, a bubble is developed … and bubbles can be good if managed and bad if they burst … it just remains to be seen how long it will continue to grow and whether we can manage it in a prudent way so that it doesn't burst with negative consequences,” he said. “We know for sure that this technology is going to be critical to our future economic development, and how we use it becomes increasingly important, and we're discovering that, so there's going to be winners and losers in that process.” Alterra's mandate is to raise $250 billion globally by 2030 to create a fairer climate finance system. Its chairman is Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc. It is less than three years since Alterra's launch at the Cop28 climate conference hosted by the UAE. Since then, Alterra has grown into three funds – Acceleration, Transformation and Opportunity – with five global investment partners: Brookfield Asset Management, BlackRock, Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, KKR and TPG. It also has more than 60 direct and indirect portfolio companies across more than 40 countries, supporting more than 100GW of renewable energy capacity. Alterra's capital activity is also accelerating. More than $51 billion in expected equity capital across its fund and co-investment activities has been mobilised, with preliminary mobilisation ratios of more than 10 times for its Acceleration Fund and over four times for the Transformation Fund, excluding Alterra's own capital and deal-level debt. Recent investments also show the breadth of Alterra's expansion, including Inkia in Peru, Wireless Logic alongside General Atlantic, and Jeppesen ForeFlight with Thoma Bravo. “What Alterra has shown through our success in the climate realm is that you can achieve the same goals, but in an economically prudent way,” Mr Al Suwaidi said. “Something that is very unique, and very underreported is how successful we've been in our model.”

events.title: US economy under Donald Trump in five charts
events.summary: A nervous US electorate is heading to polling stations across the country for Tuesday's midterm elections , and their personal finances could determine which way control in Congress swings. Recent polling suggests President Donald Trump 's shifting tariff policies, war with Iran and overall handling of the economy will be major issues this week for voters, who say they have been affected by higher prices at the petrol pumps and on grocery shelves. Half of registered voters rate the economy as “extremely important this year”, with health care costs and the war in Iran also top among 11 issues rated in an October 29 Gallup poll. Roughly four in 10 voters rate income and wealth distribution (44 per cent) and petrol costs (42 per cent) as extremely important. Forty-seven per cent of registered voters said the cost of living would be the single most important factor in their votes this week, according to an Ipsos poll conducted in August. Only 17 per cent approve of Mr Trump's handling of the cost of living, while an AP-Norc poll found 26 per cent approve of his handling of the economy overall. A Chicago Council poll also found 71 per cent of Americans think US tariffs on imports have been bad for the economy, and 81 per cent said they have been bad for their cost of living. Although not a particular macroeconomic data point, the Consumer Confidence Survey measures attitudes, buying intentions and holiday plans, inflation expectations, and where people believe stock prices and interest rates are heading. In this way, it can offer a key insight into perceptions on the economy. Fergus McCormick, senior economist at the Conference Board, said “consumers continued to express frustration with rising costs” in October, with most references pointing to the high cost of goods, groceries and petrol. Easing petrol prices saw some recovery in the Consumer Confidence Index, which rose 7.5 points to 91.7 in October, although confidence remains on a long-term and persistent downwards trend. Moreover, consumers are planning for less spending on services and goods over the next six months, reflecting enduring inflation. Despite this anxiety, consumer spending rose at a 3.4 per cent pace in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department data, showing the US economy has remained resilient amid the energy price shock caused by the Iran war. Strong business spending also accounted for US GDP to grow at a 3.4 per cent annual pace in the July to September period. US inflation has significantly eased since peaking at 9.1 per cent in 2022, and fell to 3 per cent when Mr Trump began his second term in office in January 2025. Headline inflation fell as low as 2.3 per cent in April that year. But inflation picked up again after he imposed a sweeping set of tariffs on nearly every trading partner. The disinflation process now appears stalled, and the Iran war has led to surging energy prices couple with AI-driven investment. Petrol prices accounted for nearly half of the all-items increase in September, when CPI inflation clocked in at 3.7 per cent. Even after stripping away food and energy, inflation still gained 0.3 per cent on a monthly basis and 2.6 per cent year on year. It has been nearly six years since CPI inflation registered at 2 per cent. Seventy-nine per cent of Americans agreed that prices at the pump were higher now compared to 38 per cent in February, a dramatic shift in perceptions since the Iran war began, according to an Ipsos poll conducted in September. The prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the world's energy supplies, has pushed up global energy costs. Even the US, the world's top crude producer, has not been fully insulated. Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries have exacerbated rising costs for diesel , which powers the lorries that transport food and other goods. The average driver is currently paying $4.20 for a gallon of petrol today, an increase of $1.17 from the same time last year, according to automotive group AAA. Of the six “swing states” in this year's midterm election cycle, only Georgia's petrol prices are below the national average. Diesel prices have also soared to $6.32, compared to $3.68 a gallon a year ago. The Federal Reserve was in the middle of an easing cycle when Mr Trump returned to office last year. While the Fed's announcements on short-term interest rates grab headlines, they also influence the 10-year Treasury yield through market expectations and the inflation outlook. The 10-year Treasury is the global benchmark for interest rates, car loans, corporate borrowing and consumer mortgages. Energy-driven inflation, the massive AI buildout and heavy government debt issuance have weighed on the bond market in recent months, with yields on the 10- and 30-year Treasury at levels unseen in nearly a quarter century. At the same time, the Fed has begun a new tightening cycle and has raised expectations it will raise rates further before the year ends. This combination of factors has plagued the housing market, where fixed 30-year mortgage rates climbed as high as 7.4 per cent before pulling back slightly to 7.24 per cent, compared to last year at 6.17 per cent. That means a homebuyer refinancing or purchasing a home would face higher borrowing costs on their monthly payments. Mr Trump frequently uses the stock market as an economic barometer. After suffering brief dips during last year's tariff row and the early days of the Iran war, Wall Street's major indices have surged. The S&P 500 has climbed more than 10 per cent this year and hit a new record-high of 7,818.93 on October 6, though disappointing earnings reports are fuelling a new wave of investor concerns over the AI buildout and the massive investment powering it. AI investment has been cited as the major driver behind the surge. The Magnificent Seven stocks – Nvidia, Alphabet, Apple, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Tesla – make up 34 per cent of the S&P 500. This leads to what economists classify as a K-shaped economy, in which high-earners who own assets such as stocks see their wealth climb while workers relying on pay cheques fall behind as living costs increase.

events.title: Gold climbs back from one-year low as dip buyers arrest slide
events.summary: Gold was finding some immediate support from long-term investors who see the current price as cheap, said Justin Lin, a strategist at Global X ETFs. Gold rose after hitting a one-year low, as cheaper oil eased inflation worries and buyers stepped in after last session’s 3.7% fall. The metal remains under pressure from Middle East war risks, tech stock sell-offs, and forced selling to cover losses elsewhere. Analysts said gold is at “precarious levels”; a move back above US$4,000 is needed to improve the short-term outlook. NEW YORK – Gold rose, as lower oil prices offered some respite from inflationary pressures and dip buyers were drawn by the metal’s slide on Oct 30 to the lowest in a year. Bullion gained as much as 0.7% to nearly US$3,900 an ounce, clawing back some losses after a 3.7% slump in the previous session that rounded off the worst October for the metal since 2008. Oil dropped ahead of the Oct 27 US midterm elections, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying that US President Donald Trump would prefer a diplomatic resolution to the Iran war. Still, bullion remains vulnerable to any escalation in fighting in the Middle East. Trump has repeatedly threatened to resume strikes on Iran after the US midterms, while Tehran threatened wider retaliation and several Persian Gulf states expressed concerns that another attack could unleash an even more destructive war across the region. A global rout in technology stocks is also adding pressure to precious metals. Recent sell-offs have prompted investors to liquidate bullion to meet losses elsewhere, and stocks were set to fall again on Nov 2, tracking a rout on Wall Street fuelled by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade. “We are likely to see some dip buying in the Asian session today as investors, and possibly central banks, cautiously add to positions,” he said. “But gold is undoubtedly sitting at precarious levels.” For now, liquidity concerns and technical selling were overshadowing the metal’s longer-term investment appeal, Ole Sloth Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank AS, wrote in a note. Oct 30 is close below the key technical level of US$3,886 an ounce “leaves gold vulnerable to additional downside pressure”, he said, adding that a recovery to above US$4,000 would be needed to restore “a more neutral short-term outlook”. Spot gold climbed 0.6% to US$3,899.39 an ounce at 7.45am in Singapore. Silver gained 1.3% to US$49.76 an ounce, having dropped nearly 6% on Oct 30. Platinum and palladium also gained after big declines in the previous session. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was marginally higher. BLOOMBERG

events.title: More MAGA than MAGA: How the Daily Caller turned on MAGA and Trump
events.summary: The News When Tucker Carlson co-founded the Daily Caller in 2010, it was to be the Republican Party’s answer to The New York Times. A few identity crises later, the publication has followed Carlson into a hard turn against Donald Trump’s war in Iran, and against Israel — choices that have injected into the publication the digital energy of the new online right, and cost it the support of some of its backers. “I’ve had some of the most aggressive donor pressure over this — the single most aggressive donor pressure over this, of anything I’ve seen in journalism in 20 years,” Daily Caller publisher Neil Patel told Semafor. He wouldn’t detail the cost of lost financial support to the Caller, which includes both a for-profit firm and the nonprofit Daily Caller News Foundation, but acknowledged that there had been costs. The Caller has been a pillar of Washington’s conservative media scene since its launch, an important voice in internecine Republican conflicts and a pipeline of journalistic talent whose alumni include employees of both conservative and mainstream outlets. Now it’s at the vanguard of a Republican civil war that Carlson has helped unleash. “The Iran war is a huge turning point for the conservative movement,” Editor-in-Chief Amber Duke told Semafor on Friday. Nowhere has that shift been clearer than in the outlet’s X feed since the United States went to war with Iran in February. The organization has taken to tweeting the price of diesel every day, emphasizing the war’s cost on drivers, and posts screenshots of Trump’s posts about the war in Iran, adding spicy commentary. “What if instead of “banning” a term, we stopped spending endless amounts of money on foreign wars?” the outlet wrote of Trump’s command that AI be referred to as “super intelligence.” The Daily Caller has similarly gone after Israel, questioning its decisions in the Middle East. It has blasted Benjamin Netanyahu and his policies, and repeatedly highlighted Israeli settler violence, particularly against children . The criticism has gotten the attention of pro-Israel hawks, who have accused the publication of antisemitism and crudely implied it is pro-Islamic propaganda. “Daily Caller means Al Jazeera in Arabic,” Fox News host and commentator Mark Levin wrote . The fissures at the Caller — and in the broader conservative movement — began widening when the activist Charlie Kirk was assassinated last September, according to most of the nine current and former Caller employees who I spoke to over the last week. The movement that had united around Donald Trump devolved into a frenzy of unfounded conspiracy theories, many blaming Israel for Kirk’s death. The podcaster Candace Owens drove those theories, infuriating her former employer, Daily Wire founder Ben Shapiro. Shapiro laid into Owens for perpetuating what he said were antisemitic conspiracy theories, attacked podcaster Megyn Kelly for not condemning Owens, and criticized Carlson for what he described as a cozy interview with self-proclaimed white nationalist Nick Fuentes. The Daily Caller, long a younger and slightly edgier outlet than other right-leaning publications like the Washington Examiner, The National Review, or even Breitbart, followed that online energy. Some on staff noted that former editor Dylan Housman left the publication the Friday before the Iran war started, and the tone shifted significantly following his departure. Duke, a former Caller staffer, replaced him and encouraged the publication to adopt an aggressive posture on social media. Employees also said they sensed that Patel seemed to side with Carlson, Patel’s longtime friend and business partner. While Carlson has long been unaffiliated with the outlet, Patel retains business connections with Carlson, while Carlson’s brother Buckley Carlson has served on the Daily Caller nonprofit’s board. Patel told Semafor he is not involved in day-to-day operations at the Caller, on which he defers to Duke and others, and stressed that Carlson’s stances had no bearing on the outlet. Still, he said he encouraged the Caller’s leaders to remain independent and reflect the publication’s values. That reality for average Americans, he said, has turned against Trump. “Things just aren’t going that well today. I think if you’re at all looking at this objectively, it’s hard to make the case that things are going great in a lot of areas. And so if our coverage has changed, I think it’s changed just to reflect that,” he said. Right vs. Right The concern, of course, is whether it could go too far. Some former Daily Caller staff told Semafor they are worried the publication has drifted a bit too close to the “groyper” wing of the right, whose criticism of Israel reflects its antisemitism. In October, Semafor reported that the Daily Caller tweeted a cartoon of Bill Gates and the devil posing with disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein wearing an Israeli flag Speedo. The post was quickly deleted, but not before it caught the attention of Republicans who have grown increasingly concerned about the Caller’s anti-Israel turn. The publication told Semafor that while the post didn’t meet the publication’s standards, it hadn’t been posted with any “malicious intent.” Other Caller alumni suggested to Semafor that the recent pivot could threaten what in the last decade has become an important talent pipeline and incubator for the right. The Daily Caller has brought up some of the most prominent young political media figures in America, some of whom have left the conservative media sphere (like CNN’s Kaitlan Collins and Semafor’s Shelby Talcott), and others who have built major franchises in independent media (like Breaking Points’ Saagar Enjeti) or moved into positions within the Republican Party apparatus. The previous generation’s crowd is clearly uneasy with the new crop. Max’s view The Daily Caller is clearly positioning itself for a landscape not just post-midterms but post- Trump, and for a bitter and intensifying intra-party media battle. The issue of how each side talks about Israel and the war in Iran has played out in both parties, as was clear on Sunday when Rep. Haley Stevens, the former Michigan Democrat Senate candidate, endorsed the Republican in the race over the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, citing her view that he had not done enough to condemn antisemitism. While Israel has garnered much of the attention, the Caller has taken stances against Republican Party orthodoxy on other issues. events.title: Metrocon chairman resigns after charge over unlicensed worker dormitory that was discovered in January
events.summary: Catalist-listed construction engineering company Metrocon Holdings was formerly known as Hatten Land. SINGAPORE – Metrocon Holdings chairman Alvin Lim Yee Hong has resigned after being charged with allegedly allowing an unlicensed foreign worker dormitory to operate, the Catalist-listed company said on Nov 2. The construction engineering company, formerly known as Hatten Land , also disclosed that Lim and another director had not informed its board or sponsor about earlier dealings with the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) regarding the matter, including interviews conducted during investigations. The case concerns LBD Engineering, Metrocon’s controlling shareholder, where Lim, 35, also serves as general manager. Neither Metrocon nor any of its subsidiaries has been charged. LBD faces one charge of operating a foreign employee dormitory at 58A Sungei Kadut Loop without a valid licence between July 2025 and January 2026. Lim faces a separate charge alleging that he knew LBD did not have a valid licence, but allowed it to continue operating the premises as a dormitory. The first court hearing took place on Oct 29, with lawyers attending on behalf of Lim and LBD. The next hearing is scheduled for Dec 17. Lim intends to contest the charge, is seeking legal advice and has told the company that he needs to devote substantial time and resources to personal matters arising from the case, leading to his resignation as non-executive and non-independent chairman effective Oct 29. However, Lim has indicated that he wishes to be considered for reappointment to the board after the proceedings conclude. Metrocon said any return would be subject to the nominating committee’s assessment and applicable regulatory requirements. In its Nov 2 announcement, Metrocon set out the sequence of events based on information Lim provided to the board on Oct 29. Its statement said MOM had inspected the Sungei Kadut dormitory on Jan 6, and informed LBD by e-mail the next day that the company was operating the premises without a licence under the Foreign Employee Dormitories Act. LBD was then directed to relocate all occupants by Jan 9, which it did. On Aug 5, MOM requested that Lim attend an interview on Oct 2, after which he was released on bail. Metrocon’s non-executive and non-independent director Charlotte Tay Tingyin was also interviewed by MOM on Aug 7 to assist with investigations arising from the January inspection. Tay had served as an LBD director from Dec 17, 2025, to Feb 13, 2026. She subsequently acted as Lim’s bailor on Oct 2. The board said it understood from Tay that she was only assisting with investigations, had not been charged and had received no further contact from MOM since Oct 2. Explaining why the board and sponsor were not informed earlier, Metrocon said Lim and Tay did not consider the inspection and interviews to give rise to disclosure obligations because they concerned LBD rather than the listed group. They therefore “inadvertently omitted” to notify the board and sponsor, the company said. Apart from Lim and Tay, no other Metrocon director or key management personnel had been ordered or asked to assist with MOM’s investigations, according to the announcement. The chairman’s position will remain vacant while the nominating committee identifies and evaluates a suitable candidate. In the interim, board meetings will be chaired by lead independent director Kenny Sim Mong Keang or a director elected by those present. The board said it does not expect the recent developments to have a material impact on the group’s operations or financial performance for the year ending Dec 31. Lim confirmed that the charge did not restrict LBD from continuing its construction business and that its projects were proceeding in the ordinary course. Meanwhile, Metrocon’s business transactions with LBD remained ongoing and unaffected, the announcement said. Metrocon listed on Catalist in September via a $28 million reverse takeover (RTO) of embattled Hatten Land, a Malaysia property developer whose shares had been suspended from trading since August 2024, when it entered judicial management. Under the proposed terms, the acquisition was to be paid for through about 107.7 million new shares issued at 26 cents each to LBD. It now holds about 64% of Metrocon after purchasing additional shares following the RTO.

events.title: Singapore’s STT GDC eyes $3.1 billion loan, adds to AI debt binge
events.summary: A group led by KKR and Singtel completed its acquisition of STT GDC in September, after earlier agreeing to buy the data centre company for $6.6 billion. STT GDC is in talks for a $3.1 billion syndicated loan to fund its assets, with Standard Chartered, UOB, OCBC and DBS among the banks involved. The three-year loan pays 165 basis points over SORA and has a two-year extension option, as KKR and Singtel recently completed their $6.6 billion buyout of STT GDC. The deal adds to the AI debt boom, which has raised over US$650 billion since early 2025 and is worrying investors about high bond yields and AI valuations. HONG KONG – Singapore-based data centre operator STT GDC is in talks with banks for a $3.1 billion syndicated loan, according to sources familiar with the matter, as the AI boom continues to fuel demand for debt among companies building the infrastructure. Banks working on the planned borrowing as global coordinators, mandated lead arrangers and book runners include Standard Chartered, UOB, OCBC Bank and DBS Bank, said the sources, asking not to be identified discussing private details. The three-year borrowing, which pays an interest margin of 165 basis points over the benchmark Singapore Overnight Rate Average, comes with an extension option of up to two years, the sources said. Proceeds will be used as financing for STT GDC’s assets, they said. DBS, OCBC and UOB earlier participated in a $5 billion sustainability-linked loan for the purchase. Representatives from STT GDC, StanChart, DBS, KKR and UOB declined to comment, while Singtel and OCBC did not respond to a request for comment. STT GDC’s deal adds to a wave of debt financing driven by the artificial intelligence boom that has also raised worries among investors with the binge pushing up bond yields, increasing scrutiny of what many see as lofty valuations of AI-linked companies. Globally, the AI borrowing binge has flooded markets with more than US$650 billion (S$831.35 billion) of debt since the start of 2025, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Moody’s Ratings expects at least US$3 trillion of data centre-related investments over the next five years. Established in 2014, STT GDC is one of Asia’s largest data centre operators with facilities across 12 countries, including India, South Korea, Japan and Malaysia, as well as Britain, Germany and Italy, according to its website. events.title: How a Kansas City vlogger captivated New York society
events.summary: The News On Oct. 10, an unhappy billionaire, Amy Griffin, confronted a former host, Billy Bush, at a celebrity wedding on the Hawaiian island of Lanai. Guests included Demi Moore and Tobey Maguire. It was the sort of thing that delights the entertainment media, even if you won’t often read about it in this column. But this meltdown didn’t break on Vanity Fair or TMZ. Instead, New York and LA society discreetly tuned in to the Instagrammer known as KatyinKC , who cited “multiple” sources at the wedding. When I wrote about Griffin , the wife of a hedge-funder and author of a bestselling memoir, last week, I repeatedly heard that the wealthy and powerful figures in her social world are obsessed with KatyinKC. Her name is Katy Hoffman, and she is a 33-year-old registered dietitian and mother of two toddlers who works from the sofa in her comfortable Midwestern home. Over the course of this year, Hoffman has become the chief inquisitor of Griffin’s story of abuse during a superficially perfect childhood in Amarillo, Texas. Hoffman has unmasked pseudonymous characters from her book, discovered key audio files, and given a hard-edged voice to the skepticism about Griffin’s account first raised by The New York Times . Hoffman’s Instagram account is the thing “women in the ballrooms and the Upper East Side and the Palisades and Brentwood are listening to, but not following,” said Bush, who was fired from in 2016 for a 2005 hot mic exchange with Donald Trump on , and who now hosts the podcast . Social convention dictates that you not be caught liking Hoffman’s posts or following her yourself. But she is “the internet version of Nancy Grace,” Jolie Hunt, the CEO of a New York marketing and communications consultancy, told me. Hoffman’s videos across TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram offer regular glimpses of her own life. Sometimes she dances. Once she defended a local pizza joint from another influencer’s criticism. Her home is on display, too, a well-kept place with a wood-paneled den you’d immediately rip out in the Hamptons. She doesn’t, one person I spoke to noted, seem like the sort of person who would be found on Lanai. I called up Hoffman Friday to ask how she’d become part of a new generation of social media sleuths, why she was so focused on Griffin, and, of course, her decor. Courtesy of Katy Hoffman Hoffman got on the video call Friday wearing a T-shirt featuring the lovers in the TV show . She had just dyed her blond hair red. She grew up in the well-off suburbs of Des Moines — her family loves to travel and she’s been all over the world, if not Hawaii. She attended Iowa State, where she put her energy into her sorority and personal training (and certainly not journalism). She moved to Kansas City to start her career counseling people with eating disorders, but also developed a set of hobbies that, along with fishing and hunting, includes poking around public records. “I’m just a nosy lady,” she told me. She’d be the one to tell her friends that the neighbor down the street had a lien on his house. She recalled being in a nutrition office at a local hospital where colleagues were talking about local radio personalities’ messy public divorce, and she looked up the court documents. She also closely followed the messy drama between the actors Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni; like many on social media, she grew skeptical of Lively’s well-publicized claims and was persuaded by Baldoni’s responses. She posted to a tiny audience about them, and was briefly featured in an Atlantic article last April that asked: But Hoffman had long harbored this generation’s great American dream — to be a “content creator.” She had experimented with posting recipes and talking about her professional expertise, nutrition. One TikTok about Ariana Grande has 7.2 million views. But she also edged into original reporting. When a process server in the Lively-Baldoni case was arrested trying to get into Kansas City Chiefs star Travis Kelce’s property to reach his wife, Taylor Swift, Hoffman drove to the nearby police station to get court records, posted them online, and watched the news spread. She became one of a pack of traveling social media analysts and partisans, attending hearings in New York in January and April. The Griffin case, however, has been Hoffman’s breakout moment, and it has thrust her a little closer to the world of professional journalism than she expected. “It wasn’t until this case that I’ve really figured out being an investigative journalist a bit without any of the training or whatever,” she said, adding that she wasn’t sure how to feel when she noticed New York Times and Wall Street Journal reporters sign up for the Patreon where she distributes the court documents she’s turned up. She said she felt “intimidated” by the professional journalists who have started calling her up to swap notes. Ben’s view Hoffman, who sometimes works from a small swivel chair in her children’s room, has followed a path from social video into the center of the swirling news cycles of true crime and celebrity. Her rise has echoes of podcaster Ashley Flowers and blogger Jessica Red Krauss — media outsiders who tapped into deep veins of public interest. But she’s also an obsessive researcher whose focus and work ethic remind me a bit of CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski, were his focus celebrities rather than politics. She has gone to elaborate lengths to follow hints in Griffin’s book through high school yearbooks and long-forgotten high school sporting events. Hoffman also noticed a link in a legal filing to a redacted audio recording of Griffin’s 2021 call to the Amarillo police department and posted it; later, she posted the unredacted audio, but wouldn’t tell me how she’d obtained that. In other ways, she is pure social media. In one recent short video, Hoffman dances to a pop song, Nina Nox’s , and closes by giving a middle finger to the camera and lip-syncing. It’s been a disorienting year, she said. She’s made enough money from her content to pay for court documents and a little travel, but her day job and her husband’s (he’s an engineer) still pay the bills. “I don’t know what to do with it, I’m kind of stuck in this crossroads,” Hoffman said. “I can see how someone can grow and build this — but do I want to do that?” She was amused to hear that New York’s elite were making fun of her Midwestern life. “Put their direct quotes about what they think about me so I can rip them apart,” she suggested. My New York interlocutors, sadly, declined to go on the record — though one asked that I stress that any class-inflected mockery was delivered “with love.”

events.title: Oil falls as report says Trump to give Iran diplomacy more time
events.summary: The price of diesel displayed on a fuel pump at a petrol station in Pennsylvania, US, on Oct 20. Oil prices fell after a report said Trump wants more time for diplomacy with Iran before deciding on fresh strikes after the Nov 3 midterm elections. Brent slipped towards US$111 a barrel and WTI near US$102, while attacks near the Strait of Hormuz kept market fears high. Goldman Sachs raised its Brent forecast to US$105 for December, as Middle East and Ukraine risks, plus OPEC+ output plans, keep supply concerns alive. Oil dropped after a report said US President Donald Trump wants to give diplomacy more time before deciding whether to resume strikes on Iran following the Nov 3 midterm elections. Brent slipped towards US$111 a barrel after jumping more than 2% on Oct 30 , while West Texas Intermediate was near US$102. Trump told Benjamin Netanyahu of his preference for diplomacy in a phone call , a strategy that concerned the Israeli Prime Minister, Axios reported, citing sources it did not name. The two countries started the war in late February with joint attacks on Iran. On Oct 31 , US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said no decision had been made on fresh strikes and that Trump prefers a diplomatic resolution. The push for talks tempered concerns about renewed hostilities even as attacks on vessels around the Strait of Hormuz continued. The global benchmark rallied in October, hitting a six-month high despite a revival of crude flows through Hormuz. While Trump said last week that peace talks were under way, he has repeatedly threatened to resume strikes on Iran after the midterms. On Oct 29 , a top commander briefed the US President on military options, the Wall Street Journal reported. “This is a temporary pullback” in prices, said Florence Schmit, a senior energy strategist at Rabobank. Current rhetoric suggests further escalation in the Middle East is possible and could drive oil higher, she added. Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered his top military commanders to prepare for renewed confrontation with the US and Israel, even as his foreign minister signalled progress in diplomatic talks. An Iranian delegation was in Qatar for discussions with mediators on Oct 31 . On Nov 1 , UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said it received a report that a ship had been struck by a projectile in Hormuz, following an attack on a liquefied natural gas tanker on Oct 30 . UKMTO also reported a vessel was struck east of Ras Al Khafji, Saudi Arabia, deep inside the Persian Gulf. While crude exports from the Persian Gulf are near prewar levels, oil product shipments remain constrained. The Middle East conflict, along with escalating Ukrainian attacks on Russian refiners, has helped drive fuel prices higher. Diesel prices have surged in the US and Europe. Against that backdrop, Goldman Sachs Group raised its Brent forecast to US$105 a barrel for December and an average of US$88 in 2027 , citing heightened geopolitical supply risks. “The Mid-East and Russia-Ukraine conflicts, alongside broader geopolitical fragmentation, create high disruption risk,” analysts including Daan Struyven and Yulia Grigsby wrote in note. Separately, OPEC+ agreed over the weekend to keep output quotas unchanged in December after unwinding the last of its voluntary cuts in September. The move is largely symbolic, given that hostilities in the Middle East, including in the Red Sea, continue to threaten exports and production facilities. BLOOMBERG

events.summary: Megan Cunningham, an advertising industry veteran and founder of Magnet Media, is on Monday launching Magnet Originals, a brand to help established personalities grow their media empires and to incubate the next generation of stars. Former TikTok executive Dustin Goot and former Vice exec Subrata De are both joining in senior roles, alongside media operators Alexandra Zaslow and Brannan Goetschius. Magnet Originals will provide advice and production support for media personalities, including Justin Tranter, Boyz II Men’s Shawn Stockman, and former NBA star Byron Scott. It will also build on its own original franchises. The company said it is launching with a docuseries from the poet and critic Hanif Abdurraqib and a music show hosted by Billboard executive editor Lyndsey Havens, both co-produced with Live Nation, as well as , a show co-hosted by comedian Sam Jay, Olympic gymnast Jordan Chiles, and broadcaster Ari Chambers. The company is also hoping to build a business around training the next generation of creators. Its Top Creator Academy will offer courses and one-on-one consulting with professionals. Cunningham told Semafor that she saw the program growing into a seven-figure business on its own. “Documentaries can’t count on distribution, and newsrooms keep closing because their business model is in jeopardy. … I was watching a generation of entrepreneurial, brilliant storytellers build podcasts, YouTube channels, and newsletters on sweat equity alone,” Cunningham said. “A consultancy would have reached a handful of clients at a time, and it didn’t excite me.”
