events.title: How Canada’s resource wealth makes it a strategic partner for the UAE and Europe
events.summary: “Worthy Canadian initiative” is a common joke for the world’s most boring headline. But, threatened by the US, Canada is launching initiatives that could be more world-shaping than worthy. The UAE and the EU have become two vertices of the triangle including this northern resource giant. The Canada-EU summit concluded in Montreal, one of the most European cities in North America, on Friday. Though Prime Minister Mark Carney’s hopes of “associate membership” may not be granted in so many words, a much closer relationship is on the cards. And on Tuesday, the UAE signed a comprehensive economic partnership with Ottawa . The UAE committed $50 billion of investment in the country last year. This has a strong energy component: Abu Dhabi’s renewable energy champion Masdar concluded a co-operation agreement with federal agency Natural Resources Canada. Simultaneously, Dubai’s DP World is discussing developing the northern port of Churchill, on Hudson Bay, with access to the Arctic and Atlantic oceans. Rail connects it to the Pacific. Canada’s official Latin motto translates as “From Sea to Sea”, and some have proposed amending it to “From Sea to Sea to Sea” to respect the northern ocean. Churchill’s operator suggests it could be part of an Asia-Europe trade corridor that would be as fast and more secure than traditional routes through the Red Sea. The fast-warming Arctic, itself a warning of dangerous climate change, is opening up new shipping routes through previously ice-choked straits. These moves span four global trends. First, the need for other great and middle powers to build alliances and lessen dependence on an increasingly erratic US, a revanchist Russia and a potentially overbearing China. Second, the creation of alternative transport routes as maritime security comes under threat . Third, the construction of new trade architecture while other countries try to demolish it. Fourth, the search for reliable providers of critical resources. Resource superpowers The UAE and Canada may not have much in common geographically, but they are resource superpowers. While the UAE’s bounty concentrates mostly on hydrocarbons, the northern nation has those, plus many others. At nearly 6.2 million barrels per day, it is the fourth-biggest oil producer in the world and, depending on your view of Venezuela, the second or third-largest reserves owner. It is fifth in gas output, and its shale resources ensure plenty of room to grow production. The Shell-led LNG Canada in British Columbia began exporting liquefied natural gas (LNG) last June, with an ideal geography to supply Asia. LNG Canada is set to double capacity by the early 2030s, and two other projects are due to start in 2027 and 2028. Bloomberg last month suggested that Adnoc’s international unit XRG was interested in taking a stake in LNG Canada. The company already bought Calgary's Nova Chemicals in a $13.4 billion deal last March. Canada is first in the world in extracting potash, a crucial fertiliser, second in uranium mining , and fourth in gold, platinum and nickel mining and aluminium smelting. And it is an agricultural hothouse, with huge exports of wheat, oilseed, livestock, wood and other crops. For the new strategic minerals, as well as nickel for batteries, it is a growing producer of lithium and natural graphite. It has important deposits of titanium and vanadium, crucial metals for aerospace and defence technology. In the famous and geopolitically sensitive rare earths , it has no commercial mines today, but holds large resources, and several projects are being developed. Finally, its cool climate, open land and abundance of cheap, zero-carbon hydropower – where it is the third-biggest generator in the world – make it a good site for data centres . This commodity wealth makes it tremendously attractive as a partner to the EU: a stable, Western, free-market democracy, and closer than the similarly advantaged Australia. It is further from the UAE, but many of the same attractions apply. In turn, Canada needs good friends. Seventy-six per cent of its exports go to its overbearing southern neighbour. The EU, China and the UK are each of similar weight, with about 4 per cent to 5 per cent each. This dependence makes Canada vulnerable to the US's arm-twisting with tariffs. While Canada will no doubt expand trade with China, that brings its own political exposure. A recent preliminary referendum on independence for the hydrocarbon heartland province of Alberta, backed by right-wing voices in the US, was heavily defeated. But Canadians are not amused by “51st state” taunts. They saw how their Arctic neighbour, Greenland , was intimidated by the White House, which eyes enviously its rare earths and possible oil. New routes, new partnerships Transport barriers mean Canada does not earn full value for its resources. American natural gas producers might complain about low prices, currently $2.86 per million British thermal units. Europeans’ wallets are emptied, and their energy-intensive industries hollowed out by paying around $30, as they suffer from the cut-off of LNG from the Gulf. But the wholesale price in Alberta, Canada’s main producing region, is just $1.40 per MMBtu. It is a similar story for oil. With only one pipeline to the Pacific, Albertan producers are hostage to the US market. Western Canadian crude usually sells at about a $12 per barrel discount to the US’s West Texas Intermediate. That differential has now widened to $31 per barrel. Mr Carney has sought to promote new pipelines, to integrate the national electricity grid, and in general to recharge the Canadian economy by diversifying exports and slashing inter-provincial trading barriers. Broadening its transport infrastructure is a crucial element and needs deep-pocketed investors with a long time horizon. Full development of the Churchill port and rail corridor alone will cost $57 billion. It will not replace Suez or Panama, but the current war in the Gulf shows how valuable back-up plans can become. Like Western countries in general, Canada also struggles less with mining critical minerals and more with processing them. Investors are deterred by high costs, lack of access to proprietary technologies, and the tendency of China to undercut competitors. This may be a fruitful area for triangular UAE-EU-Canada co-operation, whether investing in metals refineries in Canada or in the Gulf, as part of an integrated supply chain. Diversification – of allies, trading partners, transport routes and commodity providers – seems like a good policy today. Although technically hydrocarbon competitors, the UAE and Canada have much to complement with Europe. A new geography mingles the warm waters of the Gulf with the chilly north.

events.title: Sam Altman makes surprise South Korea visit as OpenAI builds on chip partnerships
events.summary: Altman met with around 50 Samsung executives from businesses spanning electronics, finance and biotechnology on Saturday, Samsung said. South Korean media reported that Altman also met with SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, with executives from SK Hynix and SK Telecom in attendance. The visit follows OpenAI's partnerships with Samsung and SK Group under its Stargate initiative, focused on advanced memory chips and AI infrastructure. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman made an unannounced visit to South Korea over the weekend, meeting with Samsung executives and reportedly holding talks with SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, building on existing partnerships with the country's leading chipmakers. Samsung said Saturday that Altman met with around 50 executives from its affiliates spanning electronics, finance and biotechnology in Yongin, south of Seoul. The discussions covered AI developments, potential business opportunities and the technology's impact on corporate decision-making and operations, Samsung said. Altman also met with SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won over lunch Saturday, with senior executives from SK Hynix and SK Telecom in attendance, according to South Korean media reports. The two sides may have discussed cooperation on AI chips and data centers, including existing plans for high-bandwidth memory supplies and AI data center development, according to local media reports. The participants didn't provide details of the discussions. SK Hynix told CNBC it was unable to confirm the reported meeting. Altman also visited South Korea in October 2025, when he met with President Lee Jae Myung, Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Jay Y. Lee and SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won, and announced partnerships with Samsung and SK Group as part of OpenAI's Stargate initiative. OpenAI's Stargate initiative aims to expand AI infrastructure globally, with South Korea playing a role through partnerships focused on advanced memory chip supplies and AI data center development. Under the agreements, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix outlined plans to ramp up production of advanced memory chips, while OpenAI and its South Korean partners agreed to explore developing AI data centers in the country. OpenAI cited South Korea's ranking among global leaders in AI readiness and significant public-private funding to strengthen competitiveness as reasons for expanding its presence in the country. Altman's latest visit also follows a July meeting with Samsung Electronics Executive Chairman Jay Y. Lee at OpenAI's headquarters in San Francisco, according to Samsung. Altman left South Korea on Saturday, according to local media reports.

events.title: Haze probe: Three more S’pore-registered companies agree to engage assessors
events.summary: The three companies are Singapore Exchange-listed TSH Resources, Bumitama Agri and Kencana Agri. Three Singapore-listed firms, TSH Resources, Bumitama Agri and Kencana Agri, agreed to help assessors probe links to fires that caused transboundary haze. NEA had issued notices to 10 companies under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and ministers told them to examine operations, corporate links and supply chains. The firms said they would cooperate at their own cost and share updates later; TSH and Kencana shares were flat, while Bumitama Agri fell 3.29%. SINGAPORE – Three more Singapore-registered companies potentially linked to regional fires that led to transboundary haze have agreed to cooperate with assessments by a specialist panel that will examine and hold such firms accountable. TSH Resources was not directly named in the notices issued by the National Environment Agency (NEA), but two of its Singapore-incorporated subsidiaries – TSH Global Plantation and TSH Oversea – were among the 10 companies that received them. Representatives of these companies were issued notices under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. They were summoned for a closed-door meeting on Oct 28 with Senior Minister K. Shanmugam, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong and Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu. During that meeting, Shanmugam told them that they had to engage a firm from the specialist panel to conduct thorough inquiries into their operations, corporate relationships and supply chains. In a filing on the SGX dated Nov 2, mainboard-listed TSH Resources said it has written to the National Environment Agency (NEA) confirming that the group is “very keen” to engage, voluntarily and at its own cost, the assessors from the Government’s panel , to evaluate its operations, corporate relationships and supply chains in connection with the fires in Indonesia that have contributed to the transboundary haze. The company said it will cooperate with the assessors in carrying out their assessment, in accordance with applicable laws and regulatory requirements, and as may be directed by NEA. It added that it shares the Government’s concern over the impact of the fires and haze, and welcomes the opportunity to engage constructively with the relevant authorities and independent assessors. In another update on Nov 2, TSH Resources said its two subsidiaries had responded to NEA’s notices by submitting the documents and information compiled to date, while requesting additional time to provide any remaining documents and information. It added that it continues to collate the remaining information and intends to provide them to NEA “progressively” as well as cooperate and engage with NEA. Fellow mainboard-listed Bumitama Agri also said it has communicated its commitment to voluntarily engage assessors from the Government’s panel at its own cost. The company said it would cooperate with the assessors in accordance with applicable laws and regulatory requirements, and as directed by NEA. It also noted that it shares the Government’s concern over the impact of the fires and haze, and welcomes the opportunity to engage constructively with the relevant authorities and independent assessors. In a separate update on Nov 2, Bumitama Agri’s executive chairman and chief executive Lim Gunawan Hariyanto said the company had responded to NEA’s notice by submitting the documents and information compiled to date. He added that the company was continuing to gather and compile the remaining documents and information, as well as cooperate and engage with NEA. Lim also said that shareholders are advised to refrain from taking any action involving their shares or securities that may be prejudicial to their interests, and to exercise caution when dealing in them. Meanwhile, Kencana Agri said in a filing on Nov 1 that it had written to NEA on Oct 30 confirming that it would voluntarily engage assessors from the Government’s panel at its own cost. The company said it would cooperate with the assessors in accordance with applicable laws and regulatory requirements, and as directed by NEA. It added that it shares the Government’s concern over the impact of the fires and haze, and welcomes the opportunity to engage constructively with the relevant authorities and independent assessors. All three companies said they would provide further updates when there were material developments. Also on Nov 2, Golden Agri-Resources said NEA had appointed FTI Consulting (Singapore) as an independent assessor to evaluate its subsidiary, GAI. Golden Agri-Resources had said in a filing on Oct 29 that t he company and GAI will “cooperate fully and transparently” in providing the information requested by NEA. WongPartnership has been appointed as legal adviser to the assessor, while Davinder Singh Chambers has been appointed by NEA to coordinate the evaluation of GAI, as well as those of other companies and related work.

events.title: "Petty, selfish, unhinged": Haley Stevens' staff and colleagues erupt at her "betrayal"
events.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) faced fierce backlash from fellow Democrats, party officials and her own staffers after endorsing Republican Mike Rogers for the U.S. Senate on Sunday. Why it matters: It's a stunning reversal in standing for Stevens, who came within a few percentage points of being her party's nominee for Senate in Michigan just months earlier. "Pathetic, petty, selfish, unhinged," Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) told Axios of her endorsement of Rogers. "You run out of words." Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-Calif.) said of the video Stevens posted to social media announcing her endorsement and her joint press conference with Rogers: "I've seen more pleasant self-immolations." The latest: CNN's Anderson Cooper repeatedly pressed Stevens on why she changed her mind during an at times testy interview, asking whether she still wanted Democrats to win control of the Senate. "I absolutely do. I'm just casting this vote in my own way," she replied. When Cooper pointed out that she was "publicly casting your vote," Stevens responded: "I'm just one person." State of play: Stevens' endorsement of Rogers came after her long-running feud with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed reached a boiling point over the weekend. El-Sayed, a leftist who narrowly defeated the more moderate Stevens in the Senate primary in August, said in a statement on Friday that Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago." Stevens had been pressing El-Sayed to more forcefully condemn an ad from an outside super PAC that suggested U.S. aid to Israel was partly to blame for rising prices. Stevens, in her video endorsing Rogers, said that El-Sayed "said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign, and that I should stay away," adding, "He's right. ... I don't belong in Abdul's campaign." What they're saying: Stevens' Democratic colleagues met her endorsement with shock and fury. "I am lost for words," Rep. Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.) told Axios. Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.) said in a text to Axios: "I'm shocked that Haley would do this ... right before the election." "I JUST SAW THIS BULLSHIT," Rep. Emily Randall (D-Wash.) texted. "There is too much on the line for BS like this." "What the fuck is she doing?" another House Democrat said. "This election is not about her, and this will not age well." Zoom in: "I'm dumbfounded that Haley told me one thing last night and changed her mind today," said Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who had previously said Stevens told him in a phone call she was "voting straight down the line on the Democratic ticket." Raskin told Axios in a brief interview: "There is a great sense of betrayal for this to happen at the last minute before such a critical election." Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.) told Axios: "Stevens showed her true colors and Michiganders could see right through her. It's why she lost the Democratic primary." "I'm sincerely worried about my friend," Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.) said. What we're hearing: Several of Stevens' staff members resigned shortly after her announcement on Sunday, a former staffer familiar with the matter told Axios. Her former chief of staff Justin German said in a statement that he was "shocked and heartbroken" and that "many members of our team have resigned, including myself." Curtis Hertel, the chair of the Michigan Democratic Party, said in a post on X : "Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future." The other side: "This is what happens to the far left when they go against the centrists," a centrist House Democrat told Axios. The lawmaker added: "I don't think I would have done what she did. But this is what the far left needs to understand when they burn bridges." Another centrist House Democrat told Axios that El-Sayed "created this mess," adding: "He should have just condemned the ad and invited her to church." Stevens did not immediately respond to Axios' text seeking comment. Editor's note: This story has been updated with more comment from Democrats.

events.title: Haley Stevens faces push for removal from House Dem caucus
events.summary: Some House Democrats want Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) expelled from their caucus after she crossed party lines to endorse Republican Mike Rogers for Senate on Sunday. Why it matters: It would be an extraordinary step that reflects the deep internal resentment towards Stevens within her own party. "I hope she doesn't return to work on Tuesday," Rep. Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.) told Axios, saying Stevens should be removed from the caucus. "Agreed," Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas) told Axios, arguing the endorsement "doesn't accomplish anything except hurt[ing] Haley" and that "she got bad advice." "I'd support that," Rep. Emily Randall (D-Wash.) said of removing Stevens from the caucus. Driving the news: Stevens infuriated colleagues on Sunday by endorsing Rogers over Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Stevens in the Senate primary in August. Stevens, a pro-Israel moderate, had been urging the more left-leaning El-Sayed to more forcefully denounce a super PAC ad partially blaming U.S. aid to Israel for rising prices. Stevens said the ad claimed "Jews are responsible for America's economic woes." El-Sayed pushed back in a statement saying Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago." Stevens attended church with Rogers on Sunday and released a video to social media endorsing him. The two also held a joint press conference. What we're hearing: There has been private discussion about moving to oust Stevens, a senior House Democrat said, telling Axios, "That's what people want." Stevens was also removed from several House Democratic text chains, the senior lawmaker said. A second House Democrat told Axios: "I've heard people invoking the rule about not endorsing against Democrats." "Endorsing a Republican in a tipping point state is ridiculous, especially from a Democrat ... She should be removed from our caucus altogether," a third House Democrat said. Yes, but: Not everyone is on board with the idea — even those frustrated at Stevens. The senior House Democrat told Axios that, at the very least, "we need to wait and have the discussion after Tuesday." A fourth House Democrat said it's "too bad she chose to throw her career in Congress away so easily" but that the caucus "might still need her vote in the final two months before she's gone." Several lawmakers noted that Stevens is retiring anyway and that if El-Sayed wins, the point likely becomes moot. Stevens did not immediately respond to a text requesting comment on this story. The bottom line: "[I] am not letting it distract me from the work between now and Tuesday at 8pm," Randall told Axios.

events.title: Singapore, Argentina deepen trade ties as key South American trade pact enters into force
events.summary: The agreement establishes more transparent Customs procedures, and supports expedited clearance of express shipments and perishable goods. Singapore and Argentina have started the Mercosur-Singapore Free Trade Agreement on Nov 1, marking a “significant milestone” in Singapore’s ties with South America. Argentina can help Singapore diversify food imports, improve food resilience, and open opportunities in energy, infrastructure, logistics, technology and services. The pact cuts tariffs on about 96% of products, improves customs rules and supply chains, and supports services, investment, digitalisation and cybersecurity. SINGAPORE – The Mercosur-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (MCSFTA) – a trade pact between the Republic and a key South American bloc – entered into force between Singapore and Argentina on Nov 1. The move is a “significant milestone in Singapore’s economic engagement” with South America, Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade And Industry (METI) and the Argentinian embassy in Singapore said in a joint statement. “Argentina’s position as a major agricultural and food producer supports Singapore’s efforts to diversify food import sources and strengthen food resilience. There are also opportunities in sectors such as energy, infrastructure, logistics, technology and services,” they added. Argentinian businesses can leverage Singapore’s regional hub status to access opportunities in South-east Asia, both parties said. Mercosur (the Southern Common Market), was founded in 1991 by Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, and represents a population of about 270 million people. The MCSFTA is already in force between Singapore and the three other Mercosur founding member states. Under the pact, Mercosur will eliminate import tariffs on about 96% of products for up to 15 years, with around 25% of tariff lines enjoying immediate tariff-free access. The agreement also establishes common rules of origin and more transparent Customs procedures, allows greater use of preferential tariff treatment and more efficient supply chain planning, and supports expedited clearance of express shipments and perishable goods. “Beyond trade in goods, the MCSFTA creates a more conducive environment for services suppliers and investors through greater certainty, transparency and market access commitments,” METI and the Argentinian embassy in Singapore said. Signatories will also cooperate in entrepreneurship, digitalisation, cybersecurity, sustainable development and the development of micro, small-and-medium sized enterprises. The MCSFTA builds on the Pacific Alliance-Singapore Free Trade Agreement, which entered into force in 2025, in deepening Singapore’s economic ties with South America. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Bourke filmmaker takes over reins of Indigenous film festival in Paris
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bourke filmmaker named director of Indigenous film festival in Paris In conversation with Allan Clarke on Speaking Out. ( Supplied: Michael Fairbairn ) Filmmaker and former journalist Allan Clarke will take on the role of artistic director of Europe's only Australian First Nations film festival. The Festival du Cinéma Aborigène Australien is a celebration of First Nations film on an international stage. The festival will run from December 4-6 at the Cinémas l’Arlequin et Reflet Médicis in Paris. Growing up in far-west NSW, Allan Clarke struggled to identify with "overwhelmingly negative" depictions of Indigenous people in the media. "I remember from a very young age in Bourke looking around and going, 'I can't reconcile those kinds of tropes and stereotypes and negativity with my actual loving community,'" he said. Now living a world away in Paris, the Muruwari and Gomeroi filmmaker, writer and investigative journalist wants to challenge and subvert those tropes as the artistic director of Europe's only Australian First Nations film festival. "The conversations I've been having since living in France are providing context to people and saying that a lot of those stories aren't authentically us," he said. Allan Clarke is an award-winning journalist and filmmaker. The 11 th annual Festival du Cinéma Aborigène Australien will take place in Paris this December, with this year's theme Kinetic — Tradition in Motion: Cinema in Revolt. Festival founder Greta Morton-Elangué said the festival specifically identifies First Nations cinema and takes it to a global audience. "There literally was no existing platform in France or Europe," Ms Morton-Elangué said. "There are many great films coming and they often get selected in high profile [film] festivals like Cannes and Berlin and Toronto but in terms of a whole festival, there really was nothing anywhere." Mr Clarke has directed documentaries The Dark Emu Story and The Bowraville Murders. This year's program will feature films by acclaimed First Nations filmmakers Warwick Thornton, Wayne Blair and Danielle MacLean. "Coming in sort of fresh, I really wanted to highlight our filmmakers who are really challenging the status quo and who are consistently subverting and bending genres to tell our stories," he said. Mr Clarke said the festival can expand the European perception of First Nations Australians. "There is a view that we are not modern and that we're not making a huge contribution to the international cultural landscape," he said. "Largely what they have seen, whether that's in film or TV about us, has been made by non-Indigenous people." Allan Clarke will be the artistic director of the 11th edition of the film festival. ( Supplied: Instagram ) Head of First Nations content at Screen Australia, Gillian Moody-Ardler, said international audiences were eager to connect with First Nations cinema. "It's really important for us to be sharing our stories to a broader audience than just domestically," she said. "A lot of people haven't travelled to these desert regions that some of our stories come from, "They haven't experienced the stories that we have from our coastal territories as well." Mr Clarke said that in recent times, he has seen a shift with First Nations cinema turning to genres such as romantic comedy and horror. "We are taking these very well-established genres and subverting them," he said. Ms Moody-Ardler became the head of First Nations content for Screen Australia in 2025. ( Supplied: Screen Australia ) Ms Moody-Ardler said Mr Clarke was a good fit for the role. "He's done some really amazing films that have highlighted some terrible parts of history and he's done it in a very empathetic way but also not shied away from the hardness of those projects," she said. This is the first year that Ms Morton-Elangué will not be in charge of programming Parisian film festival. "In a sense, it is like handing over a baby," she said. She said she bonded with Mr Clarke over their shared love of First Nations cinema. "We were able to have this really animated discussion about naughty Tiwi Sistergirl humour," she said. Ms Morton-Elangue and Mr Clarke bonded over their love for cinema. ( Supplied: Greta Morton-Elangue ) Mr Clarke was simply grateful for the opportunity to show an international audience the breadth of Indigenous cinema. events.title: ‘Not playing in the red ocean’: SP Group aims to triple China district cooling capacity in 5 years
events.summary: Michael Lim, deputy managing director of SP Group’s Sustainable Solutions China, says the company invests in sustainable energy solutions, including solar energy and battery storage. SP Group wants to triple China district cooling capacity to about 120,000 RT by 2031, focusing on value and sustainability, not low prices. The firm has worked in China since 2015 and now runs projects in 20 provinces and municipalities, with major sites in Chongqing and Guangzhou. Its integrated energy model combines cooling, heating, solar, storage and digital monitoring, and may cut energy use by up to 40% and carbon emissions by around 2,000 tonnes. SHANGHAI/GUANGZHOU – SP Group seeks to stand out from local competitors by offering integrated sustainability solutions, instead of competing on price. “If customers are looking for the best price, it is a ‘red ocean’. We are not there playing in the ‘red ocean’,” said Michael Lim, deputy managing director of SP Group’s Sustainable Solutions China, referring to a business term for competitive and price-driven markets. Instead, the company is targeting the “blue ocean” of less crowded, value-driven markets, by being a one-stop provider of sustainable energy solutions, Lim said on a media trip organised by Enterprise Singapore. SP Group operates electricity and gas networks in Singapore and Australia, alongside sustainable energy businesses spanning district cooling and heating, renewable energy, electric-vehicle charging infrastructure, and digital services in Singapore, China, Thailand and Vietnam. Outside of Singapore, its biggest market for district cooling is China, where it intends to triple its current district cooling capacity of around 120,000 refrigeration tonnes (RT) by 2031. “We look at the quality and the life-cycle cost savings (of our services), and we are confident that our savings are quite significant,” said Lim, without disclosing price comparisons with competitors. SP Group entered the mainland Chinese market in 2015, and now operates projects in 20 provinces and municipalities, with a focus on the Yangtze River Delta, the Chengdu-Chongqing region , and the Greater Bay Area. District cooling and heating, which involves the centralised production of water that is piped to buildings for air-conditioning and temperature control, is its flagship business and “bread and butter” in China, said Lim. Among the group’s business segments, district cooling is the third-largest revenue generator, following the sale of electricity and the use of system chargers and transportation of gas, based on the company’s annual report for the year ended March 31, 2026. The company’s first and largest overseas district cooling and heating project is at Raffles City Chongqing, which has a cooling capacity of 14,000RT. More recently, its district cooling and heating network at the China-Singapore Guangzhou Knowledge City began operations in July 2026. When fully operational, the network is expected to reduce cooling and heating-related life-cycle energy consumption by up to 40% and cut annual carbon emissions by about 2,000 tonnes, said Lim. The project now has an installed capacity of 7,300RT, with the aim to scale up to 9,000RT. The network’s cooling capacity can be scaled further to support more buildings in the area, similar to SP Group’s Marina Bay district cooling network, which is expected to serve 50 connected developments by 2030. SP Group’s district cooling and heating network at the China-Singapore Guangzhou Knowledge City began operations in July 2026. While pure-play district cooling players had a bigger advantage in the past, client demands are shifting, said Lim. When SP Group first entered the Chinese market in 2015, it chose to invest in all forms of sustainable energy solutions, including industrial rooftop photovoltaic systems integrated with battery-energy storage, rather than being a pure-play district cooling operator. For example, at the China-Singapore Guangzhou Knowledge City, SP Group integrates district cooling and heating, solar energy, energy storage and digital monitoring to reduce energy costs for commercial buildings. SP Group provides district cooling and heating, and smart and clean energy solutions at the China-Singapore Guangzhou Knowledge City. “Today, I think we are actually reaping those advantages that we set in the beginning,” Lim said. He noted that while SP Group retains its competitive advantage as an integrated player, the value of life-cycle cost savings is not widely understood in the Chinese market yet. “I think it takes time to... recognise the value from a life-cycle perspective... The key word is stewardship – you need to educate your customers and bring them along.” But this is evolving as China pursues its climate goals of peaking carbon dioxide emissions before 2030, and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060. Against this backdrop, “more and more clients are looking at sustainability as a market trend”, said Lim. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Chinese regulators to hold talks on market support tools: Media
events.summary: The benchmark CSI300 Index slumped 8.5% in October for its worst month since early 2016. Chinese regulators will meet financial firms on 2 November to discuss market support tools, as stocks and bonds face heavy pressure and the CSI300 fell 8.5% in October. The People’s Bank of China, the NFRA and the CSRC will also meet major banks to improve relending for share buybacks and purchases, which may help a year-end rebound. Investors are watching Zhuhai Huafa Group’s debt trouble after missed trust repayments and bond losses, with brokers warning that official support will shape market confidence. BEIJING/SHANGHAI – Chinese regulators including the central bank will hold meetings with financial institutions on Nov 2 to discuss tools to support capital markets, media reported, as turbulence in stocks and bonds fuels calls for policy support. The benchmark CSI300 Index slumped 8.5% in October for its worst month since early 2016, while signs of stress have emerged in the bond market over the financial health of state-owned developer Zhuhai Huafa Group. China’s central bank and the securities watchdog will hold a seminar on the morning of Nov 2 with brokerages and fund management firms to study the use of tools to support capital markets, the 21st Century Business Herald said. Separately, the People’s Bank of China, the National Financial Regulatory Administration and the China Securities Regulatory Commission will convene major banks on Nov 2 to discuss optimising the relending policy for share buybacks and purchases, the official Shanghai Securities News said. Huang Yan, fund manager of Shanghai QiuYang Capital Co, said regulators may prod more lending to support share buybacks. The measures could “drive a market rebound towards the year-end”, he added, but cautioned that a policy bottom may not be the market bottom. A growing number of listed companies have announced share buybacks over the past month. There have also signs of state-backed buying, but these measures have so far proved inadequate to arrest a slide in the stock market, given a struggling economy and worries about lofty tech company valuations. Investors will also closely monitor the unfolding debt issues of Zhuhai Huafa Group. Huafa’s bonds and shares sold off last week after news that the state-owned developer failed to repay two maturing trust products and was in discussion with banks to extend loan maturities. In a sign of potential contagion, most exchanged-traded credit bond funds lost roughly 0.5% on Oct 30 in their biggest-ever one-day percentage loss. Hua Chuang Securities said in a note that the sell-off in Huafa bonds had triggered risk aversion and pre-emptive fund redemption. “The incident is still festering, and... the government’s expression of attitude and material support will have a key impact on the market,” the brokerage said. events.title: Hong Kong plans rules for insurers’ hot new growth market
events.summary: Hong Kong’s revised guideline is expected to take effect in 2027. Hong Kong is planning new rules for asset-intensive reinsurance, a fast-growing insurance market, to give firms clearer guidance and control the risks. The Insurance Authority has finished its consultation and is reviewing feedback. The revised guideline is expected to start in 2027 and will set when insurers must notify or seek approval. Big deals are already happening, including US$1 billion transactions by Resolution Life with HSBC and Hang Seng Life, and Pacific Life Re’s first Hong Kong deal with FWD. HONG KONG – Hong Kong is considering new rules for so-called asset-intensive reinsurance, offering clarity to firms in one of the hottest segments of the insurance market, according to people familiar with the matter. The Hong Kong Insurance Authority has in recent months sought industry feedback on changes to its rules, including additions that for the first time specifically target asset-intensive reinsurance, the people said. The reinsurance market has come into the spotlight around the world in recent years, as firms like KKR & Co and Apollo Global Management closed deals worth billions of dollars. Asset-intensive reinsurance offers a way for insurers to juice their returns, but it also adds risks. At the most basic level, insurers shift responsibility for managing a pool of assets and liabilities to a third party, which can invest the money elsewhere to boost returns. Reinsurers have become an important source of demand for private credit, a market that has caused jitters after a years-long boom. Under Hong Kong’s proposed rules, insurers would either just notify the regulator or seek approval depending on the scenario. For example, insurers entering into asset-intensive reinsurance contracts with third parties need only inform the regulator – rather than get explicit approval – when the reinsurer exceeds a certain credit rating threshold, and when the firm’s overall reinsured assets are not material compared with their long-term liabilities. Deals that require approval will be assessed on factors including credit rating, collateral and legal enforceability, the people said. Hong Kong’s Insurance Authority said in response to inquiries from Bloomberg News that the consultation has ended and it is reviewing the feedback. The revised guideline is expected to take effect in 2027, the regulator said. Resolution Life, a reinsurer owned by Japan’s Nippon Life Insurance, said earlier in 2026 that it had closed two reinsurance transactions in Hong Kong. HSBC Holdings’s life insurance arm and Hang Seng Life were on the other side of the deals, two of the people said. Each did a US$1 billion (S$1.3 billion) deal with the reinsurer, one of the people said. In October, Pacific Life Re announced it had done its first asset-intensive reinsurance deal in Hong Kong. The ceding insurer was FWD Group, one of the people said. Hong Kong insurers have used asset-intensive reinsurance to cede between US$10 billion and US$20 billion of liabilities to international reinsurance markets over the past five to seven years, according to estimates by consultancy Aon. The search for yield, greater access to private markets and regulatory changes have supported this demand, said Helbert Tsang, capital solutions leader for Asia life reinsurance at the firm. Representatives for Resolution Life, Pacific Life Re and FWD declined to comment. HSBC and Hang Seng did not respond to requests for comment. In 2025, Japan’s financial regulator surveyed life insurers to examine risks tied to their growing practice of transferring policy liabilities to reinsurers backed by global investment firms, sources familiar with the matter said at the time. Globally, the International Association of Insurance Supervisors has pointed to risks stemming from structural changes in the life insurance industry, including an increase in cross-border asset-intensive reinsurance transactions. events.title: ‘Dumbfounded’: Democrats’ chaos in Michigan exposes party's divides
events.summary: The News Democratic party leaders have found themselves unable to stave off an embarrassing schism in Michigan’s must-win Senate race, a crisis that may offer a glimpse of internal battles to come. Days of frantic shuttle diplomacy and attempts to organize a joint appearance by erstwhile Senate primary rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens culminated in Stevens’ surprise Sunday endorsement of Republican nominee Mike Rogers. Stevens appeared with Rogers at a Black church in Detroit less than 24 hours after vowing to colleagues that she would back El-Sayed, winning praise from President Donald Trump and calls for her eviction from the House Democratic Caucus. But perhaps the most stunning aspect of the crackup was how hard senior Democrats had worked to avoid it. Party leaders like Reps. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., and Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., were pushing hard to get El-Sayed and Stevens on the same page for a show of unity going into Tuesday’s critical elections. Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., said on national TV hours before Stevens’ defection that she had personally assured him on Saturday night she’d be backing El-Sayed. Raskin told Semafor in an interview Sunday: “I was blindsided, and I feel dumbfounded by the whole thing.” While the Senate race remains very close, it’s not clear how much Stevens’ turnabout will affect the final balloting. She has, however, laid bare deep divides within the party — principally over Israel and the establishment’s relationships with the left wing. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ statement backing El-Sayed after the flap did not mention Stevens, a member of his caucus, by name. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who had initially favored her as a better general election candidate than El-Sayed, called her endorsement of Rogers a “ despicable betrayal .” Many in the party believe leaders were powerless over Stevens: “I certainly don’t think it’s somebody else’s fault, other than Haley Stevens,” said a Michigan Democratic operative. Yet Michigan, where El-Sayed was struggling to win over some Jewish and Black voters even before this week, is now set among the first-in-the-nation Democratic nominating states. And the party’s inability to come together during the final week of the election is likely to haunt it well into the 2028 primary. what happened Stevens kept her allies and staff in the dark through the whole process as she privately insisted she would keep backing Democrats, including El-Sayed. As she and El-Sayed squabbled publicly over the last week, a few of her staff reached out to her discouraging her from endorsing Rogers, according to a source who’d worked on her race. Stevens’ response, according to the source: “Omg why would you think I would do that?!!” By Sunday, many of her staff had resigned, slamming her Rogers endorsement. “She lied to the people that she says she respects,” said the Michigan Democratic operative. El-Sayed, who had implored Stevens not to campaign with him last week, brushed aside the news. “None of this matters,” he told reporters in Detroit. Michigan party chair Curtis Hertel Jr. said Sunday on X Stevens was expelled from the state party. Meanwhile, national party leaders across the board were united in saying they supported El-Sayed. what happens next Stevens faces rough waters ahead. She appears to have violated House Democratic caucus rules banning campaign activity for non-Democrats, and some in the caucus want to punish her. It’s not immediately clear whether Jeffries and Stevens have talked. The Stevens-El-Sayed crackup had been building in the months since she lost to him in the primary. Stevens and other Michigan Democrats kept their distance from El-Sayed over his association with controversial streamer Hasan Piker and his positions on Israel. The feud accelerated over the closing weeks of the campaign when Cenk Uygur’s Rebellion PAC began running the anti-Israel ad that would eventually convince Stevens to endorse Rogers. Uygur says he never imagined that outcome when he aired it. “It wound up creating the perfect storm because it caused two weather fronts to collide,” Uygur told Semafor. “The establishment hated it with a passion and the internet loved it with equal passion. That’s what caused this explosion.” Nicholas and David’s view Democrats are closing their campaigns this cycle with fairly unified, populist messaging about “affordability” and “corruption” that helps the super-rich stay wealthy. Underneath that messaging is a feud between the party’s left flank and centrist arm that’s bound to erupt after Tuesday’s results. If El-Sayed loses, there will be a fight over blame between Democrats who spent tens of millions of dollars to support him and progressives who’ll argue that the party establishment can’t be trusted when leftist candidates win a nomination. This is in the air already, given Andrew Cuomo’s decision to run a third-party campaign after losing the Democratic primary to democratic socialist and now-New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. But if El-Sayed wins, his faction of the party will be able to say he did it in spite of the opposition of pro-Israel Democrats. That will weaken pro-Israel Democrats’ ability to say, as AIPAC does, that their agenda is “good policy and good politics.” That’s in the air too, with Democrats already gearing up to challenge Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., who’s stopped campaigning for other Democrats after feuding with pro-Palestine activists.

events.title: China’s big banks post fastest quarterly profit growth in years as margins stabilise
events.summary: Profit growth was driven partly by the repricing of higher-cost deposits that began at the start of the year. China’s five biggest state banks posted quarterly profit growth of 6% to 11%, their fastest since 2021 or 2022, as net interest margins steadied and asset quality stayed broadly stable. ICBC, AgBank, CCB, BoCom and BOC all beat weak economic conditions, but slowing credit demand, property stress and higher impairment charges still limit a stronger recovery. Banks also leaned on bond gains and chip IPO investments for earnings, but analysts warn these supports may fade and add more volatility. BEIJING/HONG KONG – Five of China’s largest state-owned banks reported quarterly profit growth of between 6% and 11%, supported by stabilising net interest margins (NIM) and steadier asset quality, even as a slowing economy continued to weigh. Each of the five lenders posted its fastest quarterly profit growth since 2021 or 2022, bucking the broader economic headwinds and building on their resilient performance in the first half of 2026. Profit growth was driven partly by the repricing of higher-cost deposits that began at the start of 2026. That benefit is fading in the second half, but recent monetary easing and mortgage interest subsidies help lower funding costs and support margins, analysts said. Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC), the world’s largest lender by assets, reported on Oct 30 that third-quarter net profit rose 10% year on year. Agricultural Bank of China (AGBANK), China Construction Bank (CCB) and Bank of Communications (BOCOM) reported similar net profit growth rates of 10.8%, 9.8% and 10.1%, respectively. Bank of China (BOC), with the greatest overseas exposure among the big five, reported a comparatively slower 6.4% growth amid trade tensions and foreign exchange swings. Economy ‘maintains overall stability’ The results suggest the big lenders are recovering from years of squeezed profitability amid a protracted property crisis, although weak credit demand and a slowing economy continued to have a negative impact. Policymakers stepped up targeted monetary support in September, which modestly improved credit demand. But the measures are unlikely to drive a significant recovery in lending, or notably lift mortgage growth, analysts said. “China’s economy maintained overall stability, moving towards innovation and upgrading, with relatively fast growth in production and supply, strong foreign trade growth, and new achievements in high-quality development,” CCB’s management said in the company filing. “However, it still faces difficulties and challenges such as strong supply and weak demand,” it said. Net interest margin held steady in the third quarter at ICBC, AGBANK and BOC, while it edged up at BOCOM. CCB said its NIM slightly fell to 1.36%. “An earlier than expected recovery in NIM, combined with broadly stable credit costs, positions these banks for a faster profitability rebound compared with smaller banks in the sector,” said Elaine Xu, a director at Fitch Ratings. Their strong access to high-quality central and local state-owned enterprise (SOE) borrowers provides a more favourable risk-adjusted return relative to most domestic peers, said Xu. Non-performing loan (NPL) ratios were overall stable at all five lenders as they stepped up bad-debt disposals, although pressure on retail asset quality may persist. ICBC, CCB and BOC said the NPL ratios remained flat at the end of September compared with three months earlier. AGBANK and BOCOM fell slightly to 1.23% and 1.29%, respectively. Impairment charges rose as lenders moved to replenish loan-loss provisions while revenue recovered. Analysts also warned of emerging asset quality risks from loans to technology and innovation-related sectors, as banks respond to Beijing’s call to boost lending to these industries. “Loan growth to such industries remains high, with asset risks emerging gradually as enterprises in these emerging sectors have not been tested through a business cycle,” said Nicholas Zhu, a banking analyst at Moody’s. CCB said the growth rate of its sci-tech loans – lending to what Beijing defines as science and technology firms – exceeded its average loan growth rate. Bond gains remained a key driver of the big banks’ earnings in the quarter, given their longer-duration bond portfolios, analysts said. “A lot of Chinese banks rely on bond gains to secure profits,” said Xing Zhaopeng, senior China strategist at ANZ. “But the support cannot be lasting as bond yields are very low now.” The state lenders are expanding beyond fixed income into direct equity investments, through major chip sector initial public offerings. While surging debut prices boosted quarterly fair value gains, subsequent fourth-quarter share price tumbles have introduced greater volatility.

events.title: Homeowners facing thousands in costs to upgrade from gas to electric
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ATCO gas shutdown to force Albany architect onto bottled gas after building dream home Michael Roberts says he would have designed his house with electrical appliances if he had known Albany would lose its gas network. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) An architect spent thousands on gas appliances for his new home only to find out gas was set to go. Eight thousand of ATCO's Albany customers will need to change to electricity, or use gas bottles. The WA government is offering up to $2,000 for conversions, but experts say it will barely cover it. After years designing dozens of buildings in the coastal city of Albany, architect Michael Roberts finally built his dream home. The avant-garde house in Middleton Beach, about 450 kilometres south of Perth, was built connected to the city's reticulate liquid petroleum gas network, with gas appliances for heating and cooking plumbed in. But Mr Roberts is now facing a bill in the tens of thousands to refit the home after ATCO Australia announced it would decommission its Albany gas network over the next three years. "I've had a look at the compensation packages that have been put on the table," he said. "I don't know whether they've all been agreed or signed off yet, but the whole thing has come as a surprise." Michael Roberts says it will cost up to $12,000 to convert his new home from gas to electric. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) The $31 million package, which includes $5 million from ATCO, will cover the cost for customers moving to bottled gas, while those going electric will be compensated up to $2,000. Mr Roberts said the compensation would only cover a fraction of the $10,000 to $12,000 he estimated it would cost to swap his appliances from gas to electric. "We'll probably tough it out with bottles, but had I known earlier I would have made the decision and gone straight to electric," he said. The architect said ATCO's decision, and the timing of its announcement, had affected several of his firm's clients. "It's disgraceful that as design professionals, as architects, we were designing projects for people and they're making selections to use gas in good faith … that we weren't told; they weren't told," he said. ATCO and the state government faced renewed criticism last month after documents obtained by the ABC found they discussed the decommissioning of the network eight months before customers were told. Amber-Jade Sanderson says the government tried to persuade ATCO to remain in Albany. ( ABC News: Armin Azad ) Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said following unsuccessful discussions to keep ATCO in Albany, it was her preference residents move off gas entirely. "It's not going to be the long-term fuel for Western Australia," she said. "It's a transition fuel, and ultimately, we want the residents of Albany to electrify." One-year-old dies in house fire south of Perth Western Australia experienced a roller-coaster of weather in October Country town reliant on backpackers warns visa changes will cripple business Learning Auslan a 'life skill' for children Energy analyst Ray Wills said the transition from gas to electric was the right move, but the package needed to be larger to entice people away from gas bottles. "No longer burning gas should be an incentive in itself," he said. "However, if you've got to spend six or eight or 10 grand to convert your house … it's still reasonably dear." Professor Wills said a business case should determine the exact price, with the government subsidising 50 per cent of the cost. Albany residents who want to keep gas appliances will need to transition to gas bottles. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding ) He said the main concern with the package was that customers would stay on gas as the rest of the state electrified. "We can draw a metaphor … the Rio Tinto board tried to electrify, it didn't quite get there because they were getting free money from government for their diesel, so they stuck with it," he said. "This is kind of the same thing. It's about having a lower cost option being the one that's still burning stuff, and the higher cost option is going electric, which is what the state is trying to achieve." Greg Stocks says the package will not encourage all residents to go electric. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding ) City of Albany Mayor Greg Stocks said the package was not enough to achieve the state government's goal of electrification. "This transition package is about gas bottle, reticulated gas to gas bottle, the budget's not big enough for electrification," he said.

events.title: United Arab Emirates says military solutions offer no quick off-ramps to crisis with Iran
events.summary: The United Arab Emirates hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations to prevent a new confrontation between the U.S. and Iran MANAMA, Bahrain -- The United Arab Emirates’ presidential adviser said Sunday that his country hopes a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations is possible to avert a new round of confrontation between the U.S. and Iran. The Iran war , which began on Feb. 28 with joint strikes by the U.S. and Israel followed by attacks by Iran on the Gulf nations, has made it “a watershed year” for the region and the world, UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said at a security forum in Bahrain. “We don’t really want to see another round of confrontation in the region,” Gargash told the audience at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security summit in Bahrain organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, or IISS, that brings together regional and international state, defense and foreign-affairs officials and experts. Iranian negotiators are in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz soon, according to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. He said that no direct talks are being held with the U.S. and that the final outcome depends on answers provided by the United States to the “Iranian questions.” In an interview shared on his Telegram channel, Araghchi said Iran hoped that the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.” He said Iran was ready for both defense and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality.” A possible escalation cast a long shadow over the three-day security forum in Bahrain's capital, Manama. Gargash, the UAE adviser, said that the current crisis requires “a lot of wisdom, with political tools being our main tools, and the understanding that military solutions will only complicate the current very complicated scene that we have and will not actually bring any quick off-ramps.” Gargash, however, acknowledged that “the rules of logic” show that the U.S. and Iranian stances are far apart. “If these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst,” Gargash said. He said it's not in the interest of the region or Iran to withstand another round of war. It was a sentiment echoed by other Gulf and Arab officials at the forum. Egypt's foreign minister Badr Abdelatty, a day earlier, told the gathering: "The second round (of escalation) will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere.” But Gargash added that his country and the region are braced for the possibility of escalation. Before a ceasefire was reached in April, the UAE faced the largest number of airborne attacks from Iran, with more than 3,000 drone and ballistic missile attacks targeting airports, military and oil facilities, according to IISS. Most of those attacks were intercepted. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Since then, Gulf nations have spent billions of dollars to boost their defense capabilities. Gargash said that the war has solidified U.S.-UAE relations, making them “even more important” and at the heart of the UAE’s ability to defend itself. At the conference, Bahraini Foreign Affairs Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani said that his country also welcomes “every effort to reduce tensions, prevent escalation and create opportunities for dialogue.” Al Zayani said that Iran has shown what he called a pattern of attacks or threat of attacks threatening the region’s and the world’s stability and prosperity by targeting sea, air and data facilities. He said Iran has continued to do so even after a ceasefire was reached and as recently as last month, threatening underwater data cables. He described the attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels on neighboring Saudi Arabia as part of the pattern. “These attacks are part of one continued pattern,” he said. “The hands may change, the approach doesn’t.” Iran fired 500 drones and nearly 200 ballistic missiles toward Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, at the height of the war, according to IISS. The attacks hit the naval base, residential buildings, the financial district and a water desalination plant. This summer, Houthi rebels have escalated their attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and airports, saying they were a response to Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa airport. The Houthis have hit critical oil pipelines and disrupted air traffic in the kingdom. Another issue that prevailed over the forum was the lack of a coordinated defense response among the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and Oman. At the height of the war with Iran, the response from the Gulf countries that bore the brunt of Iranian strikes was at the national level, each working with U.S. command and control centers in the region.

events.title: Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson prepare for the return of war as localized ceasefire ends
events.summary: Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson region are preparing for the end of a localized ceasefire KHERSON, Ukraine -- Civilians in Ukraine’s southeastern Kherson region prepared Sunday for the end of a localized ceasefire that has marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began nearly five years ago. The White House said that U.S. first lady Melania Trump helped to broker the limited truce , which began early Tuesday and is expected to end Sunday evening. The pause in hostilities allowed besieged residents in the front-line city of Oleshky to be evacuated in a rare joint operation that ended Saturday. “The ceasefire across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack," Trump said on social media. "Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace.” An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of evacuating to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. For the safety of those who have stayed, exact numbers weren't released after the evacuation. At the Ukrainian border Saturday, family members waited for a glimpse of their loved ones, while residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet the humanitarian convoy. But Moscow and Kyiv have continued aerial strikes elsewhere, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying Sunday that Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy systems before winter. Hundreds of thousands of families were left without power overnight as Moscow sought to exploit Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses, Zelenskyy said in a post on social media. “The intensity of the strikes is extremely high, and the Russians are trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said in a post on X. Residents in the Ukrainian city of Kherson remained calm Sunday, despite knowing that the quiet of the localized ceasefire would soon end. “Don’t be afraid, keep holding on,” Oleksandr Knyha, head of the Mykola Kulish Kherson Regional Academic Music and Drama Theater, told the audience as he opened a concert. The theater performs every Saturday and Sunday. This weekend’s shows fell during the ceasefire, but the company plans to perform next weekend as usual, even as local officials warn that Russian forces have brought in more weapons and personnel and some residents expect shelling to intensify. “Of course, we want peace to finally come,” Knyha said. But “we’ve been working on the front line for four years,” he added, referring to Kherson itself, and the theater has never canceled a performance. “Whatever happens, the show is not canceled,” he said. The company now performs in a basement and is equipping an additional bomb shelter. About 100 of the theater’s 120 staff members work in Kherson, and none has evacuated. Costume maker Alla Vasylenko, 58, said that the silence of the brief truce still frightens her. “Nothing will change,” she said. “Everything will go back to how it was before the ceasefire, because believing the Russians means not believing yourself.” “I have 10 dogs, so I can’t leave,” she said. “They urge us to leave, but you need somewhere to go and the means to get there.” Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say The trip alone would cost 30,000 to 50,000 hryvnias ($650 to $1,080), a significant sum for her, she said. “Until we liberate the left bank, we have no certainty this will end,” Vasylenko said, referring to the Russia-occupied part of the region. For many in Kherson, a city that itself lived through Russian occupation, that belief is the reason they stay. Knyha is from Oleshky, on the occupied left bank, and used to commute from there to work in Kherson. He hasn’t given up hope of returning home. “That’s also what keeps me here,” he said. On the last day of the ceasefire, the theater staged a concert built around a “musical map of Ukraine,” with songs from the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014, to the Carpathian mountains in Ukraine's southwest. “This is also our job — to unite people and give them hope,” Knyha said. Elsewhere, a Russian attack killed three people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Ukrainian region of Vinnytsia when a drone hit the grounds of a vocational school, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. Four others were wounded, including two 5-year-old girls and a 16-year-old boy.

events.title: Don't get caught out by new Buy Now Pay Later rules
events.summary: If you've bought something via Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) since the summer, then you'll have been tested to see if you can afford it. BNPL has always been a type of loan, usually paid back in instalments, but it's only been officially regulated since July. This means stricter background checks on your ability to repay. If you fail, then your purchase via BNPL will be blocked. If there's a chance of this happening to you, here are some ways to approach the situation. BNPL lenders - such as Klarna, Clearpay and others - must now have regulator approval to operate, giving shoppers more access to refunds and independent rulings on complaints if things go wrong. But new affordability checks on each BNPL transaction could also leave you blocked from services for the first time. There are different affordability checks for different purchases, partially based on how much is borrowed. But, with the expensive festive season approaching, here's how to avoid being blocked when time and finances are tight. Here are four things to consider if you find your account is closed or your borrowing limit has been massively reduced, from Sara Williams, a former volunteer debt adviser at Citizens Advice who posts tips as Debt Camel on social media. Slow down your purchases: is what you are buying essential or can you postpone it? Be more careful about what you buy to avoid needing a high credit limit to, for example, buy lots of clothes in different sizes Cancel subscriptions to escape the trap of having to use BNPL to make up for the cost of previous payments Talk to debt charities for help and access to food bank vouchers if you are using BNPL for essentials If you are struggling to make repayments on any type of loan - BNPL or otherwise - you should seek help before things spiral out of control. The government-backed, independent, MoneyHelper website , external has a guide to finding free debt advice near you , external . It also suggests writing down exactly what you owe, to help plan how you will repay the money. There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, and a bill prioritiser , external to show which payments to make first and what to do if you miss a payment. You should also be sceptical of supposed debt solutions you might see on your social feeds. Have you been affected by the issues in this story? events.title: Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers amid Michigan Democratic feud
events.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) made a stunning last-minute endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, two days before Michigan's closely watched Senate election . Why it matters: Her endorsement gives Rogers a striking photo op as his party tries to peel away Black and Jewish voters in a tight race that could determine control of the Senate . Driving the news: Stevens appeared Sunday alongside Rogers at Detroit's Perfecting Church, where she praised his support for Black-owned businesses. Stevens later posted an endorsement on X. In a video, she said Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed told her she was no longer welcome in his campaign. "And he's right, and that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today," Stevens said. Stevens' appearance with Rogers was arranged at the last minute after the two spoke Sunday morning, per a person familiar. She had previously planned to attend a Detroit church service with El-Sayed and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.). How it happened: The dispute escalated last week after Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, announced he would vote for Rogers. Stevens demanded El-Sayed condemn an outside group's ad linking U.S. support for Israel to higher grocery prices and remove a campaign ad featuring Tucker Carlson. On Friday night, after El-Sayed's campaign said Stevens would not be welcome at his events, Rogers called Stevens and told her he would welcome her support, according to a person familiar with the conversations. The next day, El-Sayed explicitly rejected the outside ad's contents, prompting Stevens to publicly welcome his remarks. On Sunday morning, Stevens called Rogers back to say she would endorse him, the person said. She told Rogers she remained a Democrat and believed the party would still win a Senate majority. The intrigue: A video posted by Detroit journalist Sam Robinson showed Stevens entering the church and praising Rogers . Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), who helped organize the original planned appearance with El-Sayed, told CNN she asked Stevens not to attend because the dispute had become distracting. Stevens narrowly lost the August Democratic primary to El-Sayed but endorsed him afterward. The other side: A person close to El-Sayed argued Stevens' endorsement could actually help him by reinforcing his anti-establishment appeal. "It's good for Abdul," the person said, portraying Stevens as a symbol of the Democratic establishment, Congress and support for the Israeli government. The endorsement "shows Abdul is the candidate of change and for the people of Michigan," the person added . What she's saying: Stevens told Politico that El-Sayed had made clear she wasn't welcome in his campaign. " Abdul has run a magnificent campaign," she told Politico's Adam Wren. "He just was clear that I wasn't a part of it. I mean, I respect him. I wish him well. He very well could win. It's a close race. I mean, I'm voting for the other guy, and maybe some others are too." What he's saying: President Trump welcomed Stevens' endorsement in a Truth Social post Sunday afternoon, calling it "BIG" and praising her "bravery." Trump said Stevens has a huge following and "virtually unparalleled" respect among Michigan's Black and Jewish voters. "Haley said what few people are willing to say," Trump wrote, calling the endorsement an act of loyalty to Michigan. Trump said at an Iowa rally later Sunday: "I'd love her to join the Republican Party. Actually, I think that could happen maybe." Flashback: In August, Trump called Stevens a "Radical Left Socialist" during the primary vote count. What we're watching: Michigan voters choose between Rogers and El-Sayed on Tuesday, with Democrats facing a crucial test of whether they can reunite their coalition. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

events.title: Judge dismisses Alaska Senate election lawsuit; DOJ vows appeal
events.summary: A federal judge dismissed DOJ’s Alaska Senate election lawsuit after finding the government failed to establish the redressability requirement for Article III standing. DOJ sought to delay certification only if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan lost and reallocating every Daniel J. Sullivan vote to him would change the ranked-choice result. The dismissal is without prejudice because the court lacked jurisdiction, but Judge Sharon Gleason denied leave to amend as futile; DOJ says it will appeal. A federal judge on Sunday dismissed the Department of Justice 's extraordinary lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the Alaska Senate election if incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan loses, citing possible voter confusion from another candidate with his name on the ballot. The ruling came two days before Election Day and two days after the U.S. Attorney for Alaska said ongoing criminal and civil investigations into non-incumbent Dan J. Sullivan's decision to run for the Senate. The campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola , state election officials and outside advocacy groups had asked Judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss the DOJ's lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Anchorage. The Department of Justice quickly filed a notice of its intention to appeal the decision to the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals. Peltola is locked in a tight contest with Sen. Dan Sullivan, whose winner will be determined by a ranked-choice system. The outcome of the race is one of several contests that determine which party has a Senate majority, where Republicans currently hold a narrow lead. Neither the other Sullivan nor the fourth candidate on the ballot, Gerald Heikes, is considered a contender. But voters who rank them as a first choice could swing the outcome by ranking Peltola or Sen. Sullivan second. Alaska Gov. orders probe of Peltola Senate campaign's alleged recruitment of 2nd Sullivan Warren urges DOJ probe of Bank of America money laundering It's a 'socialist' bank — and North Dakota Republicans love it Three media outlets seek full White House access in amended lawsuit Peltola's campaign has been accused of encouraging retired schoolteacher Dan Sullivan to run for the Senate against the incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Peltola. Her campaign has denied those claims. "No sham investigation or baseless lawsuit from a weaponized Department of Justice is going to stop Alaskans from electing Mary on November 3rd so she can lower costs for Alaska's working families," Peltola's campaign said in a statement after Sunday's ruling. "Alaskans will choose their next U.S. Senator – not Dan Sullivan or his DC allies," the campaign said. In her 20-page decision, Gleason did not resolve whether another Sullivan had been recruited to confuse voters. Instead, she said the federal government had failed to establish that it had legal standing to file a civil complaint to postpone certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan lost. In that event, the DOJ wanted an investigation into voter intent and possible confusion from having two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. "The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling," Gleason said in her ruling. She noted that early voting in the state was already underway, and that ballots already cast have been commingled in a way that would prevent officials from linking individual ballots to voters. "More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," Gleason wrote. The judge also cited a Supreme Court decision that established the so-called Purcell principle, which "strongly cautions" against courts altering election rules on the eve of election. She noted that DOJ claimed it was not seeking to alter the "time, place or manner of Alaska's election." But at the same time, Gleason said, the DOJ was asking her for an order "preventing the State from certifying the election if certain circumstances occur; a court order requiring the State to segregate and preserve certain ballots; and a court order permitting the United States to conduct an investigation into the intent of those voters who cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan." "These requests certainly involve the time, place, and manner of Alaska's election, which are the responsibilities of the State, not the executive branch of the federal government," Gleason said. The judge said she would not allow the DOJ to amend the lawsuit, which was revised last week to add a new legal claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution to the first claim under the National Voter Registration Act. The amended complaint also added details of a New York Times article about the alleged recruitment of the second Sullivan.
