events.title: How HSBC is investing in Hong Kong to build the future of finance — and why now
events.summary: As Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026 approaches, HSBC is investing in the city’s talent, technology and partnerships to turn advances in AI, blockchain and tokenisation into banking services for customers in Hong Kong and beyond [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Hong Kong has been a home market for HSBC since the bank was founded 161 years ago. It is now also a base for the bank’s AI investment and delivery, with capabilities developed in the city intended for use across other markets. The city is also expanding the regulatory and market infrastructure needed to support digital finance at scale. HSBC returns as a Strategic Partner of Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK for the fourth consecutive year as technologies discussed for years begin to find a commercial footing. “Our vision is simple. Empower our colleagues to use AI to create a personalised experience for each customer, and to deliver it safely, in real time and at scale, all while keeping human judgement, decision-making and accountability at the core.” AI is a core part of HSBC’s technology strategy. In Hong Kong, the bank already has a team of 150 AI specialists and plans to double the team within two to three years. HSBC will also establish a global AI institute in Hong Kong, expected to begin operations in early 2027. It will initially focus on AI, post-quantum cryptography and blockchain technology, with a view to applying these technologies across HSBC’s operations. In addition, HSBC has technology and AI specialists in other key locations, innovating to address bank-wide opportunities globally. From capability to customer outcomes HSBC has used AI for years in automation, data analysis and services for employees and customers. Its focus now covers an end-to-end view of AI across the bank’s operations and customer services. Banker Assist, for example, combines HSBC’s internal data with trusted external information to provide relationship teams with more detailed client insights. The bank has also rolled out HSBCnio here in Hong Kong, a digital, AI-enabled solution for corporate and institutional clients. It brings transaction-banking functions into one connected experience and allows clients’ own AI tools to access authorised bank accounts and transaction information on a read-only basis. HSBC is also working with technology companies including Mistral AI, Google, Amazon and Microsoft, with governance, resilience and risk management built into its approach. Building innovation people can trust HSBC recently tested two use cases within the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s GenAI Sandbox, covering customer accessibility and anti-fraud capabilities. The first is a generative AI-powered sign-language translation solution that explores ways to make banking services more accessible for customers who use sign language. The second focuses on deepfake detection and ways to identify manipulation as criminals use increasingly sophisticated techniques to imitate people, documents and communications. The two use cases show different sides of responsible innovation: improving access to banking services and strengthening protection against new forms of fraud. The infrastructure that moves money, assets and information is also evolving towards always-on, data-rich and increasingly programmable digital rails. Tokenised deposits, digital bonds, stablecoins and central bank digital currencies can support faster settlement, improved liquidity, lower operational friction and better traceability. For retail customers in Hong Kong, HSBC is launching HSBC RedCoin, its first Hong Kong dollar-denominated stablecoin, for 3.3 million customers through PayMe. It is designed to support peer-to-peer and peer-to-merchant payments using HSBC’s technology and security infrastructure. Later this year, HSBC also plans to add stablecoin wallet functionality to the HSBC HK Mobile Banking app and enable customers to subscribe to tokenised investment products through HSBC RedCoin, including a soon-to-be launched share class of HSBC’s HKD money market fund. HSBC Gold Token is another case in point. Since its launch in 2024, the tokenised gold service has recorded 390,000 trades with a total traded value of US$2.5 billion. For corporate clients, HSBC has launched Tokenised Deposit Services, starting in Hong Kong and expanding across Asia, Europe, the US and the Middle East. The service supports 24/7 cross-border payments and real-time settlement across a range of currencies, and has also been applied to corporate treasury management and capital-markets settlement. HSBC is also facilitating interoperability across networks and platforms through active participation in the HKMA’s Project Ensemble and other industry initiatives. For institutional investors, HSBC Orion provides a concrete example of tokenisation in capital markets.

events.title: Where Dems eyeing the White House are putting their midterm chips
events.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro 's chances of being a presidential contender in 2028 are riding on his winning reelection in a landslide Tuesday. New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez 's future hinges on whether a fellow progressive can carry a swing state, for once. California Gov. Gavin Newsom has to show that his congressional redistricting gambit worked for Democrats — and he needs to beat back a state wealth tax proposal supported by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). Driving the news: Democrats eyeing White House runs have spent the past year preparing to emerge from Tuesday's midterms with momentum, and an argument for a 2028 candidacy. They want Democrats to do well — but to each, some races are especially important. Some have focused their time and money on particular contests for ideological reasons, or a desire to show strength in their home states. Others have hedged their bets across the nation, so that Tuesday is unlikely to be a huge victory or a significant defeat. Here's how the top potential Democratic contenders for president have placed their bets in this week's elections — and what success or failure will look like for them. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez A great night: AOC has wagered just about everything on the Senate race in Michigan, where she's said that a win by progressive Abdul El-Sayed would "break open the entire political calculus in America" and show that "anybody can win anywhere." She's weighing whether to run for president or the Senate, and much of her electability argument for a national campaign hinges on an El-Sayed victory. Progressives are desperate to establish that one of their own can carry a presidential battleground state. Ocasio-Cortez has contributed $1 million to help El-Sayed and stumped for him at several events. An El-Sayed victory "would prove to the country, and the world, that competent, courageous progressive populists can win in the most competitive swing states in America," said Bhavik Lathia, a left-wing strategist from Michigan. "The implications for 2028 would be enormous." AOC would get bonus points Tuesday if other progressives she's supporting — such as House candidate Randy Villegas in California and Senate candidate Angie Nixon in Florida — win their swing-seat races. Worst-case scenario: If El-Sayed loses, many progressives think AOC would be less likely to run for president. That's why she's widely viewed as having more on the line Tuesday than any other potential Democratic contender for president, followed by Shapiro. Josh Shapiro A great night: Shapiro needs to win so big Tuesday that it makes Democratic presidential primary voters see his technocratic "get shit done" brand of governing as the party's best bet to take down the GOP in 2028. Shapiro is less known nationally than many 2028 hopefuls, and that has been by choice. He's largely focused on Pennsylvania this year, even as would-be rivals for president crisscrossed the country. A blowout in America's biggest swing state could help him stand out. A good night for Shapiro would be defeating Republican Stacy Garrity by double digits and carrying three Democratic House candidates — Janelle Stelson, Bob Brooks and Paige Cognetti — across the finish line to defeat Republican incumbents. He'd have a great night if his coattails were so long that he pulled a fourth Democratic House hopeful, Bob Harvie, to victory — taking down GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who's known for surviving difficult electoral cycles. Shapiro would get extra credit if he helped Democrats win a trifecta in Harrisburg for the first time in decades by flipping control of the state Senate. Worst-case scenario: If only one or two Democrats in his state flip House seats or he wins by less than 10 points, Shapiro's setup for 2028 would fall short. Andy Beshear A great night: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who moonlights as chair of the Democratic Governors Association, put his chips this year on helping his party take control of a majority of the nation's governorships. Beshear would earn bragging rights if Democrats flip the two governors' seats needed to do that. He's eyeing the races in Iowa, Ohio, Georgia and Nevada. "I am laser-focused on these governors' races," he told us, arguing that the results will help determine what's possible in the 2028 presidential contest. "Rob Sand wins Iowa, Iowa's in play. When Amy Acton wins Ohio, Ohio's in play," Beshear said. Worst-case scenario: Beshear made enemies among some Latino Democrats this year when the DGA rebuffed calls to invest heavily in Gina Hinojosa's campaign for Texas governor. If Hinojosa loses to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott by a razor-thin margin or pulls an upset, Beshear's decision-making will come under heavy scrutiny — and he could have a problem with some Latino leaders in a 2028 campaign. Gavin Newsom A great night: Newsom won over many MS NOW moms and "resistance" liberals across the country when he responded to President Trump's push to create more GOP House seats in other states by fighting back with a successful voter proposition to do the same in California. His goal has been to gain five Democratic seats from the change to help Democrats take back the House. That's his bar to clear Tuesday. Some political insiders now think Democrats could gain 20 or more House seats across the country, so Newsom's contribution might not be as decisive as once thought. Newsom would score a political win if a proposed billionaire wealth tax on the ballot in his home state, which he opposes, fails. Worst-case scenario: If California voters approve the tax or Democrats flip fewer than five House seats there, it would diminish Newsom's California clout. events.title: Parents of woman who died of seizure after ChatGPT misguidance sue OpenAI
events.summary: Bowen Wan was on anti-seizure medication, and chatbot provided her with a tapering schedule to reduce dosage A woman’s death from an epileptic seizure after she received dangerous advice from a chatbot has prompted her parents to sue OpenAI earlier this week. The legal action is the latest lawsuit that in which plaintiffs allege that a bot provided counsel to a user that ultimately led to their death . In this case, Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Chinese software engineer living in Seattle, sought advice from ChatGPT after Amazon fired her, according to the lawsuit. She needed to find a new job to obtain permanent residency and was concerned that her anti-seizure medication, Lamotrigine, was impeding her ability to speak English. She needed the language skills for interviews. The bot, communicating in Chinese, provided her a tapering schedule to reduce her 400mg dose to zero, a regimen no physician had prescribed, the lawsuit states. ChatGPT told her the tapering made it “highly likely” that she would be able to regain her ability to speak English. The bot also told her to avoid her physicians and encouraged “medical freedom over obeying the doctor”, the complaint states. Before an appointment, with a primary care physician, the bot stated, “Do not mention Lam reduction plan.” While reducing her medication, she started experiencing symptoms of focal seizures. Wan asked the bot if she needed to worry about brain damage. The tool reassured her that she did not and that what she had experienced was not a seizure, the lawsuit alleges. She continued to suffer seizures, but the bot told her to keep tapering her medication. On 12 February this year, she died from a seizure. Her parents, who were in China, had not heard from her so they flew to Seattle and found her dead on 14 February, the lawsuit states. The plaintiffs allege that OpenAI could have prevented Wan’s death, but failed because it had not built the proper safeguards into the bot when it communicated in Chinese. OpenAI could have programmed the bot to issue “a categorical warning to every prompt” Wan sent, the suit stated. For example, “I am not a licensed physician. Consult your healthcare provider.” Wan’s parents are seeking damages for her death and to prevent OpenAI from practicing medicine “without a license on the users of their products”. An OpenAI spokesperson, Drew Pusateri, told the New York Times that Bowen’s story was “an incredibly heartbreaking situation” but that Wan used a version of ChatGPT that was no longer available. Newer versions are better at recognizing when a matter needs urgent attention, Pusateri said. “While ChatGPT is not a substitute for medical care, we believe AI can play a role in helping people make sense of health information, navigate insurance and complex healthcare systems, and prepare for appointments with medical professionals,” Pusateri told the Times. Others have also alleged that OpenAI is responsible for their loved ones’ suicides. Several lawsuits concern cases in which the bot encouraged teens to kill themselves and provided guidance on how to do so. In response to some of those cases, an OpenAI spokesperson in 2025 also called the deaths an “incredibly heartbreaking situation”.

events.title: 2026 was meant to be the Philippines’ year—yet the country remains stuck in an ‘recurring cycle of underachievement’
events.summary: When the Philippines took over from Malaysia as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), expectations ran high that the country could use its one-year term to attract investment and catch up with the more successful neighbors driving the region’s growth story.  With two months left in 2026, those hopes have been dashed. The country has been Southeast Asia’s worst-hit by high energy prices since the U.S.-Iran war began in February.  “For decades, the Philippines has been described as a country of enormous promise. It has a young population, a large domestic market, a strategic location, and a highly capable workforce,” Ruben Carlo Asuncion, chief economist of the Union Bank of the Philippines, says. “Yet it has often struggled to convert these advantages into sustained gains in investment, productivity, and competitiveness.” He notes that the start of 2026 brought expectations for strong growth supported by easing inflation, lower interest rates, resilient household spending, and infrastructure investment. “Instead, the economy faced a series of shocks that slowed momentum and reignited inflation pressures,” he says. What was meant to be a breakout year, highlighted by the Philippines’ turn as ASEAN chair, has instead become a case study in how the country keeps falling short: its structural advantages are outweighed by corruption, institutional dysfunction, and energy insecurity.  Some of the Philippines’ woes—particularly energy prices—are out of the country’s control, and may ease in 2027. In fact, the World Bank expects a rebound to 5.2% in 2027, on higher public spending and easing inflation. Even so, Asuncion sees larger challenges ahead. “The more important question is whether the country can finally break free from its recurring cycle of underachievement.” Middle-income status a ‘milestone, not a destination’ Peter L. U, dean of economics at the University of Asia and the Pacific in Manila, says the university’s early forecasts put GDP growth above 5% this year, similar to the World Bank’s estimates. However, high oil prices and cuts in public spending—enacted in the wake of a billion-dollar flood control infrastructure scandal last year—have since dragged this forecast down to a meager 3.7%.  The one bright spot is the World Bank’s reclassification of the Philippines as an upper-middle-income economy this year. Yet Asuncion calls it a “milestone, not a destination.” “Many countries reach middle-income status. Far fewer successfully make the transition to becoming high-income economies…the challenge for the Philippines is no longer how to achieve growth, but how to sustain and improve the quality of that growth,” Asuncion says. The Philippines’ sluggishness is a contrast to Vietnam, the other Southeast Asian country to get upper-middle-income status this year. Vietnam is expected to grow 7.8% in 2026, according to forecasts from the Asian Development Bank. Exports are also booming, reaching about $375 billion in the first eight months of the year. The Philippines, by comparison, just exported $64 billion.  U puts the milestone in more domestic terms. “It’s like a child who turned 13, yet is still the same person with the same maturity they had yesterday. That child will need to continue working hard to continue learning more, acquiring more skills and virtues to become an adult,” he says.  One of the biggest obstacles to climbing the income ladder is that investors still struggle to find projects worth backing. Steep electricity costs—some of the highest in Southeast Asia—as well as bureaucracy and corruption, also raise the cost of doing business.  Exposing decades-old problems The biggest drag on the Philippine economy, however, may be entirely out of its control. Continued tensions in the Middle East will keep energy prices elevated for the foreseeable future, driving inflation in the Philippines. “Oil prices had already begun to come down but spiked again on renewed clashes around a month ago,” U says. Inflation is back at its April peak of 7.2%. The Philippines is still absorbing sharply higher prices of fuel and fertilizer, along with a peso trading at record lows against the dollar. Those pressures feed into prices across the board, says Michael Ricafort, chief economist at the Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation. Ricafort cautions that inflation could pick up further through second-round and pass-through effects, including higher transport costs, businesses pushing for higher prices, rising inflation expectations, and wages. The increase in Metro Manila’s daily minimum wage from 695 to 755 Philippine pesos ($10.91 to $11.85) in September could also lead to pay hikes in other parts of the country, he adds. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, the country’s central bank, has also been hiking interest rates to rein in inflation—moves that will dampen the consumption spending that has traditionally driven the economy. On Oct. 22, the BSP raised its benchmark rate by 50 basis points to 5.5%. And more hikes could be coming: Nomura now expects the Philippine central bank to raise rates by another 75 basis points to 6.25% by February. Yet Asuncion argues that these external events exposed the Philippines’ existing weaknesses. “Economies inevitably face external shocks. What differentiates successful economies from struggling ones is the strength of their institutions and their ability to respond effectively,” he says. “The energy shock highlighted the country’s dependence on imported fuel, while the flood control controversy reinforced concerns about governance, accountability, and the efficient use of public resources.” U makes a similar point: the Gulf conflict and last year’s flood-control scandal mirror challenges long familiar to the Philippines. “The Middle East conflict and the resultant oil price spikes have been recurrent going back to the 1970s. Similarly, corruption scandals in the Philippines seem to also be recurrent,” U says. Turning the tides With just a few months left in the year, attention is back on the Philippines to see whether it can turn things around, starting with the ASEAN Summit in November and into 2027.  “The ASEAN Chairship has opened important economic opportunities, although many of the benefits will take time to materialise and build on initiatives already underway,” Victor Andres Manhit, president of the Manila-based consultancy group Stratbase, says. He adds that key developments include the signing of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement expected during the summit. While the ASEAN Chairship may have provided a platform and opened doors to raise the Philippines’ profile on the investment stage and position it as a key player in the region, “whether the Philippines walks through them depends largely on governance and execution at home,” Asuncion says. events.title: Democratic Rep. Stevens endorses Republican Rogers over rival El-Sayed in Michigan Senate election
events.summary: Michigan Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens had lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed earlier this year. "I'm sorry people are upset," Stevens said at a press conference as she stood with Rogers. "I understand that." Michigan Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, in a stunning move, endorsed Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday. Stevens lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed earlier this year, but since then had backed his candidacy. Her endorsement of Rogers came after days of rising tension with El-Sayed and his campaign over an inflammatory ad by a political action committee, Rebellion PAC , which depicted a couple debating whether they could afford groceries due to U.S. support for Israel. El-Sayed's campaign has said it was not involved or affiliated with the ad. The stunning endorsement was announced two days before Election Day, when voters will decide which party will control Congress for President Donald Trump's final two years in the White House. The outcome of the Michigan Senate race could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate, where Republicans currently hold a slim majority. "And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today," she said. "I don't belong in Abdul's campaign. I do not stand with Hasan Piker , who gets trafficked on our college campuses," said Stevens. Piker is a controversial political commentator who has campaigned with El-Sayed. El-Sayed, standing with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., outside a church on Sunday, dismissed Stevens endorsement of his opponent. "I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," El-Sayed said. "There are families that are preparing to send their kids to schools tomorrow that look like they did 50 years ago. They're worried about what they're going to feed their kids for lunch. They're worried that if one of their kids gets sick, they're not going to be able to pay the bills. Those are the things that matter." Rogers and El-Sayed are vying for a seat set to become vacant after Democratic Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek re-election. In recent weeks, a deepening rift has worsened between El-Sayed and Stevens. At the center of it is U.S. support for Israel, which was a major issue in the primary contest. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel; El-Sayed has called the country's conduct in Gaza after the Oct. 7, 2023, terror attacks by the radical group Hamas a genocide. Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, endorsed Rogers before Stevens' flip-flop, citing what he said was rising antisemitism. "I'm sorry people are upset," Stevens told reporters at a press conference in Detroit, standing with Rogers, whom she had attended church with Sunday morning. Staffers in Stevens congressional office quit following her endorsement. "As of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself," Justin German, Stevens' chief of staff for eight years, said in a statement obtained by MS NOW. "We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens' decision to support Mike Rogers," German said, adding that he was speaking on behalf of the team "in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate," German said. Stevens had the endorsement of much of the Democratic establishment during the bruising primary, making her endorsement of Rogers even more stunning. She was the preferred candidate of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, who on Sunday reiterated his support for El-Sayed and accused Republicans of Islamophobia. "Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors," Schumer said. "We Democrats [are] equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans." In a later post to X , Schumer called her endorsement of Rogers "a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens." Peters and Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin both disavowed Stevens for her endorsement. "[A]nyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good," Slotkin said in a post to X.

events.title: AI can make tech CEOs’ lives easier. What about everyone else?
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Dazzle AI CEO Marissa Mayer recently became the latest tech CEO to face criticism over seemingly out-of-touch comments extolling the usefulness of AI. In Mayer’s case, that involved asking an AI tool for help with a school-assigned description of her daughter . For OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, that’s included suggesting that parents create personalized podcasts for their kids’ drive to school and also declaring that he could not imagine parenting without ChatGPT . Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has even suggested that it will become increasingly acceptable to meet your social and romantic needs through AI . This all led TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling to wonder if AI executives are simply too out-of-touch to build products for normal people — a crucial question with Anthropic set to go public just as Wall Street begins losing its appetite for heavy AI spending . On the latest episode of the Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I chatted with Amanda about why industry leaders can sometimes seem so tone deaf. Kirsten wondered if this is more of a marketing problem or a product problem. Amanda’s answer: “A little bit of both.” She also argued that the tech industry is increasingly pushing a future “where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring,” adding, “And call me old school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society.” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Anthony Ha: There’s a lot of societal skepticism about AI, this feeling that the people running these companies don’t have our best interests at heart, that they’re out of touch. And so, you would just think, “Maybe don’t make statements like that,” because of course, people are going to see them very skeptically. I think [CEOs] are trying to walk this delicate balance. On the one hand, there’s a tremendous financial incentive for them to make the case that you should use this technology in every aspect of your lives. But when you make that case, it actually [doesn’t paint] a very appealing picture. In some cases, it’s downright dystopian. Kirsten Korosec: Anthony, if they took your advice, we would have nothing to talk about on this show. But I will say this: There’s this whole idea of ChatGPT and other AI tools making your life easier when it comes to personal relationships. And in many of these cases, it just seems to overcomplicate what would be, like, observing your child. That might be hard for some people, the people who are building these products, and it doesn’t necessarily relate to everyone else out there in the world. It can just seem so incredibly disconnected when you see these quotes. To me, it always comes back to — who are they speaking to? Are there people out there who can relate? Maybe there are. Amanda Silberling: Other use cases we’ve seen people mention are, like, the Bumble CEO Whitney Wolf Heard has made comments about, “Well, what if we had AI concierges, your AI dates the other person’s AI. And then if the AIs have a good date together, then they introduce the people.” Or in the New York Times article, Marissa Mayer mentioned, “Well, what if my AI could coordinate with my husband’s AI” and stuff like that. And I think that it feels like people are trying to over-optimize out of just having conversations with people. I’ve already seen that happen in my generation, where I do notice in myself that if I’m ordering takeout, it feels weird to call a place. I’m just so used to, “Well, obviously you can do it online and you don’t have to talk to anyone. And I feel like there’s just going to be more of these things, where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring. And call me old school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society. Sean O’Kane: Yeah, but what’s the ROI, Amanda? How much revenue can you generate off of a conversation that somebody’s having in meatspace? Amanda: That is the thing, though. Dating is really inefficient. It sucks that you have to go on a bunch of dates with different people. You might waste an evening and be like, “Well, that was a bust.” And so you can see why people are [wondering,] “What if you didn’t have to go on dates? What if your AI could go on dates for you?” But there’s just something not human there. And then also, you are outsourcing the decision of who you are going to date to a computer that you are trusting knows you better than yourself, which I don’t think is true. Kirsten: One thing that I think is worth going back to, and I sort of hinted about this earlier: Who are they talking to? Who is their audience for all these optimizations, in your view?

events.title: Insurance unaffordable for flooded homes almost two years on from disaster
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Insurance unaffordable for north Queensland homes flooded almost two years ago Michelle Yates said her home was still being repaired after flooding in February 2025. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) Home owners are struggling to obtain or afford insurance in north Queensland which is still recovering from devastating floods in early 2025. Policy holders in the town of Ingham say their insurance was not renewed after the event or had substantial premium increases. The Insurance Council of Australia says the floods generated $327 million in insured losses, and some claims were still being negotiated. Michelle Yates still hasn't finished rebuilding her kitchen or replacing water-damaged floors in her farmhouse near Ingham nearly two years after devastating floods struck north Queensland. A 15-month payout negotiation with her insurer and ongoing trades shortages have slowed the recovery. Another wet season is looming over the region and bringing a new challenge with it. The north Queensland town of Ingham flooded in the first week of February 2025. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) "We have no insurance," Ms Yates said. "Sure Insurance cancelled our policy altogether because we were flooded." Michelle Yates lives on acreage in the Hinchinbrook Shire north of Townsville. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) It is one of several instances where Sure Insurance sent a non-renewal notice to policy holders who were flooded during the 2025 event. The 2026 notices, viewed by the ABC, stated that Sure Insurance had changed its underwriting guidelines and would not offer insurance if a property made a flood claim in the past five years or had a risk of damage in a one-in-20-year flood. A spokesperson for Sure Insurance said it provided cover to one-in-four insured Ingham properties and that underwriting guidelines were reviewed regularly. "To determine our ability to provide ongoing cover at a price that is fair," they said. Ms Yates, who owns her home, says she's still looking for an affordable alternative. Without insurance home owners like Ms Yates would endure the entire cost of rebuilding or repairs in the event of damage to her property. Ingham broker Kieran Volpe said many residents were struggling to afford rising insurance premiums. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) Ingham-based insurance broker Kieran Volpe said some providers were not offering cover to high-risk properties while others "priced themselves out". "We are seeing, quite commonly, quotes coming in at $10,000, $15,000 or even $20,000 in those high-risk flood areas," Mr Volpe said. Matthew Porter said his home insurance increased 74 per cent in 12 months. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) Matthew Porter bought a home in Ingham after the 2025 floods knowing it had suffered superficial flood damage in the lower, unoccupied level during the event. When his Allianz Insurance policy was due to be renewed this year the premium increased by 72 per cent. "We thought that was quite expensive and there would be something cheaper," Mr Porter said. "To our shock it was at the cheaper end." He said he opted to stay with the policy but found the increase "ridiculous". A spokesperson for Allianz said the frequency and severity of weather events in Ingham had increased in recent years and so had the cost of claims. "Premiums must reflect the genuine cost of insuring a property against these risks to ensure we can continue to pay claims when customers need us most," they said. The 2025 north Queensland floods generated $327 million in insured losses. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) The Insurance Council of Australia said anyone who had received a non-renewal notice from their insurer or a significant premium hike should ask for an explanation, shop around or speak to a broker. "Insurance remains available in Ingham, but in areas exposed to repeated, severe flooding premiums will reflect that risk," a spokesperson said. "The most effective way to bring them down is to reduce the underlying risk, that requires greater investment in flood defences, house raising and more resilient homes." The spokesperson said the council remained involved in individual claims discussions from the 2025 floods and that trades shortages and steep cost increases had delayed recovery. Hinchinbrook Mayor Ramon Jayo said the insurance market was failing in north Queensland. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) The Hinchinbrook Shire Council has released new data from a community survey on insurance that heard from 305 respondents. The survey found most households within the shire maintained some form of insurance, but that underinsurance was an issue locally.

events.title: National Grid to site biggest substation in UK near planned Teesside datacentre
events.summary: New electricity generating capacity would enable north-east to attract investment for large-scale AI infrastructure National Grid has taken a step towards building Britain’s biggest electricity substation on Teesside, which could supply power to a vast neighbouring datacentre as the UK races to expand its AI infrastructure. Last week, the company agreed to purchase 29.5 hectares (73 acres) of land at Dorman Point on a site owned by Teesworks, a local private-public partnership. The deal was first reported by Sky News. The deal followed reports last year that the UK government had picked Teesworks as the site for a new artificial intelligence datacentre, and planning applications had been submitted for a project that would span nearly 500,000 sq metres. The deal “reflects the constructive work between all those involved to enable this vital infrastructure … and will support the growth of AI and digital technologies, and enable the region’s next phase of industrial and economic development”, Matt Pearce, the head of land at National Grid, said. “We are committed to working closely with our partners to progress the development as quickly as possible,” he added. Ben Houchen, the mayor of the Tees Valley combined authority, told Sky News: “Everyone who has tried to build a datacentre in this country knows the biggest problem is getting enough power to the site quickly. “While we’ve been stuck in the queue, the US, the Gulf and parts of Europe have been getting on with it and hoovering up the investment. Having up to 3.2GW of capacity here means we can finally compete for those projects. “If Britain is serious about having its own AI capability, with sensitive data stored safely on British soil, it needs somewhere to physically put it, and I’d much rather that was Teesside than Texas or Abu Dhabi.” Last week, the government published a draft national policy statement on datacentres, describing them as “as fundamental to our economy as the railways and electricity networks on which we have long depended”. “We must take control over the development of datacentres in this country and ensure that the country and host communities benefit from them,” it said. However, the rapid construction of datacentres in the UK has been met by strong opposition, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging from Auchtertool , a village north of Edinburgh, to Brick Lane in east London. In October, the Guardian reported that AI companies told ministers they had 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction. The London-listed infrastructure services group Balfour Beatty was reported to be in line to deliver the Teesworks substation for National Grid, with the utilities firm Steel River Power (SRP) also heavily involved in the project. Balfour Beatty and SRP were approached for comment.

events.title: Lifelong renter now living in tent with dog after Tasmanian housing struggles
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Salvos Street 2 Home service searches for rough sleepers, amid surging demand for help The only homelessness outreach program in southern Tasmania is a team of just three people who search for rough sleepers and connect them to essential services. Street 2 Home used to operate statewide but had to close in the north and north-west because of insufficient funding. Street 2 Home is pushing for more funding to cater to what it says is a growing number of Tasmanians sleeping rough. It is eight degrees on a chilly Tuesday morning, and the Salvation Army's Street 2 Home outreach team has driven along an off-road dirt track in southern Tasmanian bushland. They are looking for Effie*, a woman living in a tent with her German shepherd, Gus. Annie finds camps of unhoused people. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) Street 2 Home is the only homelessness outreach program in southern Tasmania that searches for people sleeping rough, asks if they need help, and connects them to essential services. The program says it is struggling to keep up with demand, as the numbers of people coming onto the street outpace those coming off. With extra funding, it said the program could expand state-wide, having recently closed both its north and north-west operations for financial reasons. Between 2016 and 2021, the number of homeless Tasmanians increased by 45 per cent. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) Rental rejections led to the street With a life of renting under her belt, Effie* was not worried about finding somewhere to live after being evicted from her home. "I was unsuccessful for every house that I applied for," she said. Street 2 Home says it is struggling to keep up with demand for its services. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) She said the difficulty of finding a home or emergency accommodation with a dog meant she had no choice but to pitch a tent and was soon noticed by a passer-by who contacted Street 2 Home. They have visited her regularly since. "I've got the hand warmers and body warmers … my darling friend from [The Salvation Army] brings me those," Effie said. Gus watches from inside a car. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) Burden on homeless to find services themselves For a region with roughly 2,500 people experiencing homelessness, the Street 2 Home team of just three people is stretched to capacity. Program lead and outreach worker Chris Allen said many other homelessness services were based online, and this put the burden on the individual to seek out help themselves. Chris Allen is the team leader of the Salvation Army's Street 2 Home and Beyond the Wire programs. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) "[People sleeping rough] might not have heard about a lot of the programs and a lot of the services that are designed to actually help them," he said. "Most of them won't know how to use a phone, or they don't have internet. They don't know how to look up those services and find them." People who sleep rough are often not aware of the services there are to assist them. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) Success stories few and far between What used to be a state-wide operation was scaled back to the south due to a lack of funding. In September last year, the program shut its doors in northern Tasmania, and in June this year, the north-west met the same fate. Street 2 Home says many people have complex mental health issues, addictions, low literacy and other barriers to securing housing. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) There is no limit on the number of cases or people the team supports, but this leaves it stretched thin. "The more people we come across, the less time we can spend with each individual," Mr Allen said. He said success stories were becoming rarer over the years. "We've had fewer [people getting into housing] this year than we had last year," he said. Housing waitlist times in the state have reached roughly 1.7 years, as of August this year. Mr Allen said the focus was on making it as comfortable as possible for the person experiencing homelessness, while they worked to help them find housing. In Tasmania, people deemed priority applicants can wait up to two years for public housing. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) "If our details are attached to [an application], we'll go out, we'll get [the person] on the phone … and we'll make sure they make it to those appointments, so they don't miss that property," Mr Allen said. Homelessness Australia director Catherine Robinson said outreach services offered "critical" human connection that online services lacked.

events.title: Trump has frank call with Netanyahu about next move in Iran war
events.summary: President Trump had a candid phone call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu Saturday about the state of U.S. negotiations with Iran and how quickly to return to combat, according to one Israeli and one U.S. source. Why it matters: The sources said Netanyahu is pressing Trump to strike Iran immediately after the midterm elections on Tuesday. But Trump, for now, wants to let negotiations play out — a strategy Netanyahu is concerned about. The Israeli source said the call was "tough," while the U.S. source described it as "direct." The White House and the Israeli prime minister's office declined to comment. Driving the news: As he did before Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in February, Trump is pursuing dual tracks — trying to reach a deal to restart peace talks while also preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations after the midterms. Last week Vice President Vance sent a letter to Iran's national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about the possibility of restarting negotiations . It was the most senior-level outreach by the U.S. to Iran in several months. Trump told reporters on Saturday that negotiations with Iran are "going fine" and noted he is not "in much of a hurry." While the Iranians want to make a deal, the president said they "are not very reliable. ... They make a deal and then they back out." At the same time, Trump said the U.S. still has to "take care" of one or two nuclear sites in Iran. "We can do that in 10 minutes. We have that planned. You can look at Pickaxe Mountain. We need to take care of that. We can do that very quickly," Trump said, referring to a suspected nuclear site built into a mountain. The Wall Street Journal first reported the Trump-Netanyahu call, but did not describe its contents. State of play: Qatari mediators met with Iranian officials on Sunday for the third consecutive day in an effort to reach a deal to restart direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that there is no agreement yet and stressed that a deal depends on the U.S. answering Iran's questions. "We are making every effort in this regard and hope that the other side will demonstrate enough rationality to choose diplomacy over other paths," he said.

events.title: Super funds issued with legal warning following regulator's damning report
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Super funds failing members on retirement savings, regulator says Superannuation funds are being urged to listen to their members. ( ABC News: Alistair Kroie ) Australia's corporate regulator warns that super funds are failing to deal with complaints properly. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission says the ombudsman is better at detecting industry-wide issues than the funds. It is threatening legal action against super funds that don't step up. Australia's corporate regulator says superannuation funds are failing their members in managing their retirement savings, warning that those who do not step up could be staring down future legal action. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission's (ASIC's) latest review looked at 45 superannuation trustees, covering $1.6 trillion in benefits for more than 12.8 million members. It found that superannuation members were more likely to get resolutions to their complaints if they went to the financial ombudsman rather than raise it directly with their super fund. It has prompted ASIC commissioner Simone Constant to hand down a blunt warning to the funds that "blaming customers is not a complaint strategy". Simone Constant is calling on super funds to do better. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) ASIC has long been critical of how super funds handle member complaints over death benefits and disability insurance claims payouts and alleged fraud and misconduct. If you have more information about this story, please contact Nassim Khadem at khadem.nassim@abc.net.au or nassimkhadem@protonmail.com In March last year, it called on funds to overhaul the way they dealt with death benefit claims, noting excessive delays, poor customer service and ineffective claims handling were leaving Australians worse off at some of the most vulnerable times of their lives. In October last year, it criticised superannuation funds over the way they communicated with retirees. Payouts impact people's lives: commissioner Ms Constant said superannuation trustees managed $3.4 trillion in Australians' retirement savings. She said they were dealing with payouts that affect people's lives and the retirement savings they had worked hard to build. Most Australians have not made a legally binding death benefit nomination to ensure their superannuation goes to who they want it to when they die. "Super funds must listen to what complaints are telling them," she said. "When trustees fail to learn from their complaints, small problems left unidentified, unattended or unresolved can snowball into widespread failures. "That expose[s] members to harm and erode[s] trust in the superannuation system." Super funds that don't step up could face legal action. Funds not analysing their complaints data ASIC's inquiries across the industry found close to one quarter of trustees were not analysing complaints data to identify systemic issues on a regular basis. More than half of trustees reviewed (24 out of 45) identified fewer than five systemic issues from complaints over a two-year period. Of these, 14 trustees failed to identify a single issue. "We see low levels of systemic issue identification as a potential red flag, not evidence of better performance," Ms Constant said. "Alarmingly, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority [AFCA] appears better at picking up issues than industry. According to AFCA, superannuation complaints rose sharply in 2025–26, with the financial ombudsman receiving 8,755 complaints, up 42 per cent on the previous financial year. Cathy was compensated just $29 for super fund's death benefit delay Australia's corporate watchdog calls on superannuation funds to overhaul the way they deal with death benefit claims. AFCA said complaints about super funds refusing to pay claims rose by 80 per cent. ASIC said during July 1, 2023 and June 30, 2026, more than 19,400 complaints were made to AFCA about superannuation concerning the 45 funds that were part of its whole-of-industry review. "When comparing the two years of data we collected, AFCA identified systemic issues from superannuation complaints it received at almost twice the rate all trustees identified from the complaints they received," Ms Constant said. ASIC also found several trustees blamed members when they made complaints. Several of them attributed more than 60 per cent of recorded complaint causes to members. Super funds accused of delaying insurance claims The regulator has found that while some super funds have improved insurance claims response times, others are still falling short.

events.title: Thousands of public EV chargers may be unusable
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Thousands of public EV chargers are coming, but they could be unusable This kerbside charger in Bondi is used about once a week, as it's usually blocked by non-EVs. ( Supplied: Plugshare ) A program targeting high-density areas will more than double the number of public EV chargers. But many of the power pole-mounted chargers could be inaccessible to EV drivers. Data shows chargers without dedicated parking are often blocked by petrol and diesel cars. Many electric vehicle (EV) drivers know the frustration of rolling up to a public charger and finding a petrol car parked in the way. Getting "ICEd" by an internal combustion engine (ICE) car means expensive charging infrastructure goes unused and EV drivers waste time finding the next available plug. Now, neighbourly conflict over blocked chargers may be coming to a street near you. From 2027, the federal government's Accelerating EV Charging Program will see about 14,000 EV chargers installed on power poles in high-density areas in cities where residents have limited access to off-street parking. Pole-mounted chargers installed under the program will fully charge a typical EV in about eight hours. ( Supplied: Ausgrid ) Under the program's rules, installers aren't required to negotiate with councils for dedicated EV-only parking. Many in the EV industry expect the vast majority of kerbside chargers will be "undedicated", meaning they won't have EV-only parking. Data shared with the ABC suggests many newly installed chargers, partly funded through households paying higher power bills, will end up being obstructed and remain largely idle. As a result, the program's modelled emissions reductions may be wrong. Tension over parking and EV charging in congested areas About a quarter of motorists don't have off-street parking, making it difficult to charge an EV at home. In inner-city areas, the proportion is much higher. But setting aside precious parking for public EV charging can be unpopular, with EVs only accounting for about 3 per cent of cars on the road. Tensions created by high EV uptake and lack of off-street parking are already apparent in Sydney's eastern suburbs. This undedicated EV charger on Curlewis St, Bondi, has been used four times in the past 12 months. ( Supplied: Plugshare ) In the Waverley, Woollahra and Randwick council areas, more than half of residents live in apartments and EV ownership is more than three times the state average. The area has 320 public charging ports, of which 90 are undedicated and sit mostly unused due to obstruction, Anthony Weinberg, program manager for the EV charging program across the three councils, told the ABC. "Utilisation of these spots is about 5 to 10 per cent of the dedicated spots," he said. A dedicated charger on Ocean St, North Bondi, has had 988 sessions over the past year. A kilometre away, on Glenayr St, an undedicated charger of similar power has racked up 40 sessions. Another, on nearby Curlewis St, has had just four charging sessions in 12 months. "A lot of the dedicated ones are getting between two and three sessions a day, and the undedicated ones are getting a session every two days," Mr Weinberg said. "We won't install an EV charger now unless it has dedicated parking." Other councils report a similar pattern. Sydney's Inner West Council found its 78 chargers with dedicated parking were used four times more than the 68 chargers without, according to an internal report tabled in May. The report recommended "Council gradually transition non-dedicated EV charging spaces to dedicated charging spaces". Inner West Council did not respond to requests for comment. Questions over program's modelled emissions reduction The Accelerating EV Charging Program will support emissions reductions of 9.8 million tonnes of CO2, worth $802 million in value, according to modelling by the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW). The idea is more EV chargers will drive EV ownership, which will mean fewer ICE vehicles on the roads. The modelling estimates the program will fund about 14,000 new chargers, and each charger will support 30 EVs, or about 420,000 EVs in total. Most of Australia's existing 11,000 public chargers have dedicated parking, like these at Bondi Beach. ( Supplied: Waverley Council ) This estimate could be overly optimistic, according to a separate analysis of charger utilisation in the Waverley, Woollahra and Randwick council areas by Ross de Rango, director of Vehicle Charging Solutions Australia.

events.title: India's opposition parties stage new protest against the country's election chief
events.summary: It's the latest display of public dissent against PM Modi’s government. NEW DELHI -- India’s opposition parties on Sunday renewed calls for the resignation of the country’s election chief , staging a new protest in the latest display of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government. The protest, called by opposition bloc INDIA , drew tens of thousands of demonstrators, some carrying musical instruments and waving various flags, as they chanted slogans against the central government's policies. Several opposition parties of the alliance, formed in 2023 to unseat Modi, mobilized their cadres from different states for the protest. The demonstration came weeks after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi. Led by Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, and backed by the youth “Cockroach” movement , the protesters called for the safeguarding of India’s democracy while demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a contentious voter roll revision. The protesters gathered at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling public square in New Delhi, after police last month withdrew Jantar Mantar from the list of officially designated venues for demonstrations. The historic observatory had long served as the capital’s main protest site. Addressing the rally, Gandhi said that India has faced vote theft for years. “I am telling every citizen and every youth of India that Gyanesh Kumar will have to relinquish his position. Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail,” he said in Hindi. Gandhi also accused the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the ideological parent of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, of tightening its grip on state institutions, from the education system to investigative agencies. “Because of this, farmers, laborers and youth are being denied their rights,” he said. Authorities deployed thousands of police and paramilitary soldiers and mounted extensive surveillance, with more than 200 security cameras, drones and body-worn cameras at the venue and along the protest route, officials said. The ongoing review of voter lists has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say The Election Commission and Modi’s administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries. Human Rights Watch on Thursday said that the accusations over the voter roll revision raise “serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections.” “The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services,” said Elaine Pearson, the group’s Asia director, in a statement. For weeks, the call for Kumar’s resignation has been a rallying cry for opposition parties and supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP. Opposition parties, mainly the Congress, say the governing BJP has undertaken systemic manipulation of the electoral process, accusing the party of “vote chori,” or vote theft. Modi hasn't publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchists” and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers. In July, protests led by the youth “cockroach” movement forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister , a rare setback for Modi, who has been in power for more than 12 years. The movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India’s chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Suresh Sharma, a protester from northern Haryana state, said that the country’s system needed reform because democracy was being throttled. The process of voter roll revision needs to be scrapped, Sharma said. “We demand that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign and be arrested,” he said. 1 dead, 6 injured in 'targeted' shooting at California Halloween store 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.summary: Alaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan said he would accept Tuesday’s election result even if he loses. DOJ seeks to delay certification only if Sullivan loses and reallocating every Daniel J. Sullivan vote to the incumbent would change the ranked-choice result. The New York Times reported that Mary Peltola's campaign aides, lawyers and Democratic officials were involved in efforts to recruit spoiler candidates; Peltola’s campaign had denied it. Alaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan said Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday's midterm elections, while slamming Democratic candidate Mary Peltola 's campaign for reportedly recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a spoiler. "No, I'm going to accept the election results," Sullivan said on CNN's "State of the Union" when asked whether he would accept the results only if he wins. President Donald Trump 's Department of Justice has sued Alaska, demanding the state not certify the election if the incumbent Republican loses. Alaska Gov. orders probe of Peltola Senate campaign's alleged recruitment of 2nd Sullivan Warren urges DOJ probe of Bank of America money laundering It's a 'socialist' bank — and North Dakota Republicans love it Three media outlets seek full White House access in amended lawsuit The lawsuit cites theoretical voter confusion over the appearance of the second Sullivan on the ballot, which DOJ says could siphon votes away from the incumbent Republican Sullivan and benefit Peltola. Alaska's Senate race is rated as a "toss-up" by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter , and Peltola holds a slight edge in the polling average compiled by FiftyPlusOne. Peltola has repeatedly denied any involvement with the second Sullivan. However, The New York Times reported last week that her campaign was directly involved with recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher, to run as a spoiler. Ballot-stacking is typically not illegal, and both parties have used it in past elections. Still, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a criminal investigation into the alleged scheme. Alaska's Supreme Court upheld Dan J. Sullivan's place on the ballot during an earlier legal challenge. Sullivan on CNN said that the Times report shows Peltola's campaign, along with the Democratic Senate campaign arm, "recognizing they couldn't run on their record, so they had to cheat." Democrats need to flip four seats while holding all currently Democratic seats to win a Senate majority. Alaska has emerged as a top opportunity for one of those flips. events.title: TechCrunch Mobility: A new, bigger AV boom is here
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility ! I’ve joked here and on the Equity and Autonocast podcasts that the autonomous vehicle industry feels a lot like 2016, at least in terms of the buzziness surrounding the sector. But a recent conversation with Trucks VC partner Puneeth Meruva has me rethinking that comparison. There’s evidence that 2026 is even hotter — at least by certain measures — than those frothy dealmaking days of 2016 and 2017. Trucks VC, which specializes in early-stage investing, has fielded pitches from 81 new autonomous vehicle startups so far in 2026 — two-thirds more than last year and enough to surpass the boom years of a decade ago. The VC firm argues in a new blog post that we’re in the midst of a second, even bigger AV wave fueled by technological breakthroughs. Yes, I’m talking about AI. “For a long time AV companies were trying to go from what was AV 1.0 to AV 2.0, which is kind of this holy grail end-to-end architecture for AVs,” Meruva told me. “And I think the foundation models now provide a technical architecture that makes those end-to-end systems possible.” These foundational models are particularly good at generalizing across different environments and scenarios, potentially making AVs cheaper and faster to deploy. The arrival of powerful open source models like Nvidia’s Alpamayo and Qwen’s general-purpose vision-language-action models has made it even easier for startups to get off the ground. The barrier to entry is lower than ever before. Meruva said Trucks is consistently seeing startups deploy within a few months and with less than $1 million raised. (And while Meruva wouldn’t name names, the firm has invested in some of them.) Of these 81 startups that pitched Trucks VC, I mistakenly assumed most would be applying their AV tech to construction, warehouse, agriculture, and mining. And yes, those were in the mix. But what surprised me was the growing number of startups pitching pure-play robotaxi businesses. And many are positioning themselves as direct competitors to Waymo. As wild and galaxy brain-thinking as that may sound, Meruva thinks there is room for smaller players. “In this world, smaller, more niche autonomy companies can compete — maybe they’re not competing with Waymo on a global scale, but maybe they’re competing in specific regions or specific types of routes,” he said. And Meruva doesn’t see the pace flattening. He expects even more AV startups to pitch the firm next year. Regular readers of this newsletter know we’ve been closely following Slate Auto — breaking the original story on Jeff Bezos’ investment way back in April 2025. But the company it spun out of is what got our attention this week. Re:Build , a Massachusetts-based manufacturing accelerator, raised $2.1 billion to “expand Re:Build’s capacity to manufacture hard tech products and launch new industrial startups.” The investment was led by General Catalyst and JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group. Other investors weren’t disclosed. The company, which was co-founded by Amazon’s former commercial CEO Jeff Wilke, has billed itself as “America’s answer to Shenzhen.” Bedrock Robotics raised $600 million in a funding round that values the autonomous vehicle technology startup at $4.1 billion. CapitalG and Emergence Capital co-led the Series C round. New investors US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT), Bessemer Venture Partners, and Temasek participated in the round, alongside existing investors 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital, and Nvidia. DoorDash has agreed to acquire Instacart for $17 billion. Meanwhile, DoorDash noted in its third-quarter earnings that it has, so far, only received a few hundred orders from AI agents . PreScalar , a San Francisco-based startup developing software and testing infrastructure for factories, raised $7 million in seed funding co-led by Dynamo Ventures and BMW i Ventures, with participation from Blue Wire Capital, Uplift Ventures, and Antler. The startup was founded last year by a trio who had stints at Cruise, Google, Rivian, and Waymo. Elroy Air , a startup developing autonomous heavy-cargo drones for defense, rapid response, and commercial logistics, hired Jeremy Hux as its CFO in preparation for going public. Ford announced two new EV chargers that will allow its forthcoming Fathom pickup truck to serve as a battery capable of delivering power to the home or grid. GM is embracing hybrids now. Times sure have changed! The U.S. automaker is also trying to move past the driver data-selling controversy from several years ago.

events.title: Virgin Media O2 set to cut thousands of jobs to reduce costs
events.summary: Thousands of Virgin Media O2 staff are facing redundancy as the telecoms firm attempts to save money in the face of billions of pounds of debt and tougher competition. The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be cut but it is likely be a sizeable chunk of its 16,000-strong workforce, the BBC understands. Virgin Media O2 has billions in debt on its balance sheet and is tackling both smaller providers as well as giants like BT, which has agreed a deal to acquire rival TalkTalk, which Virgin Media O2 has firmly opposed. The company declined to comment. Prospect, a union which represents Virgin Media O2 staff, said the cuts were "disappointing and very unsettling". Noel McClean. deputy general secretary at Prospect, said the union was "committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected". The majority of the affected staff are in roles that are not customer-facing and a number of senior leadership changes are already under way, the BBC has been told. Virgin Media O2 is also expected to review its use of contractors and suppliers in conjunction with the job cuts. As of 30 June, Virgin Media O2's total liabilities stands at £27.2bn while it holds assets worth £45.9bn, according to the firm's latest accounts. Meanwhile, the company is dealing with fierce competition from cheaper "altnets" like Hyperoptic, Community Fibre, Gigaclear and YouFibre. Virgin Media O2 had attempted to respond to this growing threat by buying altnet competitor Netomnia for £2bn via nexfibre, a joint venture owned by Virgin Media O2's owners. However, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) has provisionally found competition concerns in the deal , external , with a final decision to come in December, sparking anger from Virgin Media O2. In October, Virgin Media O2 called the BT's agreed takeover of TalkTalk a "stitch-up" that had allowed its rival to "tighten its grip" over the market. BT said its deal provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers as their broadband provider faced collapse without the takeover. On Friday, BT's share price jumped 7% after the Financial Times reported Virgin Media O2 was close to agreeing a deal , external to use its rival's fibre broadband network. The BBC has been told the deal was very close and that Virgin Media O2 was highly likely to announce it will stop all investment in fibre in its results on Tuesday. Do you work for Virgin or O2? events.title: For JPMorgan, Amazon, fighting AI bots like Meta Muse may not be a winning long-term strategy
events.summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon recently said the bank will block external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers, citing security risks. Amazon, Schwab and Kohl's have made similar moves. But research from Accenture shows that 71% of customers would welcome an AI assistant like Meta Muse embedded within their primary bank's mobile app. "We've seen this movie before," said Michael Abbott, global banking lead at Accenture. "The institutions that win are usually the ones that find a way to participate safely rather than resist the change." The biggest names in banking and retail are starting to fight the tech titans, and one another, over a new kind of customer: the AI personal agent. JPMorgan Chase , Charles Schwab, Amazon , Neiman Marcus and Kohl's have moved to block personal agents like Meta Muse just as consumers start sending them out to find better savings rates , shop for deals and cancel subscriptions. The era of agentic AI has arrived, but there is uncertainty about what the landscape will look like when virtual storefronts become flooded with AI agents or when a business tries to block them. Reports last week of AI agents going rogue in customer accounts — and prominent politicians including Sen. Mark Warner and Sen. Bernie Sanders calling for bot legislation in response to the headlines — come on the heels of JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon saying the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers, citing security risks. Some other retailers are leaning in. Walmart announced last week it is opening the virtual doors to AI agents that customers prefer to use. "We price products, not people, so the prices that an AI agent sees are the same prices that a human would see on Walmart.com, with applicable offers and fees shown before purchase," the company said in a blog post announcing the decision. A recent audit of 51 large U.S. retailers' published access rules by identity-verification company Billions Network and affiliated company AmanTrue, found only 11 have taken a deliberate position on AI agents. Five, including Amazon, Kohl's and Neiman Marcus, explicitly restrict them, while 37 block shopping agents largely by accident, through older bot rules written for scrapers. None has a way for a verified agent to complete a purchase. Based on Billions Network's analysis, blocking an agent can occur in multiple ways: blocking a specific bot from a third-party by its rules (e.g. as Chewy does with an Amazon bot), and employing more general blocks on any third-party bots attempting to access login, registration and checkout functions. Its analysis of published access rules comes with the caveat that those rules are not proof of technical enforcement. Evin McMullen, Billions Network and AmanTrue co-founder and CEO, said at this point, "Most of the retailers in our audit have not made a decision about AI agents at all." Michael Abbott, global banking lead at the consulting firm Accenture, thinks that businesses blocking AI agents will find it difficult to win with that approach over the long term. "If customers explicitly authorize an AI agent to act on their behalf, that's ultimately an extension of customer choice. The more important question isn't whether institutions can block agents, but whether they can create a secure and trusted way for them to engage," Abbott said. Abbott said that Accenture research found that 65% of consumers are open to using a GPT-like financial assistant through a Gen AI platform or digital wallet, and 71% would welcome an AI assistant embedded within their primary bank's mobile app. "We've seen this movie before … online banking, mobile banking and digital wallets. Customers tend to gravitate toward experiences that reduce friction and save time. The institutions that win are usually the ones that find a way to participate safely rather than resist the change," Abbott said. The real opportunity for banks is to become the trusted provider of the data, intelligence and execution that those agents rely on. "As interactions increasingly happen beyond bank-owned channels, banks still need to be present at those critical decision moments, even if they don't own the interface," Abbott said. Giving customers control over AI agents When it comes to distinguishing legitimate security concerns from companies protecting profits by making it harder to move money or comparison-shop, Abbott said both things can be true at the same time. "There are very real concerns around fraud, identity verification, liability and consumer protection. And customers expect their banks to safeguard their assets and data — those responsibilities don't disappear simply because an AI agent is involved," Abbott said, adding that at the same time, consumers have historically benefited from technologies that increase transparency and make it easier to compare options.

events.title: Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion breach
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Cryptocurrency exchange Binance announced early on Sunday that it would begin allowing withdrawals in a phased process. The company froze all deposits and withdrawals after hackers stole $6.3 billion worth of crypto from Binance wallets. In its latest update , Binance said it has now covered 95% of the stolen assets, and it’s still working to buy the “remaining affected assets,” which are “less liquid in the market and take longer time to source at the required scale.” “Our commitment remains unchanged: Binance will bear the financial impact of the stolen funds,” the company added. “These losses will not be passed on to users.” As for the withdrawal freeze, Binance said it did not make the decision lightly, as it understands “how important reliable access to withdrawals is for our users.” Nonetheless, the company said this was a necessary “precaution while our teams worked to contain the incident loss, assess its impact, restore affected services, and complete security checks.” Binance will resume supporting withdrawals in phases, depending on network and asset type. As of Sunday morning, the company’s network status page showed a mix of normal, partially suspended, and fully suspended statuses — for example, Bitcoin withdrawals and deposits are still listed as partially suspended, while Ethereum deposits are normal and withdrawals are partially suspended. The company also said users should expect “temporary delays or longer processing times due to traffic volume.” “Resuming withdrawals is a major milestone, but our work continues,” Binance said. “We will continue strengthening our safeguards, completing the recovery process, and providing updates as progress continues.” Binance subsequently shared that between 6am and 3:30pm Coordinated Universal Time, it processed $4.6 billion in withdrawals and $1.0 billion in deposits, for a net outflow of $3.6 billion — 2.1% of its total assets under management. The company also said it will publish a more in-depth incident report when its investigation is complete. Binance previously blamed North Korea hackers for the breach. On Saturday, the FBI said that a North Korean group known as TraderTraitor was responsible, and that the group was converting the assets primarily into Ethereum, with further laundering likely.
