events.title: UAE updates e-invoicing penalties for businesses
events.summary: The UAE Ministry of Finance has issued new rules to update fines for e-invoicing to support businesses and reduce duplicate penalties. Structured invoices are issued and exchanged digitally between a supplier and a buyer and reported online to the UAE Federal Tax Authority . The latest amendments – following a cabinet decision – aim to provide businesses with greater regulatory certainty and reduce administrative burdens by introducing more proportionate fines. A penalty of Dh5,000 ($1,360) applies for an initial accounting violation, followed by Dh5,000 for each month during which the non-compliance continues. Fines are subject to a maximum aggregate penalty of Dh50,000 for these breaches in any 12 consecutive months. Administrative penalties for the issuer's or the recipient's failure to notify the authority of a system failure have also been removed. This change aims to ensure that penalties are applied more appropriately, taking into account the respective responsibilities of the different parties within the e-invoicing system. The changes support the UAE's wider digital transformation objectives and reinforce the country's commitment to implementing a modern tax administration framework. A pilot phase and voluntary e-invoicing adoption launched in July, with a full introduction planned for October 1, 2027.

events.title: Binance to resume withdrawals after covering 95% of $6.3bn crypto heist
events.summary: Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, is preparing to resume cryptocurrency withdrawals in phases after covering 95 per cent of the $6.3 billion in tokens stolen in what has been described as the world’s largest digital heist . The first phase of withdrawals is scheduled to begin between 6am and 9am GMT on Sunday, covering Bitcoin , ether, BNB, Solana, XRP, dogecoin and other digital assets, Binance said in a post on X late on Saturday. The remaining 5 per cent of the stolen tokens consists of less liquid assets that may take longer to source in the required amounts, the exchange said. https://t.co/pBJaht1UGV — Binance (@binance) November 1, 2026 “Since the incident, our teams have taken precautionary measures to safeguard the platform, conducted security assessments, and worked to verify the readiness of affected services. We aim to restore withdrawals progressively as we complete security and readiness checks,” the Binance post on X said. “Deposit services remain open and are not affected by the incident,” it added. The resumption follows security assessments and precautionary measures taken by the cryptocurrency exchange to safeguard its platform and verify the readiness of affected services. Binance said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than passing the losses on to customers. “As we have said throughout this incident: user funds remain safe,” Binance said. The FBI on Saturday attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit. Members of the group were observed by law enforcement converting the stolen assets into ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected further laundering through related technology. Binance said on X that withdrawals were temporarily suspended as a precaution, “while our teams worked to contain the incident loss, assess its impact, restore affected services and complete security checks”. “We did not take this decision lightly. We understand how important reliable access to withdrawals is for our users. However, our priority was to protect users, safeguard the platform, and complete the necessary security checks before restoring services.” Despite its reputation for robust security, the cryptocurrency industry has suffered several high-profile hacks and collapses over the years. In 2014, the Mt. Gox exchange, then the world's largest Bitcoin trading platform, collapsed after hackers stole hundreds of thousands of Bitcoins, alongside a series of technical and operational failures. Eight years later, FTX, then the world's second-largest cryptocurrency exchange, imploded amid revelations of fraud and the misuse of customer funds. Its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried , was later sentenced to 25 years in prison. More recently, the FBI attributed a $1.5 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit to North Korea, highlighting the persistent security threats facing the industry.

events.title: Government will not promise net savings in budget update, despite inflation pressure
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government will not promise net savings in budget update, even as rate rise looms Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said decisions were still being made on the government's mid-year budget update, refusing to commit to delivering net savings. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The finance minister and treasurer have refused to confirm December's budget update will contain more savings than new spending, even as pressure mounts on the federal government to tighten its belt. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC Insiders pressures on the budget were growing, and decisions were still being made for the mid-year update. The mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will be delivered in December. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update, even as Australians brace for another interest rate rise amid ongoing high inflation. On Wednesday Treasurer Jim Chalmers also refused to commit to net savings in the mid-year budget update following a worse-than-expected inflation figure of 4.3 per cent over the year to September, which lifted expectations of another rate hike when the Reserve Bank meets on Tuesday. The finance minister told ABC Insiders despite pressure being put on the government to rein in its spending, she would not pre-commit to overall savings. "I can't, I don't want to pre-empt the [Expenditure Review Committee] process. We will go through that ... but there is enormous effort being placed, particularly by Jim and myself on the savings side," Senator Gallgher said. "We are doing a lot of work on the savings side but I can’t get ahead of decisions that haven’t been made yet." The minister rejected suggestions the pressure to find savings was causing tension inside cabinet, saying it was healthy for ministers to have "robust" debate and bring different perspectives. Senator Gallagher added that the government's record in each of its previous budgets and mid-year updates had been to deliver overall improvements to the budget, and that in recent budgets its policy decisions had also found more savings than new spending. The Reserve Bank's chief economist said last week that government spending remained a contributor to ongoing inflation, even if the government points to the war in Iran as the "primary driver". Treasurer downplays further fuel discounts Faced with another high inflation result and the likelihood of a rate hike next Tuesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers calls for "perspective" and points to external factors. The treasurer has previously warned that the cost of borrowing would add billions of dollars in additional costs to the budget, as long-term expectations that global interest rates would remain higher for longer were priced into bonds. Senator Gallagher said other pressures on the budget were also growing, including in health and aged care. She said the government's spending measures in those pressure areas were necessary to rescue a Medicare system "in freefall" and clear processing backlogs for veterans. "If you go back to … the Howard era, you know, they were not dealing with AUKUS, they were not dealing with aged care," Senator Gallagher said. "They weren't dealing with Medicare falling over there, all of these pressures that are coming. So there has to be some acknowledgement of that. We are living in a different world." The government maintains that the budget is helping to tackle inflation . However ahead of his departure to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese acknowledged that the Reserve Bank only had a single "blunt instrument" in the inflation fight. The remaining levers to reduce demand in the economy rest with federal and state governments. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor told radio station 2GB that the government could do more to avert further rate rises. "The government can commit tomorrow to take pressure off interest rates and inflation, that would send a strong signal to the Reserve Bank [that] they don't need to raise," Mr Taylor said. The Reserve Bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter said last week that state and federal government spending was "definitely" contributing to demand pressures in the economy, before adding that it was not the RBA's place to advice government on its spending. Frontbench minister Murray Watt told News24 demand growth in the economy tripled in the private sector last financial year, while government demand growth halved.

events.title: Data centers are now a midterm issue, even in Brooklyn
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. On Thursday evening, I slipped on my neon yellow heels and a floral mini dress. It’s New York, so I can wear whatever I want to a midterm election event full of media types, techies, policy advocates, and, well, does anyone else even exist at these things? I walked into the dimly blue-lit Brooklyn warehouse and was surprised to see the room already filling up. Newsreel, the media company founded by former Forbes and Newsweek reporter Jack Brewster, hosted the event, and the lineup was heavy-hitting. Kenneth Schlenker, co-founder of the focus app Opal, sat down for a fireside chat about “the state of attention,” and Aryan Ranjan, who built the campaign management software Baraza, gave a midterm forecast. I, meanwhile, was moderating a panel on data centers. Brewster said the goal was for people to “put their phones away and talk to each other about the election, five days out.” As the evening progressed, however, one topic consumed nearly every conversation: AI, data centers, and the backlash against the growing technocracy. Lately, as a tech reporter, I’ve noticed a growing chasm between tech and everyone else. I spend most of my days talking to people who see the benefits of AI, who are so ambitious in building it and so optimistic that it will succeed that, when I talk to people beyond the tech world, I forget how ugly it all seems to them. Outside the tech bubble, data centers and AI have become such an intense ballot-box issue that they could sway some midterm races on November 3. A recent report from Data Center Watch found that almost $200 billion in data center projects were delayed, stalled, or blocked in the first half of 2026 due to political and community opposition. Meanwhile, states like Pennsylvania, Georgia, Texas, New York, and Virginia are considering more guardrails and transparency around data centers’ rapid development. Hundreds of new data centers are planned in Virginia alone, a state already nicknamed the “data center capital of the world.” A fireside chat with New York City Council member Chi Ossé, just before my panel, set the tone. AI came up near the end; Ossé said he doesn’t really use it. To me, though, he didn’t seem to be for or against it. He mostly emphasized that he would like to see tech executives held more accountable and trillionaires like Elon Musk taxed more. He described himself as a democratic socialist, but a “law and order” one. When CEOs talk about a technology that could deplete 10% of human civilization, he said, “they should be called to testify in front of Congress.” My panel was up next. I moderated a discussion with Maia Woluchem, a technology and human rights researcher, and Hilary Flint, an environmental and public health advocate, about data centers. As I took the stage, I decided to get a better read on the crowd. I asked, “Who here is pro-AI data center?” and was promptly booed. Our conversation covered a range of topics and emotions. People are upset that big tech companies appear to be cutting secret deals with local officials to build billion-dollar data centers. In some cases, zoning rules make it unclear what is being built until it’s too late to protest. At the same time, people are struggling with the cost of living and doing everything they can to hold onto what’s left of the American Dream, while tech leaders talk about AI replacing workers, or even humanity itself. Residents feel they have lost control over what happens in their communities, and they worry about the environmental and health risks. The panel agreed that data centers are the physical embodiment of people’s fears and anger toward the tech class and the rapid pace of technology. “What is a life worth?” Flint said when I brought up the benefits that some communities have seen from data center build-outs. People still protest, she said, because they “value their lives a little bit more than a temporary check.” The panel after mine featured NewsNation host Batya Ungar-Sargon; political strategist Morris Katz, who worked on Zohran Mamdani’s campaign; and Vox’s Astead Herndon. They were supposed to be talking about the future of the Democratic Party. But once again, the conversation shifted to data centers. Ungar-Sargon noted that some labor unions support data centers because of the jobs they promise. (Reports show that data centers create many jobs initially, but those jobs are not permanent once construction ends.) “There used to be a lot of pride in a community in the Rust Belt about very ugly, enormous buildings in their communities because everybody worked there,” she said, nodding to an earlier comment I’d made about data centers being ugly. “And they knew that building represented prosperity for themselves, stability for their children, and a future and a piece of the American dream.

events.title: SA's historic Gladstone Gaol reopens with ghost tours
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Gladstone Gaol reopens after four years, with Halloween ghost tours Gladstone Gaol has 145 years of history. ( ABC News: Arj Ganesan ) Gladstone Gaol has officially reopened to the public after being closed for four years. Locals are welcoming of the new operators, which they hope will bolster tourism to the town. New licensee, Lantern Ghost Tours, has plans to expand use across the site, including the addition of a café and accommodation. Following a period of closure, one of regional South Australia’s historic landmarks has reopened its doors to the public, with new caretakers leaning into the site’s dark heritage. This year Lantern Ghost Tours licensed the Gladstone Gaol site from the Department of Environment and Water. This weekend, just in time for Halloween, the company opened the doors to the public for the first time, with sold-out ghost tours welcoming thrill-seekers and history enthusiasts alike to the now 145-year-old facility. Naomi Bailey, the project coordinator for Gladstone Gaol, said it was exciting to have people back. "The community really wanted to be here as well, they were showing it through booking of the tours, and the takeaway was the interest. We sold out," Ms Bailey said. Lantern Ghost Tours' Naomi Bailey is the project coordinator for the recently reopened Gladstone Gaol. ( ABC News: Clem Stanley ) "We had to open additional tours, and we've got really strong bookings every Saturday night." Locals also shared Ms Bailey’s excitement to have the Gladstone Gaol’s gates open once again. The Gladstone Gaol in 1929. ( Supplied: State Library of South Australia ) Gladstone Community Development and Tourism Association president David Catford said it was a surprise when the previous operators retired in 2022. "I think that the community has come to realise what it means not having it open," Mr Catford said. Mr Catford said it was a surprise when the previous operators retired in 2022. ( ABC News: Arj Ganesan ) A once-off open day in 2025 was attended by some 1,300 people , which Mr Catford said proved interest in the prison was still there. Sitting on the cusp of the Southern Flinders Ranges and Mid-North regions, authorities in 1879 at the time determined that Gladstone would become home to a new prison, aimed at taking pressure off jails at Port Augusta and in Adelaide. The jail operated in its intended capacity for just shy of 100 years. Opening in 1881, its prisoner intake varied over the years, going from an all-gender prison to male-only, to a military prison during World War II, and later took on a focus more to reintegrate inmates back to society. The jail has reopened to the public after a four-year closure. ( ABC News: Arj Ganesan ) By 1975 – and still not having plumbing in the building – the government of the day closed the facility. Gladstone local and tour guide Steve Schultz said the community acted quickly at the time to preserve the site and its history. "It's been a long battle ever since then to keep it open and at least have it accessible to the public basically," he said. In the years since, the jail's uses have varied, from previous ghost tour iterations, to hosting accommodation and events. Citing a downturn in volunteers after the COVID-19 pandemic, the previous caretakers hung up the keys in 2022. Lindi and Shelley made the trip from Clare on Friday night, with the hope of experiencing something paranormal. Both having fond memories of visits to the jail in its time as accommodation and an events venue, Lindi said its return to the community was "awesome". "I think this is fantastic," she said. Lindi and Shelley were glad to visit the tourist destination again. ( ABC News: Arj Ganesan ) Ms Bailey said the company planned to launch a café on the site, and restoration works that would allow for events and visitors’ further exploration of the site’s history. "We really want to balance the heritage nature of the site and really complement it with events and activities that are coming through," she said. Anthony Van Zeventer was passing by en route to Darwin and was happy to see the site active again. ( ABC News: Arj Ganesan ) Among the visitors on Friday was Anthony Van Zeventer, who stopped by while travelling from Philip Island to Darwin, without realising it was opening night. "I think it's great that the community's got behind it and that they're reopening it again," Mr Van Zeventer said. events.title: FBI blames North Korea for stolen billions from Binance in biggest hack in history

New York -- The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history , was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday. The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins. It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum. The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and “instant swap services.” Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, President Donald Trump suggested investigators weren't yet certain that North Korea was involved. “I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it," Trump said of the case. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea.” Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was. Crypto expert Ari Redbord said he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months. “It’s bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the Internet,” said Redbord, chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. “However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds.” Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. This week, $US6.3 billion ($6.9 million) in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange. Binance says it has enough funds to cover 90 per cent of the stolen assets. The FBI has accused North Korea of stealing $US6.3 billion ($6.9 million) in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what is thought to be the biggest crypto heist in history. In a statement, the US bureau said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the "malicious cyber activity". On Thursday, $US6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack. The FBI's statement came as Binance offered reassurances it was covering the losses from the hacking attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90 per cent of what was stolen. The FBI made the announcement on Saturday, local time. ( Reuters: Nathan Howard ) The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins. "The FBI maintains its commitment to protecting the virtual asset community by identifying, mitigating, and disrupting North Korea's illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities," it said. It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called Ethereum. Zhao Changpeng is the founder and chief executive officer of Binance. ( Reuters: Benoit Tessier ) The FBI said it expects TraderTraitor would now attempt to convert the assets using de-centralised finance (DeFi) and "instant swap services". "It is expected these assets will then be further laundered," it said. They are the same actors behind a $US1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. 'Cat and mouse game' of tracking assets Crypto expert and chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs Ari Redbord said he expected the hackers would break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months. A crypto expert says he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them. ( Unsplash: Executium ) "However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds. "It's just this cat and mouse game." 90 per cent of assets recovered, Binance says On Saturday, Binance said it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen, to cover 90 per cent of the missing assets. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X. It said the outstanding 10 per cent consisted of tokens that were less liquid, which meant they might take longer to source in the required amounts. Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but on Sunday it announced that they had resumed. events.title: Fifty years on, Julius Dam continues to sustain outback communities
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Fifty years on, Julius Dam remains a lifeline for outback communities Julius Dam's distinctive multiple-arch and buttress design is the only one of its kind in Queensland. ( Supplied: Sunwater ) Julius Dam is marking 50 years since its construction following a devastating drought in Mount Isa. Its unique design has helped secure water supplies for communities and mining operations across North West Queensland. Sunwater expects the dam to continue supporting regional growth, with ongoing maintenance helping keep it operational for decades to come. In 1971, a devastating drought exposed a serious problem in the outback mining city of Mount Isa. Despite having a major dam, the city was running short of water. Lake Moondarra, built by Mount Isa Mines in 1958 on the Leichhardt River north of town, was Australia's largest, privately-funded water scheme at the time. But as the city and its mining industry grew, the drought exposed a need for another reliable water source. The solution was unveiled five years later with the completion of Julius Dam, about 70 kilometres north-east of Mount Isa, at the junction of the Leichhardt River and Paroo Creek. The North-West Star declared "No more water worries" when Julius Dam was officially commissioned on October 8, 1976. ( Supplied: North-West Star ) An engineering solution built for the outback Constructed by Thiess Brothers, Julius Dam required hundreds of workers, including people from Scotland, England and Ireland, some of whom lived on site with their families. Building a structure with a 220-metre spillway in remote Queensland had significant challenges. Hundreds of workers helped construct Julius Dam between 1973 and 1976, overcoming the challenges of building in remote North West Queensland. ( Supplied: Sunwater ) Engineers chose a concrete multiple-arch and buttress design that reduced the amount of material needed while maintaining the dam's strength. The design helped overcome the difficulties of building in the outback, according to current operator Sunwater. "Because of its remoteness, because of the difficulty of getting materials in, that's the reason they decided to go with that structure," north region general manager of operations, William Weaver said. Julius Dam's distinctive multiple-arch and buttress design reduced the amount of concrete required for construction. ( Supplied: Sunwater ) Sunwater says it remains the only dam of its kind in Queensland. But another feature caught the attention of University of Queensland geotechnical engineering professor Alexander Scheuermann. Professor Alexander Scheuermann says Julius Dam's unique design allows floodwater to flow directly over its structure. ( Supplied: Alexander Scheuermann ) Unlike dams with a separate spillway, Julius Dam's concrete, 18m wide arches allow excess water to flow directly over the structure. "When the water rises higher than the dam is, it simply overtops the dam without harming the structure," Professor Scheuermann said. Storage capacity: 107,500 megalitres (Sunwater) Sources: Original Julius Dam engineering plaque and Sunwater. A reliable water source for the North West Julius Dam can hold 107,500 megalitres of water, equivalent to about one-fifth of Sydney Harbour's volume. While originally developed to supplement Mount Isa's water supply, its role has expanded over the past five decades. The 113-kilometre North West Queensland Water Pipeline, completed in 1998, supplies mining operations including the Ernest Henry copper and gold mine near Cloncurry. Another 38km pipeline was completed in 2010 following a drought, providing Cloncurry with an additional year-round water supply. Lake Moondarra remains Mount Isa's main water source, with Julius Dam providing supplementary water when needed. Julius Dam's built-in spillway allows excess water to flow directly over its concrete arches during periods of heavy rainfall. ( Supplied: Sunwater ) Despite the region's long dry periods, Mr Weaver said Julius Dam had spilled every year for the past decade. He attributed its reliability to seasonal monsoonal and cyclonic rainfall regularly replenishing the Leichhardt River catchment. "What Lake Julius does is it gives you that real assurance and real surety of supply," he said. "And that's allowed Mount Isa and its industry to grow." William Weaver says Julius Dam remains a vital water source for North West Queensland. ( Supplied: Sunwater ) While Julius Dam has operated for five decades, Professor Scheuermann said ongoing maintenance would be essential to its future.

events.title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
events.summary: Airbnb host Lisa says her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests When Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess. Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage. But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden. "It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes. She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher. Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her property and fears that guests leaving more mess could mean increasing costs But Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site. The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests. Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests. The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins. "We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all." While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal. "It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect." Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides". Krissi says there's a difference between being a respectful guest and being expected to help run the business you've just paid to stay in During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area. "I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says. For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests". Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine. While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says. "If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business." Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two. His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it". Anthony and his husband used to list five of their 12 cabins in North Yorkshire on Airbnb... ... but will now list just two in light of the new rules He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals. "It's common sense and common decency," he says. His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according to data from AirROI , external . Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests. Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect.

events.title: Country town reliant on backpackers warns visa changes will cripple business
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Manjimup's backpackers and businesses united in opposition to working holiday visa changes Chef Valerie Castro is one of many backpackers living and working in Manjimup concerned about looming visa changes. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) The federal government is pushing ahead with its plan to limit working holiday visas, which include ballots for second and third-year extensions. In communities like Manjimup, in southern Western Australia, businesses and backpackers say the changes are already having an impact. Regional businesses want the changes scrapped to ensure critical workers are not lost. In Paul Fowler's country pub, more than half a dozen backpackers make up over 70 per cent of his workforce. Italian travellers keep business ticking over from the front of house all the way through to his busy kitchen. It is a similar situation at many businesses across Manjimup, 290 kilometres south of Perth in southern Western Australia, with the tourism and agricultural centre heavily reliant on backpacker labour. Seventy per cent of the staff at Paul Fowler's pub are backpackers. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) Both Mr Fowler and his workers have backed calls to scrap the federal government's controversial changes to Australia's working holiday visa program. "It's only going to make things harder, and it takes away our ability to function," he said. Before the working holiday visa changes were announced, Mr Fowler bought a second pub in the neighbouring town of Pemberton, which he planned to staff with backpackers. Viola Argenta, Ilaria Dalla Valeria and Mattia Ballarini all work at a pub in Manjimup. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) Mr Fowler said that business was now under threat. "We probably go through 50 to 80 workers a year, all backpacking workers, and so without the backpacking staff, we won't have a workforce here at all," he said. Paul Fowler says his pub in Manjimup couldn't run without backpacker labour. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) The federal government's decision to initially slow down visa applications in August was heavily criticised by farming and regional communities across the country . The decision to allocate fewer second and third-year visa extensions prompted WA's Premier Roger Cook to ask federal Immigration Minister Tony Burke to reconsider the restrictions. Manjimup is a regional hub for tourism and agriculture. ( ABC South West: Andrew Williams ) A spokesperson for the Department of Home Affairs said the reduction would ensure the program's long-term sustainability, and it would work with affected industries to access the labour they need. Back in Manjimup, those impacted say the move fails to account for the benefits backpackers provide beyond their first year. Roberto Spadotto wants to build a life in Manjimup. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) Roberto Spadotto came to Manjimup to work as a farmhand, picking avocados and broccoli as part of his visa obligations. After completing his 88 days and being granted an extension, he started managing Mr Fowler's pub along with his partner Giulia Colombo, whom he met while completing his farm work. One-year-old dies in house fire south of Perth Homeowners facing thousands in costs to upgrade from gas to electric Western Australia experienced a roller-coaster of weather in October Learning Auslan a 'life skill' for children "That's where I met Giulia … one of the worst and best days of my life because picking broccoli is very tough, but I enjoyed it and I had a good outcome," he said. After spending about four years in the region, the Italian couple were hoping to put down roots. "I love the area, love the region, never really thought about moving somewhere else," he said. "And now we're planning to stay, settle, and build a new life here in Australia." Fellow Italian traveller Valerie Casto completed her farm work in a seedling nursery, before starting work as a chef once her visa was extended. Valerie Casto says second and third-year visa extensions incentivise backpackers to do hard jobs. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) She said the incoming changes were turning some of her friends off coming to Australia. "Half a year of a farm job can be very, very hard," Ms Castro said. "And some people don't know if it's worth it, if at the end the visa is not granted." Gavin Booth says backpacker workers are already leaving Australia. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) It is an experience all too familiar for truffle farmer Gavin Booth, who produces the valuable fungus on a property in neighbouring Pemberton. He relies on backpackers for sporadic and seasonal work.

events.title: Third weekend of protests in France as youth-led rallies sweep Europe
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Hundreds of thousands took to the streets across France in a third consecutive weekend of protests over living costs and education. Youth-led protests were also held elsewhere in Europe on Saturday, including in Germany and Portugal. While most people rallied peacefully, some protests turned violent and French authorities arrested more than 560 people. Hundreds of thousands of protesters, inspired by frustrated high school students, have taken to the streets across France in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education. France's protests were overwhelmingly peaceful, but gatherings in Paris and other cities ended in clouds of tear gas and scattered fires set by small groups on the margins. About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country after Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder. Protesters included a mix of high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living. ( Reuters: Abdul Saboor ) The Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge to protect stores, government buildings and tourist areas in the city centre. Authorities reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night, with the government estimating that 320,000 people protested nationwide. Mass protests on October 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew 550,000 people around the country, and demonstrations on October 24 drew 410,000 , according to government estimates. Organisers' turnout estimates are higher. The march remained peaceful for hours before clashes broke out at its end point. ( Reuters: Abdul Saboor ) Multiple groups marched together in Paris, including high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living. Footage of mass protests in Europe has been flooding newsfeeds for weeks, with demonstrators taking to the streets across the continent. Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said he lived in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats". An information technology worker protested in solidarity with the students and her mother, who was struggling with a minimum wage job. A grey-haired woman carried a sign reading, "The Old are Fed Up Too." The rallies were started last month by high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at the leadership of President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands. On Saturday, a joyful crowd streamed for hours along avenues on the edge of Paris, but clashes broke out where the march ended. Some protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police, who responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. Many peaceful marchers left the march, coughing and eyes streaming with tears. Paris police barred people from entering the Place de la Republique and Les Halles neighbourhoods from 11 pm to 6 am Saturday and Sunday, and unaccompanied minors faced a separate 9 pm curfew around the Champs-Elysees. Scattered fires were set by small groups on the margins of the Paris protest. ( Reuters: Abdul Saboor ) Protests in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life", and against any return of military conscription. Organisers said tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country. Official figures weren't immediately available. Fires were lit in the streets of Frankfurt during a nationwide protest by campaign group Gen Z regelt. ( Reuters: Kai Pfaffenbach ) In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing. "We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said. Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said authorities had to invest more money in education. While most people rallied peacefully, some protests turned violent on Saturday night. Some rioters smashed storefronts and looted stores in Frankfurt.

events.title: Liberal MP pushes for party to rule out changes to superannuation
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Garth Hamilton says Liberal Party set to shift on superannuation Garth Hamilton is drawing a line in the sand over accessing superannuation for first home buyers, saying people now want greater security in retirement. The influential MP's call goes against frontbench colleagues who favour policies for dipping into super. Mr Hamilton says he has majority support in the party room and has spoken to leader Angus Taylor about the policy. A push is underway within the Liberal Party for a fundamental shift on superannuation, with one prominent backbencher now confident he has convinced a majority of colleagues to rule out any early access for first home buyers. At the past two elections under Scott Morrison and then Peter Dutton, the Coalition adopted a policy that would have allowed up to $50,000 to be withdrawn from super to put towards a first home deposit. The Liberal Party has not adopted a formal policy position since last year's election defeat, but some senior figures have continued to argue for early super access. In recent months, Shadow Housing Minister Andrew Bragg has floated a range of options for dipping into super accounts. A push to allow Australians to use their super to make it easier to buy their first home is being floated by Shadow Housing Minister Andrew Bragg, as the Coalition works through its policy on how to help people enter the housing market. "You could take it out to pay off a mortgage or to pull together a first home loan," he told the ABC in September. He also suggested using super as "collateral or an offset" to buy a home. Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson backed Senator Bragg, arguing home ownership should be given priority over retirement savings. "This is why home ownership is so important, and we need it to take precedence as the primary economic interest for retirement and during your working life," he said at the time. Labor pounced, with Treasurer Jim Chalmers arguing the next election would be a "referendum" on super. Now, in a setback for Senator Bragg and Mr Wilson, Liberal MP Garth Hamilton believes he has convinced his colleagues to abandon any return to a super-for-housing-style policy. "I think we should be offering no changes at all to how it's invested, taxed or accessed," the member for Groom has told the ABC's Insiders. "I think it's a reasonable position for us to look at super, not as I think maybe we have done previously as a product of the Labor Party, but as being something that matters to every Australian. Garth Hamilton tells David Speers that he thinks he has majority support in the party room. ( ABC News: David Sciasci ) "Every door I knock on, they can tell you what's in their super balance. They can tell what it means at retirement. It's one of the first apps on the top of their phone. "At a certain age, it becomes the thing that you focus on. I think that's telling us that in this environment, we should be focused on that too." It is a move reminiscent of then-Liberal leader John Howard in 1995 dropping his long-standing opposition to Medicare and accepting the Australian people wanted no change to the Labor creation. "What this is trying to do is saying we hear you, we hear the challenges that Australians are facing, and we want to support that." Mr Hamilton has been quietly working to convince his colleagues to lock in behind the existing superannuation rules, and believes he now has majority support across the party room. Is super a bigger political bomb than Medicare? A political war over superannuation has been inflamed, with both the Coalition and One Nation facing a fight with Labor and the industry. He has also spoken to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor about the issue. "He sees the same challenges and acknowledges that this is an important policy discussion for us to have," Mr Hamilton said. One Nation, meanwhile, is promising a "super pay boost" policy, allowing a quarter of super contributions (3 per cent of wages) to instead be diverted into take-home pay to help Australians paying a mortgage or rent for a period of three years. Mr Hamilton says his push to lock in the current super system is about "security, stability, confidence", unlike One Nation that would "let you spend it on a second jet ski". events.title: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit over xAI data center pollution to move forward
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. A federal judge denied a motion by xAI seeking to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit accusing the SpaceX-owned company of failing to obtain permits needed to operate the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis. Suing on behalf of the NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center said the AI company had “installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.” It also accused xAI of violating the Clean Air Act. xAI sought to have the lawsuit dismissed, claiming that the turbines are exempt from permitting requirements because they’re mobile. The company also argued that the plaintiffs did not have the standing to sue. “Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not ‘mobile sources’ under Mississippi’s [State Implementation Plan], and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs’ claims will proceed,” Judge Debra M. Brown wrote in her decision . Focusing on xAI’s claim that these kinds of citizen lawsuits are unconstitutional, Judge Brown wrote, “Because citizen suit plaintiffs sue on their own behalf, in their own name, and seek penalties that redress harm to themselves, they are not exercising the federal government’s executive power.” TechCrunch has reached out to SpaceX for comment. In a statement , the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice Abre’ Connor described this as “another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.” (A similar motion to dismiss from the Department of Justice was denied earlier this month ) “The courts have repeatedly rejected attempts by xAI and the DOJ to dismiss the NAACP’s Clean Air Act case, affirming our right to pursue justice for communities impacted by pollution,” Connor said. “Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits.” The NAACP lawsuit is moving forward as public opinion seems to have turned sharply against data centers, with New York recently passing a moratorium on new data centers and other state and local governments considering similar measures. The backlash also prompted Amazon and Microsoft to promise to stop using NDAs in their dealings with government agencies, and it could be a significant factor in the imminent U.S. midterm elections . events.title: Judge tosses Trump lawsuit against WSJ, Murdoch over Epstein story
events.summary: A federal judge on Saturday threw out President Trump's lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over the paper's reporting on Trump's ties to Jeffrey Epstein, Why it matters: It's the second time this year courts have blocked Trump's efforts to sue the paper over stories about his relationship with the disgraced financier. As with the first one, courts found the president did not clear the high bar set by New York Times vs. Sullivan for allegations of defamation in critical reporting on public figures. Driving the news: Judge Darrin Gayles of the southern district of Florida issued the 20-page ruling Saturday afternoon, finding that Trump failed to prove the paper acted with "actual malice" by reporting on his links to Epstein. Gayles dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice, meaning it can't be refiled. "We're pleased with the court's decision," a representative of WSJ parent Dow Jones said. Zoom out: Trump first filed suit against the paper and Murdoch in July 2025, seeking $20 billion in damages. At issue was a story describing a "bawdy" letter, bearing Trump's name and given to Epstein for his birthday, which the president insisted was fake. Gayles tossed the initial suit last April, but allowed Trump to file an amended complaint — which was the one he dismissed Saturday, saying it fell short of the burden to prove the paper acted maliciously. What they're saying: "Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false," Gayles wrote. For the record: " President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions," a spokesman for his legal team said in a statement. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details. Sara Fischer contributed.

events.title: Tusk defends suspension of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal president as protesters gather again
events.summary: Prime Minister Donald Tusk says his government is acting to restore judicial independence in Poland WARSAW, Poland -- Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Saturday that his government would press ahead with efforts to restore the independence of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, as hundreds of protesters gathered for a second night against the suspension of the court’s president . The pro-European government said the suspension is necessary to restore judicial independence, while critics from the opposition have likened it to a “coup d’etat.” President Karol Nawrocki — who opposes the pro-European government — turned back his plane during a flight to Senegal on Friday evening and returned home. On Friday night, he made his way to the Constitutional Tribunal despite the chaos and said he helped the suspended court president enter the building. Police said they detained three protesters on Friday night after some threw objects at officers and tried to break through the security fence around the court. The dispute over the long-embattled Constitutional Tribunal is likely to deepen political polarization in Poland a year before a parliamentary election, further intensifying the standoff between the pro-European government and the national-conservative opposition party Law and Justice , or PiS. Critics in Poland and the European Union accuse PiS, which led the country between 2015 and 2023, of imposing political control over key judicial institutions. Reforms introduced under the PiS government prompted the EU to impose fines on Poland. Tusk’s pro-European government came to power in 2023 with a promise to restore the independence of the judiciary. Since then, its efforts have been blocked by vetoes from two successive presidents aligned with PiS, including Nawrocki. “Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” Tusk had earlier pledged that his government would ensure the tribunal was again staffed with lawfully appointed judges while acknowledging that his methods may not be to everyone’s liking. The functioning of the Constitutional Tribunal had been impaired for years. The Court of Justice of the European Union, the EU's top court, had said it was no longer an impartial court after PiS appointments. Even after Tusk took power, efforts to balance the court were hampered by Nawrocki and the tribunal's president, Bogdan Święczkowski. On Friday evening, the Constitutional Tribunal’s website announced the suspension of Święczkowski. Shortly after, the protesters — including PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński and far-right politicians — began rallying outside the building. Święczkowski became head of the court under the former PiS government. Tusk has accused him of blocking judges elected by the parliamentary majority from taking up their posts at the tribunal. “Since last night, we’re dealing with a massive constitutional crisis in Poland, the result of an illegal, forceful attempt to take over an important institution,” Marcin Przydacz, a top aide to the Polish president, told The Associated Press. Przydacz said that the president had invited all parliamentary parties to talks on Saturday in an effort to defuse tensions and find a solution to the crisis. The government is a broad coalition made up of Tusk's centrist Civic Coalition, the Left, and two more conservative groupings, Poland 2050 and the Polish People’s Party, or PSL. Representatives of Poland 2050 and PSL, along with several opposition parties, met with Nawrocki on Saturday, while Tusk didn't attend. The president’s camp is hoping that the crisis surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal will erode Tusk’s parliamentary majority. “Everything depends on those political parties who supported Donald Tusk so far,” Przydacz said. Speaking on Saturday night, Tusk compared PiS to a man who steals an elderly woman’s purse and then claims to be the victim when police catch him and take it back. PiS' response to the suspension of Święczkowski, including the attempts to forcefully enter the Tribunal on Friday, represents “another stage in the process of destroying the rule of law in Poland” by PiS and the president, Tusk said. 1 dead, 6 injured in 'targeted' shooting at California Halloween store 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: D.C., Virginia sue to block Trump's 250-foot arch
events.summary: The governments of Washington D.C. and Virginia asked a federal court to block construction of President Trump's planned " triumphal arch ," claiming it's unlawfully tall and would snarl traffic for years. Why it matters: It's a last-minute gambit to stop construction before the multi-year project begins, potentially as soon as this coming week. What they're saying: " This project is flagrantly unlawful," the two governments said in a Saturday filing in D.C. federal court, first reported by the Washington Post. "During the three-year period of construction, the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges," they argue. They further claim that the defendants — the National Park Service and the Interior Department — have rushed the project without the proper consultations. The city and state are asking a judge to issue injunctions to stop any site preparation or construction on the project. Zoom out: The proposed 250-foot arch would be one of the largest such monuments in the world, sparking concerns that it could interfere with other national symbols, block views and even complicate landings for pilots at nearby airports. (The FAA found otherwise.) The Park Service's own August report indicated the construction of the arch would have adverse effects on nearby monuments and landmarks. The other side: The administration has argued it will be a major tourist attraction — but also vital to national security, serving as a base for snipers and drones. "The Triumphal Arch in Memorial Circle is going to be one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. What's next: A federal judge held a hearing Friday on a separate challenge to the arch, and indicated she may block construction at least temporarily.

events.title: Binance covers 90 per cent of assets stolen in $6.3 billion hack
events.summary: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said on ​Saturday that ​it has ​been able to cover ⁠90 per cent of the amount stolen in ⁠ an unprecedented hack ​on its platform. In an update on its website, Binance said the amount to cover the stolen funds would come out of three sources: a partial use of the Secure Asset Fund for Users; a portion of the Futures insurance fund; and Binance's own corporate treasury. Users were also invited to check the balances of the first two funds online. The outstanding 10 per cent consists of tokens that are less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. The exchange said withdrawal services for users are expected to resume on November 1, with more details to be confirmed later. What happened? Binance Holdings, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, lost an estimated $6.3 billion to hackers early on Friday, in what has been described as the single biggest theft of cryptocurrency on record, exceeding the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in February 2025 . Funds began leaving Binance's hot wallets, which are connected to the internet to process customer withdrawals, at about 12.24am UAE time on October 30. A single transaction moved about 167,464 Ether, worth about $388 million, along with 63 other tokens, to an address created hours earlier and funded through the Tornado Cash mixing service, according to Etherscan data. Bitcoin shares plunged after the news, and have now fallen to about $76,450, data from CoinMarketCap shows.

events.title: Rising health costs and coverage changes are big concerns for older adults as Election Day nears
events.summary: Rising healthcare costs are a major concern for older Americans, and it's affecting their finances and political priorities WASHINGTON -- Barbara Weigand could not have prepared more for retirement. She stayed healthy and saved diligently for years. This year, though, a shoulder surgery and a bladder cancer diagnosis have really tested her finances. She recently withdrew $4,000 from her retirement account to cover medical expenses associated with her cancer treatment. “On my monthly income, I would not be able to afford my new medical expenses,” says Weigand, 83, who lives in North Canton, Ohio. She is currently on a Medicare Advantage plan and was searching for new coverage as Medicare's open enrollment period began in October. For older adults in the United States, the rising cost of healthcare is hitting where it hurts most — their pocketbooks. With Medicare costs, prescription drug prices and long-term care expenses weighing on household budgets, their concerns could carry significant political weight heading into Tuesday's elections. Weigand is part of a reliable voting bloc; 83% of voters over age 50 say they’re extremely motivated to vote in the midterms, according to an AARP poll conducted in early October. Their concerns over managing healthcare costs put the issue of affordability squarely in the spotlight. Here are some of their biggest healthcare concerns — and how Weigand sees them. THE SITUATION: Open enrollment for Medicare plans began in mid-October, and enrollees are facing a slew of changes that will go into effect in 2027. During the enrollment period, people are considering higher Part D out-of-pocket caps, the end of temporary federal Part D premium subsidies , and new drug price negotiations. Additionally, in some states, insurers put caps on the number of people who can enroll in Advantage plans, pulling out of markets or eliminating plans that people have come to rely on. Juliette Cubanski, director of KFF’s program on Medicare policy, told The Associated Press that the open enrollment period offers enrollees “an opportunity to evaluate the coverage they have and see if there might be better options for them in terms of accessing the care that they need, at possibly a lower cost.” While Weigand is grateful to have the mental acuity to do the research and the spiritual community that she relies on, she worries about other older people who are struggling to plan for the year ahead. “There are so many changes, and a lot of people my age who don’t know where to start," she says. "What do they do?” THE SITUATION: The Trump administration has made lowering drug prices a priority in its effort to show Americans that it is tackling soaring costs. Republican President Donald Trump has struck multiple most-favored-nation drug deals with pharmaceutical companies and has launched the discount drug website TrumpRx , among other steps. In September, his administration said all 50 states would join in on a program set to provide most-favored-nation pricing to some drugs within the Medicaid program, bringing the net price of selected drugs down to prices paid in certain other countries. Still, the cost of prescription drugs prevents some people from filling prescriptions. A KFF survey from March found that about 4 in 10 U.S. adults say they have not taken their medication as prescribed in the past year due to costs. events.title: From restaurant guides to payments, here’s how TikTok is building a super app
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. TikTok announced this week that it’s adding an in-app restaurant guide , marking another step in the platform’s expansion beyond social media. The company has also recently been spotted developing a feature that would allow users to send money over direct messages. The social media app has steadily expanded its offerings in recent years, adding TikTok Shop, a map for local discovery, more robust search features, games, and more. It appears that TikTok is taking steps to evolve into a “super app,” a single platform where users can do much more than just watch and share videos and that can actually handle a wide range of needs in one destination. The super app model is big in China with apps like WeChat, which is kind of like Facebook, WhatsApp, Apple Pay, and an app store all rolled into a single platform. Of course, there’s the question of whether a super app model would work outside of China, but that doesn’t mean TikTok won’t try. Instead of switching between apps, TikTok is working to become the app that people use for most of their digital activities. After taking its biggest leap with TikTok Shop, the company — which, notably, transitioned to new, primarily U.S. ownership back in January — has applied the same playbook to recent developments. TikTok has become a popular destination for restaurant recommendations, with viral videos often driving customers to local eateries. Now, the platform is looking to make that discovery process even easier with a new feature called “ Must Eat .” The community-driven guide highlights restaurants getting attention on the platform. “Must Eat” draws on more than 40 million posts and comments to compile restaurant recommendations and curated lists in one place. Users can browse restaurants by city and narrow their search by cuisine, price, rating, and location. The move puts TikTok in more direct competition with platforms like Yelp and Google Maps. It also reflects how the app is expanding its role in users’ everyday decisions, from what they buy to where they choose to go out to eat. Bloomberg reported in August that TikTok is developing a feature that would allow users to send each other money via direct messages. If rolled out, the feature would use the social media service’s TikTok Pay offering, which is already available in Southeast Asia for TikTok Shop purchases. Additionally, Reuters reported in March that TikTok had applied to Brazil’s central bank for approval to operate as a financial technology company offering lending and payment services. TikTok’s potential expansion into payments marks a significant way that the company is branching out beyond a social media platform and into a digital ecosystem. By aiming to bring financial services into its app, TikTok is looking to increase user engagement, open new revenue streams, and position itself to compete with fintech startups and e-commerce platforms. Over the years, TikTok has steadily been looking to become a place where users can come for sports highlights and content. In early June, the company launched a dedicated hub for the FIFA World Cup where users can see scores, match schedules, standings, trending videos, highlights, videos from players, and more. If people are already watching videos on TikTok but want to keep up with the score, they can do so without leaving the app or opening a dedicated sports news app or Google. The World Cup hub was made possible through TikTok’s Sports-focused product called “ TikTok GamePlan ,” which is designed to allow sports teams, leagues, and broadcasters to drive discovery and engagement on the platform. The social media giant also has partnerships with Major League Soccer (MLS) and Major League Baseball (MLB) for behind-the-scenes and exclusive content. In May, TikTok launched TikTok GO , a way for users to discover and book hotels, attractions, and experiences directly within its app in the United States. TikTok GO surfaces lodging and things to do through videos, search, and location pages. When users find something they’re interested in, they can view details, check availability, and complete a booking. Instead of directing users to third-party websites after they find a destination or recommendation in a video, TikTok has started positioning itself as a one-stop platform where viral travel content can drive bookings and revenue. While people have already been using TikTok as a search engine and replacement for Google, this latest step puts TikTok in more direct competition with Google’s core businesses, Search and Google Maps, because it’s working to not only be the app where you discover places, but also the platform where you purchase that trip. It’s widely known that one of TikTok’s biggest leaps beyond social media was the launch of TikTok Shop.

events.title: Iran's supreme leader orders "maximum" response to any U.S. attack
events.summary: Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei told the country's top three military commanders that a renewed attack by the U.S. and Israel ״must be met with an immediate and effective response, without geographical limitations״ in order to achieve "maximum deterrence," according to a statement from his office. Why it matters: This is the first publicly disclosed meeting between Khamenei and all the top commanders of Iran's armed forces since the war began. It comes as President Trump weighs major strikes on Iran after the midterm elections. Khamenei hasn't been seen or heard in public since he was wounded in an Israeli strike on the first day of the war. He has only issued written statements, which raised questions about his condition. The unusual apparent meeting took place a day after Qatari mediators held talks in Tehran for more than 12 hours in an effort to reach a deal to restart direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran and avoid an outbreak of war after the midterms. The discussions continued in Doha, Qatar, on Saturday. What he's saying: "If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Islamic Republic of Iran's Armed Forces and the Iranian nation that determine when and under what conditions those hostilities will end," Khamenei told the commanders, according to the statement. Zoom in: According to the statement, the meeting included armed forces chief of staff Gen. Ali Abdollahi, army commander Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander Maj. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi. The commanders briefed Khamenei on the state of military readiness along the Gulf coastline and around the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf of Oman, and Iran's northwestern and southeastern borders. They also reported "a several-fold increase" in production of various types of ammunition and reconnaissance, support, and combat weapons. Khamenei instructed the commanders that the "target bank" must be updated "so that all types of the American-Zionist enemy's material and non-material assets fall within the reach of the Armed Forces." Khamenei praised "the intelligent steadfastness" of Iran's proxies across the region and stressed "the unity of the different arenas" as a "decisive and strategic" element for Iran. Reality check: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera that senior-level officials have discussed a proposal from Vice President Vance and called the U.S. effort to open talks a "positive step." But he made a strict set of demands for an agreement: lifting sanctions, reducing the U.S. military presence in the region and recognizing a Strait of Hormuz shipping route agreed to with Oman. Araghchi also told Al Jazeera that reopening the strait on Iran's terms could pave the way for direct negotiations. Iran is examining mediators' proposals to address its nuclear program, a bottom-line issue for the U.S.

events.title: I took two iPhones on vacation. The Duo won me over.
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. “I think I’m going to switch back to my other iPhone.” I’ll admit, I said this multiple times during my five-day vacation with the new iPhone Duo, after encountering frustrations with broken apps, unfamiliar gestures (a return to Touch ID, argh !), and camera concerns that had me lugging around two phones. By the time the trip was over, I didn’t want to go back. When I first unboxed the Duo, a loaner from Apple, I was genuinely intrigued. I felt a flutter of anticipation as I peeled back the factory seal wrap and booted up the device. In retrospect, this was probably the first signal that Duo was going to ultimately win me over. As a tech reporter, I’ve received a lot of test devices over the years, so unfortunately, opening a package with a new gadget inside is no longer the thrill it used to be. But sometime in the days leading up to the Duo’s ship date, I found myself actually wanting one – I had started doing the math and comparing upgrade options that would allow me to afford the $2K the phone would cost. I started scrolling TikTok reviews of Duo cases . I hesitated not only because of the price but because moving to the Duo is a major change – especially coming from an iPhone 17 Pro Max. The phones could not be more different. As I was about to head out on vacation when the Duo arrived, I decided to tote my 17 Pro Max with me too, as something of a safety net. I ended up using the Duo more, and grew comfortable with it over the course of the trip, despite some frustrations. There’s always a psychological switching cost in changing phones, but particularly going from a high-end phone to a more experimental device like the Duo. For someone used to the iPhone’s long-perfected tech and thin rectangular shape, the Duo’s short, squat, and decidedly novel nature was somewhat off-putting at first. “Where is all that screen real estate I used to have?” I lamented. “Will this thing even fit comfortably in my pocket?” As it turns out, it does. Front and back pockets, in fact. Even while wearing a case. You can sit down with it in your back pocket, effectively squashing it, and it does not break. (I meant to be more careful, but I forgot to be, repeatedly, as I tend to carry phones in my back pocket when walking around. I sat on the phone countless times. It’s clearly not that fragile.) I also dropped the phone (by accident!) at least three times. Twice from about table height and once when it got pushed off the side of the bed. It did not fall on soft carpet, but rather on concrete, tile, and wood floors. It didn’t break then either, and the screen didn’t crack. I wouldn’t call these professional drop tests by any means, but it certainly was a relief for someone fairly clumsy with their phone. Of course, I did encounter some frustrations. I had to scroll more to read back through text threads because of the Duo’s small outer screen; unoptimized apps with numerous controls sometimes had key features tucked away in a “more” (three-dot) menu, leading to a hunt to find the option you needed; and, on multiple occasions, the Google Search app just froze. Though not Apple’s fault, the latter turned out to be my biggest annoyance software-wise, given that Search is one of my go-to apps especially when traveling. On vacation, I open the app repeatedly to look up points of interest, restaurant reviews, distances between towns, weather, and more. But Google’s app would just stop working, and tapping its back button did nothing. This seemed to be a problem specific to the Search app’s AI Mode, which these days you’re often dropped into without actually requesting it. (Even more reason to be annoyed by AI Search!) The workaround has been to force-close the app, so the next time you open it, your returned to the home screen with the search box. (It amazes me that, in a time when Google is facing a search decline because of AI, it wouldn’t have prioritized making its Search app functional on Apple’s latest device!) In addition, many of the early reviews pointed out how many apps were not updated or redesigned for Duo at launch, which meant they had a telltale black bar on the side, cramping the limited screen real estate when the phone is closed even further. This is true, but personally speaking, I didn’t think it was a dealbreaker for making a switch to the Duo. For one thing, companies have been pushing out their Duo-optimized updates fairly quickly. Those that have not – and there are still more than a few! – continue to be usable. They’re just kind of … ugly. Google Maps was not Duo-optimized during the trip, yet I had no problem using it for driving directions, local search and discovery, route planning, and the like.
